This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the **copyright** <note>The legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution.</note> to expire and the book to enter the **public domain**. A <term>public domain</term> <note>original: "public domain"; referring to works whose intellectual property rights have expired, been forfeited, or are inapplicable.</note> book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on **automated querying** <note>The use of software "bots" or scripts to automatically search or harvest data from a system.</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on **machine translation**, **optical character recognition** (OCR) or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

# EDITOR’S PREFACE

...this was the orator’s primary aim. And I believe those were written by him—very dry indeed, but their brevity at least will recommend them even to those who are weary of such schoolroom trifles. Nor do they please me. Therefore, <term>Hermogenes</term> <note>Hermogenes of Tarsus (2nd century AD) was a highly influential rhetorician whose works on style became the standard textbooks for centuries.</note>, who often had to be called upon, I have almost neglected, thinking of course that the rhetorical reader, without my prompting, knows full well that <term>Hermogenes</term>, the master of the art, and other technical writers should be consulted.

To produce a volume of proper size, I have added to the <term>Pachymerian</term> <note>Refers to the works of George Pachymeres, mentioned on the previous page.</note> Declamations the *Facetiæ* <note>original: Facetias; meaning "witticisms" or "jokes."</note> of <term>Hierocles</term>; not just those twenty-eight or twenty-nine very well known from the editions—the anonymous London one, those of Needham, Schier, Coray, and others—but 262 of them. These were extracted from the little book of nonsense by the grammarians <term>Hierocles</term> and <term>Philagrius</term>, to which the title is prefixed: **Philogelos** <note>original: Φιλόγελως</note>, which in the common tongue means "The Laughter-Lover" <note>The editor uses the French "Le rieur" in the original Latin text.</note>. <term>Melissus</term> <note>Gaius Melissus, a freedman of Maecenas and a librarian under Emperor Augustus.</note>, the grammarian of Spoleto and friend of Maecenas, in his sixtieth year, set out to compile a collection of that kind of jokes. <term>Coray</term> <note>Adamantios Korais (1748–1833), a central figure in the Greek Enlightenment and a prolific editor of classical texts.</note>, a serious man, almost a second <term>Socrates</term>, at sixty-four years of age, edited <term>Hierocles</term> and illustrated him with a comparison of similar anecdotes. 

I, now heavy with seventy-five years, am publishing the *Philogelos*, testing it against manuscripts and the scholarly debates of critics, adorning it with a commentary—and burdening it too—ready to defend myself with those and other such examples (for even the *Facetiæ* of the famous <term>Tacitus</term> are mentioned), but also ready to proceed securely even without examples, little concerned with gloomy and peevish censors who, misusing the saying of <term>Martial</term>, will shout that "laboring over trifles is foolish" <note>original: "stultum esse laborem ineptiarum"; a reference to the Roman poet Martial’s Epigrams (2.86), where he dismisses trivial poetic games.</note>; for I myself am also, in my way, a **laughter-lover** <note>original: φιλόγελως</note>.

The basis of my revision was a handwritten transcript of a Greek manuscript by the learned <term>Minoides Mynas</term> <note>Constantine Minoides Mynas (1788–1859) was a Greek scholar commissioned by the French government to search for ancient manuscripts in Eastern monasteries.</note>, who [brought] it...

# EDITOR’S PREFACE

## EDITOR’S PREFACE

[Minoïde Mynas] found it by good fortune while traveling through Greece and Asia in the year 1840, by order of the Honorable Villemain <note>Abel-François Villemain (1790–1870), a French politician and writer who served as the Minister of Public Instruction.</note>, the high administrator of public education. For this discovery, <term>Menas</term> <note>original: Μηνᾶς; Minoïde Mynas (1790–1860), a Greek scholar and manuscript hunter who rediscovered several lost ancient texts.</note> is entirely worthy of congratulations; yet, he is also to be blamed for not providing even a single word to indicate which library in which location possesses the manuscript, what the condition of the book is, or its age and the evidence thereof. Furthermore, the style of the language suggests that the manuscript is of a very recent date.

E. Miller <note>Emmanuel Miller (1812–1886), a prominent French paleographer and librarian at the Bibliothèque Nationale.</note>, a man most celebrated for his erudition in Greek studies, had intended to edit the <term>Philogelos</term> <note>original: Φιλόγελῳ; "The Laughter-Lover," the title of the joke collection.</note>; but, being now occupied with more serious studies which claim his entire attention, he proposed that I should undertake the work, out of the kindness he shows me. The prospect pleased me greatly; and, matching words with action, I prepared myself for this new labor without delay.

After a quick reading of the little book, I realized that an editor—even when dealing with a light and frivolous subject—would need to apply much care and diligence to ensure that Miller would not regret his choice and that I might satisfy learned readers. For the edition of a Greek work, even the most trivial, attracts learned readers and is judged by learned critics.

Therefore, while seeking resources for the edition, Fabricius <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a monumental bibliographer of classical texts.</note> informed me that “Jacobus Pontanus <note>Jacob Spanmüller (1542–1626), a Jesuit scholar known for his works on rhetoric.</note> had long ago translated the *Wits* of Hierocles, expanded from the Augsburg manuscript, and that they appear at the end of his *Progymnasmata* <note>original: Progymnasmatum; "Preliminary Exercises," a textbook on the art of rhetoric.</note>.” This book is not easily found, and was entirely unknown to the previous editors of the *Wits* of Hierocles whom I was able to consult; however, the keepers of the Library of Paris <note>The Bibliothèque Nationale de France.</note>, most excellent and learned men, kindly permitted me to use it. The jokes translated by Pontanus number 109, and they bear this heading: “From...”

## BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

# DECLAMATIONS <note>original: "Meletai" – These are formal rhetorical exercises or practice speeches, a hallmark of Byzantine higher education. In these works, the author often takes on the persona of a historical or mythological figure to argue a specific point of view.</note>

<meta>This is the opening page of George Pachymeres’ *Meletai* (Declamations). Pachymeres was a 13th-century Byzantine historian and official. These texts are rhetorical exercises where he adopts the persona of a historical figure—in this case, the Athenian leader Pericles—to argue a fictional legal case.</meta>

# OF GEORGE PACHYMERES
## DECLAMATIONS*.

---

### DECLAMATION 1.

---

After a thunderbolt struck his home, a thousand suits of armor were discovered in the house of Pericles, and he is now on trial for attempting to establish a tyranny.¹ We are declaiming on behalf of the defendant,² who speaks both in his capacity as a general and asserts his case as an orator.

Nothing,³ it seems, is more burdensome than a malicious informer.⁴ <note>original: "συκοφάντου"; in ancient Athens, a 'sycophant' was a professional accuser who brought lawsuits for profit or spite.</note> For a man who is a soldier, and who is tested daily by wars

<margin>* The title in the manuscript is fuller: "The Declamations of George Pachymeres, Guardian of the Laws <term>Dikaiophylax; a high-ranking judicial official in the Byzantine Church and state</term> and Chief Advocate <term>Protekdikos; a legal official who protected the rights of the poor and handled asylum cases</term>, regarding the preliminary exercises and the legal issues." In the manuscript, an 'η' is written over the syllable 'ρους' to make it 'Pachymere,' which is a more modern form of the name. Pachymeres himself mentions his own titles of Guardian of the Laws and Chief Advocate at the beginning of his *Histories* (see Du Cange's *Glossary*): "George, a Constantinopolitan by ancestry, but born and raised in Nicaea, who returned to the city of Constantine <note>Constantinople</note> when, by God’s will, it was recovered by the Romans <note>The Byzantines called themselves Romans; this refers to the 1261 recapture of the city from the Latins</note>. At the age of nineteen, having been saved by divine lot and distinguished by ecclesiastical ranks—reaching the honor of Chief Advocate and being honored as Guardian of the Laws in the palaces—he wrote these things, not taking unverified accounts from above..." Regarding the longer passage I transcribed, I should note that manuscript 1723 preserves a better reading: "this city under the Romans," "at nineteen," and "given to the clergy" (Rossinus defends "saved," but since he provides no suitable example, I do not yet follow him); omitting</margin>

<column-break/>

the word "in," and, since the Guardian of the Laws was an office of the palace, "Guardian of the Laws of the palaces" is not poorly phrased, though it involves a harsh inversion. Philes, whom Du Cange cited anonymously in his poem *On Offices*, verse 126: "The Guardian of the Laws, and with him the Guardian of the Statutes." The manuscript also has "from elsewhere" instead of "from above."
¹ I have already published this first declamation, in which Pericles refutes the charge of aiming for tyranny, as a specimen in the fifth volume of *Anecdota Graeca*; it seemed appropriate to repeat it here in a more corrected form, so that the entire body of Pachymeres' declamations might be contained in a single volume. As with the speech itself, the little historical backstory is fictional. At least regarding Pericles, no such event is recorded in surviving literature.
² I touched upon the declaimers' formula "we declaim" <note>original: "μελετῶμεν"</note> in my notes on Choricius, page 206. A note before the argument states: "The legal issue <note>original: "στάσις"</note> is conjecture." <note>original: "στοχασμός"; a legal term for a case where the facts themselves are in dispute.</note>
³ Note: "The introduction is based on general opinion."
⁴ Below in Declamation IX: "The malicious informer is a terrible thing, terrible indeed, O earth and gods!" This seems to recall the sentiments of Demosthenes...

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the fictional defense of the Athenian statesman Pericles, written as a rhetorical exercise by the 13th-century scholar George Pachymeres. Pericles is defending himself against the charge that the weapons found in his house after a lightning strike were intended for a coup to establish a tyranny. This page focuses on Pericles' appeal to the jury's own knowledge of his character and his criticism of 'sycophants' (professional accusers).</meta>

-># OF GEORGE PACHYMERES<-

...and in battles, if he makes the mere possession of weapons a crime, what else would he hesitate to charge? But I am grateful to the gods who protect our city<gloss>¹</gloss> that the man who disparages my deeds delivers his speeches before you—you, whom I would gladly have called as witnesses to my goodwill toward the city, had I been forced to give an account of my public life before some other audience, as often happens under democratic governments for the most rigorous examination of one's character. For it would be strange if I brought in strangers to testify, rather than those on whose behalf I have continuously spent my days struggling—both moving my tongue in the councils and wielding my spear in battles. Indeed, I have the greatest confidence that the truth will not be lost, but will prevail over every rhetorical cleverness; and it will prove, with you as my judges, that the truth alone conquers every scheme of the malicious informer <note>original: "συκοφάντου" (sycophant); in ancient Athens, this referred to a professional accuser who brought cases for money or political gain.</note>.

I would have prayed<gloss>²</gloss>—how can I put this becomingly?—that it was not I, Pericles, being the sort of man you all know, who was being judged. Instead, I wish that I were someone facing such charges for the first time and alone, stripped of all rhetorical skill, trusting only in a mind that loves the city and in my goodwill toward the people. For in that way, my victory would be above suspicion—let it be said with God's help<gloss>³</gloss>—and the informers would have no grounds to claim that this was a contest of the tongue, and not of character and truth.

---

Aeschines, *Against Ctesiphon*, § 241: <note>original: "πονηρόν, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πονηρόν ὁ συκοφάντης"</note> "A malicious informer, O men of Athens, is a wicked thing." There are endless passages concerning malicious informers. I will make do with one from Menander's *Single Sentences*: <note>original: "Ὁ συκοφάντης ἐστὶ τοῖς πέλας λύκος"</note> "The sycophant is a wolf to those nearby." Meineke cited a variation: "is a wolf in the city." I found in manuscript 1696: "is an insidious wolf." Perhaps the verse was originally complete: "For the sycophant is an insidious wolf." Scribes often omitted particles like *men, de, gar* when hunting for general maxims. Similarly, Arsenius had transcribed a sentence of Euripides in an imperfect state: "A good man loves to respect a good man," to which Wagner restored the meter in fragment 1061 by writing: "But a good man..." I myself once proposed for Philostratus's *Letters*: "The good man..." In fragment 7 of the same author, another scribe omitted "but" (*d'*) after "man." "But it is noble even to be ruled by a noble man."

<column-break/>

¹ The manuscript reads *polisouchois*. This is an error that also appears in old editions of Aeschylus's *Seven Against Thebes*, lines 257 and 822. The name was illustrated by Blomfield in his notes on the *Seven*. See also the *Thesaurus of the Greek Language*.

² Ancient note: This is a "second introduction" <note>a technical term in rhetoric</note> based on the reputation of the person himself.

³ This is a formula used by a modest speaker to ward off divine retribution <note>Nemesis</note>. One may look at the note I added to this passage in *Greek Anecdotes*, volume 5, page 352; compare also Salmasius on Aristaenetus in Abresch's supplement, page 63; and Krabinger on Synesius's *Praise of Baldness*, page 180. Procopius of Gaza, in *Letter 25*: "Our fatherland—let it be said with God's help—has looked upon us with kind eyes." Plato, *Letter 4*: "For the present, to speak with God's help, things are well." And shortly after: "Since, to speak with God's help, it will be easy." Manuscript 3009 lacks the word "speak." Compare also page 6, line 19 of this volume, and the end of Declamation II.

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of Pericles, composed by George Pachymeres. Pericles is addressing the Athenian jury, navigating the delicate balance of defending his character without appearing to be a "clever speaker" who uses rhetoric to obscure the truth. He is transitioning from his opening remarks into the narration of his lifelong commitment to the Athenian democracy.</meta>

# STUDY I.

...would be a true achievement. Since my circumstances have fallen out in such a way that there is danger on both sides: if I rely on arguments, even if I should happen to prevail, I might be suspected of winning by the power of words rather than by the truth; yet if I slacken my zeal, I would bring upon myself an accusation more terrible than all other evils. I have therefore decided on this course: to use my words as best I can and to prevail as I am able, even if someone might be suspicious, rather than to slacken my efforts in an attempt to avoid suspicion and thereby give my accusers <term>sycophants: in ancient Athens, professional informers or "legal bounty hunters" who brought cases for profit or spite</term> a handle against me. Nevertheless, taking the middle path, I shall make my defense, framing my words simply around my own conduct. I will look to you for the strength of these arguments, as you find the truth in deeds rather than in words—for it is upon deeds that a person is judged.

As I am about to <note>Scholion: This is the preliminary statement (prokatastasis), also called the pre-narration.</note> present evidence of my goodwill today, I ask those present not to attribute any self-boasting to me if I should frequently fall into such discourse. Rather, recognize that these things are a matter of necessity, and realize that I would never have tolerated such talk even from another if the accusations were absent. Forgive me, then, and grant me what each of you would do if you were placed in such a legal struggle. For what I am about to say is not strange or unknown to the many, but, I believe, familiar to all, and you more than anyone else are witnesses to it.

->### III. BY PACHYMERES<-

...of her. And I say this not to curry favor with you, but because it is the truth; and what I was conscious of in my own mind then, these things I now present as clearly as possible.

For in my contemplations, I found that other forms of government were wanting. **Aristocracy**, on the one hand, possesses a degree of utility and is justly praised by those who do not wish public affairs to depend upon a single opinion; yet, on the other hand, it is naturally blamed because it does not allow all citizens to be aware of what the "best men" <note>The Greek term is *aristoi*, from which we get "aristocracy."</note> are doing, so that the common interest might truly be common in reality. **Monarchy**, however, provides no room for praise at all, but stands entirely contrary to justice. For how could common justice be maintained in a city where a single opinion and a single vote hold power? Where the will of one man leads everyone wherever he wishes, and if anyone should dare to even mutter a sound <insert>footnote 1</insert> in secret, the penalty is death <insert>footnote 2</insert>? What useful thing could occur for the benefit of the community under such a man? For he is but one person, and he ignores even the fact that nature itself paired the senses in every living creature, as the condition of being "alone" is everywhere considered a defect. If something seems good <insert>footnote 3</insert> to him, there is no one to judge it; if it is the opposite, there will be no one to correct it. And if a passion of the soul or an irrational desire should intervene <insert>footnote 4</insert>, what counselor will prevent the harm? For everyone’s opinion depends on that one man’s will; each person seeks to endear himself to the ruler by praising his whims as if they were excellent and wise, while they fear becoming estranged from him if they should contradict him in any way <insert>footnote 5</insert>. To recount the things that happen on every occasion in monarchies would require a time of its own, and more time than the water allowed in my clock <insert>footnote 6</insert>. Clearly—

<meta>This page continues the speech of a statesman—likely Pericles, given the context—defending his devotion to the Athenian democratic system. Having previously critiqued monarchy and aristocracy, he now extols the virtues of democracy and recounts his own history of service to the city.</meta>

# STUDY I.

And what could one consider better than **democracy**? Under it, even the inequality of fortune is leveled out, and all are far from slavery; all are free. There is no one who does not share equally with the rest in liberty, just as they do in nature. Both the man in high office <note>The Greek *epi tes taxeos* refers to an official or commander in a specific rank.</note> and the craftsman who works with his own hands deliberate on war; so too do the orator, the sailor, the soldier, and every other person. Often, a man unskilled in war <note>original: "apolemos tis"</note> has recognized and pointed out something that escaped the general's notice; and what an orator has proposed, a general carries out. A man of low status may bring a lawsuit, and a man of higher status must pay the penalty. Yet the one who receives justice does not receive it for himself alone, but for the whole city, for its laws, and for its good order. Nor does the one who pays the penalty pay it to an individual, but to the entire people and the constitution, from which all social order proceeds.

I was born into this form of government; I am its child and its student. I have been its lover and its supporter—more than any other man, I believe—and its most diligent advocate. This very place, the law court, is my witness; the council chamber <note>The *Bouleuterion* was the meeting place of the Council of Five Hundred in Athens.</note>, to which I have devoted even more of my attention, is my witness. There are also worthy witnesses by whom all things are judged and held to account: I mean the comic poets and those who stage the dramas of life. Even their profession <note>The speaker is likely referring to the tradition of Old Comedy, where playwrights like Aristophanes satirized and scrutinized politicians.</note> did not persuade me to speak in any way other than I ought—to put it mildly.

When I entered the rank of a statesman along with the others—after you had approved me through the official scrutiny <term>dokimasia: a formal examination of a citizen's fitness for public office</term> and not because I had seized power for myself—I looked so little to my own personal gain that I continually advised you neither to acquire more empire nor to seek things beyond what was necessary...

not to busy ourselves with other affairs, but to remain quiet and carry through the war against the Peloponnesians <note>original: "ton pros Peloponnesious diapherein polemon"</note>¹; for as long as I stood at your head during the peace², you know how I managed affairs with moderation. But when the war broke out—and yet, what need is there for my own words? You who are present, testify if you will to my zeal at that time and my disposition toward the fatherland: that I alone, or with very few others³, knew what had to be done for you to be saved. And, if you remember—though I shall remind you even of my opening words to you: "I hold to the same opinion, O Athenians, always: not to give in to the Peloponnesians⁵." Yet nevertheless, I⁶—the one saying these things and making these introductions—restrained you from battle at the critical moment. When you wished to go out, nearly taking your weapons in your hands, I did not permit it⁷. I would not allow men in their prime to go, for I did not wish to fill Attica with war. But when I shifted the siege back against the Peloponnese and it was necessary to fight by landing in enemy territory, then I led you out, even though you were suffering terribly from the plague. I demanded that you stand firm for the struggle for liberty and not abandon your place of pride, remaining strong even against your current misfortune. I showed you, with God’s help, prevailing in war over the men of the Peloponnese, holding Megara, Nisaea, Troezen, Pegae, and Achaea⁹, and simply everything in those parts. ### STUDY I.

...peculiar, I alone advised my own people and in private, and I assisted in the tasks then, so that, if possible, they might become superior to profit <note>original: "kerdous ginesthai kreittous"</note>¹ and have their mind fixed only on the end of the war; "but if not," I cried, "let the profit from the war be the weapons of the fallen, and those alone!" I said this so that someone, even if they seemed fond of profit, might be able to defend themselves justly, saying they were collecting weapons—though despoiling something else—and would not have anyone to slander them.

It was so², and while the houses of others were being filled with riches through me and my labors, my own house was filled with full suits of armor; and while the rewards from the people brought me glory throughout the city, at home I was made more illustrious by these, as if by pillars and histories of my brave deeds, rather than by anything else³. Often a patriotic thought came to me, that again, when the opportunity arose, these weapons would be useful, and would immediately make many heavy-infantrymen <term>hoplites: heavily armed infantry soldiers</term> out of those whom nature perhaps arms with innate daring and nobility, but whose livelihood stands in their way, providing nothing for armor⁴; and only the one Peri-

² I had unwisely written *houtos* [thus], and immediately "against the those before and the" <note>original: "kata ton pro kai ton"</note>. Often "and" [kai] and "against" [kata] are interchanged. ### III. BY PACHYMERES

...-cles’ house will provoke many to battle and will produce sufficient soldiers <term>hoplites: heavily-armed infantry</term> for the fatherland.

Certainly, my foresight regarding the city and my care for the fatherland will, I know, be wondered at by everyone—as is natural—and especially by those whose disposition is reasonable and patriotic. Even Zeus, the God of Friendship <note>original: "Philios Zeus"</note>, after whom I was named¹ by a vote of your council, has, I believe, accepted my purpose; he brought down the lightning-bolt, not to punish vice, but to make manifest my virtue, since it was not yet the right time to reveal my intentions.

But this spiteful and contentious man alone subverts my good deed and charges me with an attempt at tyranny, accusing one who is merely providing for how the common people <term>demos: the citizen body of ancient Athens</term> might be sustained. He says that there is a tyranny, and he attaches the crime to me; yet he has no evidence to produce that shows I harbor the thoughts of tyrants, even if he were to "burst while speaking"² upon the orator's platform. For tell me: can you bring forward anyone—whether a free man, a slave, a relative, a stranger, or even one of my enemies—with whom I ever shared a word about tyranny? Let such a man come forward and convict me; let him speak during the time allotted to my water-clock <term>clepsydra: a water-vessel used to time speeches in Athenian courts</term>⁴, and I shall remain silent. And yet, this is the manner of accusation, and this is how you have sworn to judge, for this is how charges are brought: "Did someone strike me?" Then the witness stands by. "Is this man a traitor to the city?" Then here is the co-conspirator. "Is he ill-disposed?" Then the person who knows of it is present. But you act as if you were indicting for treason the very man who keeps watch over the city at night out of goodwill...

# THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

And just as if they were oracles from Pytho <note>The site of the famous oracle at Delphi</note> or even Dodona <note>The oldest Greek oracle, where Zeus was said to speak through the rustling of oak leaves</note>, you hold my words—and these even as they offer comfort in the face of danger? What greater honor could I have than that which comes from the entire city of its own free will, and the reputation granted by the people <term>demos: the citizen body</term>, who take joy in honoring me and consider my glory to be their very own? Is it likely that someone who holds honor from those who give it willingly would seek to wrest it from those who are unwilling? Is it possible for one who is magnified by everyone to accept being accused by everyone?

---

<unclear>...as if</unclear> sent by an oracle, I saw it <unclear>above</unclear> repeated insistently. The Greeks <unclear>pronounce</unclear> it *vradiné* <note>meaning "late" or "slender"</note>, but they write it as <unclear>βραδινή</unclear>, at least those who know how to write according to <term>grammar: the formal rules of the language</term>. But those who write the verb "to delay" <unclear>βραδυνῶ</unclear>, write the names as "slow" or "late" <note>βραδινή</note>: in the same way they write "I hasten" <note>ταχύνω</note> and "fast" <note>ταχινή</note>. They also write the word for "in the evening" <note>τὸ βραδύ</note>. The poet Christopoulos writes: "Yesterday <unclear>evening</unclear> submerged..." and "In sleep yesterday <unclear>evening</unclear>." I have also found the spelling *vradē* <note>βράδη</note>, while also seeing *vradu* <note>βράδυ</note> and *vradý* <note>βραδύ</note>. In <unclear>these</unclear> matters, much must be attributed to antiquity, <unclear>unless</unclear> a usage entirely contrary to antiquity has prevailed. Thus I find the verbs for "the evening falls" spelled as *vradiázō*, *vradiázei*, and *vraduázō*. This last one is surely to be preferred. I have often seen "early" <note>τὸ τάχυ</note> written as <unclear>morning</unclear>. I do not know if some might prefer *to tachý* just as they prefer *to vradý*. There is far too much liberty taken regarding orthography <note>spelling</term>. <term>Iotacism: the historical change in Greek where many different vowels and diphthongs came to be pronounced like the English "ee"</term> can hardly be described for how much difficulty it creates in writing vowels, even for learned men, if they are not paying close attention. There is a Bacchic <note>wine-inspired</note> <gloss>little song</gloss> by Christopoulos: "Let me get drunk, let me get drunk. To refresh my heart, and to make my mind dizzy." In the famous <unclear>recent</unclear> edition of Anacreon, I found the same: "let me get drunk, let me get drunk." In another book, the very front page displays in these same capital letters: THE LYRICS OF CHRISTOPOULOS. Similarly, <unclear>Fauriel</unclear> <note>Claude Fauriel, a French philologist</note> erred when <unclear>applying</unclear> <unclear>voices</unclear> to the first of the Folk Songs, writing *CHRĒSTOS MĒLIŌNĒS* instead of *CHRISTOS MILIONIS*. Those Folk Songs <unclear>abound with errors</unclear> of that kind.

# STUDY I.

Is it possible, when one has the chance to be loved, to choose to be hated instead? Or to trade a good reputation for a name of ill-repute? Look back at the past, I beg you, and see if I was tyrannical or violent toward you during that time. Was I not a man of the people <term>demotikos: one who favors the common citizens</term> and a lover of our city? Did I carry myself with more pride than others? Did I build a house more magnificent than my neighbors, or surround myself with a soft, excessive crowd of followers, or clear the streets with a commotion when I walked through them? These are the hallmarks of a tyrannical mind; these are the signs of a monarchy, and the clearest proof <note>original: τεκμήριον (tekmerion)</note> that one wishes to bring the hidden labor-pains of wickedness to light when the time is right.

But what else might drive an attempt at tyranny? Perhaps the desire for wealth? Truly, if I had craved riches, Fortune provided me with many ready excuses. I could have gathered money from the wars that came our way; I could have taken it from you yourselves as rewards for my excellence <term>aristeia: prizes for valor or merit</term>. But I deemed one form of wealth sufficient for me and my family: my goodwill toward the people, and their affection <note>original: ἀγάπησις (agapesis)</note> in return. May I live with this; would that I might also depart this life with it. <margin>may I live</margin>

But I fear that in what I am forced to say about my power <note>original: δύναμις (dynamis)</note>—which my accuser treats like a siege-engine <note>original: μηχάνημα (mechanema)</note> aimed at my character—I might speak of more private matters. I knew these things were happening for my sake, and I always praised the plan as something capable of preserving the order of our city. I never looked down on it because I was being watched by many out of a sense of honor; rather, because I was likely to be held up as a witness by so many, I loved it all the more. I considered those to be wise who value <note>original: πολυωροῦντας (polyoroūntas)</note> what is good with all their strength while it is within reach...

# STUDY 1.

...me, but you judge all these men, and you will appear to be a common slanderer, not a private one.

Have you ever seen—but why must I address these words to this "good" $^1$ <note>original: χρηστόν (chreston) — used ironically here to mean "this fellow" or "this so-called good man"</note> man, and not to you? Have you ever seen, O best of men, a tyrant without a council $^2$ <note>original: βουλῆς (boules)</note>, without bodyguards, and without wealth? Have you ever seen a man of the people, democratic in all things and gentle, ever face such a charge?

But nonetheless, once the slanderer settled on a single purpose—to vilify my actions—he does nothing but shout "up and down" $^4$ <note>original: ἄνω καὶ κάτω (ano kai kato) — a Greek idiom meaning to talk incessantly or to turn things upside down</note> about "the lightning bolt" and "the thousand suits of armor that were revealed." He wishes to use these to prove a tyranny is being established, and with a loud mouth he describes how suits of armor were found in my house. What is there to prevent $^6$ a general from having armor? And what law forbids a soldier from possessing weapons, even beyond his immediate needs? He cannot show such a law at all.

I will ask him this: You are surely a rhetorician and you devote yourself to books, and you cannot possibly deny this. What then? Do you not often possess books even beyond your necessity, in excess? Or do you measure your property strictly by your need? If someone else offers you a book, do you not take it? If you happen upon one at a low price, do you not buy it? And if one should come into your hands—

# III. FROM GEORGE PACHYMERES

...coming upon it [a book], would you hand it over to the fire, so that appearing redundant it might not fill the orator with great unpleasantness? But if someone else asks you for that one book, what will you do then? Answer me. Will you appear harsh and refuse the request? That would not be the behavior of one who loves his fellow man or his fellow citizens $^1$ <note>original: φιλοπόλιδος (philopolidos) — a rare term for a lover of the city-state</note>. Or will you lend it out in turn, and then wait for the loan to return to you in due time?

But perhaps you will speak this way and seem persuasive, since the situation allows for such a defense. What then? Can I also do this? When the time calls for battle, should I give my full suit of armor <term>panoply: the complete set of armor for a heavy infantryman</term> to another, and sit at home until the loan is returned to me and I can remember the war and the fight? Every city, its people, and all the city's affairs would quickly be lost to me along with that loan.

In the meantime, however, if that is how you feel about books, tell me: shall we consider this a matter of personal choice or the intent of the law? If it is personal choice, this argument does not apply to others, but belongs only to you, alone among all, and rightly so. But if it is the intent of the law, show me the law immediately by bringing it forward. Then you will be acting according to the laws and be praised by all, while you might rightly accuse others who do not act this way as violators of the city's law. I might say the same about my own affairs. If there is a law that prevents a general from having armor even beyond what is necessary, give it to the scribe to read out boldly. From that, perhaps others who did not have these in excess will be praised as guardians of the law, while I shall suffer the penalties I deserve $^2$. Yet even then, I am confident I will not be condemned for <note>original: νεωτερισμόν (neoterismon) — literally "innovation," but in a political context, it refers to a revolutionary coup or uprising</note> revolution. Rather, the charge will be a violation of the law, and I will gladly undergo the fine $^3$ imposed by the laws.

I possessed suits of armor; I possessed a thousand and more, being a general—and at that, O Zeus! Or, if you prefer, I am Pericles, whom they herald as "The Olympian" at the Pnyx <note>The Pnyx was the rocky hill in Athens where the citizens' assembly met. Pericles was called "The Olympian" because his oratory was said to thunder and lighten like Zeus</note>. Tell me, I pray, what is the special characteristic of the "Olympian"? Is it not his fellowship with the other gods, and of those...

### EXERCISE 1

->**COLUMN 1**<-

...allotted to him the abundance of divinity, so that he might share this with the others who are also—even if lesser—gods? I too have imitated him, if I may dare to say so, and I confirmed your vote through my own choice, and regarding the weapons, I devised a way to share them with the rest of the citizens. I reasoned to myself that poverty stands in the way of many who wish to defend the city, and it is hardly safe for them to risk their lives against the enemy with unarmed bodies. I said, "Let the weapons lie as a treasure in my house; let my storehouse be a common storehouse." I embody the persona of the city, serving as general, orator, counselor, and statesman; I am wholly dedicated to the fatherland. What is so strange if my home should also be common to the city, and everything in it be guarded for the fatherland in times of need? If I possessed an abundance of money, would I not also consider these common to the people, to be brought together for their needs? And how else, if I felt otherwise, could I rightly be called a lover of the city? <note>original: φιλόπολις (philopolis) — a citizen who loves and is devoted to their city-state</note>

I reckon that you yourselves feel this way: that one considers things his own—whether inherited from a father, earned by labor, or given by fortune—only until the city has an urgent need for them. When common necessity seeks them, those who were owners until then must immediately step aside for the city that nurtured them.

This reasoning, being considered just, made me a collector of many <term>panoplies: full sets of bronze armor including a shield, helmet, cuirass, and greaves</term>. Having this goal in mind, and not out of some tyrannical malice, I have filled my house with weapons just as, I might say, I have filled my soul with battle. For this reason, as I looked upon them every day, I was filled with a martial impulse. And if I should happen to touch them, I felt as if I were sounding a call to war, clearer than a trumpet. What other ornament is better for a general than weapons for those who visit from abroad? Thus, I admit I took pride in the weapons; and, looking almost upon actual war and the battle-lines of soldiers, I exhorted myself to courage and sang a song to Enyalios <term>Enyalios: an ancient title for Ares, the god of war, often used in military hymns</term> $^3$. And...

### BY PACHYMERES

...a house of glory will incite many to battle and will show forth sufficient <term>hoplites: heavily armed infantry soldiers of ancient Greece</term> for the fatherland.

Certainly, my foresight for the city and my concern for the fatherland will, I know, be admired by everyone—as is right—and especially by those whose disposition is grateful and <note>original: φιλόπολις (philopolis) — devoted to the city</note> city-loving. And even <term>Zeus Philios: Zeus in his aspect as the protector of friendship and community</term> himself, after whom I was named <note>original: ψήφῳ (psepho) — by a formal vote or decree</note> by the vote of your council, has—I believe—accepted my purpose. He sent down the lightning bolt, not to convict me of wickedness, but to reveal my virtue, since there had not yet been an opportunity for me to make my intentions clear.

Only this envious and quarrelsome man tries to overturn my good deed, and he charges me with an attempt at <term>tyranny: in this context, the illegal seizure of absolute power by a single ruler</term>—me, who is concerned with how the people might be sustained! He says that it is "tyranny" and attaches the crime to me; yet he is unable to produce anything that represents me as having the mindset of a tyrant, even if he were to <note>original: διαρραγείη λέγων (diarrageie legon) — "burst while speaking," a common Greek idiom for someone exhausting themselves with loud, desperate, or futile speech</note> burst from speaking upon the orator’s platform. For tell me: are you able to put forward anyone—whether a free man or a slave, or one of my household, or a stranger, or let it even be one of my enemies—with whom I ever shared a word concerning tyranny? Let this man come forward and cross-examine me; let him speak during <term>my water-time: the time allotted to a speaker in a Greek court, measured by a clepsydra or water clock</term>, and I shall remain silent. 

And yet, this is the proper manner of accusation, and this is how you have sworn to judge, and how charges are brought: "Has someone struck me?" A witness is presented. "Is this man a traitor to the city?" Here is the co-conspirator. "Is this man ill-disposed?" The one who knows of it is present. But you act as if one were to write an indictment for treason against a man who, out of goodwill, keeps watch over the city by night...

What was my intention in attempting to rule as a tyrant? Was it to gain some glory and honor? Or was it to acquire wealth? Or to attain a <note>original: ἐπιβῶ (epibo) — literally "to step upon" or "attain"</note> famous name? And what degree of superiority in these matters did I leave to any other of the citizens? Did you not establish me in such high honor as to hold the position of a father to the whole people, and to be able to lead you where you must go, and to make you stay where you must not? <note>This is a direct allusion to the historian Thucydides’ description of Pericles’ leadership style.</note> Who else besides me bore the address of flattery and of speaking to the assembly for favor, and not for what is best, because of having such great concession from you? Who else could restrain you when you were not "ailing" and lead you out again when you were, and persuade you in whatever I wished? # III. BY PACHYMERES

<columns>
And just as if from Pytho <note>Another name for Delphi, the site of the famous oracle of Apollo.</note> or even from Dodona <note>An ancient oracle of Zeus where the god’s will was interpreted from the rustling of oak leaves.</note> you held my words as if they were oracles, even when they urged you toward danger. What other honor could be greater for me than that which comes from the entire city by its own will, and the glory given by the whole people, who rejoice in honoring me and who consider my glory to be their own? Is it possible for someone who holds honor from those who give it willingly to seek to take it from those who are unwilling? Is it possible for one who is magnified by everyone to accept being accused by everyone?

---

Then, most eminent men, as if sent by an oracle, I recently saw a certain word repeated improperly. For the Greeks indeed pronounce the word as *vradiné* <note>meaning "of the evening"</note>, but they write it as *vradýno* <note>original: βραδύνω — "to delay" or "loiter"</note>, at least those who know how to write according to the rules of grammar. But those who write the verb *vradýno* also write the noun *vradiné*; just as they write *tachýno* <note>"to speed up"</note> and *tachiné* <note>"quickly"</note>. They also write *to vrádi*, meaning "in the evening." Christopulus <note>Athanasios Christopoulos (1772–1847), a famous Greek poet known for his drinking songs.</note> says: "Yesterday evening submerged," and "In sleep yesterday evening." I have also found it written as *to vráde* (incorrectly), and also *to vrády* and *to vradý*. In these matters, much must be granted to antiquity, unless a common usage contrary to antiquity has completely prevailed. Thus I find *vradiázo*, *vadeiázo*, and *vadyázo*. This last one is certainly to be preferred. I have often seen *to táchy* written for "in the morning." I do not know if some might also like *to táchi*, similar to *to vrádi*. The license taken regarding spelling is excessive. It can hardly be said how much difficulty <term>Iotacism: the historical change in Greek where several different vowels and diphthongs came to be pronounced like the letter "iota" (the "ee" sound)</term> creates in the writing of vowels, even for learned men, if they happen not to be paying close attention. There is a Bacchic song <note>A poem in the style of Anacreon, celebrating wine and revelry.</note> by Christopulus: "Let me get drunk, let me get drunk. To cool my heart, and to make my mind dizzy." <note>original: Νὰ μεθύσω... Καὶ τὸν νοῦν μου νὰ ζαλίσω</note>. In a celebrated edition of that modern Anacreon, I found "let me get drunk" spelled two different ways in the same line. In another book, the very front displays this in capital letters: LYRICS OF CHRISTOPULUS. Likewise, Fauriel <note>Claude Charles Fauriel, a French historian who published a famous collection of Greek folk songs.</note> erred in providing the name of the first of the Popular Songs: *CHRĒSTOS MĒLIONĒS* instead of *CHRISTOS MILLIONĒS*. Those popular songs are full of errors of that kind.

$^1$ That frequent hyperbole regarding speeches full of persuasion and truth—that they are

# EXERCISE I.

Is it possible, when one is permitted to be loved, to prefer being hated, and to exchange a name of good repute for a name of ill fame? Search through the time that has passed, I beg of you, and see if I was tyrannical or violent during that period; see if I was not a man of the people <term>demotikos: one who identifies with the common citizens</term> and a lover of the city <term>philopolis: a patriot</term>. Did I hold a pride greater than any other man? Did I build myself a house more splendid than the houses of others, or behave arrogantly with a crowd of followers, or push people aside in the streets as I passed by? These are the signs of a tyrannical mind; these are the marks of monarchy, and the clearest proof of wishing to burst forth with the labor-pains of wickedness when the right moment arises.

But what else could have incited me <gloss>1</gloss> toward an assault of tyranny? Was it the desire to be wealthy? And yet, if I truly yearned for wealth, not a few pretexts were provided to me by fortune. I could have procured money from the wars that occurred; I could have taken it from you yourselves as prizes of excellence <term>aristeia: rewards given to the bravest soldiers or most distinguished citizens</term>. But one wealth seemed sufficient to me and enough for my family: my own goodwill toward the people and their affection <gloss>2</gloss> back toward me. And with this favor I gird myself <gloss>3</gloss>; may I depart this life with this as well.

But I <gloss>4</gloss> fear that by the things I am forced to say regarding my power—which the accuser sets up like a fortified siege engine against my personal character—I may speak <gloss>5</gloss> of something more secret. It is a thing I knew was happening to me, and I always praised the intention as being able to save the constitution of our city; and not because I was kept in a position of honor by many did I ever complain, but rather I was more pleased because I was likely to be witnessed by many. I considered those men to be wise who care with all their might for what is good when it is present <gloss>6</gloss>,

### EXERCISE I.
<column-break/>

...me, and if you judge all these men, you will appear as a common slanderer, not merely a personal one.

Did you ever see—but why should I direct my words to this "honest" <note>1</note> fellow, and not to you? —Did you ever see, most excellent men, a tyrant who lacked a council <note>2</note>, bodyguards, and great wealth? Have you ever seen a man who is democratic in all things and gentle ever face such an accusation?

But nevertheless <note>3</note>, once he had committed himself to a single purpose—to vilify my affairs—the slanderer says nothing else, but talks "up and down" <note>4</note> about "the thunderbolt" and "the thousand suits of armor revealed." Through these, he wishes to establish the existence of a tyranny, and with a wide-open mouth, he relates that suits of armor were indeed found in my house. But what is it <note>5</note> that prevents <note>6</note> a general from possessing armor? And what law forbids a soldier from owning weapons, even many more than he strictly needs? He cannot show such a law, not in any way.

I will ask him this: You are certainly an orator and you devote your time to books, and you have no way to deny this. What then? Do you possess books, and often in excess of what you strictly need? Or do you measure your possessions exactly by your necessity? If someone else offers you a book, do you not take it? And if you come across one at a good price, do you not buy it? And if some should come into your hands...

...on definitions: "The common element according to substance is 'in-dwelling,' such as the form, the..." In that passage, there is a variant reading "namely" <note>original: *ἤγουν*</note>. When the moment calls us to battle, should I give my **full suit of armor** <term>panoply: a complete set of armor and weapons for a heavy-infantry soldier</term> to another and sit at home until the loan is returned to me and I can remember the war and the fight? If I did, every city, every people, and all the affairs of the state would quickly vanish along with my loan!

2 The manuscript reads "of worth" [ἀξίας]. I have written "worthily" [ἀξίως].
3 I previously wrote "law" [νόμον] by a slip of the pen.

But for now, tell me: if you feel this way about books, shall we consider this a matter of personal choice, or a requirement of the **law**? If it is a matter of choice, then this argument does not apply to others but belongs to you—to you alone among all men, and justly so. But if it is the requirement of the law, then produce that law and show it to us immediately! Then you will be seen as acting according to the laws and will be praised by all, while you might justly accuse others who do not do so of transgressing the city’s laws. I would say the same regarding my own affairs. If there is a law that forbids a general from possessing armor even "beyond what is necessary," then let the secretary read it out boldly. From that, others—who perhaps did not possess such things in excess—will be praised as guardians of the law, and I will suffer the penalty **worthily** <margin>2</margin>. Yet even then, I am confident I will not be condemned for **revolutionary plotting**; rather, the charge will be a violation of a statute, and I will gladly pay the fine according to the **laws** <margin>3</margin>.

<margin>
4 Scholion (ancient commentary): A shifting of the cause.

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s defense of his character. On the previous page, he compared his collection of armor to a scholar’s collection of books. ### EXERCISE 1.

...did He not allot the abundance of His divinity to others, so that they too—even if lesser—might partake in being gods? I too have imitated Him, if I may dare to say so, and I ratified your vote <gloss>1</gloss> through my own choice, devising a way to share my equipment with the rest. I reasoned to myself that poverty stands in the way of many who wish to defend the city, and it is hardly safe for them to risk their lives against the enemy with bare bodies:

> "Let the weapons be stored in my house like a treasure; let my storehouse be a common treasury. I embody the form of the city, acting as general, orator, councilor, and statesman; I am entirely dedicated to the fatherland. What is strange if my house too were common to the city, and everything in it were kept for the fatherland in times of need? If I had an excess of money, would I not consider that too as common property for the people, to be contributed for their needs? And how else, if it were otherwise, could I justly be called a **patriot** <term>philopolis: literally a 'lover of the city'; one who prioritizes the public good over private interest</term>?"

I believe you yourselves think this way: that a person considers what they have as private—whether inherited from a father, earned through labor, or given by fortune—only until the city has a pressing need for them. But when the common necessity seeks these things, those who were masters of them until then must immediately yield them to the city that raised them.

This reasoning, being considered just, also made me a "lover of acquisition" regarding the **panoplies** <term>panoply: the complete suit of armor and weapons for a heavy-infantry soldier</term>. Having this goal in mind, and not desiring any tyrannical wickedness, I have filled my house with weapons, just as I might say a soul is filled with battle. For this reason, seeing them every day, I was filled with martial spirit; and if I ever touched them, I sounded a "recall" as if on a flute for war, clearer than a trumpet. What other ornament is better for a general than weapons for those visiting from abroad? Therefore, I took pride in the weapons, I admit it; and seeing almost <gloss>2</gloss> nothing but war and battle-lines of soldiers, I sharpened my courage and sang a **war-song** <gloss>3</gloss> <note>original: "Ἐνυάλιον" (Enyalian song). Enyalios was an ancient epithet for Ares, the god of war, or sometimes a distinct minor war deity.</note>. And other...

This is the same way that doctors often take a stand against **expected diseases** <note>original: ἐλπιζόμενα νοσήματα</note>; it is not because they study prevention that they are already inviting the disease, but because they are guarding against it and, by expecting it, they prevent it. Such is my attitude toward the fatherland.

->### STUDY 1.<-

I speak simply and truly to you; but as for the claim that whoever possesses weapons will certainly become a tyrant—that is a point I have never conceded. For it is possible for someone to prepare weapons for another purpose entirely. And if you wish, look at this: place other examples side-by-side with this one, and you will find my argument to be true.

Consider the man who pursues other men’s wives. He is eager to draw his targets to himself, and knowing reasonably well that the natural "bait" for this is beauty, if he was not born with it, he uses artifice and adorns himself. Yet, because of this, not every person who adorns themselves will be guilty <gloss>1</gloss> of the charge of adultery. For it is possible to beautify oneself for another reason. Many people, being lovers of beauty and hating ugliness, if they were not naturally gifted, diligently <gloss>2</gloss> repair their own appearance; and though they are not beautiful, they *seem* beautiful—and that which "seems," even if it is far from the truth <gloss>3</gloss>, is often preferred. In the same way, every "night-prowler" wanders at night because the day does not grant a thief safety <gloss>4</gloss>. However, not every person wandering at night is a thief; for it is also <gloss>5</gloss> possible for someone to wander as a stranger, or perhaps because they lost their way due to some stroke of bad luck.

But you act just like someone who, knowing that honey is yellow, might then insist that everything yellow is honey—knowing little and failing in the proper logical division of things. Why then do you poorly convert <gloss>6</gloss> a statement that does not allow for such conversion? Simply because a tyrant uses weapons, you demand that I, who am using weapons, must wish to be a tyrant. You unjustly slander my noble ambition <note>original: φιλοτιμία (philotimia) - a Greek concept of "love of honor" or public-spiritedness that could be seen as either a virtue or a vice</note> and you blame what is worthy of great praise among sensible men.

But enough words regarding this man; he is completely <gloss>7</gloss> possessed by these same ideas and would not be persuaded otherwise even if one were to say more. For why...

What is more terrible than the soul of a slanderer?¹ His tongue is a viper that bites directly; even if it barely touches its mark, it is satisfied with the bite and releases its venom to spread. But I will speak my mind to you with great frankness, men of the city and fellow-lovers of what is good.

Some of you² raised me from my very³ childhood; others have joined me in doing what was possible upon the battle lines of war; and still others share with me in the councils held for the sake of the city. If I speak of my father Xanthippus⁴—how he was always a man of the people and a lover of the city—I shall not need external testimony. If I speak of my own kinsmen, you yourselves know them. If I speak of my own conduct from the beginning, I shall not summon this man or that man, but all of you together as witnesses. Anaxagoras⁵ shall bear witness for me even more, as shall his school. He reached the very core of my character, and having found me to be moderate and sociable, he trained me in meteorological matters⁶ <note>Anaxagoras was a pre-Socratic philosopher who taught Pericles; "meteorological" here refers to natural philosophy and the study of the heavens.</note>. If I should speak of my deeds and the labors I endured while standing at the head of this city—and how I was clearly most incorruptible regarding money—I held the masses in freedom⁷; the entire multitude will bear witness to me. And if I often spoke against some in anger, it was not out of ill-will, but out of favor; I struck those who were bold with insolence until they felt fear, and clearly, when you were unreasonably afraid, I restored you again to a state of confidence⁸.

And while you are aware of these things and have witnessed them in the past, I—in my accustomed manner—shall put forward my deeds rather⁹ than my words, those which I displayed in my daily life, as proof of my frankness, as I myself maintain—

# STUDY 1.

...worthy. And I shall show myself superior to the present accusation; I shall not appear lowly, nor shall I cower while being tested; I present the whole of Pericles for your scrutiny. Employ that well-disposed wisdom of yours, by which you also judge foreigners without failing in what is proper. Examine my political life in fine detail: whether I have been tyrannical and violent toward others, or indeed moderate. Question those near to me, those far away, those within, and those without. I will not take offense at these things, nor will I be deeply pained that, though you ought to ask yourselves, you seek to learn from others.

If, therefore, you condemn me based on the testimony of others, I shall accept the verdict as just; I will not struggle against the judges, I will not utter a peep, I will not make use of friends, I will not bring up my children¹ <note>original: παῖδας ἀναβιβάσομαι; it was a common custom for defendants in Athenian courts to bring their weeping children before the jury to evoke pity.</note>, nor will I beg for my life on the strength of my own labors. But if the charge is that the full suits of armor in my house are a "treasure," I will not consider this an accusation, but will rather cherish it as a point of honor. And if I should suffer anything, I would prefer that outcome many times over to being deprived of my weapons for a single day.

Come here, fellow soldiers! Come, leaders of war! If living without weapons is safe for you, then cast your vote against me. But if you consider this a heavy burden—seeing as weapons are a necessity, no less so than breathing, for men who are soldiers and who are frequently tested in wars² on behalf of the city—then give me courage for my words. Lend me the common voice; teach the nature of weapons; tell us what a soldier places his confidence in³. And if you can convince them⁴—if not, I will then accept my punishment gladly, because I am being tried for my military experience. Even if I fare poorly, I do not care at all. I only advise you to consider weapons as your one true wealth; even if someone accuses you out of envy, believe it is better to be deprived even of life than for you to both be and be called unarmed soldiers.

<header>BY GEORGE PACHYMERES</header>

## STUDY 2.

->A philosopher persuaded a tyrant to lay down his tyranny, and he asks for the reward of tyrant-slayers. But some oppose him. And we are practicing the speech for the philosopher.¹<-

The goals of our prayer and our diligence have reached their end; and already I see the whole city wearing crowns, and the people freed from the gloom of tyranny, and festivals once again being established, and the law courts and council chambers being assembled³, and all these things set right by the gods and by philosophy, with everyone rejoicing and everyone offering sacrifices of thanksgiving.

But I, the sole cause of these good things, am somber; and as if I had been condemned to pay the penalty for evils, I come before the court and practice words for a dispute, having not yet properly set aside the reasoning I used against the tyranny. And while it is necessary to rejoice with the city for its freedom and to exult together—if I had nothing more to say—instead I, who was also a victim of the tyranny in my own right, and who holds the reward (the mark of good intention and diligence) almost⁴ in my hands from the whole city...

twice; "all but" <note>original Greek: μονονοὺ καὶ</note>. Cleomedes, book 1, chapter 2, page 57 (71): "This is proven by a great many examples, which **all but** <note>original: μόνον οὐχὶ</note> possess geometric proofs." Balforeus had wandered from the correct meaning, translating it thus: "this is proven to be true from many things, not only from those which admit linear demonstrations"; rather, it should be: "which contain **all but** linear demonstrations," according to the excellent interpretation of the learned Bak. In Theophrastus's *Character* 18, from the Palatine manuscript, Siebenkees edited: "And if perhaps some relative or close friend <insert>should come to ask to borrow cups</insert>, he will lend them, but only after **branding** them <note>original: ἐπυρώσας; perhaps marking them with fire to prevent theft</note>, and weighing them, and almost taking a guarantor." The Tauchnitz edition reads: "...or... all but branding them," etc., which correction itself needs correcting, as it lacks sense. The Dübner edition reads: "...or... having **impressed a name**," regarding the authority of which reading that learned man gave no warning. Furthermore, it seems this should not be easily admitted, because the engraved impression of a name requires a great deal of time and a craftsman’s hand. Because of the similarity in the shape of the vowels "eta" and "upsilon," I have conjectured—accepting the particle "or"—that we should read "**mutilating**" <note>original: μονονοὺ πηρώσας</note>. This man of little faith lends a cup but nearly mutilates it by removing some part or an embossed ornament, the pins of which can easily be touched and fixed back again; thus the vessel entrusted to a borrowing friend, being no longer whole, could hardly be kept longer or sold. Quintilian, in *The Marian Soldier*, section 3: "nor is the accuser ashamed... to reproach the soldier for being a man, and **all but** <note>original Latin: tantum non</note> harsh and rustic, but he complains that he was poorly educated in the arts of a cour-

<column-break/>

-tesan." I think "and" was written by the author, not "but." A misunderstanding of the formula "all but" <note>original: tantum non</note> seemed to require an opposition <note>the word "but"</note>. When I noted this using the Dussalt edition, I wished for the sake of diligence to inspect the Burmann edition, and I realized that learned scholar had proposed "and," following many manuscripts, and that Valla had long ago read "and poorly." Dussalt, otherwise a man most knowledgeable in the Latin language, applied too little study to editing the *Declamations* of Quintilian. There are places where the force of the sentence separates the negation from the adverb, as I just mentioned. Valerius Flaccus will provide an example (1, 202): "with the waves **all but** <note>original: tantum non</note> indignant, may you receive this head," meaning, of course, with the waves "only just" not being indignant. Likewise Seneca, *Epistle* 119, 7: "Or does he have too little who is **all but** <note>original: tantum non</note> cold, not hungry, not thirsty? Jupiter has no more than that"; that is, he who has nothing more than "not lacking," who has only that which keeps him from being cold. More difficult is the passage from Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* 14, 5, placed by Ruhkopf next to the Seneca passage: "You see those... who ought to have been not only protected by the guards of the whole world, but even exalted, yet they are **all but** <note>original: tantum non</note> praised and loved, but are confined by walls." I propose it should be rewritten: "**not** all but praised"; "not only not praised" <note>original Greek: οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐπαινεῖσθαι</note>, as in the passage of Pachymeres cited on page 20, column 2. Heyne, in his notes on Tibullus (1, 1, 25), did not dwell on Cicero's words; but he did not say in what way he understood them.

<header>III. OF PACHYMERES</header>

Regarding the prize of honor,¹ I care very little, whether one speaks of a crown of gold, or a public proclamation by a herald in the marketplace, or the right to take meals in the town hall <note>original: πρυτανείου; the Prytaneion was the seat of government where honored citizens were fed at public expense</note>, or any other gift with which it is your custom to reward the benefactors of the city. This alone bites at my soul: that by the loss of this prize, I might also be stripped of the recognition for my devotion to the fatherland. I fear that all those struggles I undertook on your behalf—to the full extent of my character and my skill—might be erased in a single moment by a man who is both envious and a hater of the city. For in the former case, even if the prize is absent, the evidence of my goodwill is not yet obscured; but in this case, if I do not appear to have been useful to the fatherland despite my efforts, it would be utterly piteous. It would be a terrible thing <note>original: δεινὸν</note> to bear—or rather, it would be more than one could bear³—for a man who has worked beyond his strength for those he was bound to help, and who rushed with all his might against the danger, to be so dismissed!

Rather,⁴ I shall begin from a point a little further back, so that it may become clear to you both how many terrors the recent events brought upon the fatherland, and how much I struggled with all my heart, opposing that danger with everything I had. But oh! What am I to do? Being forced to remember those difficulties once again, I am filled with dizziness and despondency; my mind returns there, and I can almost see the events of that time before my very eyes:⁵ the terrifying tyrant upon the citadel, controlling everything here with a mere glance; his bodyguards passing up and down with savagery; the pious people in the greatest grief and despair. Those in the city did not dare to peek out even a little from their homes, but remained hidden in darkness and obscurity—some even in tombs—holding it better to die than to live as slaves to tyrannical decrees. I omit the plundering of houses, the dragging away of maidens, the seizing of property,⁶ the daily beatings, and those who, even if...

<header>DECLAMATION II.</header>

...if anyone so much as muttered a word, or dared to say the city's affairs were in a bad state, they met with bitter and inevitable death. I pass over the neglect of the holy houses <note>original: θείους οἴκους; referring to churches or temples</note>, the dissolution of the law courts, the inaction in the councils, and the general confusion of the city. Why must I list the events of that time and be overwhelmed by the mere memory of such hardships? Besides, anyone wishing to describe those events would find themselves defeated by the reality of them. For what words could reach the scale of those fears, those turmoils, and the dangers that appeared wherever one turned? It was a time when some even abandoned their children <note>original: γένη; literally "offspring" or "kin"</note>, so that they might not suffer the same misfortune as their fathers when they came of age. It was a time when each person sentenced themselves to voluntary exile, choosing it gladly over the tyrannical slavery of sitting at home; when the city was empty of inhabitants, and those who left were wretched in foreign lands, while those who remained by necessity appeared gloomy and downcast.

Regarding these things, therefore (and I ask you to observe my zeal), I often prayed to myself that I had military experience and was naturally suited for the spear and war. For only in this way did I think I could overcome the tyrant's arrogance and cruelty, if I were to try. Often, while sitting at home and devoting my mind to a book, I would suddenly become speechless <note>original: ἐννεὸς; struck dumb or dazed with worry</note>. The book in my hands seemed merely a book, and only my eyes ran over the writing; my mind was elsewhere, thinking of how I might see the fatherland's freedom and how the tyrant might be removed. Anyone standing by me then would have seen a man raging, possessed, like those we see who are "nymph-caught" <note>original: νυμφολήπτους; "nympholepts" were believed to be seized by spirits, leading to a state of religious frenzy or prophetic madness</note>. Often I even regretted my devotion to philosophy and the profession I had followed since I was young. "Of what use to me is the knowledge of things that are," I would say, "if it cannot contribute to the well-being of the city? Let the knowledge of both divine and human affairs perish, if it does not help the fatherland in its suffering!"

“One knowledge is best: to defend the fatherland <note>original: περὶ πατρίδος ἀμύνεσθαι; a play on Homer’s famous line from the Iliad, replacing 'omen' with 'knowledge'</note>; one pursuit is most noble: to thrust danger away from the city by every means possible.”

Night and day, I was gripped by these reflections. I suffered these things daily, and my pain was double instead of single: I felt the suffering itself, and yet, being fully conscious of my suffering, I was also searching for a way to escape it. I implored the gods <note>original: ἐποτνιώμην θεούς; a term for a tearful, desperate appeal to higher powers</note>, making prayers to the higher powers—not for this or that specific thing of mine, but for my whole life, for my very body, and for my soul forever. “For why,” I said, “should it be unbelievable if God willed it, and the city's fortune assisted, that even I—who seem to be a nobody—might be shown to be noble and useful against such an assault of misfortune? In this way, I too might become a child of my country not at all worthy of being overlooked; my work would not be superfluous, nor would I have labored in vain. Instead, it would be a prize for philosophy itself, showing that it contributed to the city's most vital concerns. Then orators will not be able to boast over philosophers regarding civic matters, if even from the philosophers something useful should happen to meet the current crisis <note>original: τύχην; referring here to the 'fortune' or 'circumstances' of the city</note>.”

Therefore, a thought from the gods came to me—for from where else could I say it came? I reasoned that in other matters, perhaps, a professional craft might differ from one's personal intent; a man wishing to handle public affairs might be hindered by his specific occupation if he had not previously been initiated into public life. But in the present circumstances, where everything depends on one’s intent, every craft and every...

<header>### STUDY II.</header>

...pursuit, wherever that [choice] might lead, the pursuit will follow. <note>original: κἀκείνη; Note 1 explains a grammatical correction here regarding how the "pursuit" follows the "choice."</note> For a person who is to receive equal crowns of honor whether he succeeds or fails, based solely on his own inner choice, will certainly not find his outward pursuit out of harmony with his inner will.

"I must attempt the work," I said, "with the help of the gods. Philosophy is also a weapon for the overthrow of tyranny. It possesses knowledge of the nature of things; it will put these truths forward. It will distinguish between things with scientific precision and will teach what remains forever and what merely passes away; it will place before one’s eyes the shortness of life. It will set down power, but set against it a most beautiful reputation. It will set down wealth, but set against it a memory well-spoken of. It will set down bodyguards and outward show and the wonder of those around him, but set against them those who are unjustly tyrannized, the hatred of all people, and being reviled by everyone. These are the weapons of philosophy; this is the test of knowledge. With these, I can put the tyrant to shame; with these, I can soften the swelling of his pride. I will occupy the 'acropolis' <note>The high point of the city, both literally and as a metaphor for the seat of power.</note>; I will philosophize about the whole world—how it is all a dream, like a shadow that cannot be grasped, like the vision of those who are just waking up; <note>Note 2 provides a deep history of this "waking dream" metaphor.</note> and that public-spirited men, both while living and after they have departed, are friends to the gods and honored by men; but tyrants, while living, are subject to public curses, and having departed, are talked about only for their wickedness, so that others might flee from their...

<margin>1. The manuscript reads *kakeine* ("and that one"). I have written the dative case here used adverbially: "the pursuit will follow that [direction] wherever the choice might lead." Regarding the use of *ekeine* ("in that way"), see the notes to Eunapius, page 225, 505.</margin>

<margin>2. Pachymeres was looking at the saying of Pindar found in Stobaeus (title 111, 12), which was later included by Boeckh among the fragments of the Lyric poets (p. 669) and explained by him: "hopes are the dreams of those awake." This saying is attributed to Aristotle by Diogenes Laertius (5.18) and to Plato by Aelian (Varia Historia 13.29). Colomesius noted this in reference to the words of Quintilian in his *Institutes* (6.2): "vain hopes and like certain dreams of those waking." I say, Basil the Great also looked to this in a</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>certain letter to Nazianzenus in the Sinnerian Collection (p. 388): "I praise the one who said hopes are dreams of those awake." Nicephorus Chumnus in Letter 112: "Someone said hopes are the dreams of those awake, and indeed, it seems to me, he spoke very well." I was briefer there. Stephane Jovius, in his *Cecilia*, says: "As for the future, he values it no more than hope; it is for him, as Saint Paul says, the dream of a waking man." Thus that writer [Jovius] often erred, for he possessed more natural talent than literary learning, and had read neither Paul nor Pindar [on this matter].</margin>
