# STUDY II.

...softening¹ [his character] through every gesture toward something more civilized. Why say more? He <note>Referring to the official or "introducer" mentioned on the previous page.</note> mentions my request; it pleases the tyrant, and immediately I am led in.

What need is there to describe how much cunning that man improvised against a humble old man, how he displayed a savage and inexorable character from the very start, and how many expressions he let slip across his face while listening to my words? Nevertheless, having once fixed upon a single goal—to free the city, if I were able—even if some unpleasantness should befall me, I did not give up. I set every reasoning in motion to persuade him, attempting by every means to soften the hardness of his resolve, to overcome his tyrannical self-will, and to achieve the object of my zeal.

One could see then a battle between both sides and an outright war. He insulted me and called me a fool if I hoped to prevail with such words. I appealed to him, setting my humility against his pride; I reminded him of death, and of the dishonor he would leave behind if he died in such a state, and of the glory he would gain if he changed. Did he mock me with laughter? I, showing my concern², shed tears. Did he dismiss me haughtily? I humbly clung to his knees. Finally, did he bare his sword? I offered my neck for the slaughter. And why should I trouble you with the telling? Barely, and after a long time, learning that I would not give in—no matter what I might suffer or whatever might happen³—he was overcome by a better reasoning, having been touched by the gods...

# 28 G. PACHYMERES

...[the hardness] of his heart, and he is seen to be humble, and after waiting a little time, he says: "But will you guarantee my safety if I withdraw from the acropolis?" And when I agreed and called the gods to witness^1 that his life would indeed be protected (and why should I say anything but the truth?), he rose up immediately, threw down^2 his arms, and having bidden farewell^3 to me as well as to the acropolis, to all tyranny, and to the affairs of the city, he departed with his kinsmen. <gloss>defense</gloss>^4

And now, with the cooperation of the gods,^5 the acropolis is empty of tyrannical cruelty, and the city is empty of tumults and disturbances. No tyrant commands; no foreigners or newcomers <term>epelydes</term> <note>refers to outsiders who have settled in the city, often implies mercenaries or unwelcome guests</note> overrun our houses; laws are not insulted; ancestral customs are not overlooked; no one's mind is enslaved, saying one thing while thinking another,^6 forced to curry favor with the times; none of the terrible things anyone might order are done. Everything is full of calm, everything full of joy. I see judges sitting on the bench, the public council gathering in the council chamber, festivals celebrated according to ancestral custom,^7 orators making public speeches, anyone who wishes speaking in opposition—everyone with the freedom to speak, everyone in the greatest liberty, those in the fields, those in the city, all offering sacrifices for their lives because of my philosophy and daring deeds.

* But this man alone—I do not know from where he came—for if he were here and had experience of these terrors, he would not have meditated saying such things—this man alone^8 belittles my bravery and seeks to deprive me of my reward.

# SECOND DEBATE

### SECOND STUDY

<columns>
...[he] desires even more honor, and he seeks the slaughter of the tyrant and bloodshed; and, because these things did not happen, he refuses to call "tyrant-slayer" the man who drove the tyrant¹—along with his equipment and all his bodyguards—out of the acropolis.

But, my good man², the patriot ought³ to have considered how the tyranny might be dissolved; I considered it as best as could be done. One ought to have dared the attempt at the destruction of wickedness, as is fitting; I dared it greatly. I went up, I confronted the tyrant who was doomed to perish, and I "set every rope in motion"⁴ <note>An ancient nautical idiom meaning "to leave no stone unturned" or to use every possible resource; original: πάντα κάλων ἐκίνησα</note> to push the danger away from the city⁵. One ought to have made the fortress empty⁶ of the tyrant and his bodyguards; this has certainly happened. And now, let everyone go up there, if they wish; let them enjoy pure freedom, and wherever they go, let them not be afraid. For look, what would have happened if he had been slaughtered has happened now that he has fled. And just as someone who was sick and became healthy⁷ does not have reason to complain about the *way* he became healthy, but will rather be glad to be rid of the disease and will feel gratitude toward the one responsible, so you should judge the present situation. Why do you question the way you were rid of the tyranny, once you have been rid of it?

¹ The manuscript reads "the, tyrant" (τόν, τύραννον). The comma was placed after the article "the" to show that it belongs not to the noun "tyrant," but to the participle "the one who drove out." # III. BY PACHYMERES

If you were not delivered from these hardships, you would have cause to blame the deed as incomplete. But if you have been perfectly delivered from these evils, and a total calm and stability smiles upon the city, and the sun is seen by you more brightly now than when the tyranny held everything in its grip, why do you enjoy the benefit, yet refuse to give the gratitude due for that benefit? Why do you embrace the work as noble, but act ungratefully toward the one who performed it? <note>original: "ἀγνωμονεῖς"; this refers to a lack of "gnome" or fair-mindedness/gratitude.</note>¹ <margin>**Scholion**: A syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>.</margin>

Lift up your eyes and look around you; see the freedom of the city everywhere. See everyone lighting fires of thanksgiving in their homes. See the dignity of our government; see the freedom of speech of the elders, and the courage of the youth for noble things. But I set aside the rest. At any rate, tell me: where did you get the ability to stand in court and speak against me, and who gave this to you? Can you name anyone other than me and my zeal? What more would have resulted beyond the present circumstances if the tyrant had been killed?² <margin>**Perhaps** "had been killed" <note>original Latin: "Fortasse ἀνήρητο"</note>.</margin> If you have an answer, show this to the judges, and I will submit myself to you to make up for the deficiency. But if you have nothing to say, why do you trouble me in vain?

I will show, from the very intent of the lawgiver³ <margin>**Manuscript**: "will," with "intent" written above and "will" marked with dots <note>This indicates a scribe correcting the text from "theleseos" to "bouleseos."</note>. **Scholion**: The opinion of the lawgiver.</margin>, that I am a "tyrant-slayer," and that the reward belongs to me.

Read the law for me, secretary.

Wait.

Do you hear, opponent, that the law says the one who acted "dissolved the tyranny"? Does it therefore give the reward for the sake of murder, or for the dissolution of the tyranny? Surely the reward is for the daring, not for the slaughter. Consider this: everything depends on the daring and the intent. On one hand, imagine someone who dared the deed but did not succeed; on the other hand, imagine someone who did not intend it but killed the tyrant (suppose, for instance, if someone hit the tyrant as he was passing by, without meaning to, and killed him). Which of the two will you honor, and to whom will you give the reward? Not to the one who dared, even if he did not succeed? If you wish⁴ <margin>**He said** "set side-by-side" <note>original Latin: "Dixit παράλληλα θεῦ"</note> on page 17, line 4.</margin>, set them side by side: someone who wanted to act but was not able, and someone who was able but did not want to, if indeed...

->### STUDY II.<-

...who actually performed the deed, but did so without intent; whom will you praise more, and whom will you love more? Is it not the one who willed it, even if he were unable to achieve it?

Holding this aim in mind, the lawgiver <note>likely referring to Solon or a legendary Athenian lawgiver often cited in these rhetorical exercises</note> accepts the **intent** in present circumstances and grants the prize to the **daring**. In these matters, you will find me even more deserving: a man <margin>Importance / Magnitude</margin> nurtured by quietude, devoted to books, and knowing nothing more than how to read and study—and perhaps sometimes to speak with children and engage in philosophy with them as far as possible. I am a man who has grown old in <term>apragmosyne</term> <note>A Greek ideal of "quietude" or "freedom from public business," often associated with scholars and philosophers.</note> and staying at home,¹ yet I threw myself into the greatest dangers. I looked past the weakness of my body; I looked past the peace of my soul, my old age, and my domestic life. I existed only for the purpose of struggling for the fatherland and freeing it from tyranny.

Transpose your mind to those times, I beg you. Reflect on how I approached the matter. Set before your logic, as if on a stage, the things that were then taking place. Imprint upon your imagination, on one side, a tyrant sitting—haughty, arrogant, and wild—and on the other side, an old man standing—weak, terrified, and humble. What man—even one like this fellow who struts about here and argues against me—could have endured that sight? Who did not shudder to see it? Who did not give up in the face of such threats? Who was sufficient to speak against so many tongues moving with such arrogance, and moreover, with such power? 

But nonetheless, with the gods granting me strength (for what else could I say?), I barely overcame all those things. I brought down his pride. That fearsome man, who at first could not even be approached, was tamed like an asp by the charms of philosophy and my own "incantations."² And he who, it was thought, would never be persuaded no matter what happened, became obedient immediately. He threw his weapons to the ground—or to put it another way, he discarded his whole tyrannical mindset. As if he had been struck by lightning, he fled; he was gone, along with his bodyguards and accomplices. And just as when a cloud passes, which for a time covered the sun...

<meta>This page continues the speaker's defense. Previously, he argued that the moral intent of a deed is more important than the physical act itself. He is now describing the immediate aftermath of the tyrant's flight and the city's celebration of his bloodless victory.</meta>

### GEORGE PACHYMERES ###

...was hidden, the morning star immediately appeared and everything was full of light. In the same way, as soon as that man [the tyrant] departed, a clear sky shone over the whole city. And before he had even properly escaped, a god-sent rumor of good news rang in the ears of the citizens. People congratulated one another, telling the story, and everyone said: "The philosopher! The citizen! The old man whom we know! This success belongs to him; this is his finest achievement. He should be crowned; he should be given public meals; he should be celebrated from the speaker's platform!"

This is how the city reacted upon learning what had happened. Nor indeed were those living in the fields unaware at that time <gloss>¹</gloss> of these events. Instead, they too came running together, and once again a second beginning for the state began, a new order for the public condition. Temples are opened and the palaces of the gods are adorned; the wooden cult statues <gloss>²</gloss> <note>original: "xoana" - ancient, highly sacred wooden images of deities</note> are cleansed, and everyone offers sacrifices of thanksgiving with pleasure. There is no one who does not call that man’s flight the "slaughter of the tyrant," and call me the "tyrannicide." For this reason, the city wished <gloss>³</gloss> to honor me with a worthy prize.

But this man [the accuser] alone prattles on about blood and slaughter. He admits, even if against his will, that the city is free; but because the freedom did not come to the city in the manner he deems worthy, he devalues the entire deed. He does not wisely <gloss>⁴</gloss> consider that it is a greater thing to repel a tyranny and free a city without slaughter and turmoil than to do so with blood and danger. For in the latter case, the victory is not purely a victory alone; there is always the chance that the one taking the risk might be defeated. And while there might be general cheer and delight, for some individuals there will be personal grief for the loss of their kin. This becomes established for the citizens as "laughter-tears" <gloss>⁵</gloss> <note>original: "clausigelōs" - a bittersweet state of simultaneous joy and mourning</note>—the citizen will rejoice for the city’s freedom, but because he has lost a son or a brother or some other relative, his joy will be tainted. But in this way, the beauty is untroubled, the good follows naturally, and the joy is shared by all. Just as they enjoy their freedom, so too do they enjoy this shared happiness.

# STUDY II. #

<sig>5</sig>

But you wanted the city’s celebration to be only half-complete, so that those who envy our success might have a share of the joy, and so our neighbors might say: “The city was freed from the tyranny, but it escaped poorly.” They will indeed remember the evils, and they will also remember the good things that followed; but nevertheless, the evils remain unmixed, while the good is mixed with the bad. What benefit did the overthrow of the tyranny bring these people? They would have been content to be ruled by a tyrant; they would have preferred to endure slavery while still alive.

How did you feel when you heard these things? How did you appear to those who reported such talk?

For my part, I judge these accusations to be heavier than the tyranny itself, more shameless than the wickedness of bodyguards, and more arrogant than the spite of armed henchmen. For being ruled by a tyrant might happen by chance, and it is not the fault of the city; but when rising up against such a power, to still be deprived of noble men is both a loss and a sin for the city.

Apart from these things, if someone else were about to take a stand against the tyrant, and then I, getting ahead of them, pushed that person aside with my words, perhaps <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "τυχὸν ἴσως" – a rhetorical formula; the gloss refers to the scholar Choricius of Gaza, p. 344</note>, while my intention might be praised, I would be giving ground against myself to those who wish to find fault. But if I had no other way to act, as my character dictated, and no one else among the citizens chose to take the risk, what was left but for me to remain quiet and sit at home? And even if something happened <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "κἂν εἴ τι καὶ συνέβαινε" – a variation found in Declamation IV: "even if something has occurred."</note> I could have chosen not to care, while others remained indifferent or even afraid (for “afraid” is a more polite way to put it). Should the city then have remained under a tyrant, with no one standing in the way of his tyrannical desires and savagery?

And what if <gloss>3</gloss> <note>Scholiast's note: "Hypothetical scenario"</note>—before I even set upon the task—I had found you all sitting together and lamenting the city's dire state (for one could not say you were gathered in a law court or a council chamber), if, I say, I had encountered you sitting together and weeping over the city’s misfortunes, and standing before you, I had said: “O fellow citizens and neighbors, this dread touches me too; I cannot bear being ruled by a tyrant along with the rest. A noble thought comes to me, and, if...”

# III. BY PACHYMERES #

<note>George Pachymeres (1242–c. 1310) was a Byzantine historian and philosopher; this text is a "declamation," a formal rhetorical exercise where a speaker argues a hypothetical legal case.</note>

My way of life provides no room for such deeds, but my resolve offers pretexts on behalf of the fatherland. I set out to go to the tyrant, to appear stripped of any equipment <note>meaning: unarmed</note>, and to use what I have against him for the common benefit. If, then, you seek to see that man slain, that is not the work of my right hand. I have placed my confidence in my tongue alone, and, I believe, through this I shall contend; even if I do not commit a murder, I will persuade him to flee. If, then, through my acting thus, you are freed from the tyranny, will you remember me regarding the reward when you sit upon the judgment seat? If I were to speak in this way, and demand your guarantees that you would truly consider me a <term>tyrannicide</term> <note>original: "tyrannoktonos" – a legal status in ancient city-states that entitled the hero to rewards, such as free meals or a statue</note> and grant me the prize, what would you have said then? Would you have hesitated and considered the matter? Or would you not have immediately voted me the prizes and no small rewards? I do not think you would have delayed; rather, even before the deeds were done, you would have called me a benefactor, and all but placed the prize in my hands.

It is therefore terrible, and beyond terrible <gloss>3</gloss>, if, when I promised to do what I set out to achieve, you were immediately going to cast your vote for the reward of tyrannicide—

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s rhetorical defense. He is arguing that his non-violent removal of the tyrant through philosophical persuasion deserves the same official reward—a "gueras"—usually reserved for those who kill a tyrant with a sword. # III. OF PACHYMERES #

...if someone strives for the common good and holds the title given as a reward <note>original: "gueras"</note>, you should be ready to grant it.

Do not, therefore, condemn me because I seek a reward and do not choose to benefit the city without pay. Rather, consider that my deed is great, and I wish for the favor to be proclaimed now, and I wish for it hereafter to remain inscribed upon ancient pillars <note>original: "kyrbesi" — these were triangular wooden or stone tablets used in ancient Athens to display public laws and honors</note>. For this reason, no matter what anyone might say¹, I desire the reward. For what could anyone give that is worthy of a man's life, which I once risked? Even if one were to give something, quite apart from it being a reward—for men accustomed to valuing honor above all else²—is it not something to be highly regarded?³

For if, while the evils of the tyranny are still almost before our eyes, and many are still skeptical because of the strangeness of the event, unable to completely wash away the "salty hearing" of those terrible things with the "potable streams"⁴ of my deeds and my daring—if this entirely wicked and envious man dares to speak against me and belittle my bravery, then what of the man who comes perhaps after him, or even after that one? Whoever he might be then, hearing of present events—that a tyranny once dared to seize the city and was completely destroyed by the impulses of a philosopher—will he then care for or call the one who did the work blessed? It is impossible to say so. But if someone were well-disposed and praised the...

They will say these things one day, and wanting to fully convince those among them who are eager, as is likely, they will bitterly increase the accusations. And the pretext for these things comes from this man, the lover of the city and "the good" <gloss>1</gloss>. I have provided for your present good reputation, providing also for that which is to come. I <gloss>3</gloss>, even if no honor should come to me <gloss>4</gloss> from you, am ready once again, whenever the occasion calls and I am able, to cooperate, and to be unsparing of my life, if it should happen. I know this having learned it from you. Each man helps as he is able, even if he cares nothing for the reward <gloss>5</gloss>. <header>STUDY II.</header>

...you are making a fuss¹ and turning away. **And well you should, men; it is only right².** Why? Because you are not so desperate or greedy for gold; rather, you wish to preserve the city for the sake of glory, to which all other things are secondary. Even now, many and varied crowns hang as trophies in the city. This one belongs to these people, with the inscription: “The Rhodians to the Athenians for the alliance against the Persians”; that one belongs to those people, with the dedication: “So-and-so to so-and-so for such-and-such service”; and so on, one after another. And while the specific act of gratitude may grow old over time, the city’s honor is made new every year by these offerings. Do you not see those who compete at Olympia or Delphi, or elsewhere? How they strive for a crown of wild olive, or laurel, or apples, or celery³, and for the sake of being proclaimed the winner? Why, O men of Athens, why do they do these things? Because absolutely nothing is greater than glory.

---

...but these things, seasonably and skillfully, absolving <note>original: "ἀπολύοντα" (apolyonta) — to release or acquit</note> those on behalf of the children and their mother. A certain manuscript—the variants of which Hasius excerpted in the margin of Bremer’s edition (for I recognize his handwriting)—reads "destroying" <note>original: "ἀπολλύοντα" (apollyonta)</note>; and that learned man adds, “most excellent.” Heliodorus, Book 1, Chapter 13: "some thought it best to pelt them with stones, others to hand them over to the executioner to be shoved into the pit <term>barathron</term> <note>original: "barathron" — a deep gorge in Athens where criminals were thrown</note>." The word "to throw" <note>original: "βάλλειν" (ballein)</note> is a better reading found in the Venice manuscript 409. Similarly, the word "they are" <note>original: "eassin"</note> is poorly written for the standard form <note>original: "easin"</note> in an Epigram by Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and influential theologian</note>, Anthology 8, 10; I gave warning about this in my notes on Theophylact Simocatta, page 235. Incidentally, I will remove another error from that same epigram: “An eight-year-old <note>original: "octaetes" — functioning here as a noun/adjective describing a person</note> having held the reins of a god-fearing people, this alone of your deeds, O King, is a small thing.” Now, if Basil had held the reins of the pious people as an eight-year-old boy, that would not be a "small thing" in the story of his life, but a total miracle. An ancient manuscript shows the much better reading "for eight years" <note>original: "octaetes" — used here as an adverbial form meaning 'for a duration of eight years'</note>. The adverb for "seven years" <note>original: "heptaetes"</note> has a similar form.

# C. OF PACHYMERES
<page-num>40</page-num>

This honor is what I, too, seek from you today; this is what I hold fast to. Even if I receive it, the profit will not be mine, but will belong to the city once again¹, and you will have many who are zealous for what is good. The prize of a philosopher will provoke a soldier <note>i.e., to emulate his excellence</note>, the honor of an old man will inspire the young, and the public acceptance of a private citizen will stir the statesman. Everyone will take heart immediately; everyone will compete for honor in return. Each man will sharpen his sword, another his tongue, and another will prepare whatever else is needed for the occasion. And I pray to the gods who protect the city that you never have to experience such hardships; but if² once again—as is the way of human affairs—some setback should occur and the moment calls for it, one would see then even an old man overcoming through his eagerness, and the man of peace acting with courage, and no terror shall overcome the city, I say this with God's help³.

...entering, which he wished to correct. The Codex correctly reads "entering" <note>original: "εἰσιοῦσαν" (eisiusan)</note>. In an incomplete oracle in the *Palatine Anthology* (14.149), Timocrates, who was consulting the god, is ordered to wrap himself in the skin of a goat: "A wandering creeper from a girl rich in sheep" <note>original: "ἐϋῤῥήνου" (eurrhēnou)</note>. See the scholarly note <term>scholium: a marginal comment or explanation in an ancient manuscript</term> added by the learned editor from the codex, though it was not well read in all parts. I correct it as follows: "Theognostus the Democritean, in his 38th year, explained this oracle thus: among flocks of goats, the head naturally becomes pregnant with many worms at the base of the brain; when the animal sneezes, the worms of the goat leap out (so the manuscript, not 'are exchanged' as the learned gentleman thought he saw, correcting it to 'many depart from the nostrils,' which is how the edition has it), and so on." Nowadays, editors very often make mistakes regarding the connections and abbreviations in manuscripts; even when they represent them with diligent

care, they usually lack success. <meta>The previous page concluded a rhetorical address by George Pachymeres regarding the psychological power of public honors. This page begins "Declamation III," a new rhetorical exercise (melete). In the tradition of the Second Sophistic, these are fictional legal cases used to practice the art of persuasion. This specific case deals with the intersection of art, public safety, and civic law.</meta>

<header>DECLAMATION III.</header>

## DECLAMATION III.

**A painter**¹ who, having painted scenes of shipwrecks and displayed them near the harbors, is being tried for public crimes² because sailors are no longer putting into port. We are practicing the speech on behalf of the painter.

It was inevitable, it seems³, that at some time even a painter—charged with public [crimes]⁴—should have to appear here, hiring advocates and orators to defend him against such a novel offense. Now, I do not consider it a hardship (lest anyone judge⁵ me to be suffering greatly) that I am seeing, for the very first time, a court in session, judges in their seats, advocates, accusers, and the court officers⁶ whom I have never had the occasion to see frequently. This lack of experience is due, on one hand, to my calm disposition and my preference for enduring a wrong rather than having⁷ legal troubles; and on the other hand, it is due to the quiet nature of my art. For if one were to surrender art to disturbances and turmoils, he would strip it of its unique character. I do not, therefore, complain of this—knowing that a man can only be a genuine citizen of his city and его people if his character is tested by you against life's circumstances—but rather I am distressed that the tongue of an accuser has reached me first, for things I never did. Indeed, I have been found to be in "error" as much as if I were being accused of seeking a Persian tyranny! Nevertheless (for what else⁸ is there to do?), I shall defend myself against the accusation as best I can, requesting of you, gentlemen, not to pay attention to bare words unless—

# III. BY PACHYMERES.

...that I might be able to speak with skill, and in the manner that orators know. Rather, I ask you to take the starting points provided by my words, fill in what I have left out, and prove to be supporters of my just cause. For in this way, I shall take heart, find the strength to speak, and stand firm against the accusation.

The accuser¹ then, O judges, is heavy against me; the charge is greater than I am; and the present contest is not on equal terms³ for him and me. But he himself—and I cannot⁴ say anything harsh⁵ as I begin my speech—yet he stirs up the whole multitude against one who has done no wrong. He is supported by many tongues, all sharing one wish and aim: to help themselves and the common people, and to consider my death so much a matter of justice that they believe it a ransom for the souls suffering from the current famine <note>The "famine" results from the sailors being too afraid to bring grain ships into the harbor after seeing the painter's realistic depictions of shipwrecks.</note>. But for me, alone and a private citizen, charged with such a great evil, what tongue could be sufficient for words, unless⁶ I should immediately fall down and draw judgment upon myself? For the accuser is so formidable that he forces me to defend myself not only against him, but against everyone: the common people and the whole city, whom I would rightly be wronging—I admit it—if something heavy happened, even if against my will, and they suffer because of my art. However, since <term>charge</term> <note>original: *enklema*</note> and <term>deed</term> <note>original: *pragma*</note> are terms close in name but differ in their power; a "charge" is what someone does intentionally and on purpose against someone with bad intent⁷, but a "deed" is what one often does out of goodwill, even if the opposite happens. The former is hateful, while the latter is within the realm of forgiveness. I now entreat the multitude of the city not to be hostile toward me, even if something unintended⁸ and unpleasant occurred. For to this...

### STUDY III.

...judging me so bitterly for public crimes, I shall make my defense as best I can, even while the court itself rejoices <note>The speaker suggests the court might be enjoying the drama of the trial despite the gravity of the famine.</note>.

**Rather,** <note>original: *prokatastasis* — This is a rhetorical term for a "preliminary statement" or introduction before the main facts are laid out.</note> it is right to say a few words first and demonstrate my true intentions toward this city and its people.

**I,** <note>original: *katastasis* — The formal "statement of facts" in a legal speech where the speaker describes the events and his character.</note> O those present, have always been the man my neighbors testify I am by my deeds. Let them say if I have been wicked or arrogant, if I have been greedy or a lover of strife, if I am quick to file lawsuits and accusations, if I am a lover of profit, or if I bear ill-will toward anyone in the city. Let them say if I am a meddler—or to put it more lightly, a busybody—constantly interfering in the city's affairs just because I say I have been wronged when I truly have been. My simple character has always been this way from the beginning, far removed from any cunning. My profession, in which I have now grown old and from which I have earned my living, has contributed not a little to this character.

And I was not restricted to painting one thing and forbidden another, nor told to depict this but avoid that. Instead, every action performed by others served as the subject for my art. Did someone distinguish themselves in war? It was mine to paint the battle lines, the maneuvers, the war itself, the men falling, others conquering, and finally, the victor. Was another admired for his public speaking? His speech became my project. One could see in my colors the city’s council-chamber, the seated councilors, and the orators speaking—and there he would be, standing in their midst <note>original: *meson apantōn* — The editor notes that the word "middle" or "midst" is often used with this specific grammatical phrasing in ancient Greek.</note> and all but delivering his speech right there in the painting. Did someone want to give advice on what should be done? Just as my art allowed, I would craft that advice visually. I would show the figure of a humble man in a portrait and place others there, looking on in awe...

### III. BY PACHYMERES

...I would show the hallmarks of arrogance <note>He likely refers to personified figures in his paintings.</note>, and I would advise one figure to love humility, while turning another away from being prideful. I sketched <note>original: *dieskariphoumēn* — to outline or sketch lightly. See note 1.</note> the ways of a "strife that is not good," showing how she is small at first, but then raises her head high and rests her crown upon the heavens while still walking upon the earth; indeed, what Homer chanced to say about her <note>A reference to the goddess Eris (Strife) in the Iliad. But since it was also necessary to depict the sea, and to paint waves, surges, and shipwrecks—and if I were to say for what reason, perhaps I would not be believed by some for the time being—I painted these as well. A man might see a sea growing terribly wild, and a violent wind there (such as painters are accustomed to creating), and storm-tossed waves, the breaking up of a ship, and a shipwreck. And seeing that the image of these various forms was well-executed and capable of drawing the eyes to the sight, a certain thought occurred to me; and judge for yourselves if it was a good one, befitting a citizen of our educated city.

For I reasoned that while different men have different pursuits, whether inherited from their fathers or developed at home, and each man here is able to benefit both himself and his neighbor; therefore, let this image be for me a demonstration of a good intention, as well as a demonstration of my skill. I will set this up where it is beautiful: if inside the city, the citizens will praise the hand that crafted the image, and it will be nothing strange to me if I am praised by those from whom I have often received praise before. I will set it up by the harbors, where foreigners also put in. It will attract them too...

...history. Standing by, they will behold it; they will marvel at it, as is natural; they will ask their father about it; they will understand; and when they return home, they will speak highly of the work. And let no one condemn me, I beg you; for my intention did not stop there, but rather that by frequently looking at the image <note>original: *eikona* — an image, painting, or representation.</note>, they might be cautious of the sea, and not suffer shipwreck by sailing at the wrong time. And thus there would be praise for the craft itself, and there would also be a benefit to those who see and praise it.

This is exactly what happened. And those men, it seems, were so captivated by the painting <note>original: *graphē* — can mean a drawing, painting, or even a written description.</note>, and so intimidated by it, and paid such close attention to it as though it were the truth, that they even renounced the sea they had been familiar with since childhood and refused all seafaring; and, saying goodbye to all trade, they sought other ways to support themselves <note>original: *ekeinoi* — "those men." As a result, the city's necessities grew scarce, I admit, and a famine <term>famine: *limos* — a severe food shortage, often a matter of life and death for ancient city-states</term> immediately followed—which I did not bring about by my will, nor did I satisfy any desire of my own by longing for it. Rather, it was some heavy stroke of fortune <term>fortune: *tychē* — fate or luck, often viewed as a semi-divine, unpredictable power</term>—I would not say of the city (for the city is good), but of myself alone.

This event, which happened by my own ill fortune (for otherwise I would not have been forced to come before this platform and court just now)—finding this event, this "noble" man, so "devoted to the people," has used it as a sufficient pretext for an accusation. And he has dared to bring a charge of public crimes <term>public crimes: *dēmosiōn adikēmatōn* — serious legal offenses committed against the state or the general public</term>—a charge that does not belong to me—and he turns this famine and the citizens' want upside down <note>original: *anō kai katō* — literally "up and down," an idiom for creating total confusion or distorting the truth. See note 3.</note>. Because the sufferers are the people, he deems the crime "public" as well, and says that the offense is a public one. But what a "public crime" is, and who is liable for it, he is completely ignorant. And because a painting of shipwrecks was set up at the harbor...

<header>C. OF PACHYMERES</header>

And those who put to sea ceased their work, and from this, famine and scarcity rush to and fro. But what law <note>original: *nomos*</note> is there that forbids doing these things? And from where does the restriction <note>original: *kōlyon*</note> against me come? He [the accuser] cannot show it, regardless of what he might say.

Tell me then, my good man. You also practice a certain craft, so that you might have the means to provide for your living. Are you a shipbuilder? Or perhaps a mason? Or someone who sits in a workshop? If I must speak, setting other things aside, you are surely an orator <term>orator: *rhētōr* — a professional speaker and legal advocate in the Byzantine world</term>. And this is clear from the fact that you have stripped for action in these verbal contests against me.

What then? Is it permitted for you to write and offer counsel about whatever you wish, both in the council chamber and anywhere else?

->“Certainly,” you will say.<-

Consider this same principle for all the crafts, whether one is a manual laborer or not. I do, however, exclude those actions directly aimed against the city; for it is not safe for you to write in such a way, nor for them to act <note>original: *poiein*</note> thus. Let the work of the craft be performed according to its nature <note>original: *kata tropon* — properly or according to the standard method</note>, and if some failure occurs, let there be no charge of intent—and then there is no case against it.

How is it then that what is permitted to all craftsmen and not forbidden should stand against me <note>original: *prosstaiē*</note>, such that I am even convicted of public crimes? Why is that? Does this charge belong to me and to those like me? Does it not belong to generals? To war-leaders? To councilors? To ambassadors? To presiding officials? For those men, I believe, are the ones who will be charged with public crimes, as they are the ones who handle public affairs entirely. But how could such a charge apply to a private individual <term>private individual: *idiōtēs* — a person not holding public office; the root of the word "idiot," though here it simply means a non-official</term>? 

Take care that, by confusing everything and not leaving each thing in its proper station, you do not accidentally fall into a charge that does not belong to you, nor one you ever hoped to receive even in a dream. For just as a public official—if he should perhaps fail in some matter regarding my craft—would never be held accountable for it, so neither should I, as a private person, be convicted on account of public matters. But you are doing something similar <note>original: *homoion*</note> to this: it is as if someone were to judge a doctor for public crimes because, after he mixed a potion and gave it to some people for their benefit, others who were present...

<header>### SPEECH III</header>

...seeing those people and being distressed by them, they suffered something unintentional; their stomachs turned, and they lost their appetite <note>original: *kakositousi* — a very rare verb meaning to suffer from a stomach ailment or loss of appetite</note>. But, my good man, no one would call their loss of appetite an accusation against the doctor, but rather a coincidence of circumstance, even if the starting point of their illness came from the medicine. Likewise, no fair-minded person will make the citizens' hunger a charge against me, even if those putting into port were deterred by the painting.

You say—and here you define the nature of the crime <margin>Scholium: A "Definition" <note>original: *horos* — a rhetorical term for defining the specific nature of an act under the law</note></margin>—that I have wronged the city in a public capacity. Tell me, what did I do, and what was my plan? Did I betray a fortress to the enemy? Did I intentionally sink a ship along with its crew? Did I reveal the city’s secrets to our rivals? While serving as an ambassador, did I surrender my fatherland for bribes? While serving as a general, was I responsible for the defeat of our men through negligence? These are the signs of a most wicked intent toward the city; these are the charges of public crimes. Show that I, the painter <note>original: *zōgraphon*</note>, am guilty of any one of these. On this basis, bring the public charge forward. But as long as you cannot show that my handling of the matter was a public concern, do not call the crime "public"—even if some mishap occurred through others and not from me.

On what grounds do you judge me? <margin>Scholium: This is introduced as an "objection" <term>objection: *paragraphikon* — a legal tactic to block an opponent's argument based on procedural grounds</term>. It is characteristic of this kind of inquiry and does not have a fixed place in the argument.</margin> Only on what I have done, or on what happened later? If on what happened later, why do you seek a defense <note>original: *apologia*</note> from me for what the sailors have done? That was their act; let the defense be theirs as well. Accuse them and judge them, whether for public crimes or not. They will explain why they do not put into port, for they alone are conscious of what they have done. Why should this concern me? For I did not do it, nor would it be just for me to defend myself for what was done by others. But if you judge me for what I did—setting up the image of the shipwrecks in the harbors—I confess that I am only human; I know that knowledge of the future belongs to the gods alone. If, then, I did this in ignorance of the future, as is likely, it was your turn not to remain silent, if indeed you knew what was going to happen. Who, then, saw you stopping me? Who heard your voice on this platform, saying...

<header>III. BY PACHYMERES</header>

> “A terrible mistake has been made, terrible, O bystanders—and by a painter, at that! By painting shipwrecks, he places them right in the harbor. I do not know what this is or what his purpose was, but my soul is deeply disturbed. I fear for the merchants, lest they somehow become possessed by the image¹ (for it is, indeed it is, a masterpiece of the craft), lose their courage at the sight, and subsequently abandon their voyages, leaving the city in a shortage of necessities.” Who ever heard you² utter such a voice? If they have witnesses to it, let them testify.

Indeed, if you had known this, these are the things you should have said; you should have called witnesses and used every ounce of zeal to stop me and tear down the panel. But if you remained silent while knowing the danger, you are proven to be ill-disposed toward the common people. Even before you "catch" me, you have tripped yourself up, betraying through your silence those for whom you now pretend to feel pity. You are accusing not only me, but also those who voted for me <note>Presumably the judges or officials who allowed the painting to be displayed</note>. If, however, you did not know what was coming and remained silent for that reason—just as I, certainly, did nothing with any knowledge of the future—then come now and you too must pay the penalty to the people for your ignorance. You must answer for the future just as you demand I be punished for it. From here on, I am accountable, and you are accountable. Let some third party accuse us both—someone who did not happen to see the image standing by the harbor, but only knows that the merchants are no longer putting into port.

**Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, 8, 1:** "be satisfied if at least for the rest of your life, however long your nature wills you to live." <meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of a painter. On the previous page, he challenged the legality of the accusation, arguing that no law forbids the depiction of shipwrecks. On this page, he uses an analogy from medicine to argue that art, like medicine, is inherently "philanthropic" (humanitarian) and should be available to everyone, regardless of the consequences perceived by others.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

to someone, gather together that art of painting as well and attempt to reason it out. Can you show a law of medicine that permits one person to heal but forbids another? Indeed, the art is called **philanthropic** <note>original: φιλάνθρωπος - literally "lover of mankind," a common term in Greek for the professional ethics of doctors and artists</note> and is common to all; it is not philanthropic toward one person while being, as it happens, "misanthropic" toward another.

"But," you will say, "what is this? Do you, being a doctor, heal even a tyrant or an enemy?" $^1$

I do not say this $^2$, nor have I reached such a point of madness as to think it right to benefit the common enemy of the people. But that case is not equal to mine. In that instance, the action is liable to prosecution because the wrongdoing is manifest; the one who heals a tyrant necessarily prepares disease and death for the people. But here, the act is far removed from the resulting evil. Famine, the scarcity of necessities, and the city’s want do not follow *necessarily* upon the one who paints shipwrecks—or, let me add, even the one who sets them up in the harbors. The work itself is blameless, even if the event that follows is harsh.

And I $^3$, unless I shall seem a burden to the city, would even go so far as to maintain that it is permitted for a doctor to heal a tyrant.

And I ask you, before you hear out $^4$ the whole of my argument, not to make a disturbance. For I know you are lovers of your city, and you feel unpleasant at the mere name of a "tyrant."

I say that it is permitted for the practitioner $^5$ to heal even a tyrant, provided that he heals him entirely $^6$ as a **human being** and not as a tyrant—when there is no ill-will in the doctor's soul, and he does not heal him for the sake of the city being under a tyranny, but...

->### STUDY 3. 51<-

...as he has sworn. And how has he sworn? To take care of all as far as possible <note>The speaker is referencing the Hippocratic Oath, which requires physicians to act for the benefit of the sick according to their ability.</note>, so that he may heal. Even if the sick man be an enemy, even if he be a foe, let the doctor neglect nothing, but rather extend his cures to both citizen and stranger, to both rich and poor, and to both friend and enemy. This is the **law of the art**, according to which he might even heal that tyrant who is destined to perish most miserably. 

Those in power, perhaps, upon hearing this will be tolerant; they will forgive what has happened and accept the situation—not as if the tyrant remained healthy because of some deliberate care to keep him in power, but as if he had been healthy from the start—provided they perceive the doctor to be well-intentioned based on the circumstances. Yet for those leaders, there will remain a concern that admits no excuse: the task of removing the tyrant from their path and from the city.

Meanwhile, if you remember, I was seeking a law that either permits or forbids [my painting]. But my accuser cannot show one, no matter how much he labors or what he tries to do. Thus, in the case of my art as well, you can conclude its lack of accountability from other examples, such as those I might relate <term>kathistorein: to set down in history or relate in detail</term>. For just as you would find a law for other professions that distinguishes between different types of actions, you should reason out our case as well. For our standards were established by us, as was necessary. So again, since you cannot show the legal distinctions of actions according to your own craft in other cases, assume the same applies to mine.

Except, even if it were permitted to write new laws and no existing law forbade my work, I would still have needed the help of a seer or even a **dream-interpreter** <note>original: ὀνειροπόλου - a specialist who interprets messages from the gods found in dreams</note> to know what was going to happen. For who could know the future, being only human and led by timid reasonings and mere guesses? This power belongs to the gods alone, and to those upon whom they might bestow it. 

Would that the gods had then put into my mind what was to happen! If they had, they might have given courage and strength to *you* yourself to forbid, from the very beginning, both the painting and its placement at the harbors, and everything else done there. For it would have been excessively vain if someone had merely suggested it, without having foreknowledge from God...

...place in the common fund? They are the noble offspring of a noble city$^1$ <note>original: "γεννήματα γενναῖα γενναίας πόλεως"</note>, possessing a natural drive that could lead them in any direction. Should I not teach them to rise from their seats$^3$ when elders approach them, and to appear civil and gentle to everyone? But if the fatherland should ever fall into danger—may it never be!—then these same young men, filled with courage, will stand in the battle line, strive for victory, and liberate the city from its terrors.

For this very reason$^4$ <gloss>Scholia: This marks the Epilogue.</gloss>, I appeal to you, fellow citizens and members of my district: never block the drive of the people. # III. BY PACHYMERES

...will criticize those who act or who are even about to act. <note>original: "ἢ καὶ πράξειν" — Thus in the manuscript. Perhaps it should read "or might act" or "or will act."</note> And what follows from this? No one would be willing to act if they were to face trouble from every person who wished to cause it. For each person will prefer to do nothing and avoid accusation, rather than to act and have trouble.

I may have failed in my aim through my actions, yet the whole of my judgment rests upon my aim and my **intent** <note>original: "προαιρέσει" (prohairesis) – a technical term in Greek philosophy for a moral choice or internal purpose.</note>; another might succeed in their aim through their actions, and various people might succeed in various things. I believe it is better that the power to act and the manner of that action <note>original: "τρόπον τῆς πράξεως" — The editor suggests the word "manner" seems to lack an adjective such as "free," "autonomous," or "self-willed."</note> remain with those who choose it, and that each should act as they intend—even if they sometimes err—and that everyone who wishes to act should do so, <note>original: "καὶ πάντας τοὺς βουλομένους ποιεῖν" — The editor notes they would prefer: "and for everyone who wishes to act, to do so."</note> rather than having the manner of doing good depend on others. For if it were up to others, an act would only seem good if it pleased them, and if not, it would be deemed a mistake; and from this, fearing malicious accusations, even those who wish to act would be prevented. For the man who looks only for ways to catch me, whatever I might have done, would be restrained from accusing me. <note>original: "ἐπισχεθήσεται" — Thus in the manuscript. It appears that something is missing here.</note> If that is not enough, you may pass a law for the future that one must first reveal and share their plan with you, attempting nothing on their own even if it seems beneficial, unless it is permitted by you to the one who desires to do it, according to what they have willed. <note>original: "τεθέληκε" — see page 32, note 3.</note> But as for the past, since the law was not yet established and ratified, no one is accountable for having acted as they chose.

Upon these grounds, let me also be the painter. If I wished to present my reasoning for how I painted the shipwrecks and how I placed them in the harbors—showing that the act was civic-minded, patriotic, and contained nothing malicious or deceitful—then even if the **malicious accuser** <note>original: "συκοφάντης" — in Ancient Greece, a 'sycophant' was a professional informant who brought vexatious lawsuits. See page 8, note 2.</note> should burst with his lies, I seek no other **water** <note>original: "ὕδωρ" — a reference to the 'clepsydra' or water clock used to time legal speeches in court. See page 4, note 6.</note> and no other time for the court.

Yet art itself will bear witness to my words, and my profession will reveal my intent. For it is not troublesome or vulgar, nor the sort of thing that meddles in other affairs. Art is for those who love peace...

### EXERCISE III. 57

# PAINTING

Painting. Unless you close the door, unless you gather your mind, unless it withdraws from external things, you do not know how to excel. For other arts, men require the movement of the mind and transitions from one thing to another; but for me, the mind’s tranquility <note>original: "τὸ ἠρεμεῖν κατὰ νοῦν"</note> and the refusal to be buzzed about by outside distractions—this alone is my luxury and the very foundation of my art. I do not investigate politics, I do not seek out wars and battles, I do not study the city councils, I do not serve on embassies, I do not lead armies, nor do I perform any other public duties.

Even if I were to excel in such things, my fame and praise would be confined to a very narrow circle; and if I should fail, the blame would remain at home, or at most among my neighbors. What do I have in common with the city, that a failure of mine should be treated as a common or public disaster? I have more people to look upon in the images I create with my own hands than there are living and moving people in the city. And if the urge to speak and converse comes upon me, I will speak and converse with these figures—yet not like a fool or an eccentric. 

Instead, perhaps when I am successful, I might say to the person I am painting: "How well you stand! How excellently you have been shaped! You will bring me praise when you are seen in the public squares." But perhaps if I fail, I shall say: "How unfortunate you are, not even carrying a sense of happiness in your image! How many times have I reworked this painting! I take pride in the forms, but you do not accept the <term>ideal form</term> <note>original: "τὸ κρεῖττον" (to kreitton)—the "better" or idealized version of a subject.</note>, as if by your own choice." These are the conversations of a painter; these are my gatherings, my "busy-work," my words, and everything else. I have never even let a thought of public life enter my mind. Not even a professional slanderer could say otherwise, if indeed...

There was a law, as **Aelian** testifies (Historical Miscellany 4.4), among the **Thebans**—which is surprising, considering they were people born in such "thick air" <note>A common ancient Greek stereotype that the heavy atmosphere of Boeotia made its inhabitants dull-witted.</note>—by which painters and sculptors were ordered to imitate images **toward the ideal**, and a fine was imposed upon those who ever modeled or painted things **toward the worse** <note>original: "εἰς τὸ χεῖρόν"</note>. Aelian says the law threatens the one who committed the act with a penalty **to pay** <note>original: "δρᾶν" (dran—to do/to act)</note> the valuation. **Korais** <note>Adamantios Korais (1748–1833), a famous Greek scholar and editor.</note> thinks the word *dran* is corrupt and suggests the fine was "one drachma." I do not agree with him; rather, a shorthand for the word **drachmas** <note>original: "δραχμῶν"</note> may be hidden in the word *dran*, the number having been lost, unless it was "50" (ν′), so that it might read "**50 drachmas**." <header>-> C. WORKS OF PACHYMERES <-</header>

It was his intention to profit greatly from this. But I know he attempts this in vain, at least until I see you judging according to the laws and the oaths you have sworn.

Why do you bring such empty slanders <note>The Greek "sykophanteis" refers to a "sycophant," which in ancient law was a professional accuser who brought malicious lawsuits for profit.</note>, and hold up before the city a lack of necessities and a scarcity? You do not realize that you are the one creating a scarcity of public-minded citizens. For if you listen to him and hand me over to the courts, there will be some other enemy against another of the commoners, and then another against another, and each will accuse the other of whatever charge happens to arise. In the end, you will lose many of your citizens for no reason. But if this wave of slander stops with me, every other wicked man will grow quiet, and there is no reason why everyone should not live in the proper peace and tranquility.

### Summary of the Arguments^2

You perhaps—I know not why—forbid the merchants from appearing, and you insist that we would never see foreign ships in our harbors even if something were to happen^3; but I, for my part, expect many ships, and cargo ships at that. Fear will not always grip their souls; they will set aside their cowardice. It is difficult to abandon one’s habitual work. They will hear our news, they will learn of our scarcity of necessities, and they will run toward a ready profit. It is not always winter and storm and surging waves; spring will come. They will set out to sail again, and again they will come together, some from one place^4 and some from another, and others will do the same, and they will fill our harbors with ships, and fill them with all kinds of good things. And again, if the gods will it, the city will be <note>original: "ἐσεῖται" - an archaic or poetic form of "will be"</note>^5 in an abundance of necessities, and our people will be filled with joy. And then, if they wish, let them pull down the statue; but if not, the benefit they have from it^6 will surely remain, and you will likely praise the painter.

# EXERCISE 4.

**A general, having burned his ships because he deemed them unnecessary, and having won the battle because of this, is accused of public offenses.** <note>The charge of "public offenses" (demosion adikematon) was a serious legal category in ancient Athens used for crimes against the state or official misconduct.</note> **We are practicing the speech for the defendant.**

I, for my part, assumed, gentlemen, that I would be receiving a reward for my deeds. I thought the voice of the herald, which usually gathers you together, was leading you to the council house <term>Bouleuterion; the meeting place of the city council</term> to deliberate on how it was fitting to honor me and with what kind of prizes, on account of this present victory—as would be expected. For it seemed to me, as I reflected on it, that since you had been shut in for a very long time and were unable even to peek out from your houses, let alone the city, because of those enemies who were destined to perish so wretchedly—since God has granted this and I have overcome the foe—you would, upon finally seeing the light of freedom and being rid of your hardships, judge it right to reward the man responsible for the victory. (And indeed, it was so, and it was necessary). I expected you to first open the council house and deliberate on how you might worthily repay the gods for their kindness toward you, and then to deliberate on how you might show yourselves grateful, to the best of your ability, to me, the one who, after the gods, was responsible for the victory. 

But since you have not yet fully caught your breath from the terrors of the siege, nor I from the labors of the wars, this malicious man <note>original: "baskanos" - a term implying envy or the "evil eye," often used for a spiteful prosecutor</note> has immediately come forward. I do not know what excuses moved him or what he suffered at my hands—unless it is this victory and the freedom of the city that you are all talking about, and I do not know if that victory bites at him—he is the first...

# G. PACHYMERES <note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "melete," a rhetorical exercise where he adopts the persona of a historical figure to practice the art of persuasion.</note>

...would take on these labors, but those [accusers] would not only feel no gratitude, but would even fabricate charges against them that are entirely ill-fitting. And indeed, [I know] neither that those men will ever be silent once they have reached this state, nor that they try to seem well-disposed toward you when they speak ill of the citizens, nor that you will restrain <margin>The original manuscript (Codex) uses the future tense "will restrain," while the editor suggests the optative "would restrain."</margin> them, even if one were to catch them in an obvious lie.

For this is the way of a democratic <term>politeia</term> <note>Politeia refers to the form of government or the "body politic." Here, Pachymeres is using a classic trope in Byzantine rhetoric: criticizing the "excessive freedom" of ancient democracy.</note>: to allow anyone to say whatever he wishes, and to consider it better to hear even falsehoods so that the truth might be found in the middle of them <margin>Regarding the use of the word "middle" with the genitive case, see page 43, note 3.</margin>, rather than to disregard those speaking by judging them as liars, and thus often losing the truth itself.

Because of this, men grow lazy regarding the practice of politics, and each person chooses to live for himself alone. From this comes a scarcity of people willing to govern, and disorder and confusion for the common wealth. As a result, our internal affairs become clear to our enemies. For great and illustrious cities are by nature impossible to ignore, no matter what they do; like great beacons visible from afar, they are seen from a distance by those they allow to watch them.

And those enemies who, until then, had kept their distance from our affairs as if they were sacred offerings—because of our common defense and the way the statesmen guarded <margin>A previous note on the verb "to care for" or "to guard" was provided on page 11, note 6.</margin> the city—once these men withdrew from the public sphere because of the attacks of certain individuals, the enemies began to despise us. And every day it was reported: now this fortress is being besieged, now that one has been captured. And again: now they are overrunning this territory, now that one, and then another after it. We have more people announcing disasters than those who will deliberate about the dangers, and more people spreading fear than those suggesting how we might be delivered from those fears. Finally, having subdued the surrounding areas and taking great courage, they dared to attack the mother-city; and having gathered a massive host worthy of war and battle, some by land and others upon ships, they attacked the city.

### DECLAMATION IV. 63

If I were to speak now of the many hardships that have befallen the city since then, and the terrors that gripped us, I would do nothing more than surround you with a siege once again through my words. I would bring these horrors before your eyes and lead you back into those dangers. Perhaps this would even play into the accuser’s hands—if I, like him, were to disturb your souls by describing the actual siege and its horrors. He hoped to win by brandishing danger and fear over the city, claiming that the ships were destroyed by fire—which I argue were not only unhelpful for our needs but actually harmful—while he claims it was impossible to be saved without them. Thus, he tries to terrify you by setting up another "siege" in your minds. If I were to intentionally recount the past siege and its hardships, I would be throwing a city that has finally found peace and the courage to overcome the worst dangers (with the gods' help) back into helplessness and the fear of wars that are not present, and—as I believe—will never be.

Nevertheless, since this terror came upon the city like a cloud gathered from a fierce whirlwind, you had to consider to whom you would entrust the city’s affairs. You needed to find, through careful searching, a general to appoint for the war. One person proposed one man, another proposed someone else, each for different reasons (for, by the gods' grace, our city is not lacking in good men <note>original: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀμοιρεῖ σὺν θεοῖς ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν ἡ πόλις</note>); yet, passing over all the others, you chose me alone to take charge of affairs.

As for my reluctance, it was not because I was unwilling to contribute what I could to my fatherland. Rather, it was because I was intensely worried that—since war involves many unforeseen innovations <term>kainotomia</term> <note>Kainotomia literally means "innovation" or "novelty." In a military and political context, it refers to emergency measures or unconventional tactics that break from tradition, which were often used by rivals as grounds for legal prosecution later.</note>—if I were forced by necessity to innovate something for the benefit of those in the city, some might seize upon it. I feared they would find handles <note>A "handle" (labē) refers to a rhetorical or legal opening that an opponent can use to seize upon and attack someone’s reputation.</note> to accuse a man who, until now, has never been charged by anyone. “Do not fear, man,” they said...

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

The city said:
> "Do not be afraid; we elect you general and master of affairs, the kind of leader the Romans would call an **Autokrator**. <note>The term *Autokrator* literally means 'self-ruler.' In this context, it refers to a commander with absolute, supreme authority, similar to an Emperor's military power.</note> You shall take care of both what is present and what is not yet present; you will keep what you deem worth guarding and cast aside what you do not."

But why do I bring up the speeches of that time? You yourselves can testify to the events through which you confirmed my total authority, nearly placing the city’s very existence into my hands with your own hands.

What followed from that? I took command of the soldiers—which is the same as saying I took charge of the city’s affairs. I marched out and drew up the battle lines. I saw the enemy attacking from two directions. If they attempted a naval battle, they also ravaged the surrounding land; if they chose to remain on land and fight the infantry outside the walls, they destroyed everything by sea. One might have called that a "two-faced" battle. It required a man of two faces, like the figure of **Hermes** that the Egyptians fashion, <note>The speaker refers to a 'two-faced Mercury' (Hermes). While Janus is the famous two-faced god of the Romans, late antique and Byzantine writers sometimes attributed similar multi-faced iconography to the 'Egyptian Hermes' (Hermes Trismegistus).</note> except that this figure should not merely have the double appearance <margin>3. The original manuscript read "having the sight," but these words were deleted and "appearance" <note>original: ἰδέαν</note> was written in the margin.</margin> of an old man and a youth at once, but the combined strength of so many old men and youths. For that battle did not require courage for one side and wisdom for the other, but both qualities for both fronts. At that moment, I needed a plan from God on how to manage that double war.

Then, from God—for where else could it come?—a thought occurred to me: to make the battle "single-faced" as much as possible.

For even if I had a fighting force so excellent that they could man ships and fight on foot at the same time, I still could not have fought with any security. A general cannot divide himself between two fronts, fighting at sea one moment and engaging with the infantry the next. To hand over command to others for a task for which I alone was held responsible seemed to me the least appropriate course of action. Nevertheless—though there were many men capable of leading—the small number of our soldiers was a constant obstacle, and the impossibility of the situation became clear to me. I saw...

### EXERCISE 4.

<column-break/>

And while the enemy was doing even more damage by land than by sea, our men were clinging more to the ships. Even if they tried to do anything, I lacked the power to pull them away from there; instead, the ships and the confidence of the city were failing¹ <note>original: ἀπελογοῦντο. The editor notes this likely means the ships were "giving up" or "exhausted."</note> up and down. There was also a fear that if our men retreated, the enemy would set the entire fleet on fire. From that point on, I was paralyzed; I didn't have the strength to fight by land, and using the ships for war did not seem safe, as there were so many of the enemy, and besides, it was a foolish prospect.

Therefore, as time was being wasted,² and the enemy had gained control of the land, I saw that we were achieving nothing else except guarding the ships. I wanted to stop that distraction, as it held nothing useful and was actually doing harm—(for how long were we to stay parked by them?³ Or were we to wait until our city was captured?)—and if we did move away, it was inevitable that the ships would be burned anyway, and a great shame would be rubbed into the city on top of the defeat. Seeing these things, and being able to do nothing else—especially since I saw that some men (and let this not be called a sign of cowardice, but rather the circumstances of the time persuaded them to act this way) were taking courage only in fleeing to the ships—because of this, I imitated the doctors. When a terrible ailment strikes the joints so as to deaden them, doctors, wishing to preserve the rest of the living body, cut off the dead part with a blade.⁴ So did I. I cut away what was serving no purpose, and I acted before the enemy could, doing what they would have done by necessity if we had retreated. This act was a way to prevent us from suffering such a great disgrace and to remove the obstacle that hindered all our military operations.

For before every action, a mind <term>νοῦς (nous): the intellectual faculty or "common sense" behind an act</term> and a purpose lead the way. If you strip away the intent, if you ignore the purpose, and look only at the action itself, I do not know what you can say in a fitting manner⁴ <note>original: κατὰ τρόπον. It seems to me that all counter-argument would be abolished, and the first speaker would necessarily be justified, if intent and purpose were not judged in every case.

For these men will say—the one: "I did indeed take the sword, but my purpose was to rescue the owner from danger, because he was angry and seeking to lay hands on himself, perhaps suffering from an outrage or even being mad." And the doctor: "I did deceive the sick man, yes; and when he was annoyed by being offered cold water and was longing for undiluted wine, I gave him the water instead of the wine without him knowing. And my purpose was to heal the sufferer."

# 68
->FROM GEORGE PACHYMERES<-

...will you condemn one man for theft and another for deceiving his neighbor, simply because they did these things? Or will you grant their intentions some consideration, and not merely blame the bare actions or condemn those who speak? I, for my part, believe that if one judges justly, he will accept the intent <term>γνώμη (gnome): the inner purpose or resolve</term> rather than condemn the deed.

Why then in the present circumstances, by separating the deed from the intent, do you find fault? Why do you strive in vain to prove that a citizen who is well-disposed to the city—and a victor—is actually ill-disposed? Why do you belittle the victory as if it were worth nothing, just because something happened out of necessity and against our wishes?

I, too, wanted the ships to be saved for the city; I wanted the victory to happen and for the enemy to have no leverage against me. This was my concern, and this was my prayer. This is the very reason I appeared slow to enter the battle. For I was gripped by a terrible and unbearable fear—not that I might be put on trial even if I won, or that the joy of victory would be tainted (for such a thought never even entered my mind)—but rather that I might fail to achieve victory after having already committed the ships to the flames. And how could I defend myself¹ to the citizens if, while being required to save the ships and win besides, I instead brought loss upon the city and was defeated in the fighting as well? This reasoning made me tremble; it was this that made me appear sluggish in action. If I had any other way to handle the war, I would not have cast my lot upon such a roll of the dice.

But since there was no other way to act (and please², I ask you to consider this), I made Fortune <term>Τύχη (Tyche): the personification of luck or fate in Greek thought</term> my only protector. And, staking my very soul (for what else can I say?), I attempted the deed with Fortune at my side. I said to myself: "If I win, I will build and equip even more and larger ships than these; and if I fail, I will either fall in battle or perhaps escape the hands of the enemy." And then, if the people of the city are forgiving when they look upon my purpose—but if not³, I shall accept their judgment with joy...

² <note>Regarding the formula "I pray/please" (parakalō), see page 80.</note>
³ <note>Regarding this ellipsis (leaving the conclusion unsaid), see the note I provided on page 19, n. 4.</note>

---

¹ <note>original: "Ekeinon sphage est sphazonton, non sphagenton"</note> "Their slaughter" refers to those who slay, not those who are slain. The meaning of certain nouns changes to active or passive depending on the context. Thucydides 1.41: "regarding the war of the Aeginetans" <note>original: "pros ton Aigineton polemon"</note>—meaning the war brought *against* the Aeginetans, not the war they themselves waged. Homer, Iliad 1.203: "so that you may see the insult of Agamemnon" —meaning "the injury committed by Agamemnon." Livy 1.13: "the Sabine women, from whose injury the war had arisen." Phaedrus 2.8: "The stag, so that he might escape the impending death of the hunters"; which is "so that he might escape the slaughter [inflicted] by the hunters." Gellius discusses this syntax learnedly in *Attic Nights* 9.12. See also the commentators on the passage in Phaedrus. Xenophon uses the full expression in *Anabasis* 1.2.18: "Cyrus was pleased, seeing the fear [felt] by the barbarians for the Greeks." This is characteristic of Xenophon’s style, as noted by Wyttenbach in his *Selecta*, p. 370. Even in the French language, the genitive has a double sense. Racine’s *Andromache*: "Tell him that the love of my son is strong enough" <note>original: "de mon fils l'amour"</note> [meaning love *for* the son]. Fénelon: "the respect of antiquity must be great" [respect *for* antiquity]. J. J. Rousseau: "the assistance of beggars" [assistance *given to* them]. Rousseau the poet, speaking of God to an impious man: "You never placed a barrier between his fear and your furies" <note>original: "sa crainte"</note> [meaning the fear He inspires]. Harpius Lycaeus, regarding this passage, asserts that he is not speaking French correctly when "his fear" signifies "the fear he inspires." But that critic seems to be mistaken and overly critical. "The fear of God" and "the love of God" are the most common formulas of speech, and there are other similar ones. It must be admitted, however, that a certain rarity, unusualness, and obscurity arises from the pronoun, but it is something no one would reject in poetry. We owe this style of speaking to the Latins—or perhaps not—for whom "fear of Pompey" or "Punic fear" was said not of Pompey or the Carthaginians feeling fear, but of them causing it. Valerius Flaccus 5.526: "the terrors of Scythia"—those which Scythia struck into the Greeks. A minor writer, Rochon, said something that seems to depart from our usage: "your accusations are struck out"—meaning the accusations prepared *against* you. This passive meaning is frequent in the Greek word <term>κατηγορία (kategoria): accusation</term>, and not unusual in Latin nouns. Livy, regarding Africanus (33.47): "he considered it beneath the dignity of the Roman people to subscribe to the hatreds and accusations of Hannibal"—meaning the accusations leveled *against* Hannibal, as noted by Drakenborch. And "the hatred of Hannibal" is also passive. Likewise, in Sophocles' *Electra* (342), "the hatred of these" is the hatred with which they are hated, not that which they themselves feel.

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of a general (likely a historical or legendary figure like Themistocles, used as a model by Pachymeres) who has burned his own fleet to prevent retreat and ensure victory. # BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...city, and your own authority, along with that of others, to go wherever you might wish? Do you see the people in the fields remaining untroubled, and pursuing their own labors with total security, since there is no one left to frighten them? Do you see the freedom of travelers, the gatherings, and the transport of necessities from foreign lands, and a city overflowing with all good things? These are the offspring of that burning of the ships. 

Those ships, by being burned, created a source of comfort for us; their fire lit a fire of gratitude to the gods. Because those ships no longer *exist*, the *existence* of the city was secured. You accept the outcome, and you confess it is both good and the salvation of the city; yet you condemn the very means from which this result came. You do not consider that this outcome could not have happened if that deed had not occurred first. It is just as if you loved having regained your health, but refused to accept the treatments that made you healthy—not even in the slightest degree. 

For if it were possible to win by other means, then speak and I shall accept it—or rather, do not even speak of it now. You should have spoken then, if you had anything to say, when you were acting as a citizen among the rest of us; I would have listened and acted, if you had seemed to speak well for the people and the city. But if there was no other way to secure our common freedom, then grant what was done and be glad to see the city saved. 

Indeed, you might see many wise men sacrificing small things for the sake of great ones, and accepting minor losses for the sake of many benefits. Look at sailors for me: when they face a terrible storm, they throw many of their goods into the sea with willing hands so that they might save both the ship and themselves. And many, in times of famine and siege, cast out those of "useless age" <note>This refers to the "non-combatants"—the elderly, the very young, or the infirm—who were sometimes expelled from a besieged city to preserve limited food supplies for the soldiers. It is a harsh example of sacrificing the few for the many.</note> from the city so that they might preserve the city itself. And what do the orators among us advise in times of crisis? 

> "Let us give," they say, "a few things, that we may receive more; let us abandon our property, if necessary, and our houses, that we may gain glory and not lose our freedom." 

And what of that famous deed performed by our ancestors <note>The speaker is likely referring to the Athenians during the Persian Wars, who abandoned their city to the Persians to fight at sea.</note>...
