### FOURTH EXERCISE

...but to eat while armed, to sleep while armed, to fulfill the needs of the body while armed! Is it possible for a man in such a state, acting thus against the enemy, to be secretly allied with them and to betray the rights of the city? Is it possible for one who plots against the enemy by night and charges against them by day, encouraging all others, to hold a mind that favors those very enemies? Show me some other time besides night and day, and in that time label me as ill-willed and thinking poorly of the city. But if you cannot, cease this audacity and do not condemn me.

"I am of a most wicked mind—the most wicked, O Zeus the Liberator!—and of a disloyal opinion," says my accuser; I, who cannot even bear to hear of an enemy performing a brave deed! I cannot bear the charge, citizens; I find the very words of the accusation unendurable.

### STUDY 4.

...if that <note>Referring to the fleet mentioned on the previous page.</note> is not also contributing? I only wish the city could conquer even without weapons, and that it might always prevail even without allies and military cunning!

I want the results to be achieved, even if the tools are missing. Ask the craftsmen. If the saw exists for the sake of the wagon, let the wagon be presented to me, and I shall have less need of a saw. If the <term>compass</term> <note>The Greek word is *perigra*. In this context, it refers to a tool used for drawing or measuring, likely a compass or a tracing tool used in carpentry.</note> exists for the sake of the door, let the door be made for me; even if the compass is missing, I shall certainly care less. Let victory come to the city, and let it come through whatever means possible. It is better to be in safety while building ships than to be hedged in by wars and turmoil, dragging along ships that are less useful for the immediate need <note>original: *tō tote*</note>, even if they might be useful at another time.

If, then, you do not accept this victory—if you consider it a small thing and believe it holds little honor for the city—then I have nothing more to say to this. There are others who can judge and offer a defense. But if you hold victory to be a great and wondrous thing, and would not trade it for many other blessings, yet you still argue that "this was not the way one ought to conquer," then you provide the method! Do not simply say "another way," but suggest exactly how.

Should it have been done differently? I say so too, but it was not possible. What then? Should we have also refused the victory if we could not have the ships as well? Or <note>original: *ē*</note> is it not better to have both the ships and the victory? But if both were not granted, then at least we have the victory, because from victory it is possible to acquire <note>The author notes a variant reading: "to keep acquiring" vs "to have acquired."</note> ships as well. However, having ships did not necessarily result in victory.

### [BOOK] C. OF PACHYMERES

You will perhaps say that a loss has come to the city, and a part of the military battle-line has vanished, and it is a most great shame for the city to have no ships—and many other things besides—as if you were accusing me while stripping the city of its joy in victory. But I consider this the greatest profit and a provision for military strength; not a shame for the city, but rather an honor and good reputation, if anyone should hear of it.

For perhaps someone, having heard this, will say <margin>Scholion: A forced definition</margin> that it is truly a mark of military excellence to innovate for the sake of advantage, and to consider oneself to have resources even if they are lost. This is victory, this is the good fortune of a city: that even when losing those things upon which one hoped to win, one wins again. It makes it clear that success for those who govern well does not naturally come in only one way, but from every circumstance that falls upon them—as if virtue itself makes even the unlovely lovely, and the general's intelligence makes even the useless useful. For <margin>Scholion: Proposition</margin> the one who commands well must not have the form of a statue <note>original: *eikonos schema*</note> <note>Note 3 below explains this metaphor in detail.</note> that always maintains the same appearance. For if the affairs of war were immovable and certain, then the general too, standing on a single form, would have to fight. But since nothing in the world is as unstable and uneven as war, he too must change along with the circumstances, and now...

# FROM THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

You, who now strut about making a fuss <note>original: *ano kai kato sobon*—literally "shaking things up and down," meaning to act with self-importance or to cause a stir</note> concerning the ships, were the very first to vote for their burning.

But if the people previously elected me as supreme commander <term>autokrator</term> over all others, and gave me their full trust for whatever I might do out of goodwill, consider, I pray, the power of that election. Just as in all other matters you credit the things we achieved during the war to those who elected us, accept this action in the same way. You will find that the whole populace and the city, at that time when they were holding the election, were essentially the ones setting the ships on fire.

And, if you wish, consider the argument as I state it simply and plainly, without any cleverness or persuasion. For why is it that when I defeat the enemy, the *city* is said to be victorious, and the people wear crowns of victory and are celebrated with great divine honors? Why? Because good harvests come from good farmers, and good fruits come from good seeds; the action belongs to those who chose and elected the leader, not just to me, the one who was elected.

Accept the opposite in the same way: this perceived failure is not entirely mine, but belongs also to those who entrusted me with these affairs. Yet neither are they worthy of blame, nor am I worthy of condemnation for these things, as long as they remain lovers of the city and I am seen to be well-disposed toward the fatherland and a man of the people.

And, if you wish, examine my character once more; examine my intent again. Do not be satisfied with the citizens' former opinion; apply a second test. Do you think the people chose me in a completely simple or unexamined way, based on the first person who happened to be there? Did they not look into my lineage, my character, who the father was that begat me, how I was raised, and how I have lived my public life? Did they not check if I was a man of the people and moderate toward the citizens, or rather tyrannical and arrogant—someone who treats this man as nothing, insults another, and curses the people? The city would not...

<column-break/>

What do you say to this? Are these the signs of a wicked mind? A mind treacherous toward the fatherland? If these are the marks of a soul that chooses evil, then other marks of nobility will hardly be found.

I have now defended myself sufficiently against the accusation, and I think you require nothing more to recognize my true intent <note>Perhaps the text should read *hymas* (you). "Furthermore... my intent."</note>. But let this suffice, for I am not practiced in the art of long speeches.

Give me one thing, I implore you; grant me one favor, yes, by—

# DECLAMATION IV.

...by my labors, yes, by the struggles in which I have nobly competed, by the very victory from God which you now enjoy—if you have condemned me based on the accuser's words, then vote so, and I shall not care for the prize of honor <term>geras: a reward, gift, or privilege given to a hero or leader for their service</term>. Let there only be a common proclamation for the city: that Envy, which lies in wait for the good and flows uncontrollably against others, met you as judges and was halted; and turning back again, it consumes the soul of the envious man. But if you wish to impose some penalty, let it be death. I would gladly accept this; indeed, I would rather <gloss>The adverb "rather" is implied here by the context of the Greek.</gloss> accept death than live to see my city lose its reputation among those who slander our affairs. I shall lie with the great Pericles; I shall lie with Cimon; I shall share a tent with Themistocles. They will receive me into their midst as they sit in Hades; they will ask about the present state of things; they will be the ones to judge me.

And I wish and pray that your actions are not slandered even in Hades, but that I might be the one condemned there. But if it must be so, then it will surely be your concern how you might wipe away the ill-repute and shame that follows you both here and there. For once I am dead, I care less for how you might maintain your eternal glory, or how you might keep the trust of others when you speak—even if a time of struggle should arise again and you elect certain generals, who will then pay attention or be persuaded? <gloss>The manuscript (Codex) reads *peisthēsōntai* (a subjunctive form). The preceding future tense *prosexousi* ("they will pay attention") suggests the future form *peisthēsontai* ("they will be persuaded"). The use of the particle *an* with a future verb is acceptable here. See page 68, note 1, and the remarks on the *Greek Anecdotes*, volume III, pages 115 and 477.</gloss>

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

## DECLAMATION V.

->The law commanded that there should be deliberation concerning war for three days after Philip had seized Elatea. Demosthenes¹ advises setting out and fighting on the same day.<-

I believe, O men of Athens, that it is appropriate for you to struggle against Philip for many reasons. It is not only because that man’s race is alien to yours, and barbarian characters cannot harmonize with Greek ways; nor is it simply because, as your neighbor, he attacks and harms our interests whenever he wishes. Rather, it is because he treats plotting against us like an inheritance received from his father Amyntas. He never ceases now to overturn this region by deceiving the city and breaking treaties, and now that region, so that it would seem more profitable for you to have him as an open enemy than a friend. One could see that it is always beneficial for Athenians to wage war against him, but never more so than now, when he has seized a city that has belonged to Athens of old and is an ally—for you all know what sort of people the inhabitants of Elatea are regarding their loyalty to us. Therefore, having seized such a city, which alone stands as a bulwark for us⁵, and having disregarded those pledges, oaths, and treaties he made with us as if they were nothing but empty words, he displays great arrogance against us, as if we would never come to the aid of those whom he might attack. We must certainly not allow him to do those things for which one might⁶ condemn us for the greatest failings; rather, we must assist our interests in every way, with both our bodies and our wealth⁷—

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

## DECLAMATION V. 83

...others, so that everywhere people would know they will have us to stand against any who might wrong them.

The present moment, this very evening, brings news of great and terrible evils: Elatea has been captured!² <note>Elatea was a strategic city in central Greece. Its capture by Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE signaled that his army was only a few days' march from Athens, causing a famous night of panic in the city.</note> It calls us all together to the council chamber, bearing an unexpected disaster.

And indeed, everyone is stunned by this terrible news, and there is no one who does not call it evil and destructive to the common good, saying that we must go to war against that man, and that there is no other way to restore safety to our own people. But regarding when and how we must set out for war, there are some here who argue against the rest, putting forward a law stating that the citizens must deliberate for three days concerning war. Why? Because each of us, for the sake of reputation, desires victory; one would wish to win while facing a strong opponent³, rather than to prevail by fighting someone weak and worthless. Now, to use these points to encourage us to set out boldly and more quickly would not make sense; but let me speak of the things that can be said even without these to urge an expedition against our enemies, and I will attempt to go through them to the end.

I believe that if someone were to propose what is to your advantage, and this became clear to the city, you would choose it in exchange for much wealth⁴, not even sparing your own bodies to achieve what will benefit the city, even if the tasks are laborious and difficult. That this is the case requires no prophet, nor do I say it by guesswork; but every day I see the assembly gathered, the orators speaking, and councils and actions proceeding for no other reason than the common interest. And if someone—either a god from Olympus or someone with a god-given gift of speech—stood by and gave you a choice as to what you would accept to happen—

### DECLAMATION V (CONTINUED)

I know I am making an argument that some of you have not yet accepted. Nevertheless, let this stand as a settled point for those who do not merely *desire* to wage war against him, but are forced to do so by necessity.

What then? Because of this, must we abandon the war? Or will we need three days to deliberate on how we must fight? Why, O Athenians—why is this happening? Who could possibly accept the argument that, while under such pressing necessity, we should be idle? That we should fail to march out, fail to fight, fail to save our allies, and prevent the city from doing what it always does—all because Philip is "fearsome"? When has anyone ever heard such a thing in our city?<margin>1</margin> If someone else steps forward and says:

> "Men, we must march out and attempt to fight that fearsome man for two reasons<margin>2</margin>: both to save our allies and to secure safety for our own people. For if we do not, the horrors currently occurring there will soon be much more terrifying here at home."

If someone speaks this way, and another person argues against him in our current manner of debate, to whom will you give more weight? Whom will you listen to? Would it not immediately be the former, if you truly care for your own survival? For no one would dare say the things [the opposition suggests]—things you couldn't even bear to hear when facing those terrifying Persians.

Do you not know<margin>3</margin> what happened to Cyrsilus<margin>4</margin>? He dared to bring up the proposal of "earth and water" <note>The traditional Persian demand for total submission.</note>—something it was neither fitting for him to say nor for you<margin>5</margin> to hear. ### STUDY 5.
### [Page] 87

...drawing up against them day by day, they proved superior to the fears of that era and the circumstances of the time, showing that they preferred a glorious death over shameful slavery. And even now, there are conspicuous monuments to those who struggled then—their very tombs—so that we might be able to look toward them and do those things which, having been done, bring a glory to the city that never fades.

If we should waste time <note>original: καιροὺς τρίβοιμεν</note> and put off the matter with delays, will the glory inherited from our ancestors that we now possess still remain? I certainly do not think so. Rather, even the glory we were destined to gain by marching out swiftly and waging war would never come to pass, even if we were to labor much afterward. For the people of Elatea <note>A strategic city in central Greece whose capture by Philip in 339 BCE signaled his imminent invasion of the south, causing panic in Athens</note> will, I think, wait in anxious expectation and court Philip more than is reasonable, acknowledging him as their benefactor and master, and yielding to him in everything. And he will grow arrogant, as is his habit, and say with bitter irony: "Do you see what you suffer by clinging to the city of the Athenians? Did I not say, in my messages to you, that you hope in the Athenians in vain? What benefit did you gain from trusting in them?"

And he will say these things. For the rest, we will spend the three days wasting time deliberating against him; but he, for his part, will not hesitate to surround this city with every form of infamy, and he will fill the ears of many with his many drunken outrages <term>paroiniai</term> <note>The term "paroinia" refers to the violent or insolent behavior of someone who is drunk; Demosthenes often characterized Philip II as a drunken barbarian to insult his character</note> against us. For this reason <note>Scholiast note: Epilogue, or the concluding section of the speech</note>, men, I exhort you: let us not let the opportunity pass <note>As the Latin poet Publilius Syrus says: "Opportunity has difficult retreats"—meaning once it passes, it is hard to catch</note>, for everything after it works against us. Let us not waste this time in vain. Instead, let us take up our arms and go out almost directly from this very council chamber. Let no one appear unhelpful for the present need, no one lazy, and no one discouraged. Instead, let some of you vote, while others <note>The manuscript uses a specific Greek phrasing "and those" here and in the following lines</note> get ready for the departure; let others arm these men, and—before putting on the armor—provide them with appropriate words of encouragement <note>The Greek term implies an "encouraging speech"</note>, while the rest of you send them off with good fortune. And you, the presiding magistrates, prepare the provisions.

If there is also a need for mercenaries <note>literally: foreign troops</note>, the city will support them too. We do not lack money; there is enough for what is required. At other times, perhaps, the public will contribute to these needs, and the people will give together as if for a communal feast-offering. For now, however, the public treasury and the Acropolis <note>The public treasury of Athens was historically kept in the Parthenon on the Acropolis</note> will suffice for the war that has fallen upon us.

Indeed, long ago when men set out for the sake of the Olynthians <note>A reference to the famous opening of Demosthenes's *Third Olynthiac* speech: "There is a need for money." The Byzantine scholar Nicephorus Chumnus also famously quoted this line in his letters</note>, there was a need for money, and we looked toward the festival funds <note>The *theorika* were funds used to pay for the poor to attend religious festivals and the theater; Demosthenes famously (and controversially) suggested they be redirected to the military</note>, since there were absolutely no other military funds available. But now, even the festival funds will remain untouched...

<column-break/>

<header>EXERCISE 5.</header>

...and we will rely on public funds, and no lack of resources will hinder our departure from this very place.

### Summary of the Argument¹

I have shown, as far as was possible, how to seize the moment according to our present needs and advantage. It is easier now than ever before; moreover, it is both necessary and glorious for the city. I add this as well²: that the mere act of voting for this and marching out will not be something to be looked down upon—at least in my judgment. It will ensure that either Philip, out of fear and seeing our readiness, will withdraw from Elateia <note>A strategic city in central Greece; its capture by Philip in 339 BCE signaled that he was within three days' march of Athens, causing massive panic.</note>, or, if he remains contemptuous, he will be caught off guard.

This is my stance and my counsel. But you—if you can speak against it and show there is another way to aid our allies or defeat the Macedonian <note>Philip II of Macedon</note>—stand up and speak now. Do not let time be wasted in endless talking, lest you gain no benefit from our words even if we have given good advice. If you cannot, then grant me your obedience. Give all our allies firm assurances based on these current actions: that no enemy shall prevail over them so long as the city of Athens remains safe. Set an example for your children, so that they too may be eager when their time comes, looking back at your zeal just as you looked to your own fathers as a model. Our rivals will then learn not to look down on Athens so easily or attack our allies, seeing that you are willing to touch even the <term>untouchable reserves</term> <note>original: τῶν ἀκινήτων; this refers to the "Iron Reserve" of 1,000 talents set aside by Pericles, which carried a death penalty for anyone who proposed using it for anything other than a naval invasion of the city itself.</note>³ and set aside ancient laws, if only you can secure the safety of your allies.

# EXERCISE 6.

A man who performed a <term>heroic deed</term> <note>original: ἀριστεύσας; refers to an "aristeia," a supreme act of valor in battle</note> requested the death of a fellow citizen as his prize. The city granted it. However, it was discovered that he had already killed the man before the prize was official, and he is now being tried for murder. We are declaiming the case for the prosecutor.

Regarding the young man’s heroic deeds, I am far from finding fault—on the contrary, I have admired him greatly, for he did not hesitate to offer what he believed were fine "rearing-fees" to his fatherland. I might have been thought to envy his reward if, after his victory, he had asked for and sought something great and illustrious. But since the reward he sought was the murder of a citizen—a matter distressing even to hear of, let alone a cause for envy—which he indeed sought while many wondered at the time (the reason for his request being then unknown), and which you granted, obeying an ancient and well-established law: how could I be accused of envy if I come forward to speak for the city's legal rights? For I have no wish to slander his heroism as insufficient, nor to disparage his request for a reward as cruel. Rather, while the victory was noble and beneficial to the city, the reward would also have appeared noble and a point of honor for the hero if he had acted as he requested—doing the deed <insert>only</insert> after receiving the right—and not if he received it by asking for it in one way, while having already committed the act beforehand without having sought it.

Nevertheless, I leave the whole matter to you, as you hold the power to judge justly and according to your oaths. You must say whether it is just in a city governed by democracy and laws for such things to be permitted: that anyone can kill another <margin>Perhaps "any of the others"</margin>, provided only that a pretext is fabricated.

I see the people <note>original: δῆμον (demos); the citizen body or assembly</note> at once rejoicing and grieving. They rejoice because each man considers the <term>heroic deed</term> <note>original: ἀριστείαν (aristeia); a supreme act of valor</note> his own, even though only one man performed it. Yet they grieve again because of the nature of the request: this hero did not ask for things as other heroes have—though many such men, as is likely, have served the city—but rather, as if he had learned to act heroically against enemies and then decided this skill was useful even against his own city, he pursued his request with trickery. He wished to display today another new kind of "heroism": if one wants to call it that, it is heroism against a fellow citizen; or rather, it is heroism against you, the ones granting the prize. For my part, I wish for the <term>prize of honor</term> <note>original: γέρας (geras); a gift or privilege granted to a hero</note> which you have already given to remain his; I would not deprive him of it, no matter what or how he asked.

For even if what he puts forward is dishonorable and full of cruelty, nevertheless, since in such matters the will of the petitioner—not the granters—is what counts, no one could blame you even if he had asked for the execution of even more citizens and you had granted it. To him alone—not to say anything harsh at the beginning of my speech <note>Note 2: Similar formula. The editor notes that a previous conjecture on page 42 is confirmed by this passage.</note>—it would result in the greatest dishonor emerging from his supposed glory.

As for the prize, as I have said, and the gift, I would not <term>begrudge</term> <note>Note 3: The manuscript (Codex) reads "φθονείην" (phtoneiēn); the editor notes a common vowel swap between 'ei' and 'oi' and corrects it to "φθονοίην" (phtonoien).</note> it to him; let him have it exactly as he asked. But regarding the murder of the citizen, I question it deeply: whether a man, being a member of this community and subject to Greek laws, dared to do things that one cannot see attempted even among the barbarians.

...in a fitting manner <note>original: κατὰ τρόπον (kata tropon); see page 67, note 4</note>, so I might speak and you, having heard, might judge.

I consider it unnecessary and quite tedious to describe how the enemies attacked the city, how they surrounded it and laid siege, and the terrible things they did to us <note>Concerning the phrase "doing terrible things," see page 67, note 1</note>—especially if I were to merely circle back to things obvious to everyone and bring in a heap of confusion. For we know those events well <gloss>Setting the scene</gloss>; and again, we know these truths: that we humans are such toward one another that one cannot imagine a time without wars, turmoil, and human strife. But, even if someone is outside of war, disputing in the courts, or indeed in the council chambers and the marketplace, has never ceased. We have often bothered one another, and others have bothered still others. This happened in your time too, and it has occurred before. Yet it was not as though we should give up <note>The manuscript originally read "you all" (hymas), but "we" (hēmas) was written above it by a corrector.</note> and become lazy in the face of those terrible attacks; for it was necessary to fight with both wealth and our very bodies <note>See page 82, note 7</note>. We lacked one thing: a <term>general</term> <note>original: στρατηγοῦ (strategou); a military commander or leader</note>. And we hoped for victory if we would elect a man who was truly worthy.

A council was therefore gathered, and a deliberation took place, and we examined with precision the qualities befitting a leader of noble soldiers.

And someone, stepping into the midst—and you remember the words, I know; but if not, I will remind you, for the time that follows former events, bringing its own concerns, entirely takes those things away from the memory—standing there, then, said: "Men, citizens, we absolutely need a general, a general alone, to move our forces. We must seek him out, we must choose him. We will find many immediately; for, by God’s grace, our city is not without such men. One person will name this man, another that man, and another someone else; and all will seem useful, and all worthy of some consideration. But we must distinguish the power of choice and what this name signifies: that, when many similar men are present, we prefer the one who excels. Let the one preferred be someone, I propose, who knows how to arrange the people well in battle and how to wield a spear excellently, and against the enemies..."

# EXERCISE 6. 93

...to be intertwined; knowing also that he should love the <term>people</term> <note>original: δῆμον (dēmon); the citizen body as a whole</note>, and be disposed toward each individual exactly as if he were a father, a son, or a brother. He must not look down on a citizen just because he is only one person, nor turn away from one because he is poor or lacks a reputation. Rather, because the community is composed of each individual, and the "people" is indeed this fulfillment of the many, he must love even the least among them. As for private enmities or political quarrels, let him have as much interest in them as he does in the affairs of the Britons or the Sarmatians <note>The Britons and Sarmatians (nomadic tribes of the Eurasian steppe) represented the furthest ends of the known world to the Greeks—this is a way of saying he should have zero interest in local squabbles.</note>.

He said these things, adding the reason: that a man who holds a grudge against one or even a second citizen will be diminished in his capacity to fight for the whole. Although he may appear to be a statesman toward all and generally a lover of the people, if he holds a grudge or an adversarial spirit against anyone at all, he will not be fully devoted to the cause.

To this—why should I speak at length?—you gave such approval to the counsel that nearly everyone agreed, and some said to him: "Certainly, orator, the first trial of a military campaign is the mind <note>original: γνώμη (gnōmē); one's inner disposition or character</note>. If this is not upright, democratic, and philanthropic toward every individual in the city, it is impossible for that man to lead the whole correctly as a <term>general</term> <note>original: στρατηγεῖν (stratēgein); to command as a military leader</note>."

He said these things then <note>original: Ταῦτ᾽ ἔλεγε τότε. The editor notes: "Perhaps: These things were being said then" (Latin: Fortasse, ταῦτ’ ἐλέγετο τότε).</note>. And, out of many candidates being proposed, you preferred this man over the rest (for his murder of a citizen was not yet known), and you entrusted the affairs of the city to him as a man of the people and a lover of the city.

And immediately the entire <term>hoplite force</term> <note>original: ὁπλιτικόν (hoplitikon); the heavy-armed infantry</note> was around him. Having become a single unit, they marched out, drew up their ranks, and conquered through the city’s good fortune. They returned as victors, shared their joy with the city, displayed their trophies, and were hailed by all as the bravest. But since it is the custom to attribute success to one man rather than to everyone—and specifically to the one who leads the others—and since the evidence (for one must speak the truth) spoke in the general's favor, the city accepted the testimony. Through the voice of the herald, the city made a public declaration <margin>He perhaps remembers a Demosthenic sen[tence] <note>The editor suggests the author is imitating the phrasing of the famous Athenian orator Demosthenes.</note></margin>. And the general alone was proclaimed both the victor and the recipient of the <term>prize of valor</term> <note>original: ἀριστεύς (aristeus); the award given to the soldier who showed the most distinguished bravery in battle</note>.

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

As it was the next day and the deliberation concerned the prize of honor <note>original: γέρως (gerōs); a gift of honor or privilege granted to a hero</note>, and it was necessary to seek from the hero whatever prize he might want, the man who had been the city's benefactor was asked through the herald what gift he desired. He was asked whether he would accept a crown, or a triumph <term>triumph</term> <note>original: θρίαμβον (thriambon); though a Roman concept, it is used here to mean a grand victory procession</note>, or a statue, or even maintenance in the Prytaneion <note>original: πρυτανείου σίτησιν (prytaneiou sitēsin); free meals at public expense in the city's town hall, one of the highest honors in ancient Greece</note>. If not these, the herald urged him to say what his plan was and what his purpose might be.

These things the city asked through the herald. But he—oh! <note>original: ὤ (ō); an exclamation of shock or grief</note> How can I say it? How can I report the request? After pausing for a short time, rubbing his head, and casting his eyes downward (for he knew, perhaps, that his listeners would take it hard), he looked past all those honors. Judging them to be trifles—as one might say—he asked, oh Zeus! for a citizen to be put to death. If I were to call this citizen a man of the people and well-disposed toward the fatherland, I would likely not be disbelieved. For of necessity, when the community as a whole is doing well, each individual within it must also be good. Nevertheless, whatever sort of man he was, he was still known as a citizen of a city from which this tyrannical and cruel behavior had long ago been exiled.

Immediately, therefore, your reaction to this was exactly what it should have been. I saw everyone feeling hatred and loathing for the plan, taking it as a heavy burden that, having fled the cruelty of barbarians, they should now face such things from a fellow citizen...

---

### DECLAMATION VI.

...they themselves might surpass even those others, in so far as while those men sold strangers, these men were selling their own people to be slaughtered. At that time, I heard many people speaking and criticizing the victory, considering it a misfortune if, having conquered immediately and from the very start, they were now to betray and butcher their fellow citizens as if they were enemies. Nevertheless (for the law compelled them, and it was not possible to refuse), they fulfilled the request willingly, though with an unwilling heart <note>original: ἑκόντες ἀκούσῃ γνώμῃ (hekontes akousē gnōmē); a common rhetorical paradox meaning "yielding under pressure." See note 2 below.</note>, and they granted the murder of a citizen to this "noble" man and hero. However, they did this after a long delay, putting it off in the hope that that wretched man might somehow hear of it and, as is likely, come to plead for himself. But since he was not to be seen (for it was not possible <note>original: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἦν (oude gar ēn); the editor discusses this reading in note 3</note> for one who had been dead for a long time to appear alive and speak as a suppliant), they ratified the vote under pressure and confirmed the gift with a written decree. And now, he himself takes the prize and leaves the council chamber, having achieved nothing more than the mere act of taking it. But that citizen has been found to be the handiwork <note>meaning he was a victim of a previous action or a "trophy" of sorts</note> of a time before this "fine hero" was even risking himself for the citizens and the city.

Is this a good thing, O men? Is it a good thing that citizens are taken from anyone...

---

By a contrary reasoning, the conjunction should be removed from Hypatius’ *Anatomy*, page 152: "the buttocks, the spherical flesh <unclear>and</unclear> lying upon the limbs." The best version is in Codex 3035, in which that treatise lacks the author's name: "flesh lying upon..." As the poet said: "I will it thus, so I command it" <note>original Latin: "Huc volo, sic jubeo" — a quote from Juvenal, Satires 6.223, indicating a tyrannical whim</note>.

# FROM THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

...to be killed at any time; and from where do we get victory, and from where do we get the prize of valor? Unless this man, and that one, and another—being noble children of the city and knowing they must pay back the cost of their upbringing to the fatherland—come together at the right moment, draw up for battle, and struggle with every bit of zeal, just as has happened now. For could anyone say, O men, that the prize of valor <term>aristeia; the reward given to the most "excellent" soldier in a battle</term> fell to this gentleman apart from our fellow citizens? How, and in what way?

For if it is possible for the general <term>strategos; literally "leader of the army"</term> to win without soldiers, let this be so, and let the citizens be killed; then one general would suffice—whether it be this man <note>The original Latin note suggests reading "this man" here</note> or another—for the city's struggle against enemies and for the prize of valor. But if it is not possible to draw up for battle without the people and an army (for he was named "general" for "leading an army," and there would be no "genuine" army for the city unless it were local and made of citizens), where is it just to allow this man or that one to murder a citizen and a child of the city?

The people <note>original: δῆμος (demos). An ancient commentator notes that this section refers to the arrangement of rhetorical "places" or topics, comparing it to the "regions" discussed by the Roman orator Cicero in his work "On the Orator" 2.34.</note> do kill; but they do so according to judgment and a long-standing law. You also gave up a citizen to death; but you did so while obeying the law of the prize of valor. But this man kills too; why, O men? Why? Does he possess a tyrant’s power, or has it been granted to him by you to do whatever he wants, and to murder whichever citizen he wishes under any pretext whatsoever?

As for me, even if he were a hero from the very beginning, I do not think you should assume that that prize of valor is enough for him to thus kill—without trial <note>original: ἀκρίτως (akritōs); this and the following term describe the nature of the killing</note> and without cause—anyone he wants. And what then? Is this the act of a common citizen subject to the laws, or that of a bitter and relentless tyrant who considers his own character to be the law? You murder, fellow, a citizen—and yet you wish to be called a lover of the city? You kill without trial—and yet you say you do not lord it over the laws of the city? You kill without cause, as I say—and you fashion excuses against your neighbor. Therefore, men who love the city and fellow-citizens, do not accept this pollution and this curse. A murder of a citizen by a citizen has been dared, a terrible murder...

Was it not yours, the one who asked? You, having avoided blaming yourself—having murdered the man beforehand—now attach the crime of cruelty to the People!

But the People (for I must speak in defense of them too), caught between lawlessness and cruelty—having the law as a shield for not giving whatever you might ask, but considering nature and Greek customs as the things that forbid such giving—decided to secure themselves on both counts: to fulfill the law by giving, but to escape barbarian cruelty. They hoped that those who were surrendering the man would show a cheerful face to the one being handed over for the time being, if he appeared anywhere, and would say what was just on his behalf.

...and great things—or rather, the dignity of our city and the unprecedented nature of such an act. One might argue that the victim was a loyal citizen who perhaps raised children for the city and was useful to his fatherland. By speaking against this <note>The orator uses the word "good" ironically here to describe the hero’s questionable character.</note> "good" man, the speaker will persuade the listeners and invalidate the decree. In this way, it is not the People’s will, but that man’s own version of "justice" that will overrule the justice derived from the laws, and thus the decree will be rightly declared void.

This is what these men thought; for this reason, they gave what they did not actually wish to give.

But you—consider this: if you were planning to grant me your own cloak as a favor, but I went ahead and snatched it by stealing it before the proper time, you would be indignant. You would charge me as a thief for taking what you were previously willing to give. Being in this situation, do you not realize how far apart "willingly" and "unwillingly" truly are? If these two things were the same and indistinguishable, why do we bother to set up courts? Why do we judge cases, acquitting one man because he received something from a willing giver, but convicting another because he took from an owner who was unwilling and had surrendered nothing? We call the first instance a "gift" or a "wage," or some other voluntary term, but the second we call "theft" and "plunder"—or some other term for involuntary loss on the part of the owner.

If you wish, let us ask the people themselves. For they are the ones "giving," as you claim.

### III. FROM PACHYMERES <note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a Byzantine historian and philosopher; this text is likely from his rhetorical exercises called "declamations."</note>

But this man, as if he were ignorant of the way of the world, knowing nothing of its affairs and never having been raised in the city—as if he were born **from an oak or a rock** <note>original: "ἀπὸ δρυὸς ἢ ἀπὸ πέτρης." He relates the present gift back to that former time, reasoning out things that have no connection. He claims that because the People gave to him now when he asked, they *also* gave when he did **not** ask, and he insists there is no difference between "then" and "now."

Is there no difference <gloss>Scholion: Definition</gloss> between "then" and "now"? Tell me. Is there no difference between a thing being a gift and it being based on your will alone? Will you, then, remain a general forever just because the People once granted it and you appeared as a general? Because they gave you the command then, do you now insist on leading our army forever? If you wish—because you have excelled now through fortune (whether yours or the city's, I know not) and received a gift—to force yourself to have been a general and a hero *then*, when you were nothing of the sort and were worthy of no such honor?

Everything has its time, my good man: fortune, the People, and the gods. A man acts as general when and if the gods grant it; he performs heroically when fortune allows, and not always. Even the People grant gifts when a benefit to the city is clearly evident and demands a return favor. But if you confuse the seasons and twist the facts, see if you do not rather admit by this very argument <gloss>Scholion: Syllogism</gloss> that you are rightly accused: because you were once a murderer, you have no right to receive a gift, even if you later performed heroically as a general. And what follows...?

# SIXTH STUDY. 101

Having unworthily obtained the gift from the people, will you hold fast to it throughout, and use it to shroud your crime? Did you perform heroically in war? Yet you do not receive the gift on the basis of having committed a murder. Therefore, submit to the penalties for the murder, for you hold nothing from the people that would allow you to cover up your transgression.

For do not tell me that this is a gift—that you received nothing because you murdered. For the forgiveness of murder is not a "gift" in the sense you mean. Why? I shall explain.

If you set the time of the murder at one point—the past—and the time of your heroic deed at another—the present—your argument might have merit, and a good deed could be set against a crime; perhaps then you would escape punishment. But since you confuse the time periods, claiming the "now" is the "then," <note>The prosecutor argues that the defendant is trying to blur the timeline to make his past crime look like part of his recent service to the state.</note> and you treat both as one—as if to show that you committed the murder with the people's approval—then you must accept the timing of the murder as being the same as your heroism. And just as you were then destined to be loathed by all as one polluted <note>original: "ἐναγὴς," meaning a person under a ritual curse or "blood-guilt" due to murder.</note>, so you are loathed now; and your heroism is nothing in the face of this pollution <note>original: "μύσος" (mysos), meaning a moral or religious stain.</note>. Since this is not taken into account,

---

¹ **Perhaps**, "the now for the then."
² **Perhaps**, "the same as that of," or "and that of."
³ **Manuscript:** *mŷsos* [with a circumflex accent] and similarly below. Scribes everywhere err regarding the accent of this noun because the pronunciation <note>In the Byzantine period, the Greek vowels 'i' and 'y' sounded identical, leading to constant spelling confusion known as 'iotacism'.</note> deceives them into confusing *mýsos* (pollution) and *mîsos* (hatred). For this reason, grammarians treat both nouns together. The commentator on *Euripides' Andromache*, line 135, says: "*mýsos* is the stain or pollution; it is accented on the penultimate syllable and has a short 'y'. But *mîsos* is that which comes from being 'hateful'; it is long and takes a circumflex accent." The same rule is found in Moschopulus, Book II, page 129. The text should be restored to *mýsous* [of pollution] in *Themistocles' Letter 9*: "nor shall we allow the Athenians to become cursed by our pollution <note>The Latin editor argues that the manuscript's "hatred" (*misous*) should be "pollution" (*mysous*) based on context.</note> and cast some murderous or sinful thing upon the city which is not pleasing." The Caryophyllian edition correctly reads "to rub pollution... upon the city." The exchange of the vowels 'i' and 'y' is very easy and occurs everywhere. # FROM THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

The gift <note>The "gift" (dōrea) refers to the reward traditionally granted to a war hero, which the defendant is trying to use as a pardon for murder.</note> has no place here. Henceforth, you shall be brought in as one defiled, and you will pay the penalty for your audacity, even if you have performed ten thousand heroic deeds.

And do not consider this a mere premise of my argument. For it is not just a premise, based on what you assert and say, that you are condemned as a murderer; rather, this is the intent of the entire argument—a just intent and a true aim. It would only be a "premise" <note>original: "λῆμμα" (lēmma). In logic, a premise; here, the speaker argues that the defendant's guilt is the fundamental conclusion, not just a starting point.</note> if you yourself were to agree that the aim of this argument is just, based on how you confuse the timing—claiming that you received this gift "then" (at the time of the crime), when you actually received it "now."

> "Yes," he says¹; "but so-and-so was worthy of death, especially since the people, having only heard of his deeds, voted against him."

To whom is it clear that the man was worthy of death? Was he a criminal? Did he betray the interests of the city? Was he ill-disposed toward the state? Did he reveal secrets to our enemies? Did he steal? Did he commit sacrilege? Did he murder someone else, just as he himself has now been murdered? For all these things there are trials and courts, which carry both small and large penalties. The wretched man ought to have been judged; he ought to have had the opportunity for a defense, and the hand of justice ought to have been the hand of the public executioner, not yours.

Suppose he *had* committed a murder. Do you thus justify him being led away without a trial? If so, you should also be led away to your death without a trial, for you too have murdered a citizen. If you performed heroically, perhaps he too, had he survived, would have performed heroically as time went on, or benefited our city in some other way. And if you think you should escape the penalties of murder because of your heroism, he too might have escaped his penalty by achieving something else for the city.

Nevertheless, prove his villainy, and do not falsely accuse the people of things that do not belong to them. The people voted against him—but not as a villain or as someone otherwise useless to the city, as you claim. Rather, they were forced by you, or perhaps were following the laws; they were forced, by Zeus!

# III. THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

...and the list of his supposed evils, so that I do not have to list each one individually and waste my **water** <note>original: "τὸ ἐμὸν ὕδωρ" (to emon hydor). In Athenian courts, speeches were timed by a clepsydra, or water clock. To "waste water" was a common idiom for wasting the court's time.</note> in vain. Take my argument as well, and consider it fair and public-spirited, containing nothing terrible. If no one spoke upon the rostrum to recount that man’s good deeds, why is that surprising? How many good things could one say about this or that person sitting here among us? Yet no one, standing on the rostrum, weaves together a formal praise for every single person. If you wish, you surely think that you yourself excel many others because of certain natural gifts; yet no one has brought these forward in public. But if a certain man is "bad" simply because his good deeds were kept silent, then you must also be considered "bad" for the same reason. Furthermore, you are fleeing from a charge of manifest murder—a deed which even you do not dare to deny. Finally, the appeal to mercy, which is customary in this court, belongs to anyone more than to you; so submit to the penalty for the murder immediately, without being excused by anyone.

You see where the argument has arrived as it proceeded, and how you are caught by your own—I would not say **wings** <note>A rhetorical flourish referencing a proverb about being defeated by one's own weapons.</note>, but for now by your own **words**, which you used against others...

->### SPEECH VI. 107<-

...except for the good and benefit of the citizens. And just as one who has become a <term>hero<note>original: ἀριστεύς (aristeus); someone who has excelled in battle and earned a public reward.</note></term> was right to seek a reward for his honor, so too one who has been revealed as a murderer would justly receive the appropriate punishment. Do you possess a noble hand and a martial courage? Then do not attempt anything against your fellow citizens. There are enemies and adversaries of the city; show your ambition against them, and direct your rage toward them; arm your right hand against *those* people. <note>original: Fortasse ἐπὶ τούτοις; the editor suggests the text might originally have meant "against these."</note> Your <term>contest<note>original: ἀγώνισμα (agonisma); a struggle or feat performed for a prize.</note></term> will then be beautiful for you; the citizens will crown your right hand and lead a brilliant **triumph**. <note>See page 94, note 1 regarding the use of the term "triumph."</note>

But if, overlooking the enemies, you set upon your friends, this is the way of those who perceive nothing; this is the way of those who are insane. Such people bite their caregivers; they suspect their own kin and turn away from the doctor bringing them treatment, as if he were doing them the worst harm; and when they find the opportunity, they strike and murder. <note>Plutarch, in his essay *On Progress in Virtue* (section 11), depicts the insane as being so sick that they cannot even tolerate doctors visiting them; they drive them away or flee because they do not even realize they are ill.</note> If you act heroically against enemies but murder a citizen, you act just as if a ship’s captain or a farmer, while choosing to save the entire ship, tore away one of the planks and thought it of no consequence; or, while tending an entire tree and grafting it, you pulled up one branch or cut off one root and did not think the whole thing was being destroyed. Renounce the heroism; renounce the gift.

Reflect upon the murder of the citizen, and consider whether this is what you should have done—especially to a man who was both a citizen and a reputed hero, and who believed he was risking his life for you just as much as for every other person. Are you a citizen? Love your fellow citizen. Are you famous? Do not turn away from the obscure. Are you rich? Provide for the poor from your own resources if you can; but if not, at least do not trample upon them in your pride. <note>See page 105, note 5.</note> Have you been wronged or even insulted? Look to the court, and do not seek justice lawlessly, showing contempt for judgment. For this is the way of a democratic <term>state<note>original: πολιτεία (politeia); the administration or character of a city-state.</note></term>, and far removed from the arrogance of a tyrant.

### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...having done [evil], and having decided that it is necessary to kill whomever he wishes? I speak to you, the **people**, and I ask if these things should be permitted; if this tyrannical and arrogant behavior is appropriate and beneficial to the city. If I do this to one man, and he to another, and another to someone else—simply because one wants to and has the will—will he do evil? How does this differ from **tyrannical cruelty** and total chaos?

Indeed, when were such things ever dared, even under those famous tyrants? In the times of the accursed **Peisistratos**? <note>Peisistratos was a 6th-century BCE ruler of Athens who, though sometimes seen as a "good" tyrant, became a symbol of the loss of democratic freedom.</note> In the times of the **Thirty**¹? In the times of each of those villains and destroyers of the city? Though we have forever heard their tyrannies described in song as harsh, we have never received such a report from our fathers, nor did we expect such a thing for the future.

And if you indeed choose to punish this pollution, why do you not pass judgment immediately? Thus you might show that you are eager for justice for each of us who are still living, should anyone suffer evil at the hands of a neighbor. But if you yield and do not punish² him, you permit this behavior entirely. It would then be fitting to first level this courthouse to the ground, to cease having judges or even considering them, and then to permit these crimes. If these things are good for the city, let them happen! But what kind of "city" is this place then, and how are we "men"? We would be nothing but a desert, and those living in it nothing but **wild beasts**, having no share in reason, civility, or citizenship.

Remove **reason** <note>original: λόγος (logos); meaning both speech and the capacity for rational thought.</note> and judgment from among men, and consider what remains: nothing but the irrational and unrestrained cruelty of beasts. For the anger that dwells in the heart and its partner, desire, exist in both beasts and men; through these, they achieve much, but also fail much. Therefore, **reason** was allotted to us as a help. Even if I am not moved by reason—because the passions have defeated the reason within me—there is the **public**³ judgment. This brings order to disorder by punishing the one who has been defeated by his passions; it places **reason the charioteer**⁴ above them and subordinates...

### STUDY 6.
<note>original: ΜΕΛΕΤΗ Ϛ'. This is the sixth "declamation" or practice speech in a series of rhetorical exercises.</note>

->**BY GEORGE PACHYMERES**<-

...ordains worse things. But if these [laws and institutions] are taken away from men, what will remain for us but to live the life of beasts? Let the courts be abolished; let the council chambers, the judgments, the legal arguments, the punishments, and the rewards be abolished from now on. For this is what this "excellent" young man and "hero" <note>The speaker uses "hero" (aristeus) sarcastically to mock the defendant's claim that his crime was a noble deed.</note> commands. And let this be his first "heroic deed": the destruction of our customs and our government—and I might even say, the destruction of all human order.

I myself¹ would never ask anyone who knows him about his previous life, for I know that anyone who dares to do such things would not hold back from any other form of vice. Would a man who has committed murder not have felt envy before? Would he not consider it nothing to seize what is not his, to do wrong, to hurl insults, or to set himself up against everyone? For it is likely that one who has arrived at the very extreme of evils has also passed through all the others. Therefore, just as he would not have done these things if he were currently paying the penalty for those [previous] crimes, so now, if he is released, he will dare even worse things.

Consider that [deceased] citizen, and imagine his stance before the court², and his pitiful tears. Let each of you consider what happened to him as if it happened to yourself³. If he were your brother, your son, your father, or some other relative⁴, how would you feel toward the man who did this? Does that man have no children? But other men do; and do not think that just because no one from his family is here to accuse him, the common good of the city is also nothing.

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical argument against a man who, despite having performed a heroic deed for the city, has committed a murder. The orator argues that his "heroic excellence" (aristeia) does not grant him immunity from the law, as the safety of the city depends on the rule of law rather than the whims of powerful individuals.</meta>

<header>BY GEORGE PACHYMERES</header>

Are they not fitting? I think so, and many of them; but someone might say they are also good men. Nevertheless, even if they wish to bring charges, they perhaps shrink back—partly out of respect for his <term>heroic excellence</term><note>original: ἀριστεία (aristeia). This refers to a formal recognition or prize for supreme bravery in battle.</note>, and perhaps out of fear of his cruelty. Or perhaps they are waiting to see your own zeal. Those men too will act heroically, they will act heroically with the help of the gods; but if not, they will at least perform some other useful service. At the very least, they will not commit murder, nor will they attempt to hide an evil deed behind a good one.

If he puts forward his heroism, set his murder against it. It is a fine thing to be a hero, but not to be a murderer. If he kills, even if he performs heroically, his hateful nature will not disappear. Someone might say, "He is the hero," but another will say, "He is the murderer." And perhaps another, remembering your role, will recount how the <term>people</term><note>original: δῆμος (demos), the citizen body.</note> overlooked the murder of a fellow citizen. They overlooked it because they were swayed by a person’s status, and this has caused the very image of heroism to become a great reproach to the city.

If he brings forward children—the children of a murderer—do not consider them the children of a hero. With the honors you gave their father—granting what was requested and leading him toward heroism—you should now punish him for the murder, and thus train them for a life within a <term>democratic society</term><note>original: δημοτικὴν κατάστασιν. A state where all are equal under the law.</note>. Give these children a guarantee: that if they become good men, they will not be overlooked because of a wicked father. Tell them that it is more just for us to believe this than to allow a most wicked father to remain in the city for the sake of his good sons.

If he offers his "reward" as a defense, do not accept it. Say to him:

> "Do you see this reward? It was harsh and entirely out of tune with our customs. What then moved us to this, acting even against our own judgment and far from the character of this city? The Law. It was the Law, not mere words, that overcame our choice. Even if you had spoken many times, you would have achieved nothing if we did not have the Law commanding it."

So be it: there is a law here as well—the law that punishes murderers, the law that is the educator of the citizens if they act wickedly, and the champion of the citizens if they suffer unjustly. The Law will persuade us to punish.

Therefore, the law will make your judges harsh against you, just as it once made those granting rewards harsh against a citizen who had done no wrong. We were called harsh when you were forcing us and demanding your gift <note>original: δωρεάν (dorean). Now is the time, men, to take up the opposite reputation from the former one, and to show that we would sooner overlook anything than a standing law. For this reason, though we previously seemed harsh and against a citizen, now once again—because the law commands it—we have appeared harsh on his behalf. And just as before, the "goodness" of that citizen (if he was good) and his moderate behavior had no power against the standing law to keep him from suffering what the petitioner desired, so now, this man’s virtue in his <term>heroic excellence</term><note>original: ἀριστεία (aristeia). The formal prize for supreme bravery.</note>—even if it belonged to him alone and not to all the citizens—will have no power against the standing law on homicide to keep him from suffering what he himself, and not you, has primarily willed. And thus, the murder will be avenged, and he will be punished...

For they were of this mind, and I often heard people saying: "How well it has gone for you, the stranger—if indeed you can still be called by the name of 'stranger' and are not already among our most prominent citizens! And even better for you⁴, because you have been enrolled as a citizen not by descent from fathers and grandfathers like the rest, but by offering your heroic deed as your payment—properly and as is right!" Such was the attitude of the city's people toward me, and they were preparing gifts and rewards from their great abundance. But this "patriot," this "noble" champion of the laws...

I will show who I am, and whether I scaled the wall out of contempt for the established laws, or out of zeal for the city—and how, perhaps because of your own piety and the gods' granting it, I performed my heroic deed.

A heavy war <margin>Narrative <note>original: κατάστασις (katastasis), the section of a formal speech where the facts of the case are presented</note></margin> came upon the city—a war that broke out instantly, neither expected beforehand nor even announced. This is what truly troubled the citizens and threw them into a state of helplessness. For when the unexpected arrives, it enslaves the spirits even of those who are firm and brave in the face of terrors. This war also trapped me and forced me to stay inside; I was unable to leave, nor could I travel home <note>original: ἐπ’ οἴκου (ep’ oikou), meaning to his native country</note>. For I did not settle here as a wicked man condemned to exile from my own city, nor did I set out from my homeland as some other kind of wanderer or redundant person with nothing to do there. But—I cannot speak of my own circumstances; and even if I do, perhaps I will not be believed—I only present this to you: that I went abroad without my homeland having any grievance against me, no more than I had against it. And I went abroad...

...perhaps for the sake of seeing other things; however, it was also so that I might see the cities of many men and know their minds <note>original: ἄστεα ἴδω καὶ νόον γνῶ; this is a direct allusion to the opening lines of Homer’s *Odyssey*, connecting the speaker’s travels to the legendary journey of Odysseus</note>, and having known them, I shall also learn much. ³ **"To speak concisely"**] Our author in his ***Preliminary Exercises*** <term>Progymnasmata: a set of traditional rhetorical exercises for students</term> **chapter 3, page 554, line 20**: "to speak concisely, being useful neither to the public nor to their own kin, but, like a 'burden upon the earth' <note>A common Homeric expression for someone useless</note>, the mind is carried along by every wind in its lightness, distinguishing nothing in between (the manuscript reads 'middle' correctly) the helpful and the harmful." **Athenagoras, *Embassy* § 17.** **Julian, *Oration* 1, page 19**: "to speak concisely." **Demosthenes, *Philippic* 1, § 7**: "to speak simply, in short." There, the most excellent editor omitted "to speak" based on two manuscripts, which more recent editors have not followed, and rightly so, it seems. nymous source **"Semirameian walls."** **Herodian, *Epim.* page 122.** "Semiramis... from whom also the Semirameian walls [come]." The constant exchange of the vowels *i* and *ei* <note>A common feature in Byzantine Greek manuscripts where these sounds were pronounced identically</note> favors my spelling. Hence, in an **Epigram of Constantine the Sicilian, *Anthology* 15, 13**, the Palatine manuscript incorrectly shows *kleismos* for *klismos* <note>a type of ancient Greek chair</note>. But concerning that Epigram, I have somewhat weightier matters to advise. **Jacobs** says he found, "I, a couch (*kleismos*), [carry] men who are masters of wisdom," and he published it as "a couch (*klismos*) for carrying." **Reiske** had better provided "carrying" (*phoreon*), which I testify the manuscript clearly bears. There is also a gap in the earlier verses: "If you are a wise man, sit down; but if you have tasted the Muse only with the tip of your finger... Stand far from me and seek a seat elsewhere." In the manuscript, the second verse ends with the adverb "far," and the third begins with "Stand." From this, I think the gap can be filled in this way: "...you have tasted, O stranger, far; Stand far off"; which does not lack emphasis. For eyes and a pen in haste, the repetition of an adverb was an easy cause for omitting the second one. That famous speaking formula "to taste with the tip of the finger" <note>meaning to have only a superficial knowledge of a subject</note> brings to my memory a passage of **Himerius, *Oration* 1, 16**: "It was for Sappho, then, to compare to an apple..."

---

Regarding the maiden, who was so gracious to those hurrying to pluck her before the hour, that they might "taste with the tip of the finger." <note>original: ἄκρῳ τοῦ δακτύλου γεύσασθαι; a Greek proverb meaning to touch upon something briefly or superficially</note> Wernsdorf suggested: "not even with the tip." But without the negation, the sense is "more Lesbian" <note>likely referring to a specific stylistic or dialectal quality noted by the editor</note>. In either case, there is something of a harsh sound <note>term: κακεμφάτου (kakemphatou) — a technical term in Greek rhetoric for a word or phrase that sounds unpleasant or suggests an accidental obscenity</note>. In the *Florentius* of Nicephorus Gregoras, this proverb is slightly corrupted on page 512: "The Italians and those who, according to them, have reached the porches of education 'with the tip of the finger' [having become]." It should be restored as "tasting," which is found in the Paris manuscript. The metaphor of "tasting the porches" is acceptable. The same error occurs on page 510: "I do not know how you imitated those who are in a frenzy and mad, 'having become' [instead of 'tasting'] their own flesh." The Paris manuscript has "having tasted," which must be fully accepted.

¹ This refers to the *Odyssey* 9, 34: "As nothing is sweeter than one's own country or one's parents." Duportus compared similar passages in his *Gnomologia*.

² The manuscript reads *perikathesantes*, using a vowel swap already noted on pages 7 and 39 <note>term: Iotacism — a common error in Greek manuscripts where different vowels (like 'i' and 'e') were pronounced the same way and thus swapped by scribes</note>. So too *kapesetai* appears on page 118, 19. Georgides, in his *Gnomologia* in my *Anecdota Graeca*, vol. I, p. 30, says: "The care of those in need is a loan of wealth." Following the same pronunciation habit, I changed the manuscript's spelling *danitikon* to *daneistikon* [loan], though it added little to the meaning. In another manuscript, I found the better reading *dapanetikon* [extravagant]. In the Anthology, 15, 4, of the Vatican parchments...

Having reasoned these things, immediately (for the chaos of the combatants was pressing) I saw a sight both terrible and pitiful, O men: your forces were being defeated, yet they were not falling completely, only insofar as they considered it shameful to show their backs to the enemy. They retreated step by step, facing the foe <note>term: ὑπὸ πόδα (hypo poda) — a military term for a tactical retreat where the soldier moves backward while still facing and fighting the enemy</note>, even as they were on the verge of falling. ### SEVENTH DECLAMATION. 119

Then I, the stranger, the foreigner, having no connection to the city and owing it nothing, my heart was set on fire and I took up a warm zeal. I saw the enemies fighting right up against the wall <note>original: ἐν χρῷ τοῦ τείχους (en chrō tou teichous). This phrase literally means "to the skin of the wall," signifying they were in extremely close quarters.</note>, and they were already expected to overcome that army and seize the city. I therefore let out a shout worthy of such courage. I stretched out my spear and released it; I struck one, and then another again with stones, and then another in turn. Finally, learning that the enemy general was by the wall encouraging his own men, I struck a fatal blow. He fell immediately, and his standard <note>The "symbolon" or military banner representing the commander's authority.</note> fell with him; then those who were just now winning were turned to flight. As I again struck the others and roused the people of the city, they took heart again, and the battle shifted. Some were slain, others fell, and others were captured. Finally, the people of the city raised a trophy against them; now there was a clear victory for the city, with hymns of praise and trophies, and I, the stranger, was proclaimed a victor, a champion, and a benefactor <term>Benefactor: original "euergetes," an official title of honor bestowed by Greek cities upon those who provided extraordinary service.</term>.

And while you were for a time considering a gift and a reward for me, this man—envious of everything and not even made cheerful by the benefit he received <note>original: ἱλαρός (hilaros) — meaning cheerful, gracious, or light-hearted.</note>, as if he had been greatly wronged or suffered a loss—breathes fury against me. With total eagerness <note>original: ὅλαις προθυμίαις (holais prothymiais) — with his whole heart or full enthusiasm.</note> he ignites the common people. Gathering them from the council chamber to the court, he proposes a law—I know not where he got it or when he saw you using it. And not only does he refuse to give a reward, but he also chooses to punish me, as if he were being benefited contrary to the law. He attempts to kill a stranger who went up onto the wall, perhaps reading the literal text <note>original: γράμματα (grammata) — the "letters" or literal wording of a law.</note> and not paying attention to the intentions <note>original: διανοίαις (dianoiais) — the spirit, meaning, or "mind" behind the law.</note>, to which it is more worthy to pay attention in all things.

See, I ask you, the intent of the lawmaker. For what reason does he forbid the—

# GEORGE PACHYMERES

Is it a strange thing to go up on the wall? Look at my intent$^1$. How did I go up, and for what purpose? I will ask you. You, in turn, answer me.

Is it possible for someone to speak without first thinking about what they might say? Is it possible for someone to write laws for the public on tablets without first considering what they should legislate and write—whether it will benefit the state, and whether it will cut away harm or provide an advantage? I would say that even a simple word—not to mention an action$^3$—is never uttered in vain.

Consider, then, the purpose of the lawmaker, and set aside the literal text. Explain the law and match your explanation to its words. The lawmaker knows that foreigners are not all good, nor are they all well-disposed toward wherever they might be stationed; rather, many of them are spies. He considered the one at Troy$^4$, and again the one at Babylon$^5$. To the citizens, it was clear they were foreigners; they would not have been allowed to enter$^5$ had they not seen the welts and punishments upon their bodies$^6$. And so, they brought evil$^7$ upon themselves, as the deed itself showed$^8$.

Because of this, the lawmaker saw fit to legislate on these matters: to prevent the foreigner from ascending the wall and from standing upon it.

Examine me and my whole case; look at my action and understand my intent. For that lawmaker did not think it necessary to simply block *all* foreigners, but rather those who come with ill-will and to spy on the city$^9$. But as for the man who, if he were to go up$^{10}$, would act as a benefactor and—

### STUDY 7.

...he would have urged him to go up; for he is not a stranger, but a true-born citizen. 
I did not go up there because I was wicked, O Zeus, or a villain, or because I was meddling in the heights and depths of the city. Just because a foreigner is usually a spy does not mean that I, too, am wicked for going up. The action reveals the person. If you take away the specific action of each individual and judge based on appearance alone, you might call even the most ill-disposed person "well-disposed." If you condemn a man based only on the location where he is found, you will call even the most decent man a lecher. 

For both this man and that man are citizens; one might be loyal, while the other is an enemy to the city. Will you acquit the latter just because he is a citizen, showing favoritism to his status while ignoring his actions? For example: one man enters a brothel again <gloss>1</gloss>, and another man also visits there frequently. But the first goes to indulge in drunkenness and lust, while the second goes perhaps to purchase supplies <gloss>2</gloss>. 
What do you say? Will you condemn this second man as well, without investigating the deed—who he is and for what purpose he entered? 

If so, what is the point of this court? Why do the judges here trouble themselves? Why should the defendant even bother to plead his case, if whatever he says is insufficient to release him from the charge, provided it is shown he was simply present at the scene? I know many men—and you will bear witness if you wish—who are judged...

---

...[he gave] a servant to Admetus <note>Admetus was a mythical king served by the god Apollo</note>. *Planudean Anthology* 5, 353: "If envy would remain quiet and they wished to judge the contests." Themistius, *Oration* 1, p. 10: "A bad shepherd who only knows how to milk heavily and fill the pails with milk, cutting off the nourishment of the future flock, not caring for good pasture, and, if he happens upon it, stealing it away." I believe this unusual form belongs not to Themistius, who is a most refined writer, but to a scribe. There is something in the participle "caring for" (*melousēs*) that might give a reader pause. 
The Latin translator read "pasturing" (*nemousēs*), for these are his words: "to deduct the food from the herd which he pastures." But we will deal with "pasture" (*nomē*) shortly; for now, we speak of milk. I would read "future" (*mellousēs*), as noted from a good manuscript. That bad shepherd who only knows how to milk and fill the milk-pails,

### BY GEORGIOS PACHYMERES
<note>Georgios Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "declamation," a formal rhetorical exercise where a speaker argues a hypothetical legal case.</note>

...of murder or some other crime, which they have clearly committed; nevertheless, judges who have gathered do not immediately condemn them. Instead, they grant them a place for defense as well, in case they might justify themselves righteously.

> "You went up," you say, and you do not consider the intent. I went up, I admit it, being a stranger; I do not deny it. But I did not do so with ill-will or for spying. As for the reason I went up, do not ask me; rather, look at the outcome, and learn.

> "Let him die," says the lawmaker, "if a stranger should go up." I say so too. However, I do not attend only to the literal letters; I also enter into the intent of the writer—that he certainly forbids the ill-disposed person, not the one who goes up out of goodwill and for the benefit of the city. And this is the will of the lawmaker. For what else does he want, or what does the lawmaker mean by making such a declaration about strangers?

But if he did not specifically define <gloss>1</gloss> what a "stranger" is, and what kind of distinction this carries, it is because writers often omit things that are obvious. For the whole matter of condemnation or acquittal does not come solely from the written word. They have left something also to the judges; for they know that wise men will receive the laws and will wisely interpret the intent <gloss>2</gloss> of these things <gloss>3</gloss>. Search through the entire book of laws, and examine the laws in detail <gloss>4</gloss>, to see if it anywhere forbids anyone—whoever they may be, whether citizen or stranger—from doing good to the city. This is especially true in times of necessity, and when inescapable dangers are looming and about to seize the city, unless some hand of the gods is held over it through any of those present. Look for specific definitions <gloss>5</gloss> for each of the necessary matters, since it seems to the writer to omit them as being obvious, and you will use the laws well, both for the honor of the fatherland and its advantage.

> "But <gloss>6</gloss> there is a fear that perhaps even that city, and the laws, and every good thing might fail, while you are meddling with what is missing from the laws as if it were obvious, and seeking what the lawmaker did not specifically define."

<meta>This page continues the speaker's argument regarding the interpretation of law. Previously, the speaker established that laws against strangers entering certain areas were intended to prevent espionage, not to punish those acting for the city's benefit. Here, he explores the philosophical difference between the literal "written" word and the "unwritten" intent that a wise judge must discern.</meta>

### STUDY 7.

Defining something clearly or not is essentially the same thing, and these differ in nothing except for the mere fact of being written or unwritten. If the lawmaker defined it, it is written and clear as something beyond doubt. If he did not define it, it is simply not written, but it is clear to those who interpret it properly <gloss>in the appropriate manner</gloss> and understand why, after all, he left it out. The fact that the missing part is clear—as if it were heard from the outside <gloss>implied</gloss>—also makes the lawmaker’s intent clear, showing what he was looking toward when he omitted it. 

But you, acting as if you know nothing of laws or the mindset of lawmakers, accept the written word but have not learned to perceive the underlying meaning. You call one thing this and another thing that, failing to realize that by this very distinction, the wise man is set apart from the layman <term>layman (idiotes): in Greek, an 'idiotes' is a private person or an unskilled amateur, as opposed to a professional or an expert</term>. On one hand, the layman knows the written word and nothing else, and you will never bring him to understand more, even if you were to labor long at teaching him. On the other hand, the wise man is he who dives deep into the text and joins the unwritten meaning to the written word. For if the lawmaker were still alive and breathing, or if the written words themselves had breath and life and could speak when questioned as to why they were written <gloss>original: "ἐγράφησαν"</gloss>, there would be no need for a wise interpreter; but once—

The manuscript reads better as "groaned from below" (hypestenaxen), which Bekker published silently.
