Symeon Metaphrastes, *Life of John the Evangelist*, page 28: "The elder, groaning somewhat from his depths with a warmer spirit, will weep pitifully (hypodakrysei)." It should be restored as "having wept over" (epidakrysas), by comparison with Clement of Alexandria, *Who is the Rich Man?*, section 42, whom Symeon follows. Nicephorus Basilacas, *Preliminary Exercises* 17, page 510: "For that which he suffered as a simple misfortune caused by one (hyph' henos), I suffer many times over from many." Perhaps also "from" (aph'), since "upon" (epi) and "from" (apo) are often confused, and not rarely "from" (apo) and "under" (hypo). Leon-

-idas of Tarentum, *Anthology* 7, 480: "Already my bone has been worn away and uncovered (hypekkekalymmenon), and the harmony, O man, of the slab leaning upon it." I propose "uncovered" (apekkekalymmenon) <note>original: "ἀπεκκεκαλυμμένον"</note>. For if the bone is worn, it ought to be completely exposed. There is another more serious error there: "For people had not yet cut the path before then (prin iten), coming down against my head." So the manuscript says. Jacobs published it, with the letters separated, as "before the path" (prin iten). This emendation is worthy of a man both learned and ingenious, yet it is, unless I am mistaken, more attractive than it is true. I dislike the two nearby synonymous words, and especially such a sudden change in number. I would prefer to read "not yet trodden" (stipten) or "worn" (tripten); these epithets do not stray far from the corrupted syllables "prin iten."

<meta>This page continues the speaker's defense regarding the spirit of the law versus its literal letter. Having previously argued that laws are created with a specific intent, the speaker now addresses how judges must act as interpreters (hypophetai) for authors who are no longer present to explain themselves, specifically regarding a foreigner who acts as an ally.</meta>

### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

One might ask and learn from the author if they were in doubt about a point. But since this is impossible, the wiser citizens are chosen to judge, and they become interpreters <note>original: ὑποφῆται (hypophetai) — literally "under-speakers" or those who interpret a divine or authoritative will</note> for those who wrote the laws. They do not seek to learn the clear meaning from the authors themselves; instead, by applying their own reasoning, they understand the intent from the existing text and judge according to the author's original goal.

Suppose, for instance, there is a law to punish an enemy, even if he begs or pleads for mercy. What should you do if that man comes to love your customs, disregards his own, joins your side, and fights alongside you? Will you follow the letter of the law and punish him without mercy, sticking strictly to the written words? Or will you reason out what is missing from the written text and receive him with open arms <gloss>1</gloss> when he defects to you? I, for one, believe the latter. Why? Because he is not performing the work of an enemy, but the work of a friend.

And I, then, though a foreigner by birth, have not acted as a foreigner while fighting as your ally; rather, I have acted as a native-born citizen. I am a benefactor and worthy of a reward.

"This," you say, "was not specifically defined." But it is necessarily implied in the established laws. For he who orders a stranger to be punished...

---

<columns>2</columns>

...training. Nay, rather *by form* <note>original: εἴδει (eidei)</note>. The same is found in the Gospel of John, page 42: "as if it were necessary to be surrounded <note>original: περιστοιχείσθαι</note> by a multitude." Nay, it should be *surrounded* <note>original: περιστοιχῆσθαι</note>, as Hasius wrote in his notes to Leo the Deacon, page 472; unless perhaps, by another exchange of letters, it should be written in the better form *to be hedged in* <note>original: περιστοιχίσθαι</note>. In passing, let us correct a mistake from that small work of Symeon, which should not be cited too often. The Oxford edition, page 10, reads: "behold the *passing* <note>original: παριόν (parion)</note> of confidence," which Brettius interprets as: "attend a little to the present confidence." In that sense, "present" <note>original: παρόν</note> should have been used. But it should read *abounding* <note>original: περιόν (perion)</note>: "behold the abundance of confidence." Suidas says: *perion* means "exceeding." Pachymeres says in another place: "the abundance of divinity." Add the note to Choricius, page 9. The usual confusion of the prefixes *peri-* and *para-* is a fountain of errors. Themistocles, Letter 15, section 6: "for the final calculation... revealed that so much of my property still *remained* <note>original: παρεῖναι</note> with you." So says the Bremer edition, though it is correctly read

<column-break/>

in the Caryophyllian and Schoellgenian editions as *to remain/be left over* <note>original: περιεῖναι (pereinai)</note>, which the manuscript also shows.

John the Deacon, in his poem to John Palaeologus, verse 203: "He received you with open hands, as the saying goes." <meta>This page continues the speaker's defense, moving from the general principle of interpreting a lawgiver's intent to the specific case of a foreigner who has performed a heroic act of valor (aristeia). The speaker argues that the result—the safety of the city—justifies the technical violation of the law.</meta>

### STUDY VII.

...just as if he were a wrongdoer, yet that same lawgiver orders that even a foreigner who has acted as a benefactor be crowned. For if punishment is for expected wrongdoing, then much more is acceptance due for a benefit already performed.

"I went up," you say, "as a foreigner." But I did not perform my act of valor <note>original: ἀριστεία (aristeia) — a prize for supreme valor or the heroic deed itself</note> like other foreigners do. Let my ascent be an offense, and let my action be contrary to the law; <gloss>Objection <note>original: ἀντίστασις (antistasis) — a rhetorical defense where one admits the deed but argues it was right or necessary</note></gloss> let the act of valor also be a benefit to the city from me—not from elsewhere, but through this very action. For if the law had been strictly observed and the city had been captured, what would remain but for the laws themselves, the state, and all the city’s rights to vanish? Let the violation of the law be the ransom <note>original: ἀντίλυτρον (antilytron)</note> for the fatherland, and let the city be saved by laws—except in both cases, so that the city they save by guarding, they might also save by overlooking.

If they save the city because they are guarded, but destroy it if they are overlooked even slightly—and this will happen in every manner—then show this, and win your case; let the one responsible for the city’s destruction face justice. But it is not right for me to pay; for I saved it, I did not destroy it. And it is clear that I did not even ignore the law, but acted according to the laws. For if I had ignored them, I would have destroyed the city, not saved it, according to the premise. Since the law was not truly transgressed, and I benefited the city to the best of my ability, I should be worthy of honor, not punishment.

Why then do you press me, saying "you are a foreigner" and "you went up" over and over, while you run past the facts of my valor? Is this intentional? It is just as if you were judging a doctor for the most painful "cutting and burning" <note>This refers to the common ancient medical practice of cautery and surgery</note> of a patient, but did not consider the health that followed. For that doctor would say with boldness to you: "Man, do you want health? Then accept these treatments too. For there is nowhere you could obtain health without those things." But you do not accept this; and know that you would not have received this act of valor from any other source.

Do not say: <gloss>Transference <note>original: μετάληψις (metalepsis) — a rhetorical shift in the grounds of an argument</note></gloss> "He should have shown valor, borne arms, and gone out in another way..."

### C. [WORKS] OF PACHYMERES

...to be drawn up in rank, to fight; for these things were not strange to me, though I was a foreigner, even though I had no right to be numbered among the citizens nor to be ranked under the city’s general.

What if there were another law laid down for the city, even better than this one, and issued by a greater authority, and that law forbade a foreigner from standing in the ranks with the citizens? Who would not have stoned me while driving me away? Who would not have brought the case before the judges? And if I had performed a heroic deed <note>original: ἠρίστευσα (ēristeusa) — from 'aristeia', meaning to perform a supreme act of valor</note> in secret, would I even then have escaped accusation? For if you yourself were not the one prosecuting, then perhaps someone else would, sharing your disposition and wishing to appear "secure" regarding the mandates of the laws, hunting for a reputation. That person would have brought the same charges against me then as you do now.

How else, then, should I have acted? Speak, and I will accept it. Should I have given money? But I had none. Should I have offered advice? And who would not have suspected the advice of a foreigner? Indeed, if you do not accept my prize for valor <note>original: ἀριστεία (aristeia)</note> now because I am a foreigner, how much more would someone have turned away from me when I was just a man speaking? Should I have stayed quietly at home and not meddled in affairs? Would that have been good and salvific for the city? Would you have received that act of valor from some other source?

But forgive me for acting under necessity, I entreat you. For I do not say these things because I wish to disparage your soldiers; God forbid! For I know them to be both brave and full of spirit for war. I know that they were drawn up excellently then and fought nobly, and I recognized them as foster-sons worthy of such a city; I know they were even willing to fight against a divine power. But it was not in their power to win, for the enemies were pressing upon them like wild boars <note>original: dikēn syōn — a traditional simile for a fierce, reckless, and unstoppable charge</note>, emboldened partly by their sheer numbers and allies, and partly not so much by military skill as by a barbaric and irrational mindset. I have already seen other wars and have encountered other men; but who could even tell the story of such a battle without shuddering, let alone seeing it?

# EXERCISE 7.

...but armored in solid weapons$^1$, brandishing a spear, singing of Ares <note>The god of war; here referring to battle-hymns or the spirit of combat</note>$^2$, and mounting his horse in a fearsome way$^3$. With a noble and warlike$^4$ spirit, everyone surrounded the general. Their one impulse and aim, as it seemed, was an unyielding drive to attack the walls. For these things were reported to you, and we heard them as well. 

I too saw what happened next along with many others: how, when your men nobly clashed with them, the enemy did not give in at all. Instead, they withstood the encounter, and drawing closer together in their ranks, they pushed back those they were striking and did not let up. Their archers were also shooting from behind, not allowing anyone to look them in the eye <note>meaning the defenders could not face the enemy directly due to the barrage of arrows</note>, until they reached the walls. And if it had not been for the frequent objects thrown from above, they would have prevailed by force, and the most terrible of things would have happened.

At that time$^5$, when the city’s affairs were in such a state, if I had stood beside you—you who now champion the laws—and shared my counsel with the senate, saying: 

> “I am deeply pained by your sufferings; I see the danger; my heart urges me to help. But I know the law, and I am afraid to go up to the battlements;” 

if I had said these things and added my hopes in God that I would conquer, and I sought your advice, what would you have said? What would you have advised? To abandon the goal and not rush in? Not to go up, not to help from above, not to conquer—even if it were possible—because the law is an obstacle? Or would you have told me to go up and take part in what was possible$^6$, fearing nothing? 

I believe you would have interpreted the law then and revealed the intention of the lawmaker; the very things I am arguing now, you would have said then, and you would have urged me toward whatever help I could provide.

Therefore, do not now turn your words around and condemn your benefactor—you who would have had to say these things and urge me then, out of necessity, being a lover of the city <term>philopolis: a person who loves their city-state and prioritizes its welfare</term> and desiring the city’s salvation.

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of a foreigner who broke the law by fighting to save a city. Having previously described the terrifying enemy siege, the speaker now transitions to a philosophical argument: comparing the permanence of law with the fleeting nature of opportunity and heroism.</meta>

# BY PACHYMERES <note>George Pachymeres (1242–c.1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "melete" or rhetorical exercise, a common teaching tool where students or masters argued hypothetical legal cases.</note>

For I ask you:¹ Which seems greater to you—the <term>heroism</term><note>original: "aristeia," referring to a singular, outstanding act of bravery or excellence in battle</note> for the city’s sake, from which your victory came, or the overlooking of the law? A law, I believe, if it should be overlooked for a moment—and that for the sake of the public good, since it was written for the public good in the first place—is preserved once more for the city in its established form. And if, while being bypassed, it provided great benefits, how much more might it provide the greatest benefits at another time when it is strictly observed? It was perhaps overlooked slightly (for this was advantageous), but it has not been annulled. Let it stand for the city, undisturbed, and let everyone await the protection and benefit that comes from it. It possesses its authority again alongside the other laws; and by turning this law in two directions, solely out of goodwill for the city, one is able to contribute to the common interests from both sides. Perhaps it found a moment to be useful even before this; it awaits a moment once again, and again it will show itself providing the ultimate benefits.

But what of heroism? Is it possible for a <term>noble deed</term>, if it falls upon someone at a specific moment, to be overlooked as if it might happen again another time? Is it possible to say to <term>Fortune</term><note>original: "Tyche," the personified goddess of luck, fate, and opportunity</note> as she tips the scales—whether of her own accord (for she too is a god) or from some other source, such as the alignments of the stars: “I do not want your gifts; I do not want to conquer right now. Wait for a better time; come to me next year, and then I will conquer. In this way, I will owe you thanks, and I will receive thanks from those I have benefited, for whom I performed my heroic deed at the right moment”?

It was heroism that established the city, and it has given the city and those within it the power to use its established laws³ freely—to ratify one law and annul another, and to act as they wish. The bypassing of the law in this instance did no harm to the public interest.

If you wish, send for the enemies and ask them. You will learn the truth even from your foes, I know well: what it was that pained them, and what it was that persuaded them to retreat—a few men out of many—in shame. For what do they say, or what⁴ do they practice saying, if perhaps someone should find them...

### EXERCISE 7.

Will you bring before those people an account of their shameful retreat? Is it the oversight and turning aside of the law—for which I am liable to punishment—or is it my victory, my <term>heroic excellence</term><note>original: "aristeia," the pinnacle of soldierly virtue</note>, and the trophy you won because of it? Would not everything have been overturned? And you, the "lover of laws," what would you have become then, seeing both laws and courts being trampled underfoot? Do you see the scale of the harm, men? Do you see what a true "nullification" of the laws looks like? If that outcome would have been the destruction of the laws and the city, then the act that prevented it is the preservation of the laws and the city. If those disasters seem "good" to you, then these successes are naturally distressing. Finally, go ahead and admit that the capture of the city is a "good" thing. And then it would be worth—

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...and that I should pay the penalty for what I did wrong. But as long as you cherish the victory and consider my <term>heroic excellence</term><note>original: "aristeia," the peak of military achievement and virtue</note> as beautiful and life-saving, you have no grounds against me as one who has done wrong.

I would have wished that the lawmakers themselves were present, to be questioned and to say what they had in mind when they wrote these laws. If they looked toward the downfall and ruin of the city—if their goal was for the city to be captured in one way or another, either by the citizens being powerless or by foreigners not being admitted—then one of these has already happened. It was obvious that your men were not strong enough, <gloss>even though they fought nobly</gloss><note>The editor notes this particular Greek syntax—"kàn kai gennaíōs emáchonto"—is used frequently by Pachymeres throughout his work.</note>. And if I, by not being admitted, had still tried and succeeded in preventing the evil, then I would submit to the penalty; I would not speak against it. <margin>The manuscript is corrupt here; it perhaps should read: "I submit to the penalty and do not speak against it." But there seems to be a more serious error.</margin>

However, I say clearly that I have been utterly deceived. Thinking those men were citizens, wise and well-disposed, I thought they would be disposed as citizens, legislate as wise men, and seek what is beneficial for the city as well-disposed men. It was proper to believe this; I saw this in my own fatherland and city, and I thought it was the same in this one. Nevertheless, having missed the mark regarding their intention, unless someone shows mercy, I would not be able to escape condemnation.

But if this is not the case—for it is not even worthy to think such a blasphemous thing against those wise men—but rather they wanted the city to be saved at all costs, and for the sake of its salvation they legislated and did all those things, then I, by providing the end goal of their intention (salvation), though I did not use the means toward that goal as they commanded, let them be questioned. And if they say this is the ruin of the laws rather than their <term>composition</term><note>original: "systasin," refers here to the preservation, establishment, or fundamental structure of the legal system</note> and security—as I strongly maintain—then I immediately submit again to the penalty for the law’s <term>composition</term>, as I call it, or its <term>dissolution</term>, as they judge it.

I believe <margin>Scholiast's note: This marks the "thesis" or the core argument of the speech.</margin> that it is fitting—not just for a foreigner, a newcomer, and a free man like myself, but even for a slave, every citizen, and even one once thought an enemy, provided he is well-disposed at the time—to neglect nothing and to help a city in danger in which he might find himself, by whatever means he can. <margin>This phrasing—"by whatever means"—also appears on page 132.</margin> For it is a noble thing...

<meta>This page continues the speaker's defense, moving from a general justification of his actions to a specific argument about the nature of citizenship and the toxicity of envy. Having previously argued that the city's survival justifies his temporary bypass of the law, he now challenges the definition of "foreigner" versus "citizen" based on loyalty rather than birth, while anticipating the petty criticisms of his detractors.</meta>

# STUDY 7

...to work together for the common good: one person advising, another contributing, one fighting, another encouraging and welcoming those who are eager; and while one goes out to battle, another stays inside, yet performs no less work for the general benefit.

**It is right** to judge a foreigner solely by his actions: whether he harbors ill will toward the city, whether he betrays the citizens, whether he spies on the wall, or whether he reports secrets to the enemy. These are the characteristics of foreigners. But if he works with those inside and <term>is well-disposed</term><note>The Greek text here is "ennoei," but the editor suggests "eunoei" (well-disposed), which fits the context of loyalty better.</note>, and fights alongside them, and assists them, and rejoices with them in victory, and does nothing that is not beneficial, then that man is no foreigner, but is a citizen in the highest degree. For a man’s character can make a citizen into a foreigner and the most hostile of enemies; likewise, it can make one who is technically a foreigner into a citizen and the most well-disposed of all the people.

**It is right** not to give any ground to the false accusers when someone has performed a <term>heroic deed</term><note>original: "aristeia," the ultimate display of valor</note>. For envy, which necessarily lies in wait for beautiful things, <term>creeps</term><note>original: "herpoi." This is a literary allusion to Sophocles, suggesting envy moves stealthily like a serpent.</note> toward such a man, trying to turn his good deed into an evil one and throw affairs into confusion. For when will a pretext ever be lacking for one who is envious? One person perhaps slanders what was done and refuses to accept it as good; another might accept the deed but say, "It ought to have been done differently"—and there is the disagreement. One says, "He should have consulted with the captains, the leaders, and the city’s general"; another says, "He should have gone out to fight, not fought from the wall"; and another, "One who is not a citizen should not be performing heroic deeds—only the native-born and the citizens should." Each says something different, but all have one goal: to disparage the achievement.

**What are you saying?** Do you not accept the foreigner when he does good? But the city desires and accepts him. Do you disparage his heroic excellence and say "It should have happened differently"? But the people will perhaps say: "I cannot bear defeat, even if it comes at the hand of a citizen who acted with foresight. Let there always be victory, and let the one who helps be even a foreigner."

### BY PACHYMERES

Is it called a foreigner's victory now, or the city's? Is it a foreigner's <term>heroic deed</term><note>original: "aristeia," the ultimate display of valor in battle</note>, or that of the entire people? I contributed only a small part; I laid the foundation, I provided the pretext—but the whole of the struggle belonged to those fighting below.

It was possible <gloss>Objection</gloss>, just as I wished, to act as a benefactor. It was possible; and who would hinder someone choosing to excel in valor? "Do you say otherwise?" But it did not occur to me in that way. "Do you say otherwise?" But the opportunity did not allow it. And even if there had been an opportunity, I was afraid that I might be suspected and thus stopped. And if I had been stopped—for suppose this had happened—what more would you have had than to simply lament your misfortunes?

The law hinders the foreigner. What of it? Will it also hinder the man who chooses to do good for the city? Do not regard him as a foreigner only, but also as a man of noble purpose. If I am hindered as a foreigner, I shall never be hindered as one of noble purpose.

Consider these things then and place them side-by-side. I am a foreigner, yet I am rushing toward an act of benefaction. One of these is hindered by the laws, the other is not. Which shall overshadow the other: shall the act of benefaction cover the status of foreigner, or shall the status of foreigner cover the <term>heroic deed</term>? If the latter, I still win, for even as a foreigner who has performed a heroic deed, I do not receive the reward. Let that be so. But why do you even seek a trial, seeing that I have already been deprived of the reward? Has this not satisfied your envy? Have you not had your fill of malice? Let him be a hero without a gift, and a benefactor of the city without a wage, simply to satisfy your will.

But if the former is true, and the act of benefaction shall overcome the foreign status—which is the side I take <gloss>I agree</gloss><note>original: "tithemai," here used to mean assent or agreement</note>—then why do you still call me a foreigner after I have struggled for the sake of the <gloss>Perhaps: citizens</gloss>? Why do you not prepare the reward, having received the favor? Is it permitted for you to bring charges and accuse whomever you wish? Was it not permitted for me to act heroically in the manner I saw fit? Is it for you to slander the victory, and for me not to win it? Even if you slander me ten thousand times, know this: even if you <term>burst yourself</term><note>original: "diarrhageies," a colloquial expression for someone bursting with rage or effort</note> in opposition, you will be slandering the *manner* of the deed, not the *deed* itself. As for me, as long as you praise the deed, I hold the "manner" in contempt, and I am <term>exalted</term><note>original: "kudroumai," to be filled with glory</note> in victory, regardless of how it happened. For I, indeed, shall pass away...

### STUDY 7. 133

...and you will die; but two monuments shall stand for us, placed in the middle of this city: **A FOREIGNER WHO EXCELLED HEROICALLY**, and **A CITIZEN WHO ENVIES**. Which of these will urge future generations toward the good? If you wish for the citizens to be envious, then this matter will serve as a school—as I say, of the extreme vice, though another might call it—but I fear to speak blasphemy—but if you want them to be heroes, it is not possible for someone coming to my city to fail to learn how those who excel heroically shall be honored. Remaining within, they shall take up the lesson. Hearing of a foreigner who performed heroically, being citizens themselves, they will feel a zeal to emulate him; learning of one who came from elsewhere and benefited the city, being native-born themselves, they will be stirred to action. If they also learn that the newcomer was honored, how do you think they will tremble with excitement and rush toward heroic excellence?

Democrates, page 63²: **"The world is a stage, life is an entrance; you came, you saw, you departed."** Two manuscripts offered me the spelling *eides* [saw]. But it seems that *ides* [an older Ionic form of "saw"] should be retained, since that Democrates mostly **used** the Ionic dialect. <column-break/>

The same spelling confusion seems to have harmed the text of Arethas, *Anthology* 15, 32, 11: "parents [singing] a hymn for all, the aged [singing] a dirge, worn down by gray hair." I propose the word *tillomenoi* <note>meaning "plucking out one's hair" as a sign of mourning</note>. In the same poem, the sixth verse is published thus: "Nor did I see any beautiful child playing." No note is made regarding the manuscript, in which one can read clearly: *oud’ epi*, which is a "splitting" <note>term: "tmesis," where a compound verb is broken into two parts</note> of the verb *epidov* [beheld]. Thus Homer in the *Odyssey* 16, 144: "Nor to look upon the works." The similarity of sound caused Gregory Nazianzen, in his poems on Basil, to treat the name **Basileios** as a certain rhythmic foot. We now rightly write **Basileios**, which I think the Church Father himself neglected. There is great variety in the manuscripts. But in the headings of the *Anthology* 8, 2, 156, 163, **Basilion** or **Basiliou** should not have been written, since the common form with **ei** uniquely suits prose. And the headings in the very ancient manuscript I saw show the name with all those letters. Likewise, there is an error in the heading of Poem 164, "**to Theosebion** sister of **Basileios**." The neuter form is a fiction, like many female names changed into diminutives. In the poem itself, it is correct: "**And you, Theosebion**"; but the manuscript also correctly displays "**to Theosebia**" in the heading.

### STUDY 8. 135

...the son into dishonor. Rather, once he had sufficiently received from me exactly what he wanted—and it was for this reason he issued the <term>disinheritance<note>original: "apokeryxis"; a formal public renunciation of a son by his father, a common theme in Greek rhetorical exercises</note></term>—he seems to be setting you up as judges once again, to speak on my behalf, so that you who know the truth may dissolve that disinheritance. For he did not send me away from his home out of hatred then, nor did he do this of his own whim without your consent. Instead, being a father, it seems, and longing for his son’s good reputation, he wished to cause a little pain to the one he had loved all along. And knowing that you, being wise, would grasp the secret of his intention and, as men who love children, would grant him his wish, he came forward here. After putting on a great show of being against me, he achieved what he sought: he led out of the house the one whom he perhaps still held close in his heart, waiting for the right moment to undo these things.

And while my father acted thus, as I have heard many people say, this man <margin>That is, the adversary</margin>—being more oppressive, I think, and wishing to seem even harsher than Fortune—strives to take away whatever honors she <margin>The manuscript reads "to her," but I have written "she," meaning Fortune.</margin> granted me through my own hard work. # 136 — GEORGE PACHYMERES

...so that, if I should ever seem to be saying things that are unbelievable, he <note>Referring to the father.</note> being present might bear witness to them and resolve the doubt. For in this way, I seemed to speak credibly, and my only struggle was for the sake of the ship, for which I have struggled greatly even against the waves.

I had a father, both good and noble—let the truth be witnessed—and a man who loved his children and his home so much that he wanted all his sons to be well-regarded and longed for his household to increase daily. To him, I know not from where, the thought occurred that his wealth could not become greater unless his own offspring worked together. For he suspected the hired foreigners, fearing that they might even be destroyers of the household, even though they appeared to serve his needs diligently. He believed the cost of their upkeep was greater than the income they brought in. Because of this, he sent them away and preferred that the entirety of his business be handled by his sons. Indeed, he concerned himself with the daily tasks and introduced a youthful counsel <note>Or "vigor."</note>. Those born of him obeyed his commands with the greatest compliance; but I was negligent. And why should I hide it? Yet this negligence was not, after all, from a wicked character. Heaven forbid, judges! Rather, it was the confidence of being younger than the others; it was the lure of youth toward toys and games, and the way children of my age spend their time, and many such things that made me neglectful, causing me to consider all my father’s preoccupations with those matters as secondary.

But while I was thus, and spent all my days with younger companions, my father—and what would a father do?—reproached me, insulted me, and threatened the worst. There were times when he even inflicted heavy blows, unwillingly, but out of necessity. Since I would not turn back at my father’s words, having once given myself over to idleness and—

### STUDY 8. 137

Since I was hostile to all household drudgery and the serious pursuits of life, and because I longed for every kind of freedom and wished to associate unrestrainedly with those of my own age, my father saw this. He looked toward the future, fearing that I might persist in these habits even into the next year, and that I would not only be useless to myself but even harmful to the city. "For the idle man," he would say (and I remember the phrase), "gathers many evils in his heart." <note>The speaker is quoting Hesiod's "Works and Days," a standard text in Greek education.</note> Seeing this, therefore, and wishing to drive me out of that youthful state as something that would later be harmful <margin>or: "slippery/deceptive" <note>original: *sphalerās*</note></margin>, he first deprived me of the table and my usual clothes, and banished me from his presence. Finally, becoming discouraged, as it were—for I do not think a doctor can remove a disease immediately if he does not use the proper timing, nor can a father strike out a son's love of freedom if the son is not at the age that gently receives such admonitions—becoming discouraged, then, as I said, and acting at an improper time...

### PAGE 138

-># III. BY PACHYMERES<-

...treating the disease, with your leave, he drove me from the house. He did something that seemed harsh to most people, and even to me for a time, though it turned out to be extremely beneficial.

For when he disowned me <note>original: *apekyrytte* — a formal legal process of disinheritance in the Greek world</note> and made me a stranger to my own kin, I accepted the penalty with tears. My youth did not yet allow me to recognize what was good, to repent, to prostrate myself before him, or to give guarantees of my future obedience to whatever my father might wish. I was left to struggle by myself, living as best I could. To turn back to my father, to put forward mediators, and to beg for mercy seemed, for a time, petty and servile—especially since I had reached full maturity, an age at which there was hope I might do something noble, gladden my father, and offer my conduct as a form of mediation so that I might cross my father’s threshold once more, once the disinheritance was revoked. For I knew that while my laziness grieved him, my diligence would gladden him; and he who disowned me for being idle would welcome me back home once I became industrious.

For this reason, having a constant goad <note>original: *myōpa* — literally a "gadfly" or "spur," a metaphor for a persistent internal sting or motivation</note>—my estrangement from my father—I was not content to sit idle. Instead, night and day, I turned over every thought: where should I go and what should I do? "I shall go to war," I said, "and fight in battle, and the weapons of the fallen shall become my wealth. Or shall I work for hire for anyone who wishes, and my wage will provide not only food but even a modest surplus? Shall I take up a trade? Then I will not lack for necessities."

The exchange of these words is very frequent. See many examples I have collected for Theophylact Simocatta p. 187; compare Diodorus Siculus 1, 28, p. 81; Athenagoras *On the Resurrection* p. 203 H. St. Asclepius to Hammon after the *Poemandres*, p. 97: "always and likewise holding his own knowledge." Manuscript 1220 reads "kin/domestic" <note>original: *oikeia*</note>.
2. The manuscript reads *esetai* [he/it will be]. I think the author intended to write his own *eseitai*, or better

<column-break/>

*estai* [will be]. And perhaps the word "for/into" <note>original: *eis*</note> is missing in the following: "obedience *for* whatever he wishes."
3. "As best I could" <note>original: *Ek tōn dynatōn*</note>: see page 112, note 4.
4. The Manuscript reads "to gladden" <note>original: *euphranai*</note>. By a more useful change of accent, a passage of Libanius (vol. IV, p. 827) can be understood, which currently makes almost no sense: "Therefore, lest I suffer this and miss out on death, and adding money to life, a life much harsher than death, I have left behind that injurious death." It should probably be written: "and, adding money, *I might live* <note>original: *zōēn*</note> a life..."

### STUDY 8. 139

Finally, after much consideration, I decided to travel abroad and devote myself to commerce, moving from place to place and disposing of my wares. Since I thought it necessary to sail, I reflected to myself how fortune has often favored men, especially at sea, and has suddenly made the wealthy <note>The original manuscript is corrupted here; the editor notes that the scribe swapped syllables, writing "poor" instead of "wealthy."</note> out of the destitute, provided they manfully faced the waves as they should.

> "If I board a ship, it is possible to reach my destination; but it is also possible, if Poseidon <note>The Greek god of the sea, often depicted as temperamental and easily angered by sailors.</note> is angry, to show even more courage than expected. And perhaps, while the others flee, I shall remain with the storm-tossed ship, and immediately I will either sink with her or become rich, as the law commands."

Having these thoughts in mind, I boarded. The ship, as it happened, belonged to my father. But nevertheless, acting as if I had no connection to it, but just like the others—as a stranger and a complete outsider—I stayed with the rest of the crew, <note>The editor suggests "companions" or "crewmates" here.</note> without being meddlesome. I did not ask what the cargo was, to whom it belonged, or its destination; nor did I ask who the overseers were, or why those specific men were chosen and not others. I asked nothing about the owner of the ship—whether he had sent it off with a kind heart or with bitterness, or if he had made any mention of me while preparing the voyage. And if any of them asked their neighbor about me—whether this was the son of that man, the one who was disgraced just the other day—and how he could be here...

***

¹ The manuscript reads "poor," having swapped the syllables as often happens. Aristotle, in his Third Letter, says: "It is beautiful and just to pity all those who are unfortunate." Two other manuscripts read "those who are unworthily fortunate"; one indeed reads "unworthy," but it is a slip of the pen. It should be written "unworthily unfortunate." For "fortunate" does not fit the context of the whole passage. In passing, I will fill another gap in the sixth of the letters attributed to Aristotle (said to be from Philip): "You will compel us, who are indifferent to what is noble, to take up a zeal for noble things." <column-break/>

In another manuscript, I found it correctly written as "to be wounded" (infinitive). Since these verses are not entirely lacking in elegance, I would like to repeat them here in a slightly corrected form:

"Alas! Against us once again the Archer <note>A reference to Eros or Cupid, the god of love, whose arrows cause the "disease" of passion.</note> sends his fire-bearing arrows, inflaming hearts; arrows that are bitter and yet sweeter than honey (as he had read in Meleager: 'the sweet-bitter arrow of Love'); arrows that are terrible, yet craved by the one who suffers the disease. I acted as if I had no concern for my father's affairs, even while being present myself. "I was once a son," I would say; "but now, thanks to my father, I am not."
— "What then?" said someone, "Does this disinheritance <note>The Greek term is *apokeryxis*, a formal legal process in which a father publicly renounces a son.</note> not bother you?"
— "Even if it does," I replied, "what more will I gain than simply scratching at the wound and cursing my own fate? For I would not speak ill of my father; it was fate that provoked even my father against me." Thus I seemed so indifferent to what had happened that it caused wonder how I would not even participate in a conversation regarding my father's estate.

For some days, while Poseidon <note>The Greek god of the sea.</note> happened to be favorable, we sailed with fair winds<gloss>1</gloss>. Each of us was considering where we might go once the ship reached land to find what was necessary, paying only for the ferry-fare<gloss>2</gloss>.

While we were considering these things, suddenly a cloud gathered in the sky, a terrible whirlwind broke out, and a frightening wave rose up. The East wind and the South wind clashed together, and the North wind, born in the clear air, rolled a great wave; night rose up from the heavens, and a dark storm made the sea surge<gloss>3</gloss>. Then, indeed then, all the ship's gear—sails and forestays—were proven weaker than the storm; some were torn, others were cut, and those parts of the ship<gloss>4</gloss> that were loosed were carried away in vain. The man at the rudders began to describe the danger in a tragic and vivid manner, and being the first to despair of safety himself, he threw himself into the sea, judging it safer to float on the open water than on that ship which was just about to be submerged; after him, another, and—

# DECLAMATION 8

...then another, and simply everyone, leaving the ship, committed themselves to the sea.

When I, having barely looked up from that great despair and opened my eyes, saw no one left inside the ship, but saw others here and there being carried along by the sea like some water-dwelling birds, I too was then drawn along with them. And, fearing the worst for myself, I would have fallen into the waters, if some other, better and more noble reasoning had not held me back. For I reasoned that we shall all die, and no one who is born will live an eternal life. It is terrible indeed to die "gaping at the wave" <note>The author is quoting Homer's Odyssey 12.350: "I would rather lose my life at once, gaping at the wave [as it swallows me]."</note>, but it is even more terrible if one lives while laboring in dishonor and intolerable poverty.

Either the possessions that once belonged to my father will belong entirely to the sea, or they will be a windfall of fortune. However, the sinking <note>The manuscript uses the term *katadynai*.</note> of this ship will happen of necessity, even if no one helps it along; for it belongs to the surging wave alone. But to be saved is as difficult <note>The Greek implies "more" difficult than can be imagined.</note> as it is even for someone to imagine. 

Yet, the disinherited man <term>apokleros</term> <note>A son legally cut off from his inheritance.</note> must attempt even the impossible, as one who will either gain or perish completely. Therefore, the one who has been cast out must struggle against fortune; and perhaps if she appears favorable, even a small portion <note>original: *to ep’ elatton*</note> might remain. For in this, fortune stands and holds her seat, if only one does not despair. Will a father drive me out of his own property? But perhaps fortune will drive me in, making my father's goods her own; and the cargo will become not a father's inheritance <note>The manuscript reads *kleron*.</note>, but a windfall of fortune. Does a father disinherit me from his own? He certainly does not wish to deprive me of things belonging to others, even if they come from fortune. There is also a wise and ancient saying <note>A quote from Sophocles' play *Electra*, line 911: "Truly, the same spirit does not always stand by the same people."</note>, that the same spirit <term>daemon</term> <note>In Greek thought, a *daemon* is a guiding spirit or a person's lot in life, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> does not always stand by the same people. Even if it was harsh then, perhaps it will now smile kindly upon me."

Having said these things, and having braced myself with these thoughts, as is natural <note>Footnote 1: The editor notes a parallel on page 152: "I brace myself with certain thoughts." Oh, how many times was I dragged down with the vessel, and then again, as if pulled up by some invisible hand, I saw myself and the ship suspended in mid-air! How many times did I collapse upon the decks, having no foothold for my feet! smoothed the sea for your ship.” From Basil the Great: “A deep calm smoothed over the sea that was raging and boiling with the surge.” From Theodoret: “The sea was smoothed over and freed from its wintry roughness.” This same phrasing supports a reading in Themistius: “Some of the waves have already been smoothed over.” An anonymous poet in the Anthology addresses Christ as: “O calm one and smoother of the storm.” Gregory the Presbyter, in his Life of Gregory Nazianzen, writes: “The sea, which until then...”</note>

### EXERCISE 8. 143

...and a gentle breeze began to blow, a sort of West wind <note>original: "ζεφύρου" (Zephyrus) — the West wind, often personified as a gentle or favorable breeze</note>, I think, and my heart steadied. I looked up, and I could just barely see land. As best I could, I steered toward it. I was not using oars, nor was I steering with a rudder or being guided by one, nor was I setting the stays and sails for the voyage (for all those had been lost to the sea), but rather I used some planks lying there which, I believe, had been ripped from the ship and found lying there. By these alone, churning the water and steering the ship—with great difficulty and barely succeeding, yet succeeding nonetheless after that great struggle—I brought the ship to land¹ and, falling upon it and kissing the ground, I lay there for a long time, rejoicing.

Then I gathered my thoughts and composed my reason. For the first time, I began to examine whether anything of the ship remained. Upon searching, I found it all, and I realized I was now the master of these things, knowing the law accurately and what it commands for one who remains. For the law appoints as master of the ship and all things within it whoever stays behind when the others have fled a storm-tossed ship at sea.

I, therefore, remained. I struggled firmly even unto death itself, and a ship that had belonged only to the sea I have made my own through those many toils and labors of mine. I hold this possession not by some inheritance from my fathers, as is the case for most people, but from my own zeal and greatest struggles—something that is rare for anyone.

And I hoped that, from this point on, I would have no one to oppose me, but that everyone, knowing the law, would call me fortunate, having grown wealthy in an instant and having hidden the shame of my disinheritance.

### III. BY PACHYMERES

<columns>
But indeed, envy is a terrible thing, touching even the untouchable, as it creeps against everyone who possesses something¹; it arises from somewhere, and it assembles judges² against the person whom fortune long ago³ attacked. It tries to exclude me from what fortune has given, and it puts forward another law—one that is good in itself and not at all to be despised, yet not at all applicable to my circumstances. <gloss>Another proposal from the text:</gloss> "For being disinherited⁴," it says, "you have no share in your father’s estate. For the disinherited person, the law says, must not share in the paternal goods." And by putting forward the literal word, my opponent does not consider the meaning, not realizing plainly that the intention of words has often caused many to stumble and just as often set them right again.

I am disinherited, I say so myself, and, knowing the law⁵, I stay away from my father’s goods. For when and who ever saw me, after⁶ 

<column-break/>

the disinheritance, laying claim to a paternal inheritance? Am I now seizing my father's goods? Am I now, against his will, forcing myself inside the house and seeking to be an heir? For the law⁷ forbids this; this is what it means: that the one who has once been rejected by his parent should receive nothing of the father's possessions. For such a person is no longer a son for the rest of time, from the moment he was disinherited. And since he is not a son by his father's will, how could he become an heir? I have once and for all become a stranger to those things which belong to...

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s legal defense. Having established that he is not claiming his father's house or estate by right of birth, he now addresses the specific insults and legal barriers thrown at him by his opponents, who view him as a "stranger" due to his disinheritance.</meta>

# STUDY 8.

<columns>
...to the legitimate heirs; I will never make a counter-claim, I will not trouble my father, and I will not fight against those who were once my brothers. I will not seek a portion of which I have become a stranger. I do not dare to call them "brothers," and yet shall I claim to share in the inheritance with them? I call him my "former father"¹—and shall I now insist on receiving things that he has cast away? This too would be fitting for my ill-fortune, if, in addition to my misery, I should also be charged with folly for seeking things that do not belong to me at all.

For if I am holding onto this ship as one intending to inherit, then judge me as a lawbreaker, pelt me with stones, and send me away to *Kynosarges*² <note>A place in Athens associated with those of "impure" or illegitimate birth.</note>, or indeed, to the crows!³ <note>A common ancient Greek curse equivalent to "go to hell."</note> Bring forward the law and condemn me; explain it, and judge me! Say to me, "Why are you here to inherit, you stranger, who have no connection to your father’s affairs? The law confirmed your disinheritance while your father was living, and the law confirms your exclusion now that he is dead. Anyone else will inherit sooner than you, who are excluded by law." Say these things, and do not think me worthy of a share.

But if it is because the ship belonged to my father, and there was a sea-storm, and I alone—while the others fled—stood against the danger, and [risked] my life...

***

¹ <margin>I call him my former father] From this it seems that earlier one should write: *I will not trouble my former father.*</margin>

² <margin><note>original: "Κυνόσαργες"</note> Kynosarges was a place in Athens where illegitimate children were formerly cast away. It is mentioned in many places. See Psellus, *Short Works* p. 105, with my note; Bartholinus, *On Childbirth*, p. 78. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 3*, p. 99: "the rest should be thrown into Kynosarges, just as they used to do with illegitimate children of old." Add Nicephorus in the following note.</margin>

³ <margin><note>original: "εἰς κόρακας"</note> An Attic expression, often used by Aristophanes, by which they would call down evil upon someone. You may see, among many others, Erasmus’ *Adages* "go to the crows," *Chiliads* 2, 2, 96. The manuscript I follow says "to the crows" (*eis korakas*). Perhaps the author himself had written "to the crows" (*es korakas*), which Helladius reports was uniquely in use among the Attics. Nicephorus, *On Images*, cited by me in *Greek Anecdotes* vol. II, p. 413: "let him be cast far away, let him go to the crows, let him be sent...

<column-break/>

...away to Kynosarges." And today this formula of curses still seems to flourish. Lazaras, in *To the apparition of the suffering Mark*, p. 30: "To the pit, to the crows with the men of blood! And let the Greeks live, sons of the immortals!" I did not show the error of the edition "to the crows" (*eis korakas*). Those "men of blood" are the heartless, cruel, and murderous Turks. Corayus [Adamantios Korais], in the *Second Dialogue of Demochares and Pasicharis*, p. 35: "send them to the crows." They use another curse which has more novelty: if they wish to curse someone, they send him to "Cairo." Alexander Soutsos, in his *Satire*: "Do you not send your own poor goddess to Cairo?" There the excellent poet notes: "In the Peloponnese, and especially in Lacedaemon, they use as a curse the phrase 'let him go to Cairo! send him to Cairo,' which phrases are equivalent to 'let him go to the Devil! send him to the Devil!'"</margin>

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s legal defense in a rhetorical exercise by George Pachymeres. The speaker, a disinherited son, argues that his right to the ship he saved during a storm is based on the law of maritime salvage, which is entirely separate from the law of inheritance that excludes him from his father's estate.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES

...compared to the perils of the sea, I saved myself. I hold these things because I took them, as the law commands and grants the vessel to the one who stayed behind. Why then are you so arrogant in your speech? Why do you try to strip away the reward of my labors—or should I call it a windfall from fortune? For what purpose did the lawmaker deem the one who stayed behind worthy of such a great reward? Surely <note>original: "Ἦ"</note> because the danger involves one's very life, and nothing is more precious to a person, no matter what anyone says. It is only right that rewards be proportional to the hardships endured, so that if someone were inclined to be lazy or to shrink away from such immense danger, they might be strengthened by looking toward the reward—knowing they will either suffer the worst of fates or receive the greatest of blessings.

Thus, with two laws before us, I do not violate either one: I do not claim anything as an heir, for I have no share in that, yet by staying with the ship, I become its master.

And if you ask why the lawmaker did not specify in the law regarding disinherited children that they are excluded from the father’s estate *only* when they try to force their way in as heirs, then I will ask you why he did not specify in the law of the "one who stayed behind" by saying: "except if he is disinherited." But just as you would say in your defense that he omitted it because it was obvious, so I give you the same answer.

***

¹ <margin>Concerning the phrase "if on the other hand," understand "I hold onto" from the preceding clause "if on the one hand." I refer the pronoun "that" to "the storm-wave." I have added the word "toward" <note>original: "πρός"</note> before "the affairs of the sea."</margin>

² <margin>I added "why" <note>original: "τί"</note> after "the one who stayed behind," following that rule of omissions which I just mentioned on page 144, note 4.</margin>

³ <margin><gloss>Scholion:</gloss> A different reasoning regarding the other law and the lawmaker.</margin>

⁴ <margin>The manuscript has "or" <note>original: "ἤ"</note>. I have written "surely" <note>original: "ἦ"</note> meaning "certainly." I do the same below on page 147. Libanius (vol. I, p. 508) writes: "Whom, indeed, which of the gods should be blamed? Surely <note>original: "ἦ"</note> all of them equally? Having abandoned the guard they owed to that noble head..." I would prefer "Surely <note>original: "ἦ"</note> all of them equally, having abandoned..." as "all, surely all." In the repetition "whom indeed, which of the gods," there is a certain Platonic flavor. See the note on Aristaenetus, p. 632.</margin>

<column-break/>

⁵ <margin><gloss>Scholion:</gloss> The lack of specification, which is handled as an equalization.</margin>

⁶ <margin>The manuscript has "I answer" written with an *omega* over the second-to-last syllable. The letters *omega* and *omicron* are swapped everywhere in these texts. For example, Gaetulicus in the *Greek Anthology* (6.190) writes: "Take... a poor handful of a few barley-cakes." I would prefer to swap the *omega* and *omicron* to write: "a handful of a few poor barley-cakes." I slightly dislike having an epithet attached to every single noun. Though this strikes me as too delicate an objection here, I will tolerate it elsewhere. For in judging these trivial matters, there is something moody and varied, governed by no fixed law. The same phrasing I take from Gaetulicus I would give to Anyte in the *Anthology* (7.646): "O father, I am yours no longer; already dark death, a blue-black cloud, covers my eyes as I waste away." Critics do not tolerate the double mor-</margin>

### STUDY 8

<columns>
Furthermore, I have even more to say: that while my law is the decree of Lycurgus the Spartan <note>Lycurgus was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, famous for the "laconic" or brief style of his laws</note>, brought here for our use, yours is that of Solon the Athenian <note>Solon was the famous Athenian reformer whose laws were known for being more detailed and descriptive</note>. It is certainly not unreasonable that Lycurgus, being a Spartan, should use brief speech. Consider this law and then another; see how many necessary points are understood from the outside <note>i.e., implied rather than stated</note>. But what reason would Solon have for being brief, since he was an Athenian and was someone who clarified his laws to the point of exact precision?

Therefore, in the case of your law, one would have to argue extensively to prove that the same conclusion is reached even if the missing part is not written down. There is a great difference between something being written and not being written. In the case of my law, however, one could easily connect the unwritten intent to the written word; that which the writer left out will be taken exactly as if it were written, and the intended meaning will be logically concluded¹.

> "The disinherited <term>apokeryktos</term> <note>A child formally cast out and legally disowned by their father</note> shall not share in the father's estate," it says.

Which "father's estate"? Surely³ it refers to whatever the father holds in his possession—the things he has acquired by his own will and provides to others when he wishes. If he does not wish to give to this person, who could force him? If he wishes to give to that person, who would stop him? However, he may or may not wish to give to the disinherited son; and if—

---

...an epithet of something. Jacobs edited "eye... dark blue." <note>original: "ὄμμα.... κυάνεον"</note> Brunck preferred "but my eye is black... dark blue [sea?]." <note>original: "μέλαν δ' ἐμὸν ὄμμα.... κυάνεος"</note> I agree with Brunck. A dying maiden speaking of the black shadows of her own eyes must have thought of this first. But there is a great difficulty at the end of the Epigram of Gætulicus: "If you drive away my heavy-limbed disease, as you have done, you shall also drive away poverty, and he will give a fat goat." <note>original: "Εἰ δ' ὥς μευ βαρύγυιον ἀπώσαο νοῦσον, ἐλάσσεις Καὶ πενίην, δώσει πιαλέον χίμαρον"</note> One is struck by the transition from the first person "my" <note>original: "μευ"</note> to the third person "he will give" <note>original: "δώσει"</note>, and various conjectures are made. But it must be remembered that Gætulicus speaks not in his own name, but in the name of Leonidas: "Accept, honored goddess of Cythera, these humble gifts from the humble poet Leonidas." <note>original: "Λάξεο, τιμήεσσα Κυθηριάς, ὑμνοπόλοιο Λιτὰ τάδ' ἐκ λιτοῦ δῶρα Λεωνίδεω"</note> Since Venus had restored him to health, Gætulicus promises the goddess that if she can likewise relieve Leonidas's poverty, he—Leonidas, that is—will give not just figs and grapes and such gifts, but a fat goat. After this explanation, the change of person will not

<column-break/>

disturb the reader. But if anyone desires a more explicit mention of Leonidas's poverty, it is easy to correct "you will drive away for him" <note>original: "ἐλᾷς οἱ"</note> instead of "you will drive away" <note>original: "ἐλάσσεις"</note>, thus preserving the future tense and adding the pronoun. It is well known that "elâs" <note>original: "ἐλᾷς"</note> is an Attic form of the future. Aristophanes, *Frogs* 203: "You shall not talk nonsense, but exerting yourself, you shall row" <note>original: "Ἐλᾷς"</note>. Sophocles, *Ajax* 499: "Fate will drive" <note>original: "ἐλᾷ"</note>; where the scholar’s note says: "instead of *elasei* (will drive)." And so too in *Oedipus Rex* 407. Aeschylus, *Eumenides* 76: "they will drive" <note>original: "ἐλῶσι"</note>, with the note "they will drive forth." And likewise Euripides, *Alcestis* 972. Furthermore, I observe that the reading "these humble things from a humble man" <note>original: "λιτὰ τάδ' ἐκ λιτοῦ"</note> is a conjecture. In the Palatine manuscript, it was found as "quickly these things from the famous" <note>original: "αἶψα τάδ' ἐκ κλυτοῦ"</note>, and in Planudes as "quickly these things of the famous." <note>original: "αἶψα τάδε κλειτοῦ"</note> I would accept "quickly these things from the famous." Leonidas could be called "famous" <note>original: "κλειτόν"</note> by Gætulicus, or "renowned" <note>original: "κλυτόν"</note>, if the meter had allowed it; and it was also an epithet that might move Venus.

³ The manuscript reads "or." <note>original: "ἤ"</note> See page 146, note 4.

<meta>The previous page discussed the distinction between Spartan and Athenian legal styles, specifically focusing on the law regarding disinherited children. The speaker argued that the father's intent determines what constitutes the "estate." This page continues that argument, moving into a second law regarding the ownership of a ship abandoned during a storm.</meta>

### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

<columns>
...if he chooses to give, he immediately dissolves the disinheritance, and there is no reason for that person not to receive what is provided; for a man is certainly no longer disinherited if his father appoints him as an heir. But if the father does not choose to give, let the father not give, nor let the child receive against the father's will; for he is no longer a son. **And shall he then share in the father's estate?**

Do you see what kind of "sharing" the law speaks of? Do you see how, while the disinheritance remains in effect and the property belongs to the father, the law bars the disinherited person? Why then does the law need any further clarification <term>diastixis</term> <note>A legal distinction or specific qualification added to a rule</note>, when "sharing" is understood in the context of inheritance and carries only this specific meaning?

Let us come then to the remaining law, which grants the ship to the person who stayed on board during a storm. Surely the lawmaker was aware of many people who were disenfranchised <term>atimos</term> <note>In Greek law, 'atimos' refers to a person who has lost their civic rights and status</note> or disinherited <term>apokeryktos</term>. He knows of both young and old, of friends and enemies, and of those for whom the storm-tossed cargo will be beneficial and those for whom it will not. He knows about ships: that one is private and another public; that one carries a large cargo necessary for the city, while another carries a small load not worth a thought; that one is a fast-sailing trireme <note>A classic ancient warship with three banks of oars</note> and another is almost stationary, moving only when a heavy wind aids its path. If he had intended a distinction in these cases and did not simply legislate the same for all, the law would necessarily be bound by many such clarifications. But just as with the objects themselves—where we count them as one and the same whether they are many or few—so also you must accept it regarding the persons involved. Do not investigate whether the one who stayed on board is poor or rich, an enemy of the city or a friend, one of the honorable or the disenfranchised, a legitimate son or a disinherited one. Observe <gloss>1</gloss> <note>Scholium: Here the intention of the lawmaker is clearly seen.</note>, if you wish, the intentions of the lawmakers. One lawmaker bars the disinherited from the father's estate, not because the son is hated by the one who sired him; for if he disinherited him out of hate, you might have a point. But since he does so for the sake of discipline and admonition—even if it seems somewhat harsh—for "bearing children is a powerful thing" <gloss>2</gloss> <note>He uses the words of Euripides in Iphigenia at Aulis, line 917: "Bearing children is a powerful thing <note>original: 'Deinon to tiktein'</note> and brings a great love."</note>, or rather "begetting," and not...

<column-break/>

And, since it concerns the father, he adds "or rather begetting" <note>original: "eit’ oun gennan"</note>. I would almost believe this addition to be a marginal comment <term>scholion</term>, since "to bear" <note>original: "to tiktein"</note> can also be used for a father, and immediately...

</columns>

<summary>Pachymeres argues that laws should be applied generally without extra "clarifications" unless specified, using the example of a person claiming an abandoned ship regardless of their social or legal status. He cites Euripides to emphasize that disinheritance is often a tool for parental discipline rather than a sign of true hatred.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal argument regarding disinheritance and maritime law. The speaker is justifying why a father might disinherit a son—not out of malice, but as a harsh form of "tough love" to build character. This leads into a discussion of a second law where a person who remains on a ship during a storm earns the right to own it, contrasting this "earned" property with inherited wealth.</meta>

# STUDY 8.

<columns>

...even if a parent, though suffering, should feel a sense of hatred toward his offspring—it is not that he excludes the child from the father's estate because he is hated. Rather, it is so that the son, struggling by himself in poverty and facing dangers, might be compelled to acquire things through labor, to create wealth through his own efforts, and to cast aside the luxury and laziness for which he was disinherited. This is what I appear to have done myself; and having persevered, not over small matters but over the greatest ones, I have fulfilled the lawmaker's intent alongside fortune. 

But the law gives the property of others to the one who remains on board, teaching even the helpless man to endure, and rousing the lazy man with great rewards and things he would never have expected. For if, even when such a great reward is offered, people still cling to their lives and, looking toward danger, become fugitives from the sea—throwing away the ship like a shield <note>original: "τὴν ναῦν ὡς ἀσπίδα ῥίπτοντες" — a play on the Greek term 'rhipsaspis,' meaning one who throws away their shield in cowardice</note> and bargaining for their safety—what then became of those trapped in terrible storms when only a small reward for endurance was offered? One not even large enough to please a man who loves wealth and money?

I,^1 for my part, feel this way about these things, and I consider those men to be wise teachers of diligence, temperance, obedience, and courage...

---

<note>The following section is a Latin scholarly commentary on the Greek text above, discussing word choices and historical parallels.</note>

The author did not hesitate to say, "hatred for his children would not arise in the parent." <note>original: "οὐκ ἂν τῷ γεννήτορι μῖσος ὧν τέκοι προσγίνοιτο"</note> In the context of tragedy, the term "to bear" <note>original: "τὸ τίκτειν"</note> must be understood as referring to mothers; however, in a verse torn from its dramatic sequence and not even complete, the sentiment stands on its own, and no one remembers Clytemnestra <note>The wife of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy, famous for her hatred of her husband and complex relationship with her children</note> or the chorus. 

Yet, upon reflection, the author might have added the phrase "or rather to beget" <note>original: "εἴτουν γεννᾶν"</note> himself for the sake of explanation. He speaks similarly in the Tenth Declamation: "In what part of the chorus, or rather [the rank] of dignity, does he place this woman?"—here he intended to clarify the metaphor of the word "chorus." Likewise in the twelfth: "they run back to our [property], or rather their own." Pachymeres’ book *On Harmonics* displays this title: *On Harmonics, or rather Music*. The learned editor retained the spelling *ētoun* [ἤτουν]; but it should have been replaced with *ēgoun* [ἤγουν], since the letters Gamma (Γ) and Tau (Τ) are commonly swapped, or *eitoun* [εἴτουν] due to the common swap of the vowels

<column-break/>

*eta* (η) and *ei* (ει). The conjunction *eitoun* <note>Meaning "that is to say" or "or rather"</note> is very common among later Byzantine writers and is not rare among the ancients. 

Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian</note> says in Oration 3, page 100: "of your madness, or rather [eitoun] your god-forsakenness"; and in Oration 33, page 533: "introducing the one through the windows, as the Scripture says, or rather [eitoun] through the senses." An anonymous author in the work *On Hair*, edited by the learned Miller (page 31), writes: "armed men attacking the unarmed, or rather [eitoun] true things attacking plausible things." After the fall of Thessalonica, Nicetas writes to Eustathius that he wishes to share in the lamentation with "our Jeremiah, or rather [eitoun] Ezekiel" (page 359 of Tafel’s *Thessalonicæ*). This should be added to my note in *Greek Anecdotes*, volume IV, page 475; see also Bernhardy’s notes on Eustathius, page 910.

^1 <note>Scholion: A counter-accusation <term>antegklematike</term>—a rhetorical strategy where one deflects a charge by accusing the opponent—and a topical attack against the disinherited son.</note>

</columns>

<meta>This page continues the speaker's defense in a declamation (a formal rhetorical exercise) likely written by George Pachymeres. The speaker is defending his right to a ship he salvaged during a storm, countering an opponent who is using his past disinheritance by his father to discredit his character. This page moves from the general theory of "tough love" to the speaker's personal experience of hardship and his "athletic" struggle for the ship.</meta>

# III. BY PACHYMERES

...and of all, so to speak, education. This man has reached such a point of madness, or malice, or envy—or I know not what to call it—that he now brings forward my disinheritance as a criminal charge against me. He brings up the very things I previously confessed against myself, for which I was justly disinherited by my father, and presents them as evidence: claiming that I am disobedient, a lost soul, a source of grief to my parent, and "this and that," <note>original: "τὰ καὶ τά" — a Greek idiom used to summarize a list of insults or specific accusations of wrongdoing</note> on account of which he deems me unworthy of any paternal possessions whatsoever.

But, my good sir, if I was disobedient to my father and undisciplined, I have paid the worthy penalties; <note>Latin note 2: The editor notes he decided not to change the word "worthy" (ἀξίας) based on a previous reference.</note> I became a stranger to my father’s house, a stranger to the inheritance, hated by my kin, dishonored by the citizens, robbed of my status among my peers, poor, helpless, a wanderer, living by myself and weighed down by worries for which there was no remedy. Were these penalties not sufficient for my former life? It was for these reasons I went abroad; for these reasons I committed myself to both land and sea, so that by struggling I might call back my father’s goodwill, and that through hard work I might grow wealthy. Even if my father seemed to still hold onto his anger while testing my resolve, it would be possible for me to live on my own means, looking to no stranger’s hands for my livelihood. This reasoning cast me onto the sea. And having found a ship, I embarked. But who could find the words to describe the terrors I first encountered?

Do not merely consider the fact that I survived. Instead, consider what came before, and weigh the end result against the events that occurred. Only then—considering that I, and I alone, have struggled through so many things <note>original: "παμπληθὲς" — meaning in great number or with full intensity</note>—will you judge the ship to be my prize. Many run in a stadium, but the prize is reserved for only one. He who looks only at the finish line will declare the prize a stroke of luck, a mere godsend; but he who considers the struggle before the end knows the pain of the feet, the weight on the loins, the constant sweat, the tension of the whole body, and the agony that he might somehow slip and be crushed, or perish being trampled, or after much labor, bring home only shame in the end. See these things in my case as well. Do you see the ship? Then pay attention also to the labors by which I acquired it.

---

<note>original: I should not have changed "worthy" [ἀξίας] page 14, note 2.</note>

<note>original: "Παμπληθές"] see page 84, note 2.</note>

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s harrowing account of the shipwreck. # G. [GEORGIOS] PACHYMERES

...to do? For the terror lay heavy upon me, and the shipwreck that followed was great. I fortified <note>original: "συγκροτῶ" — literally to weld or strike together; here meaning to strengthen or brace oneself</note> myself with certain reasonings that seemed to me not ignoble, and I emboldened myself <term>andrizesthai: to act with manly courage</term> against the danger in an unexpected way. I resolved either to live well, if I should survive, or to die well, and in either case to hide the shame of my disinheritance <note>original: "ἀποκηρύξεως" — the formal, legal act of a father disowning a son, a central theme in Byzantine rhetorical exercises</note>. And who would be able to recount the terrors of that entire night? What wind did not gather its blasts against me? What wave did not strike me as its only target—as if I were a projecting rock—only to be shattered into thin foam? There were times when the sea overcame me, throwing me down onto the decks repeatedly, or dragging me toward the water and pulling me away from the ship, as if in an outright contest for my life. I was submerged many times as I went under, but not even once did I surrender my place on the ship to the wave. I came close to drowning many times, but I held on, in part, to the ship itself. Many times I was sinking, but my mind remained fixed there, and having suffered these things, I endured until that terror abated and I barely conquered that wild and irresistible surge. I conquered by holding on while the storm turned away, having first outlasted the terrors.

Then do you wish to deprive of the gift the man who has struggled <note>original: "ἀθλήσαντα" — Pachymeres uses the language of athletics and martyrdom to describe the struggle for survival</note> so, who has suffered such misery, who has run such a race for his life? And do you not judge this gift to be a worthy trade for those many labors and struggles which I fought even beyond all my strength? For what reason, then, did I endure those great trials and hold out against so many hardships, when it would have been easy for me to seek safety for myself as the others did, and to lean toward whatever path would save me?

"But," he says, "you should have shown your courage in other matters."
Do you say this to me? Say it to Fortune; say it to the divine spirit <note>original: "δαίμονι" — referring to one's lot in life or a guiding supernatural power</note>. ### EXERCISE 8. 153

...I am shut out from my father’s house. What seer said these things? What watcher of portents or dreamer of dreams was initiated into the things that would come to pass?

"You ought to have shown courage <term>andrizesthai: literally "to act like a man"; a core virtue in Greek rhetoric involving bravery and endurance</term> in other matters." This is a saying that would suffice to destroy any good reputation. Why, then, do they give prizes to athletes, when it is possible to say: "You should have won in other contests"? Why give rewards <note>The word "give" must be understood here from the previous sentence.</note> to those who do good for the city, when one ought to say that they should have done something else and not what actually happened?

In *these* matters it was necessary to show courage, my good man—in the very things where I happened to be present. In these it was necessary to labor, for it was through these that I could solve my desperate situation and heal the wound of my disinheritance <note>original: "apokeryxis" — the formal, legal act of a father disowning a son, a common theme in Greek rhetorical training</note>. For the sake of these things, it was necessary to fight both the sea and the winds; if I had shirked this labor, I would have been justly deprived of them. Was I a disinherited son? Yet I showed courage even beyond my strength. Was I hated by the one who begot me? Yet I stayed with the ship. Am I a stranger to my father's property? Yet I held the fruit of my labors as my own. What farmer, who sows his seeds with great toil <note>The manuscript says "toils," but perhaps a preposition like "with" or "in" has been lost.</note> in the winter, yields the harvest to others in the coming year? What athlete, having competed and won, steps aside so others may take the crowns? Who, sailing on a ship when a storm has overtaken it and the others have fled, stays behind to meet the surge, the squalls, and the winds face-to-face—and then, having overcome the terrors, allows others to take the gifts of fortune? I would be a fool if, expecting such a result, I had stayed for even a single hour. Why did I do it, men? Why? So that I might go away with empty hands and receive only praise and applause? That would be a "worthy" prize for such great and massive labors, and for that long and perilous circuit! Or was it so that I might be dragged back into court, and see judges and the speaker’s platform, and be forced to contend again? That would indeed be a "splendid" award for my toils, and truly worthy of wonder!

Why do you speak so pointlessly, man, and appear even more burdensome than my own fate? For while fate, however reluctantly, has finally made peace with me <note>The phrase used here, "oïs hoti," is a specific idiom used by Pachymeres and other rhetoricians like Choricius and Aristides. It functions like the French "en ce que" (in that / because).</note>
<column-break/>
by sparing my life...
