# FROM THE WORKS OF PACHYMERES <note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a rhetorical exercise, a "declamation," where a student or scholar argues a fictional legal case to practice oratory.</note>

...comparing myself against the dangers of the sea¹, I saved myself, and I hold these things because I took them. Since the law commands and grants the ship to the one who remained, why² do you act so arrogantly and speak this way, trying to strip away the reward of my labors—or should I call it a windfall from Fortune? For what³ was the lawgiver looking at when he deemed the one who stayed behind worthy of a great reward? Was it⁴ not surely because the danger involves one’s very soul <term>psyche: in this context, it refers to one's life or physical existence</term>, than which nothing is more precious to a man, no matter what anyone says? It is surely just that rewards should be offered in proportion to the labors, so that if someone were inclined to be lazy or to shrink away from such a massive danger, he might be strengthened by looking toward the reward. He knows that he will either suffer the worst of evils or carry away the greatest of goods.

Therefore, with these two laws before us, I am not breaking either one. I do not claim the property as if I were an heir—since I have no share in that—but by having remained on board, I have become the master of the ship.

But if you ask⁵ why the lawgiver did not specifically define, in the law regarding disinherited sons, that they only lose their share of the paternal estate when they try to force a claim as an heir, then I will also ask why, in the law regarding the one who stays with the ship, he did not add the condition: "unless he is a disinherited son." But just as you might say in your defense that he left it out because it was obvious, so I respond in kind⁶.

### STUDY 8

However, I have even more to say: that my law is an ordinance of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with establishing the city's military-oriented reformation.</note> the Spartan, brought here to us, while yours is from Solon <note>The famous Athenian statesman and lawmaker known for his efforts to legislate against political, economic, and moral decline.</note> the Athenian. It is, therefore, not at all unlikely for Lycurgus to be brief, as he is "Laconizing" <term>Laconizing: speaking in the brief, pithy manner characteristic of the Spartans/Laconians</term>. Look at this law and then look at another; see how many necessary points are understood implicitly from the outside in these Spartan rules. But for Solon, what reason would there be for brevity, since he is Athenian and clarifies his laws with such precision? Thus, regarding your Athenian law, one would have to argue at length that the same conclusion follows even when the missing part is not explicitly stated. Indeed, there is a great difference between whether a point is written down or not. But in the case of my Spartan law, one can easily join the unwritten to the written; that which the writer omitted, the reader will take as if it were directly written, and will logically conclude¹ the intended meaning.

"The disinherited son² shall not share in the paternal property," the law says. What "paternal property"? Surely³ it refers to whatever the father holds in his possession, which he has acquired by his own will and provides as he wishes. If he does not wish to give to this son, who could force him? If he wishes to give to someone else, who is there to stop him? He may wish to give to the disinherited person, or he may not; and if...

<column-break/>

...the epithet. Jacobs edited it as *eye*....
*dark blue*. Brunck preferred *but my black eye*.... *dark blue*. And I agree with Brunck. A dying maiden speaking of the black shadows of her own eyes should have thought of this first. But there is a great difficulty toward the end of the Epigram of Gaetulicus <note>A poet of the Greek Anthology, likely Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus.</note>: *But if you have pushed away my limb-weighing disease, you shall also drive away poverty, and he will give a fat goat.* One is struck by the transition from the first person (*my*) to the third person (*he will give*), and various conjectures are made. But it must be remembered that Gaetulicus speaks not in his own name, but in the name of Leonidas <note>Leonidas of Tarentum, a famous epigrammatist known for writing about the lives of the poor.</note>: *Receive, honored Cytherian [Venus], these humble gifts of the singer Leonidas from a humble source.* Gaetulicus promises the goddess that if she can likewise relieve the poverty of Leonidas—whom Venus had restored to health—then Leonidas will no longer offer just figs and grapes and such gifts, but a fat goat. After this explanation, the change of person will not

hinder the reader. But if anyone desires a more explicit mention of Leonidas's poverty, it is easy to correct it to *you will drive away for him* instead of *you shall drive away*, thus preserving the future tense and adding the pronoun. It is well known that *elâs* [you will drive] is the Attic form of the future. Aristophanes, *Frogs* 203: *You shall not keep talking nonsense, but having stepped against it, you will drive.* Sophocles, *Ajax* 499: *The divinity will drive*; where the scholar's note says: *instead of "elasei" [will drive]*. And similarly in *Oedipus Rex* 407. Aeschylus, *Eumenides* 76: *they will drive*, with the note *they shall drive*. And so too in Euripides, *Alcestis* 972. Furthermore, I would observe that the reading *these humble [gifts] from a humble [source]* is a conjecture. In the Palatine manuscript was found *quickly these from the famous*, and in Planudes *quickly these of the famous*. I would accept *quickly these from the famous*. For Gaetulicus, Leonidas could be called *famous* or *renowned*, if the meter allowed it, and it was also an epithet that might move Venus.

¹ The manuscript reads "concludes" (subjunctive).
² Scholar's note: Syllogism (logical deduction).
³ The manuscript reads "or" [interrogative]. See page 146, note 4.

# G. PACHYMERES

<columns>

...to give, he immediately dissolves the disinheritance, and there is no reason for that man not to receive what is provided; for he is no longer disinherited if the father appoints him as heir. But if the father does not wish to give, then let the man not give, and let the son not take, against the father's will; for he is no longer considered a son. And will he share in the paternal estate?

Do you see what kind of "sharing" the law describes? Do you see how, while the disinheritance remains in effect and the property is paternal, the law excludes the disinherited person? Why then does the law need further distinctions, when sharing is understood in the sense of inheritance, and has this meaning alone?

Let us come now to the remaining law, which deems that the one who stayed on the ship should receive it. Surely the lawmaker knew many people who were dishonored, or disinherited. He knows both the young and the old, both friends and enemies, those for whom receiving a storm-tossed vessel would be beneficial, and those for whom it would not. He knows the ships—that one is private, another public; one carries a heavy and necessary cargo for the city, another a small one hardly worth a thought; one is a fast-sailing trireme, another almost immobile, requiring a strong wind to move it along. If, then, he intended a distinction based on these factors and did not simply legislate the same for everyone, the law would necessarily have been bound by many distinctions. But just as in the case of objects, where we consider it one and the same law whether the value is much or little, so you must accept it for persons. Do not ask whether the one who stayed was poor or rich, an enemy of the city or a friend, of high status or dishonored, legitimate or disinherited. Consider¹ then, if you will, the intentions of the lawmakers. One lawgiver excludes the disinherited from the paternal estate, not because he is hated by the one who sired him; for if he disinherited him out of hate, you might have a point. But since it is for education and admonition, even if it is a bit sharp—for "bearing children is a powerful thing²," or rather, to beget, and not...

### STUDY VIII

<columns>

...even if a parent, suffering ill, should come to feel hatred for those he fathered—he does not exclude the son from the paternal estate as one truly hated, but rather so that, toiling by himself out of necessity and exposed to dangers, he may be forced to acquire things through his own labors. Thus, he might gain abundance through his own efforts and cast off the luxury and laziness for which he was originally disinherited <note>The Greek term is *apokeryxis*, a formal legal process in antiquity where a father publicly disowned a son.</note>. I myself now appear to have done exactly this; having endured not merely small trials, but the greatest of all, I have fulfilled the lawmaker’s intent alongside my own fortune. The law gives the property of others to the one who remains, teaching even the helpless to endure, and rousing the lazy with great rewards such as they would never have expected. For if, even when such a great reward is offered, men still cling to life and, looking toward the danger, become fugitives from the sea—throwing away the ship like a shield <note>This is a rhetorical play on the "shield-dropper" (*rhipsaspis*), the ultimate symbol of cowardice in Greek culture.</note> and bartering for their own safety—who then were those men caught in the terrible storms, when only a small reward for their endurance was offered, one not even sufficient to please a lover of wealth or money?

I, for my part, hold this view on these matters, and I consider those men to be wise teachers of diligence, self-control, obedience, and courage...

<column-break/>

...would not hesitate to say, *hatred would not come to a parent for those they begot* <note>original: οὐκ ἂν τῷ γεννήτορι μῖσος ὧν τέκοι προσγίνοιτο</note>. In the context of tragedy, the word *bearing* <note>original: τὸ τίκτειν</note> must certainly be understood as referring to mothers; however, in a verse torn from its dramatic sequence and incomplete, the sentiment stands on its own, and no one remembers Clytemnestra or the chorus. Yet, upon reflection, he might have added the phrase *that is to say, to beget* <note>original: εἴτουν γεννᾷν</note> for the sake of explanation. He speaks similarly in the Tenth Declamation: *where in the dance—that is to say, the rank—does he station her?* <note>original: ποῦ χοροῦ, εἴτουν ἀξίας, τάττει ταύτην</note>, intending to clarify the metaphor of the "dance." Likewise in the twelfth: *they run back to our—that is to say, their own—affairs* <note>original: πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν, εἴτουν αὐτῶν, ἀνατρέχουσι</note>. Pachymeres' book *On Harmonics* features this heading: *On harmonics, or rather, music* <note>original: περὶ ἁρμονικῆς, ἤτουν μουσικῆς</note>. The learned editor retained the word *ētoun* <note>original: ἤτουν</note>, but it should have been restored to *ēgoun* <note>original: ἤγουν</note>, following the common exchange of the letters G (Γ) and T (Τ), or *eitoun* <note>original: εἴτουν</note> from the habitual swapping of the vowels eta (η) and ei (ει). The conjunction *eitoun* (meaning "that is to say") is very common among later writers and not rare among the ancients. Nazianzen in Oration 3, page 100: *of your madness, that is to say, your god-blindness*; Oration 33, page 533: *introducing [sin] through the windows, as the Scripture says—that is to say, through the senses.* An anonymous author *On Hair*, edited by the learned Miller (page 31): *those armed attacking the unarmed—that is to say, true things attacking the plausible.* After the capture of Thessaloniki, Nicetas writes to Eustathius that he wishes to share in his lamentation *with our Jeremiah, or rather, Ezekiel* <note>original: εἴτ’ οὖν Ἐζεχιήλ</note>, page 359 of Tafel’s *Thessalonica*. Add also a note to my *Greek Anecdotes*, volume IV, page 475; and Bernhardy on Eustathius, page 910.

<meta>This page continues the declamation where a disinherited son justifies his claim to a ship he salvaged during a storm. The speaker is now addressing his opponent's attempt to use his past legal "disinheritance" as a reason to deny him the "prize" of the vessel.</meta>

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...of discipline, and of every kind of education, so to speak. This man has reached such a height of madness, or villainy, or envy—or I know not what to call it—that he now presents my disinheritance <note>The Greek term *apokeryxis* refers to a formal, public act where a father legally severed ties with a son, usually for moral failings or disobedience.</note> as an accusation against me. He brings forward those things I previously admitted against myself, for which I was justly disowned by my father; he cites these, calling me disobedient, a lost soul, a cause of grief to my parent, and "this and that" <note>original: *ta kai ta*. A Greek idiom used here to summarize a list of grievances or "all sorts of evils."</note>, because of which he deems me unworthy of any part of my father's estate.

But, my good man, if I was disobedient to my father and ill-bred, I have paid the proper penalty. I became a stranger to my father’s house, an exile from my inheritance, hated by my kin, dishonored by the citizens, undignified among my peers, poor, helpless, a wanderer, living by myself and weighed down by cares for which I had no remedy. Were these punishments not sufficient for my former life? It was for these reasons that I went abroad; for these reasons I committed myself to land and sea, so that by struggling I might call back my father’s favor, and that by my diligence I might grow wealthy. Even if my father still seemed to hold onto his anger while testing my resolve, I wanted to be able to live off my own means, looking to no stranger's hand for my survival. This reasoning is what threw me into the sea. And having found a ship, I boarded her; but as for the terrors I first encountered, what words could ever do them justice?

Do not simply consider that I survived by staying behind. Rather, consider also the things that came before, and weigh the end result against what happened. And so, because I and I alone have struggled through such a multitude of trials, you should judge the ship to be my prize <note>original: *geras*. In ancient Greek, this refers to a "prize of honor" or a gift of privilege given to a hero.</note>. Many men run in a stadium, but the prize is reserved for only one. He who looks only at the finish line will declare the prize a stroke of luck <note>original: *hermaion*. Literally a "gift from Hermes," the god of transitions and luck; a "godsend."</note>; but he who considers what happened before the end knows the pain of the feet, the weight on the loins, the constant sweat, the strain of the whole body, and the agony that one might slip and be crushed and perish, or that after much toil one might carry away only shame. Look at these same things in my case. You see the ship? But turn your mind also to the labors by which I won her.

---

### STUDY 8.

<columns>
2

For it was just now night and darkness across the sky, with the sun hidden by the clouds, and a bright Hellespont wind <note>original: Hellespontias; a strong north-easterly wind blowing from the direction of the Dardanelles.</note> was descending, and the sea **was in labor** <note>original: ōdine; a common classical metaphor for a churning, swelling sea.</note>¹, and the water, which until then had been calm, **began to swell**², and the continuous expanse was divided, and wave upon wave pressed on. The ship at one moment would rise up in disorder, tossed high by the waves—you would have said it was hanging in the air, with nothing supporting it—and then again it would descend as if into Hades, and the hearts of the voyagers sank down along with the vessel. Tackling, sails, and stays were torn to shreds and carried away beneath the waters. And the pilot, giving up in the face of the terror, lay haphazardly upon the decks, allowing anyone who wished to trample him. Everything was full of turmoil: the things outside, the things inside, and the things still further within the soul. Everything was filled with uproar and a mingled cry of those about to die instantly. Finally, having lost all hope, some trusting themselves to poles, others to whatever came to hand—since they could see the shore nearby and the danger was manifest—they cast themselves into the waves, bidding farewell to that ship and all its cargo. I, left behind all alone, at first lay there, unable to move at all of my own accord, moving only as the ship moved. But later, having collected my thoughts and looked toward the danger, and having already before my eyes that **bitter death in the waters**³ , I began to bewail my own fate and to lament that foolish disobedience of mine. For the first time, I began to understand what terrors those who have offended their parents cast themselves into. But nevertheless—for why should I prolong—

---

¹ Our author is similar to himself in *History*, vol. I, p. 396, 8: "They experienced a terrible shipwreck; for immediately the sea **was in labor**, and a bright Hellespont wind descended, and with clouds it covered both the earth and the sea." He was imitating Homer, *Odyssey* 5.293: "and with clouds he covered the earth and the sea together." He was also imitating a fragment of Aristides which Hermogenes preserved in *On Types of Style* (1.26), and which Jebb wrongly omitted in the *Collection of Testimonies*. For Aristides says: "...for just as the sea-battle was joining, the sea **was in labor** and a bright Hellespont wind descended." These passages were conveniently provided to me by the learned diligence of L. Dindorf, who enriched the Didot *Thesaurus*. # C. BY PACHYMERES <note>Georgios Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a Byzantine historian and philosopher; this text is likely a "progymnasma" or a rhetorical exercise written in the voice of a character.</note>

...stay? For the terror pressed harder and the subsequent shipwreck was great. — With certain reasonings, as they seemed, not ignoble, I **strengthen**¹ myself, and against the terror I strangely **act with manly courage** <note>original: andrizomai; a Greek verb meaning to behave like a man or to show courage.</note>, as if either to live well, if I should survive, or to die well, and in either way to **hide the shame of my disinheritance**².

And after that, who could have the power to recount the terrors of that entire night? What wind did not marshal its blasts against me? What wave did not fall upon me alone, as its target, as if against a projecting rock, only to be dissolved into fine spray? There were times when it overwhelmed me, throwing me down upon the decks repeatedly, or even dragging me down toward the sea, tearing me from the ship as if in direct dispute over my body? I was **submerged** <note>original: ebaptisthēn; literally "I was baptized," here meaning to be dipped or plunged under water.</note> many times by sinking, but not even once did I yield my place on the ship to the wave. I came near to drowning many times, but in part I clung even to the ship. Many times I was submerged, but my mind was there, and having suffered these things I endured, until that terror eased, and I barely conquered that wild and irresistible surge; I conquered by holding on while it turned away, having first endured the terrors.

Then do you wish to deprive of the gift one who has struggled so, who has suffered so, who has run such a race for his life? And do you not judge this worthy of those many toils and struggles, which I have fought even beyond all strength? And for what reason, then, did I endure those great trials and hold out against so many hardships, when it would have been easy for me to seek salvation like the others and lean toward wherever I might be saved?

> “But,” he says, “one should show courage in other matters³.”

Do you say this to me? Say it to Fortune, say it to the **divine power** <note>original: daimōn; referring here to a personified fate or a guiding spirit.</note>. As if I would have boarded the ship on purpose—since it was my father’s, as you say—being a prophet, O Zeus! Or knowing from some god that a storm would certainly surround us, and the sailors would turn cowards before the terror, and I would then struggle beyond my strength, and receive from Fortune what from...

³ Scholion: **Metalepsis** <note>A rhetorical figure involving a shift from one context to another, or a specific type of word-play.</note>.

# C. BY PACHYMERES <note>Georgios Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "progymnasma," a rhetorical exercise written to demonstrate style and moral reasoning.</note>

...and may you find praise from many. Be humble toward everyone; be temperate; stand noble against pleasures. Keep your tongue free from lies, and your hands free from bribes. Share what you have with your neighbors. Choose to do well for yourself, but prefer the city even over yourself. And if you have the strength for counsel, do not grudge the resulting benefit to the people <note>original: dēmō; referring to the citizen body or the public interest</note>. From this you will become famous and esteemed by the city. Many, as is likely, will envy <note>original: baskanousin; to look upon with malice or begrudge success</note> you as you prosper; but do not even so desist from doing good for the city as much as you are able. Hold your father's words as your soul, and let them move you toward the good. Regarding your character, I could speak and advise you to follow your father, and I have confidence that this advice will generally benefit you; for I am not at all a ruined man, nor stingy, nor a striker, nor envious, nor a lover of lies, nor crooked in mind, nor a lover of evils. But as for me—I do not wish to speak of my own deeds; but you, choose what is better, and take what is useful from me, and take also from others what is profitable, considering as "fathers" all those whose actions you see you can benefit from. Yet, for your part, desire to lack nothing of what is noble; and to others, and to your father, give—

participle: *syllabōn antigraphous labōn* [collecting copies, having taken]. # STUDY 9 <note>The Greek word "Meletē" refers to a rhetorical exercise or declamation, common in Byzantine education, where a writer adopts a persona to argue a specific case.</note>

...and what is fitting for the mind, and what is necessary for custom, and that which follows for a time from innate choice. For what does it matter if you had a searching father, guarding tutors, and advising teachers, and benefited from being well-raised, while I—or perhaps someone else—lacking all these things by chance, was not able to maintain a blameless life in every respect? We are perhaps already old and have passed most of our life; we misused our youth, and habit became almost nature¹. Contrary to your mother, we associated with courtesans <note>original: hetairais; women who served as high-status companions in ancient society, often contrasted with the "temperate" wife</note>, which was not good. But you have a mother who is most venerable, capable of preparing you to embrace temperance <note>original: sōphrosynēn; a core Greek virtue involving self-control and excellence of character</note> through her own ways. Even if you do not gain this from me, take the example from her; do not imitate those things in which I am perhaps not praised by all, but follow in the footsteps of your mother, who is admired even by those who have not seen her, and gather what is useful. And if you wish to learn from me, listen to what I say, and turn away from what is blamed in me. For many things are distinguished and judged by the cutting edge of reason, and the better is separated from the worse. For no one can deceive themselves, even if they wish to; yet what one judges is not beneficial...

### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...better, he acts while being defeated [by his impulses]; and what disease is to the body, passion is to the soul. Just as no one who is sick would turn away from health, so too one who errs in soul would not consider virtue to be an evil. Because of this, a word once spoken for the purpose of advice alongside what is good is beyond suspicion, no matter who might say it. Why do you seek to know how the speaker acts? Action is a slave to passion, habit, and custom; but reason is free from all these. If you wish, you will gain even more from one who has been overcome by passions, insofar as that person knows exactly what that shame is like, and how bitter the defeat is; just as, surely, one might learn most reliably from the sick how great a good health is. Be stronger than pleasures. Do not be fluttered by the beauty of women, "nor let a woman with a swinging backside <note>original: *pygostolos*; a colorful term used by Hesiod to describe a woman who dresses to emphasize her anatomy to deceive men</note> deceive you," says the man from Ascra <note>Referring to the poet Hesiod, who was born in the village of Ascra</note> who was fed wisdom by the Muses. And if you should often be carried away or even caught, leap away immediately and do not remain there. For in the former case, you will be called a lecher; but by acting thus, you will be forgiven for the absurdity of the act, as a human being. I know that this passion is even valued by the laws themselves—

...valued, except especially in the case of women, whom they specifically call "companions" <note>original: *hetairas*; a term for high-status courtesans in ancient Greece</note>, who bring consequences upon both themselves and their children. This is what my father used to say; this is what I heard every day. Consequently, it was my constant labor and my one great effort to act according to his instructions.

But when I was enrolled among the ranks of men <note>This refers to the *ephebeia*, the formal transition from youth to adult citizenship</note> and reached the age when one must choose a profession, I appeared—how shall I say it?—as a lover of the people, and I admit I was an extreme devotee of our form of government. Setting aside the management of my household and the consideration of how I might amass as much personal wealth as possible, I devoted my energy to public affairs and, to the best of my ability, I took part in political life. I do not serve on embassies, I do not lead armies, I do not oversee the tax collectors, I do not preside as a magistrate, nor do I pursue any other such political office. But, if a council is ever called to discuss how something might be done properly and for the common good, and the councilors must gather to speak their minds as best they can, I too am summoned; I lend my mind to the city, and I lend my tongue to give voice to the thoughts of my mind. To what extent I succeed, and with what spirit I approach the task of giving counsel, you yourselves can bear witness. Bear—

### NINTH EXERCISE (CONTINUED)

The time I have spent in public life testifies for me; during this period, no one ever found cause to condemn me. Not only did no one bar me from this rostrum <note>original: *bematos*; the speaker's platform in a public assembly</note> or from the common council, but no one ever brought even a moderate complaint against me.

But this man, having arrived recently—from where, I do not know—stirs up a legal tribunal against me and agitates the Council. He judges me as a lawbreaker, even though I conduct my public life, as I maintain, according to the laws. Indeed, he brings this very charge against me: that my act of speaking and participating in politics is a violation of the law.

He rushes up and down, agitating the claim that there is a law preventing me from speaking. Yet, what this law is and what it decrees, he does not have the courage to state openly. But I am carrying the book of laws under my arm <note>original: *hypo males*; literally "under the armpit," an idiom for carrying something discreetly or ready for use</note>, and if it pleases you, I will read the law myself.

The law says: "The son of a companion <note>original: *hetairas*; a term for a high-status courtesan</note> shall not speak." Do you hear that, my good man? Let me repeat it; I will read it again. Pay close attention. Do you think, gentlemen, that I am attempting to deceive you by tampering with the text? Pay attention, I beg you: "The son of a companion shall not speak." You have heard the law. And it says: "The son of a companion I bar from the rostrum." What are you saying, man? That I am the son of a companion? What has possessed you to say such—

### NINTH EXERCISE

What are you saying? Do you speak thus of my mother <note>A word is missing here in the original, likely omitted through a scribe's error</note>, that venerable woman, the very ornament of womankind, she who practiced silence <note>original: *hē sigēn askousan*. This refers to a classical Greek ideal of female virtue where modesty was expressed through quietness. A famous line from Sophocles' play *Ajax* states: "Silence brings ornament to women."</note> and was so temperate? Either you are a stranger come from elsewhere and do not know her, or you are utterly mad. Call the neighbor women for me; call the female relatives, those from afar, and those who are strangers! They, being women themselves, will bear witness concerning a woman. For it is not entirely forbidden for women to bear witness. They too have their proper places to testify, especially regarding the most sacred matters where men are not permitted to be present, and they testify faithfully. One of these most sacred things is my mother's modesty, which was not only free from the plots of men but nearly beyond the reach of even being tested. It would have been better for you to call me a male prostitute, or ill-disposed, or any of the worst things, and to drive me from the Pnyx <note>The Pnyx was the official meeting place of the Athenian democratic assembly; the speaker refers to it as the heart of civic life</note>, if you could, than for you to dare to speak thus of her. Speaking these things, do you not shudder before Hera Zygia <note>original: *Zygian Hēran*. Hera "of the Yoke," the goddess who presides over the sanctity of marriage and the marriage bond</note>, the goddess who oversees venerable weddings? ### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

...of the council. Look for the son of a courtesan <note>original: *hetaira*, a term for a high-class female companion or prostitute</note>, and justly bar whoever you find engaging in politics here.
“But,” he says, “you were born of a male prostitute <note>original: *pornos*</note>, who associated with many women besides your mother.”
And what does this have to do with the ordinance of the laws? What security does this provide for the laws? Is the male prostitute not a man? Is the courtesan not a woman? What does a woman have in common with a man regarding the deeds each performs? Let me count the differences for you one by one. A man is able to travel abroad and provide for necessary needs; a woman stays at home and is devoted to wool-working <term>wool-working: *talasiourgia*, the traditional domestic labor of weaving and spinning that epitomized female virtue in the ancient world</term>. He goes to war and stands against enemies; she commands the maidservants and manages the household. He deliberates in council; she remains silent. He is permitted to be free with his pleasures; the law restrains her in her self-control, down to even a minor oversight. If you strip away the dignity of women, you will have stripped away their most defining characteristic.
Why then do you bring together things so far apart in their actions and reason through the unreasonable? You hear “courtesan” and you look for a “male prostitute.” Did the law not know nature, and mention the woman who is a courtesan, but also mention the man who is a male prostitute, if indeed these were the same thing according to your divination? For I have no explanation to give. If it intended to show both from one, it should rather have shown the worse from the better, implying the other.
I condemn your great foolishness, if you flee from wickedness, because in unfolding a civic law, you do not read it as it is written; but while it stands one way, you interpret it differently...

### STUDY 9

Show then what is unclear, and pride yourself on your interpretations, and gather arguments that do not exist according to your whim, but only from those which the text is able to provide.

Seeing these things, the legislator <note>original: *nomothetes*</note>, guarding against disgrace, restrains the son of a courtesan from the public assembly <note>original: *synedrion*</note> and strips him of all freedom of speech <note>original: *parrhesia*, the right to speak one's mind freely in public</note>, as if saying: "You, sir, have no part in the common freedom of speech and the status of a free man, of which <note>The grammar here suggests a link between the mother's behavior and the loss of the son's rights</note> your mother, by living poorly, deprived both you and herself. # STUDY IX.

->...to consider the laws as otherwise empty¹ words? Is this tolerable, O city-protecting gods and Hermes, from whom it was granted to the legislators—guided by you—to set forth the laws of the city?<-

I, for my part, say: these things are not tolerable, nor are they at all bearable to those who are prudent. And who would reach such a height of madness as to say it is right for the laws to be trampled upon, or to consider our most precious traditions as nothing? But nevertheless: show us the laws being set aside, and only then bring these charges. Present the lawbreaker, and only then judge and condemn him. For as long as you cannot point out the one who has erred, even if you speak of the crime as great, you cannot claim victory at all. Since a murderer is a terrible thing, a traitor is a terrible thing², and this or that evil is a terrible thing; what of it? If that thing is terrible, will the one you accuse be caught immediately, even if he does not admit to it?

Away with this "plausible" rhetoric! I know your mind, I know it. You calculate the zeal of the citizens, knowing that no one would allow—even in the slightest—to see a law set aside, and that they would sooner give up their lives than any of the city's customs³. Knowing this, you seize upon that zeal; you magnify the crime, and you think that by magnifying it you can lead the people astray. You hope that, even before you have shown that the crime actually applies to the accused, they will wish to punish him without mercy, cutting off the defense itself. But you will strike your oars against dry land, appearing like an ignorant fisherman⁴,

---

In any case, *pax* and "pax" <note>The Latin and Greek words for peace</note> have more probability.

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

### 178

...to train the child born of him better than the mother would, even if she were temperate and among the most dignified of women. Since he who is to have a share in public life and the council <note>original: βουλῆς (boules), the governing body</note> ought to possess experience in practical affairs from the very start, even if the councilor lacked knowledge, he would not be approved by the others, even if he were of noble and temperate birth. The vice of each of the two parents is scrutinized, and for this purpose alone: which of the two is capable of bringing more shame to the child and attaching **dishonor** <term>dishonor: *atimia*, a legal status in Ancient Greece involving the loss of a citizen's rights</term> to one who is otherwise handsome, temperate, and has reached the height of knowledge. 

Where is the justice in not examining the parents individually? If the father is a profligate, will he bring more shame upon his offspring—even when the son is delivering a speech to the city—than a mother who is a courtesan, surrendered to all who desire her, and possesses none of the equal rights of free women? This remains true even if she overflows with knowledge, or is weighed down with wealth, or is another **Lais** in beauty <note>Lais of Corinth was a famously beautiful and wealthy courtesan of the 4th century BCE</note>, and her son appears no less gifted in beauty, wealth, and intelligence. 

Will the child follow the father and live as a wastrel just like him? In that case, the son must certainly be driven away from the **Pnyx** <margin>Pnyx: see p. 169, n. 4</margin> <note>The Pnyx was the official meeting place of the Athenian democratic assembly</note>; but he should be driven away because of his *own* profligacy. Why should we seek out the father to condemn the young man? Each man’s own transgression is enough to bring him dishonor. But he will not follow the mother; even if she is dishonored, he will not be made equal to her at all. Yet, he will remain dishonored even if he is handsome, temperate, and dignified. Why? Because the shame of the mother descends even to the son. 

For so it seems to the law, and it is one of the legal penalties imposed on a prostitute: that not even the one born from her shall be honorable in the city, but like her, he himself shall be driven away from the public assembly. Thus, a mother being dignified, temperate, and intelligent does not benefit the son much if he, when put to the test, appears unworthy. A mother’s advantage does not necessarily pass to the son; but her defect *will* pass to him. Just as this defect keeps her from the freedom of speech enjoyed by the noble and dignified, so too will this same defect of the mother exclude him from the speaker's platform. She was shameless...

<summary>Pachymeres explores the legal and social inheritance of "atimia" (dishonor), arguing that while a mother's virtues do not automatically grant a son status, her "shame" as a prostitute legally bars him from public life and the speaker's platform.</summary>

### STUDY 9

...and a prostitute, neither truly devoted to this man nor loving that one, but surrendered to all, and submitting to no one as a husband. She holds onto this one while seeking another; she leaves that one and woos yet another. She is shameless, she is without affection; she is the **corruption of the city**, the source of disorder among women, a variegated hook of youth <note>original: ἄγκιστρον (ankistron), literally a "fishhook," used here as a metaphor for a seductive trap</note>. What father among all men can the child born of her know? Even if he should name this man, another disputes it; even if he names that one, another marks the offspring as his own. And so, having no father, he is suspected of belonging to everyone. 

Finally, the law assigns illegitimate children <term>illegitimate children: *notha*, children born outside of legal marriage</term> to the womb, and he who is suspected of belonging to many fathers becomes the child of his mother alone. Consequently, having nothing to be named for from a father, he is confined to the name of his mother. And the name of the mother is **courtesan** and **prostitute**, shameless and undisciplined, and whatever else might be of that kind and most wicked. Therefore, the son of the courtesan hears himself called the offspring of a harlot, the nursling of a shameless woman, the product of an undisciplined upbringing. 

Fine things these are for a city councilor! Fine indeed for a public speaker and orator! Will he speak out with vigorous boldness <term>boldness: *parrhesia*, the right of a free citizen to speak the truth plainly</term> against an enemy? Will he speak freely? Will he compete with confidence? In my view, he will be a cowering wretch <note>original: πτὼξ (ptox), a "cowering" person, often compared to a hare</note> before everyone; he will speak to curry favor, and he will flatter those who actually deserve a rebuke.

What will prevent such things in my case as well? Has my mother sold her own prime for shameful gains? Did she choose a disgraceful life for the sake of pleasure? Did she cast herself away into shame and clothe herself in the ultimate insults? Do I too not know the man who fathered me? Am I not even named after a father...

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

I have been named from of old; I am not merely called the son of "so-and-so," but of an honorable man, a citizen who suffered no legal penalty from the laws. Who stopped my father when he wished to participate in public life? Who spoke ill of him? Who turned away upon seeing him? Unroll the tablet of the **disenfranchised** <term>disenfranchised: *atimoi*, citizens who lost their civil rights and were barred from public speaking</term>; search, I beg you, if my father’s name is written anywhere in that book. But even if it were there (let us suppose this for the sake of argument), I certainly should not mention it; for it is not worthy. Yet, what is that to me? No matter what sort of man he was <note>The editor notes that Pachymeres uses a specific grammatical construction here that he repeats elsewhere in his works.</note>, he nonetheless raised his son as a free man. He brought me up under the care of **initiators and tutors** <term>initiators: *mystagōgoi*, literally those who lead one into the mysteries, here meaning high-level teachers</term>, and he spared no expense for my success. I should even say that from him I received the foundations for all good things, as he was always advising me, to the best of his ability, on what must be done and what must be avoided.

Do you wish to learn of my instruction? Look at the end result, consider my purpose. Nature has given to me—but I do not wish to say it, lest I seem burdensome by boasting about myself—but nonetheless, if it has given me anything, I do not keep it for myself alone. Instead, I set it forth for the common good; I engage in public life, and I offer counsel that is beneficial. And I say, "I do no wrong." But if I do wrong, as you claim, then you must demonstrate the wrongdoing, while I shall present to you the benefit.

And consider each point with me: through my counsels, I once made the people wealthy when they were in poverty. I brought war against those whom no one else dared to face, but at the mere report of whom they would tremble and seek to flee to the ends of the earth. I dealt with ambassadors, and having received **lions**, I sent them back as **hares** <note>original: λέοντας... λαγωούς (leontas... lagōous). A common classical metaphor for turning brave enemies into cowards.</note>; I sent out our own ambassadors with courage. As for the rest, so as not to dwell on each detail, I established matters properly and in a manner that you yourselves would say was fitting. These are the offspring of my "wrongdoing"; these things I did while "breaking the law," as you yourself claim. These actions...

# EXERCISE 9.

Indeed, while admitting that these things are for the good and benefit of the city, instead of giving due thanks, do you bring a **suit of illegality** <term>suit of illegality: *graphē paranomōn*, a legal action in ancient Athens used to challenge a decree or law on the grounds that it contradicted existing statutes</term> because of the manner in which they were done?

"But you should have helped the city *in another way*."

In another way? Tell me how; or rather, prove that my way was not fitting. And if you can show that it was unbecoming, then condemn me, and do not look for "another way" in which my service to the city should have occurred. For if it were not right for things beneficial to the city to come from me, then find fault with me, the method, and the actions themselves. Say to the people with all boldness: "It is not permitted for so-and-so to participate in public life because he is barred by the laws; even if his actions are extremely <note>The original Greek text is missing a word here, likely "noble," "good," or "useful."</note> and beneficial, yet they are not beneficial when they come from a lawbreaker <note>original: "para paranomountos"</note>. We must block every purpose of one barred by the laws, even if we are to be saved by him. Let us not prevent him from doing this, but allow that <note>The manuscript (Codex) variant here reads "let us see this."</note>." For one who is simply shut out by the laws has no "manner" of action that can be introduced.

If, therefore, I am barred by the laws, why do you seek a "manner" of benefit and say that I should have helped the city in another way? But if there is a way of being a benefactor <note>Perhaps: "of the act of benefitting."</note> while managing public affairs, and you disparage mine while introducing yours as "lawful," you shall hear quite rightly from me, I think, that this was how I *wished* to help the city, and this was how I was *able* to benefit my own people.

Do not, then, **object** <term>objection: *antilēpsis*, a rhetorical term for a counter-claim or a point of contention</term> on purpose, nor speak of another way—for you would have found reason to disparage that one too, had I acted according to it. For consider: if I had helped in another way, and had applied myself to embassies or the safeguarding of public interests, would you not have been able to say then too, if you wished, that it should have been done "in another way" and not like this? It was possible, my friend, being a citizen, to benefit the city to the best of one's ability; it was possible, having knowledge from **Hermes** <note>Hermes was the god of eloquence and communication; the speaker suggests his political skills are a divine gift of rhetoric.</note>,

### GEORGE PACHYMERES

I will not mutter a word <note>original: γρύξω (gryxō); literally to make a small sound like a grunt or a "humph." See footnote 1.</note>, nor will I offer some chance objection. For I shall know that I am being judged by those who do not envy me, but rather love me. I will be content to be condemned by you, rather <note>The original Greek implies the word "rather" here. See footnote 2.</note> than to be justified by this man. I will trust your words as if they were laws. I will depart rejoicing that a slanderer had no power against me, but that men learned in the law and zealous for civic customs and statutes have passed judgment. Even if someone should wish to advocate for me out of favor, or to soothe my grief, I will not accept it. I will trust you more when you condemn me than others when they acquit me. I will say then that the whole city condemned me, and the law of the common council excluded me, with those men judging and those men interpreting. For who else is a reliable guarantor to interpret the law in the future, and to declare innocent one whom they themselves dispassionately condemn?

I too love honor <note>original: τιμή (timē); in a Byzantine context, this refers to public status, rank, and the respect accorded to it</note>. And how could I not? Being a human being and a citizen of such a city, where so many people put into port. And there is much talk <note>The scribe likely omitted the preposition "about" (peri) here. See footnote 3.</note> among them concerning the men of rank; wherever they might appear while passing through the city, there is much discussion about them. "This man," they say <note>If the punctuation in the manuscript were shifted, this word could be read as a description of the listeners rather than a verb. See footnote 4.</note>, "is the illustrious <term>senator</term> <note>original: βουλευτής (bouleutēs); a member of the city council or Senate</note>; that one is the excellent <term>general</term> <note>original: στρατηγός (stratēgos)</note>; another is he who conducts public affairs justly. These are the men one must honor, and they must be honored by us, since we are strangers and in need of patrons." Whence they approach them, and honor them, and **bring them gifts** <note>original: δωροφοροῦσιν (dōrophorousin); the editor suggests this might be a mistake for "acting as an escort" (doryphorousin). See footnote 5.</note>, as is fitting. This honor I too love. I confess this passion; I want to be illustrious, I want to be admired. For why else have I labored so much—while others were slaves to their pleasures—and regulated my life in moderation, if not specifically so that in due time I might reap the fruits of my labors? I am a victim of <term>ambition</term> <note>original: φιλοτιμία (philotimia); literally "love of honor." While it can mean "ambition," it was often viewed as a positive trait of a civic-minded aristocrat</note>, for which I have been diligent. I am a victim of glory, for the sake of which I lived attentively and with self-restraint; even if I inherited any stain from my father, I wished to erase it and overwrite it with better things. I wanted these things to be present throughout my life, to adorn me and to make me great in the eyes of all.

->### STUDY IX.<-

->24<-

But what should I do? I have nothing else to ask of you but to attend strictly to the **law**, to read it frequently, and to be judges not of this person or that, but of the law itself. One person might be able to reason <note>In the sense of drawing a logical conclusion or "syllogizing."</note> according to this man (and I grant this); but another might be able to distinguish the argument and take the <term>literal text</term> <note>original: τὸ ῥητόν (to rhēton); the explicit, written word of the law as opposed to its perceived intent or spirit.</note> as it is set down, setting aside misinterpretations—those mental assaults that lean this way and that, justifying one thing and condemning another according to one’s whim. The first clarity of the law is the literal text, read as it is, just as it was written. If someone introduces something from the outside, one person will say this and another will say that, and from this comes ambiguity and a battle between interpretations. But why must I teach men who are well-versed in laws and judgments? Why not simply speak to the others with the confidence I have in you, and be rid of these present troubles more quickly?

Fellow citizens—for I must also address the **epilogue** to you—it is a fine thing for everyone to be zealous for the city. It is a fine thing to pay the <term>rearing-fees</term> <note>original: τροφεῖα (tropheia); the debt of gratitude and support a child owes a parent, here applied to the citizen's debt to the state that "nurtured" them.</note> to the city that raised us, as far as we are able. We should not, having once taken the **form of a statue** <note>original: εἰκόνος σχῆμα λαβόντας. See footnote 1 below. The speaker suggests that citizens should not be stiff and unmoving like a monument.</note>, each seek only our own interest, but rather we should change along with the times and the events that befall us. Thus, one might appear humble and gracious when the time is right for it, but at another time appear uncompromising and even abrasive to the majority, when it is necessary to give counsel that might not please the masses. At one time, one might be silent and fight with no one; at another time, one might be troublesome and stubborn if the occasion calls for persuading and stirring the lazy majority to struggle on behalf of the city.

And if no one prevents him, it is a fine thing to **act** <note>See footnote 2 below regarding the likely correction of "mold" to "act."</note> without having excuses. But even if someone does try to prevent him by making excuses, it is right not to abandon one's original zeal. Instead, one should hold fast again to common discourse and good counsels, and speak against the one attempting to stop him, labeling him as someone ill-disposed to the city and a domestic enemy. Nevertheless, one must entrust the final judgments to the common councilors. If they do not declare against you or exclude you from the council, you should pay little heed to your accusers and the things they use to bar you. But if the councilors, in their judgment, should condemn you, and—

->### STUDY X.<-

...[presenting her case], as she is not permitted to do so at all by the laws. Since she is barred by the laws, I am advocating for her according to the laws, simply and justly. For it is granted that others may speak on behalf of the **disenfranchised** <term>disenfranchised</term> <note>original: ἀτίμων (atimōn); individuals who had lost their civil rights and were legally prohibited from addressing the court or assembly themselves.</note>, lest any justice they might possess be overlooked and vanish, and the judges inadvertently do wrong to that party. I do not think it is reasonable for those who have sworn to judge according to what is just to commit an injustice. Therefore, **I lend my tongue to the prostitute**¹ <note>original: Κιχρῶ τοίνυν τῇ πόρνῃ τὴν γλῶτταν; a rhetorical metaphor where the advocate provides the "voice" for a person legally silenced.</note>, and while she stands aside, I have come forward to offer her just arguments, intending to present to you whatever assistance is available to her from the city’s laws.

Let no one, therefore, look at the fact that she is such a person; rather, let him lend his ears to the fact that every person is permitted—by both laws and customs—to speak on their own behalf and offer whatever they believe will help them. Listen, then, not to her recounting the matter, but to me speaking. For perhaps by understanding the matter from this perspective, you will render a verdict according to the intent of the laws, and you will not be led astray by the persuasive speech of this bitter orator.

Now², the present contest involves the daring and shamelessness of a prostitute, and her presumed disregard for the established laws; on my part, it involves a lack of daring and a sense of dread in advocating for her. But you must not at all condemn me for impropriety <note>original: ἀκαιρίαν (akairian); literally "untimeliness" or acting at the wrong moment, here meaning a breach of social decorum.</note> because I have set out to speak for her. For if I had proposed to show that the deed she committed was blameless—wearing gold jewelry and parading through the streets without a blush when the laws explicitly forbid it—I would perhaps seem to many, or rather to all, to be shameless. I would be carrying more shame than the prostitute herself if I, being an **orator** <term>orator</term> <note>original: ῥήτωρ (rhētōr); a professional public speaker and legal advocate.</note> raised on the laws and a foster-child of this very courtroom, dared to say such things and, as it were, perform wonders <note>original: τερατεύεσθαι (terateuesthai); to speak in a way that is marvelous, deceptive, or unnatural.</note>. From such speech, she might perhaps be pardoned ...[but I] would be [regarded] as just [to be punished]³ if I were going to attempt such daring in front of all of you⁴—a daring that far surpasses even that of the prostitute. But, since this man [the accuser] puts forward a law against the act, yet misinterprets the law because he wishes to impose the fine, and—

<header>III. BY PACHYMERES</header>

He makes this matter more bitter for the woman, and by changing the pronunciation, he adds a sharp accent to the word¹ <note>original: παροξύνει (paroxynei); a pun meaning both "to sharpen an accent" and "to provoke/exasperate." I wish to say a few things³ to him and show that he either ignores the city's laws by skimming them superficially, or else he is acting maliciously to the bitter detriment of the wretched woman. 

Therefore, let whatever pertains to the prostitute—leading her to the punishment and retribution appropriate for her actions—be hers alone and not mine. But my task is to interpret the laws exactly as they were originally written. If someone reads them otherwise to satisfy their own desires, I will immediately expose their malice. My purpose is to assist the laws themselves no less than the citizens. And let no one say from now on that the prostitute or speaking on behalf of a prostitute is shameful; rather, let them say that the established laws and speaking for the laws is a truly noble thing⁴. For in this way, you too, setting aside the prostitute and her affairs, will belong entirely to the city's laws. You would surely consider it just to support these laws, so that if they are not diverted in any way, certain people cannot intentionally do wrong to many others.

I wish⁵ to remind your **Decorum** <note>original: κοσμιότητα (kosmiotēta); a formal, respectful way of addressing a jury or a body of citizens, similar to "Your Honors."</note> from a point slightly further back in time. I will discuss—ostensibly concerning the woman herself who is the reason for this present assembly, but in truth concerning the nature of the vice itself—how it crept into your state long ago like some other grievous disease.

<header>DECLAMATION 10.</header>

Lais¹ lived in Corinth—Lais, whose mere name, unless one guards themselves with <term>temperance<note>original: σωφροσύνῃ (sophrosyne); a Greek ideal of excellence of character and soundness of mind, involving self-control and moderation.</note></term>, sets the soul on fire with pleasure. The Corinthians held her as if she were one of their most illustrious spectacles. Though they ought to have dishonored her or driven her from their city as if she were a <gloss>pollution</gloss>² and a common ruin of the youth within it, they instead pampered her. They granted her such freedom of speech that she would swagger through the streets, draped in all kinds of finery and escorted by many followers, just like one of the sacred and great personages revered by the city, or those who are entitled to public honors.

Since she attracted not only those who wished for her but also foreigners visiting the city to her charms, the "disease" of this passion found a foothold in other cities as well. Because the Corinthians did not punish Lais but instead praised her excessively³, other "Laises" appeared everywhere, including here. You all know that famous Athenian "Fly"⁴, and after her another, and then yet another.

This passion is ancient, I believe, and has been nurtured over many ages.

In those times, the wise men of our ancestors' day—whom one would not be wrong to call "common benefactors"—saw this passion spreading even into this <gloss>city</gloss>⁵ of ours. They thought deeply about the matter, realizing that once something has taken root and been solidified by time, it is not easy to remove—especially when it provides the citizens with no ordinary pleasure. Simply...

# OF PACHYMERES
<columns>2</columns>

They <note>Referring to the ancient lawgivers.</note> believed that legislating to prohibit such behavior would be like trying to divert or transform any other established custom of the state. For just as a doctor cannot stop a disease of its own accord—especially one that has become chronic—neither can the **fathers of the state**² immediately put an end to a city's habit, particularly when it leads to the ease and pleasure of those who pursue it and is therefore not easily abandoned. However, they considered it the mark of a truly skilled statesman to treat the matter gently: to take foresight on how the "passion" might diminish over time and, as if cutting out the roots even if they could not yet pull down the tree, to allow time to wither what was previously blooming.

Consequently, they wisely set forth laws, not strictly barring the courtesan <term>hetaira<note>A high-status professional companion or courtesan in ancient Greece, often educated and influential, distinct from common prostitutes.</note></term> from her trade, but rather passing many significant judgments against her if she persisted in this passion and placed every warning second to her own choice. One of these laws is that she may not wear gold ornaments when appearing in public, nor may she take pride in her display and beauty. If she should do anything prohibited while disregarding the law, they would exact the appropriate fine for each offense. In this way, they preserved for the woman who had turned to courtesanship the freedom inherited from her fathers—as something necessary and unchangeable—while subjecting her to specific fines. This was done so that, while her freedom remained intact, she would not be ready to descend into total **shamelessness**³, and by counting herself among the free-born, she might still have the opportunity⁴ to relearn **temperance** <term>sophrosyne<note>original: τὸ σῶφρον; a Greek ideal of self-control, moderation, and excellence of character.</note></term>, to repent, and to change for the better.

As for this woman, who is the subject of our current legal struggle, I cannot say what sort of parents she had, what kind of upbringing she received, or how she took up this profession. For now, let it suffice that her parents were of our own city. When I say "of our own city,"

That I should call them solemn, temperate, and$^1$ beautiful, and that you—the listeners—should suspect this, is only to be expected; for **temperance** and **solemnity** are the city's own particular ornaments. Whether these qualities have been cast aside here by chance, let this be granted to the people and the masses, as if to some complex living body which finds it difficult, or rather impossible, to remain entirely the same throughout.

Certainly, I believe that those who sired her, being fathers and obeying the laws of nature, educated the little daughter worthily and as was necessary. For who would ever choose for their own offspring to appear base, bringing dishonor and reproach upon their own family, even if they stood to gain much from the child's wickedness? **Away with such an impulse**, you who say this! Let nothing else close your mouth but your own personal care for your own child. You would easily, I think, sacrifice life itself$^2$ so that your child would not be considered unpleasant—to say nothing more—especially when being educated by you. They, too, gave warnings, as is likely, they gave warnings; and while they were alive, the daughter was perhaps temperate and solemn. But what can one say when the **divine power** <note>original: *daimonion*—often referring to fate or a guiding spirit</note> proves more dominant? For they perhaps kept their daughter as a "secluded housekeeper,"$^3$ according to the custom of the city, and were preparing a marriage for the girl and testing the one who would take her. ### STUDY 10.

She is excluded from common gatherings and driven away from those places where **temperate** women spend their time. She accepts the legal fines mandated by the law, and she understands—as much as a woman can who has no part in the <term>parrhesia</term> <note>original: "parrhesia"—the right to speak freely in public, a privilege of male citizens</note> of the city—what the laws require of her. But having once embraced the worst path, her own character has become her law; she lives among the dishonored and pursues only that which satisfies her desire.

Since she has chosen a life of desire—even if someone might mock her for it—she also desires to be adorned with gold, which she has indeed received in abundance from many men. She does this not out of contempt for the laws (heaven forbid!), but by chance, being a slave to her cravings in this as in all other things.

But she could not escape the notice of the **inspectors** <note>original: "epoptas"—public officials who monitored behavior or religious rites</note> while living in such a manner and conducting herself contrary to the laws of the state. She was immediately caught wearing gold jewelry, and she was brought under the power of the laws so that she might pay the prescribed penalty. Thus, she learns that her <term>anaideia</term> <note>original: "anaideias"—shamelessness or lack of modesty</note>, for the sake of which she dared such things, leads to a precise financial loss. And look, having learned what the legal fine for her action is, she is certainly distressed—and how could she not be?—at being deprived of her own finery. Nevertheless, reluctantly and against her will, she is prepared to surrender the gold so that these items may become **public property** according to the laws.

For the law explicitly declares: "If a <term>hetaira</term> <note>original: "hetaira"—a professional companion or courtesan of high status</note> should wear gold, let it be public." If a courtesan should adorn herself with gold, it says, let these things be public property. Thus, she, having adorned herself contrary to the law, is sentenced to be fined according to the law.

But this man—I know not where he comes from—being a truly heavy and bitter accuser, says: "The law does not want the gold, but the **courtesan herself** to become public property." He provokes the written text and interprets the word "let it be" <note>original: "esto"—a singular verb form</note> as a singular command. "Let her be," he says, "the woman herself public property, because she wore gold."

What are you saying, man? Do you define the greatest punishments even for chance transgressions, and for things which one might rather...

<meta>This page continues the declamation by George Pachymeres. In the previous section, a woman was caught wearing gold jewelry in violation of the law. Here, the speaker argues against a literal or "incorrect" reading of the law, using a technical point of Attic Greek grammar to suggest that the prosecutor is being unfairly harsh by misinterpreting the text.</meta>

<page-num>194</page-num>
->### C. BY PACHYMERES<-

...would you forgive what was done, or would you wish to prosecute? Are you such a bitter avenger and an unyielding punisher, simply because you found someone who has committed a fault? Know that you are not reading the law correctly. Shift the accent of the written word back <note>original: "proparoxune"—meaning to move the accent to the third-to-last syllable, which changes the grammatical form of the word</note>, and use the Attic custom—being an Athenian yourself—and make the word "let it be" <note>original: "esto"</note> plural.

If you had not been born or raised here, but somewhere else, and were therefore ignorant of the Attic custom—and how they pair a singular verb with plural nouns, provided they are <term>neuter</term> <note>The "Attic Schema" is a rule in ancient Greek where plural nouns of the neuter gender take a verb in the singular. The speaker is arguing that a specific verb in the law should be interpreted this way.</note>—then perhaps someone might forgive you for reading the law that way. But since you are an Athenian man, and have mastered our dialect to the highest degree—hearing even the women here, and those who live a rustic life, and the manual laborers speaking this way, as they possess a native and noble tongue—how is it just for you not to understand this, and not to read the law¹ according to the Attic syntax? 

And even if someone² moved the accent and the book has the text written that way, you ought to have gone back to the legislator³ and examined his intention⁴, and from there taken the resolution of the ambiguity, employing what is truly **fitting**. For the **fitting** is found everywhere among beautiful things, and no one who employs it has ever gone wrong.

Indeed, look at what is **fitting** in every action, and see how much strength it gives to the speaker. It is fitting for a father to be caring toward his own offspring; and it is fitting, conversely, for a pirate to be harmful to those he encounters. For suppose a father, sailing with his only son, had happened upon pirates, and the boy was submerged under the waves while the father was present; and the pirate and the father were disputing with one another about that event, and which of them was the cause of the boy’s drowning. If you were the judge of their dispute over the boy’s fate, would you—based on what is likely—condemn the pirate or the father? Is it not absolutely necessary to condemn the pirate? Thus, in every case, the **fitting** serves as a revelation even for things that are unknown.

***

¹ <margin>The negation "not" should be understood as repeated before the word "read."</margin>
² <margin>Meaning, some scribe or copyist.</margin>
³ <margin>original Latin/French: "Sic vernacule dicimus: 'recourir au législateur'" — As we say in the common tongue: "to have recourse to the legislator."</margin>
⁴ <margin>Scholion: The intention of the law-giver.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical argument attributed to George Pachymeres, an 13th-century Byzantine scholar. The speaker is challenging an opponent's interpretation of a law, arguing that legal texts must be understood through the "intent" of the lawgiver and the principle of "what is fitting" (to prepon), rather than a strictly literal or grammatically incorrect reading.</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>STUDY 10.</header>

Tell me, from what grounds do you speak when you claim that the lawgiver is well-disposed to the city, and that whatever he might legislate is for the common good <gloss>1</gloss>? How can you say this when you know nothing of that man, nor how he felt toward the city in his opinions and his purpose? Or <gloss>2</gloss> do you simply grant him the benefit of what is fitting? For you assume that if he had legislated otherwise, the people of that time would not have accepted his laws. Do you think they would have accepted them if he were ill-disposed <gloss>3</gloss>? Indeed, if he were even merely suspected by some of not being well-disposed <note>original: "eunous"</note> <gloss>4</gloss>, they would hardly have tolerated his laws—in fact, they wouldn't have even tolerated the man himself standing there in silence.

**Do you see** how much power the concept of "what is fitting" <term>to prepon</term> <note>A central principle in ancient rhetoric and ethics, meaning what is appropriate or suitable to a specific character or situation.</note> has over things that are unknown or ambiguous? Examine, then, the mind of the lawgiver in this same fitting manner.

**Was it** <gloss>5</gloss> fitting for him to legislate the greatest penalties and punishments for accidental or minor offenses? Or was it more fitting for the legal reckoning to be in proportion to the sins committed? Please, consider this.
**Did someone** insult so-and-so? Look at the law concerning insult, and see what kind of penalty the law considers just for the victim to take from the offender.
**Has someone** murdered another person? Look at a different law, and a different penalty to which the murderer is subject. Would you say the penalties in these two cases are equal? Where would be the justice in thinking that penalties should be equal for unequal crimes? Furthermore, if someone is going to <gloss>6</gloss> undergo the one and same penalty whether they have committed a small sin or a great one, why would a person wishing to do wrong only attempt small crimes? They might as well commit great ones, if they are to be caught and punished in exactly the same way.

<gloss>1</gloss> **To be for the common good**] In the phrases "for goodwill" (or rather "misfortune") and "for ambition," I previously understood the word **to tend** <note>original: "teinein"</note> (referring to page 52, note 2). From this passage, however, the word **to be** <note>original: "einai"</note> is better understood as the implied verb.

<gloss>2</gloss> **The manuscript has "ē" <note>unaccented</note>.** I have written it as **"ê"** <note>accented as a confirmation or "or"</note>, as I have done elsewhere. The poet Meleager (Anthology 5.191), as he approaches his girlfriend's house, says to himself: "...will I see that luxury-loving girl still in her bed, wakeful, weeping much by the lamp? **Or** [ê] does she have a bedfellow? Having withered at the porch, I will hang my suppliant garlands wet with my tears..." The question mark seems to fit poorly with what follows. Perhaps it should be read as "Or she has...

...a bedfellow. **At the porch...**" The poet must be imagined to have seen a rival lover admitted inside by his girlfriend through the cracks of the door or some other way. He speaks the rest in despair. Doors that were poorly closed often brought trouble to courtesans. Rufinus says to an incautious young woman in the Anthology 5.41: "Bolt the porch." It could also be read: "If she has a bedfellow, at the porch..." But that is less fitting; if that were the reading in the manuscript, I would still propose **"ê"** [meaning "or"].

<gloss>3</gloss> **I have phrased this as a question.**

<gloss>4</gloss> **The word "well-disposed"** <note>original: "eunous"</note> **seems to have been omitted from the text.**

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense or legal commentary attributed to George Pachymeres. Following the previous page’s discussion on the "intent" of the lawgiver and the principle of what is "fitting" (to prepon), the speaker now applies these principles to a specific case: a law concerning a prostitute (hetaira) who wears gold jewelry, arguing that the penalty should be proportional to the offense.</meta>

<page-num>196</page-num>
<header>OF PACHYMERES</header>

Did the prostitute sin by wearing gold jewelry? What was the nature and magnitude of her sin? Because, it is said, she acted shamelessly toward everyone, spoke with excessive boldness <note>original: "peparresia-stai". In a Greek civic context, "parrhesia" or free speech was a right of citizens; for a marginalized woman to speak boldly was seen as a subversion of social order.</note>, adorned herself, and behaved luxuriously before those who saw her. She does not know in which rank—that is, which status<gloss>1</gloss>—the law places her; for it is not the highest rank, which others share in, but rather the law shoves her aside and deems her worthy of the lowest portion, a place without the right to speak, and one that offers nothing to make the person stationed there proud. Yet she even takes pride in being seen and adorns herself by putting on gold jewelry. This is the way of the harlot; this is the sin of the unrestrained woman; this is the prostitute’s transgression. Truly, then, the law punishes her. What penalty should it impose? Perhaps the greatest and most inescapable? Or <gloss>2</gloss> entirely in proportion to the transgression?

I, for my part, believe that the lawgiver considered the confiscation of the gold jewelry to be a sufficient punishment. For in the very things about which she was so proud, by having them taken away, she will be humbled. A sufficient loss will be added by becoming poor suddenly after being wealthy, losing in a single hour the wealth she collected over a long period from the wages of prostitution. This is just as if someone, having gathered all their wealth and placed it on a ship, then encountered an unkind sea and barely escaped with their life while losing everything <note>A common rhetorical metaphor in Greek literature comparing sudden reversal of fortune to a shipwreck.</note>.

> “Let the wealthy woman then become poor,” says the writer of the law, “and let her who did not know how to use wealth well be disciplined by its loss, so that having experienced the terrors of poverty from then on, if she should ever happen upon wealth again, she might have the lesson sufficient from her suffering and guard herself against deceptive luxury. This fine will both discipline her—since she will no longer have the means to adorn herself—and will strike the greatest fear into other women, lest for the sake of a small pleasure they lose their entire wealth, which alone among many things they found delight in.” This is the prostitute’s sentence; this is the intent of the lawgiver.

For it was likely <gloss>3</gloss> that he, being wise, would also discern that she, being a woman and spending her leisure on other matters, and being ignorant,

### EXERCISE 10.

...should act in this way. For the penalties for those who act out of ignorance are one thing, and the penalties for those who act out of contempt are another. If someone breaks the law out of contempt, they shall bear a double penalty: once for the contempt they showed, and once for the law they broke. But if one sins out of ignorance, they fall within the bounds of pardon. Because they sinned, they shall be punished; but because they did so without knowing, they shall receive a moderate sentence, because the transgression was involuntary <note>original: "akousion"</note> and happened not according to their own will, but because of their ignorance.

Surely it is more likely that a courtesan <term>hetaira; a high-status prostitute in ancient Greek society who was often better educated than average women but still socially marginalized</term> sins against the law out of ignorance rather than contempt. For who is there to educate her? What kind of assembly of virtuous people, and for what purpose, would prepare her to learn what she was previously ignorant of? She is barred from every assembly; she is cast out of every council. Even if she should hide herself and slip in secretly to sit beside the other women, she is immediately sent away as one who is bold and shameless. And if she should weave herself into gatherings to learn something useful, she is driven out as a pollution <note>original: "agos"; a source of ritual contamination or a curse</note> to the virtuous women. Even if a teacher should present himself, he becomes a lover instead of a teacher; abandoning those laws and what they proclaim, he proves himself to be entirely devoted to her passions.

Therefore, you will justly grant pardon to her when she sins out of ignorance. Furthermore, whatever small penalty is imposed is a sufficient punishment for one who has transgressed due to this ingrained ignorance.

In this way, you too should reconcile the text. Thus you are able both to "Atticize" <note>To write or speak in the prestigious, classical style of ancient Athens—a key goal for Byzantine scholars.</note> this common and everyday usage, and at the same time to impose penalties for wrongs <note>original: "adikematon"</note> according to reason upon those who sin...
