...the text is sharpened. I demand that she herself becomes public property in this way, so that even if I do not act according to the specific intent of the law, I may nonetheless satisfy the law in abundance. **Since the woman has been established as a public slave, her gold ornaments will follow her, and those too will be dedicated to the public treasury. Is this not what you say, searching up and down <note>original: "ano kai kato"; a Greek idiom meaning to search thoroughly or "inside and out." See page 168, note 3.</note> for security regarding the laws? Have I clearly explained the aim of your arguments? You say you do not know where the law leans or what it clearly defines. But let us suppose the law refers to the courtesan, or let us suppose it refers to the gold. Let the woman become public property, whether the law wills it or not. If the law does not intend for her, but rather the gold, to be public property, let the woman be public anyway; in either case, the gold will become public property for me.**

**But**, my good man, the danger to this wretched woman is no small thing—that she should be enslaved to the whole populace even if the law does not intend it, simply because you command it for the sake of "legal security," as you put it. If the law commands her to be enslaved to the public <margin>The manuscript reads "publicly." Also found on page 47, line 8.</margin>, then let her be both a slave and public property; let her be punished not by you, but by the laws which so command. But if the law does not command her [to be enslaved], but rather the gold to be public, how is it just for the woman who sinned to pay such a heavy penalty? It is a penalty that neither the law knows, nor the humane <term>philanthropon; the principle of "philanthropia" or legal mercy, often invoked in Byzantine law to favor the less harsh interpretation</term> character of the people allows.

**Moreover**, there is another law, one of the ancient ones: if a law should appear ambiguous in any way, the judges should interpret it toward the more humane side. For it says, "**In ambiguous matters, let humanity prevail.**" What cruelty then would you not surpass if—when there is an ambiguity as to whether this woman or the gold is intended by the law to be subjected to the public treasury—you choose to place this woman, and not the gold, under the ultimate accountability <term>euthyne; originally a public official's end-of-term audit, here meaning a severe legal reckoning or punishment</term> and thus condemn a human being? You say, "**The prostitute contains the gold as one possessing a possession.**" But it is not right for her to be condemned because of this. There are many things that lie in ambiguity, and there one will find both...

The city certainly contains the Piraeus <note>The Piraeus was the famous port of Athens, connected to the main city by the Long Walls.</note>, and there is a law that those Athenians building ships in the Piraeus must be <term>joint-contributors</term> <note>original: "synteleis"; citizens who shared the financial burden of public works, like building warships.</note> to the public treasury. And finally, aside from the fact that many others would unjustly suffer such a reproach, will even the Athenians be called traitors to the glory of their fathers? The Athenians—O gods who protect the city, and sacred oracles, and glorious Salamis <note>The site of the great naval victory against the Persians in 480 BCE.</note>, and all the brilliant and greatest achievements there!

Do not, therefore, consider only this: that the "contained" are brought in along with the "containers." Rather, consider whether it is fair and just that, if someone is condemned by the laws in a specific part, they should be forced to pay a universal penalty. And if the intent of the law is to hold the courtesan accountable by means of her gold ornaments—an existing law which you are ignoring—you instead condemn her person, making a "public slave" of one who is forever free, even if she has committed the most shameful acts.

Nor should you merely consider that she is a courtesan, and from that point attack the woman as "dishonorable." She is a courtesan and dishonorable; I say so too, and so does everyone—

<meta>This page continues the rhetorical defense of a woman accused of being a courtesan. In the previous section, the speaker argued that social ostracization—exclusion from festivals and civic life—is already a severe punishment. Here, the argument shifts to a psychological and economic defense, exploring how poverty (Necessity) forces women into such lives, and questioning whether wealth can ever truly erase the "habit" of one's past or the stain of legal trouble.</meta>

<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>BY GEORGE PACHYMERES</header>

<note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "declamation," a formal rhetorical exercise used in Byzantine schools to practice legal and moral arguments.</note>

...[poverty makes one] wandering and foolish, helpless in all things despite being resourceful, a scorner of the gods though previously very pious and God-fearing, and negligent toward civic order though only yesterday and the day before he was solemn and well-behaved. If poverty takes hold of a woman—especially one who is young, tender, and <term>easily deceived</term> <note>original: "euexapatēton"</note>—since she cannot obtain the necessities of life from any other source, poverty prepares the woman to use the only thing she possesses. And since she has nothing else besides her body, she uses it to provide for her own nourishment. For most women, this <term>misconduct</term> <note>original: "akolasia"; refers to a lack of restraint or a licentious lifestyle.</note> comes not from their own choice, but from sheer necessity. Womanhood and poverty meeting in the same place: from the one comes the opportunity for deception; from the other, the assault of necessity. Even if she attempts to act wisely and with endurance, standing more manfully against the deception, the violence of necessity prevails. Thus, she who was once modest and in control of her desires is led away as a captive by necessity, and she turns to misconduct as a means of procuring food. This is how the character of many women is corrupted.

It is not far from the truth to suggest that this woman, in the same manner, appeared to be "bad."

But if you say she possesses something now, and you point to her gold as proof of her wealth, let that be so. Nevertheless, <term>habit is a second nature</term> <note>original: "ethos... physis"; a common Greek proverb suggesting that long-term behavior becomes as fixed as biological nature.</note>, and in many people, it is difficult to shake off. What then? If she loses these things to the public treasury according to the laws, will she not be destitute again, possessing nothing more than she had at the beginning?

Do you really think that she, having scorned the established laws, has "repaired" herself simply by means of gold? To what end do you devise these arguments, and for what reason? Is it because she has frequently "conversed" with the laws, or frequently stood before the law courts, or because she has associated with free and modest women and was able to hear what is lawful? Tell me, what opportunity—

### STUDY 10. 203

Who, I ask, could ever show me that this woman was a student of the laws? Who would be the one to teach a woman—especially one living such a life, and therefore barred on all sides from those places where she might have learned something useful? She was ignorant, then; she was truly ignorant. And there is much room for forgiveness for such ignorance among those who sit in judgment. Perhaps from this case, another woman will learn the requirements of the laws and will keep them, out of fear for what has been commanded.

Therefore, just as another woman, learning from this one, will guard against such an action as being unlawful, so too might this woman have learned from someone else, if only it had happened that another had faced this accusation before her. But the one who is ignorant, and is the first to be caught for these reasons <note>The speaker refers to the specific circumstances of her trade and the laws she broke.</note>, is within the bounds of forgiveness.

But you—if you insist, do not forgive her. Take the penalty according to the laws and make her gold jewelry <term>public property</term> <note>original: "demosia"; property confiscated by the state.</note>. Why do you increase the fine, when it would be more just to relax even the penalty already set? You would make this woman—who has already lost her sense of shame—destitute. You would force her, who once made a poor showing of herself in public splendor, to slink back into the corners and skulk about the house. If you take away her gold, you take away her entire wealth. How much time must pass before this trade of hers makes her wealthy again? You take her wealth, and poverty will seize her again like a prisoner of war. And while you might set her free from this court, Fate will enslave her once more. You, as is likely, will show mercy—or rather, this present compassionate court will—but poverty will weigh upon her more heavily, forcing her back into her old ways. You—but why must I say more?—you will perhaps spare her as she pleads for pity and will lower the intensity of the legal struggle. But she will suffer many things before she finds any kindness from <term>Necessity</term> <note>original: "ananke"; the personification of compulsion or dire need, often depicted as an irresistible force.</note>, whose strength is unyielding, whichever way it may lean.

# G. PACHYMERES

...to be adorned and beautified. Otherwise, there will be no lack of those who will report you to the public. And thereafter, if for a time you happen to find judges who are humane, you will merely turn from being wealthy women into poor ones. But if—as often happens¹—the arguments of your accuser prevail, what do you think you deserve to suffer? I myself, through my ignorance of the laws, appeared to treat them with contempt and was instantly placed in extreme danger. I might even have been stripped of my very freedom <note>In ancient and Byzantine legal contexts, extreme debt or certain crimes could lead to a loss of status or "civil death."</note>, had not some kind fate protected me before the judges. To some, I seemed worthy of pardon, as one who stumbled out of ignorance rather than defiance. But you—what will you say then, having seen what I suffered and knowing that the law is open to interpretation when its meaning is unclear?"

But enough of her words to those women. Speaking a few brief words to you in her place, I shall now conclude my speech.

***

¹ **Often** <note>original: Πολλάκις (pollakis)</note> should apparently be understood here as "perchance" or "perhaps," a meaning I already noted on page 73, note 2; it will likely appear again in Declamation 12, if I am not mistaken. I am not quick to accept this sense, as it is so contrary to the very nature of the adverb *pollakis* (often). In a famous passage of Thucydides (Book 2, Chapter 13), Pericles is said to have suspected that Archidamus might "often" <note>meaning: perhaps</note> pass by his lands. Those translators who today render *pollakis* with the Latin word *forte* (by chance/perhaps) find, I believe, few readers who agree with them—and rightly so. For, according to Thucydides, Archidamus would not act by chance, but either because he personally wished to do a favor, or because the Spartans ordered it. And in that sentence of Plato which I used on the page cited above, *pollakis* can also be understood in its usual sense. Heliodorus (Book 1, Chapter 10) writes: "Our common child, whom I have 'often' loved more than you." If one translates it as "whom I have *perhaps* loved more than you," it suits the character speaking; but it is more consistent with the Greek words if one takes the adverb *pollakis* in its usual sense and renders it: "to whom I have **frequently** shown even greater love than to 

<column-break/>

yourself." The Roman poet Lucretius, writing on the origin of diseases (Book 6, line 1098), says: "or they 'often' [saepe] arise, having sprung from the earth itself." If the adverb here is taken in the sense of doubt (perchance), the poet is better served than if we change the word to the ablative of the noun *saepe* <note>meaning "hedges" or "fences" in Latin</note>, which has occurred to some scholars. But nothing prevents it from simply meaning "frequently." Virgil seems to have followed Lucretius in his noble comparison: "And just as when a riot has 'often' [saepe] broken out in a great crowd." In this verse, many learned men since the scholar Abresch have taken "often" to mean "perchance" [forte], without any necessity; they did not consider the following verse: "if by chance [forte] they see some man..." Goeller disagreed with them in his notes on Thucydides, and the scholar Heyne interpreted the verse correctly. Thus "often" [saepe] and "perchance" [forte] follow one another in the *Aeneid* (Book 10, line 723): "Just as a hungry lion, 'often' [saepe] ranging through the deep stalls—for maddening hunger drives him—if by chance [forte] he sees a fleeing goat or a stag with rising antlers, he rejoices." There too, there is no need to depart from the common meaning of the adverb.

# G. PACHYMERES

...beyond what was necessary, I have been honored for my deeds as a hero <note>original: "aristeus" — in ancient Greek society, this was a title for a warrior who had been formally awarded a prize for supreme bravery in battle.</note>, whenever I performed heroically. But regarding my feelings toward my own kin—and especially those whom nature made more dear to me than most—to produce other witnesses before those very people would perhaps seem foolish and redundant. For those who happen to benefit from good things do not need to be convinced by others to admit it; rather, they themselves would sincerely bear witness to what befell them, when the time calls for it. But if I were to be judged for murder, having done away with a son who did not conform to my ways—I, who am a hero and who moreover <note>original: "kai tauta" — regarding this specific phrasing, see page 163, note 1.</note> prize risking my life for strangers above all else—I would be astonished.

Nevertheless, the accuser’s arguments prevail, and I have come forward to be judged. I do not resent this tribunal <note>original: "bema" — the raised platform where speakers and litigants stood in a court.</note>, knowing it is open to all who wish to bring charges, even if they be harassers or professional informers <note>original: "sykophantai" — malicious accusers who brought lawsuits for profit or spite.</note> on purpose. But I am deeply pained if, after having shown my character many times by fighting even for the common man, I now risk being seen as a child-killer because of the malice of this bitter accuser. I ask you, gentlemen, not to receive this accusation simply or at random, but by looking deeply into my purpose, thus to conduct your investigation of what was done. For I am convinced that in this way you would pity me, rather than hate me, for what has been committed.

The manuscript uses a slightly different spelling for "happened" which is more pleasant.</note> for the boy—am driven even beyond my natural duty? I, who many times prayed to the gods for him, am forced to kill him myself, thus darkening the succession of both my lineage and my virtue at once. What could anyone say is more wretched than this?

### EXERCISE 11. 209
### 27

If, then, it were your custom to bring votes of condemnation against those who are simply unlucky, then kill me immediately, and I would have no reason to deny that the sentence was just. But if you judge only those who do wrong—as indeed you have sworn to do, and as everyone would agree is right—then I am not guilty at all, but rather utterly unfortunate. Mine is a misfortune that was indeed voluntary <note>The speaker acknowledges he performed the physical act, but argues the outcome was a tragic accident of fate rather than a crime of intent.</note>, yet necessary and admitting of no excuse. 

Even this accuser of mine, if he truly wished to act justly toward me, ought to have joined with the others in calling upon me and offering comfort for my calamity. And if he felt envy toward me before, he should cease his passion now, having sated his desire; for what greater evil could he wish upon me than this present state in which I am held? If he truly felt my pain, he ought not to be accusing me, for until now he should have been comforting me and sharing in the burden of this suffering. 

But since envy possesses him to such an extent that he wishes to reopen so great a wound and organize a tribunal <note>original: "dikasterion" — See page 144, note 2.</note> against me, I beg you to listen to me for a moment <note>The original manuscript (Codex) repeats "I beg" twice, but the second instance is marked with dots underneath, a traditional way for scribes to indicate a deletion.</note>. Once you have learned how these events regarding my son befell me, then you may judge. Whatever you decide after a calm hearing, I will accept with good grace—not because of the slanders of my accuser, but because of your votes. These are the votes I have been accustomed to receiving many times after winning prizes for heroism <note>original: "gera" — The original manuscript (Codex) writes "gerra" (meaning wicker shields), but the context clearly intends "prizes of honor."</note>, and I shall carry away this judgment, no matter how it falls upon me.

I had a father <note>original: "patēr" — The speaker here is likely a fictional persona used in a rhetorical exercise.</note> who was brave in war, public-spirited in his ways, moderate and cheerful toward the citizens, but quite bold toward those who were hostile to the city. > “O child, you are my child by nature, but strive to become mine in your character as well. For the natures of bodies and souls are very different. One might often see those who are legitimate by nature, and whom the kinship of bodies unites, being very different in character; while those who are far removed in lineage may be truly legitimate in their ways. Wish, therefore, to appear as the image of your father as the archetype. Strive not merely to be called the son of such-a-man, but to truly be so in reality. Do not merely associate yourself with the family line, but much more with the character—just as a barbarian might align himself with a Greek, or a foreigner with a native. For physical resemblances do not reveal a person as much as the dispositions of the soul. You have the spur for this. The example is not from elsewhere, but ‘from the hearth’ <note>original: "aph’ estias" — an idiom meaning "from the very beginning" or "from one’s own home."</note>, as they say. # 212

### GEORGE PACHYMERES

<columns>

These things my father said, and he was grand in his exalting of self-control <term>sophrosyne: a classical Greek concept of excellence of character and soundness of mind, often characterized by temperance and moderation.</term>, bringing me as close to this virtue as was possible.

What of it? While he sang the praises of virtue in this way, was I only concerned with living according to my desires, making my father’s commands secondary to my own appetites? Let those who know the truth bear witness. Even if they should speak otherwise—denying that I was obedient to my father—I will not argue the point further; instead, I myself will cast the vote against myself regarding the charges I face, defeated only by my own silence. But if I must, I will present my own actions, which all but bear witness to my obedience toward my father. For if a man imitates his father as much as possible in the things he did while he was alive, how could he be proven disobedient in the things his father said when urging him toward that very imitation?

Take for me then, O reader, this decree of a gift; take this second one, and another after them, which I hold in my hands and offer in succession.

These are the prizes of my excellence <note>original: "γέρα" (gera) - rewards or marks of honor given to a hero.</note>¹; look upon them. These are a monument to the gratitude of the people. These things persuade me to bring my whole family to be useful to the city. For since the entire city admires my acts of excellence <term>aristeia: a scene or series of deeds where a hero is at his peak of bravery and skill.</term>, and it is not just one man or a second or a third who gives these prizes, but everyone together—because I have benefited the community—how is it not just that I, with my own hands, my own children, and my whole family, should be devoted to you and struggle on your behalf?

---

->·<-

This argument seems to me to possess no small power, yet I do not believe that Aristides <note>Aelius Aristides, a 2nd-century orator who was a major influence on Byzantine rhetoricians.</note> wrote in this manner. For Herodotus, according to Gravert, joins the names: the polemarch <term>polemarch: originally a high-ranking military official in ancient Greek city-states.</term> Callimachus, Stesileus the son of Thrasyleus, and Cynaegirus the son of Euphorion, designating Callimachus by his title of office, as Polemon and Aristides do. **Furthermore**, in the words of Polemon, "some necessity existed or virtue led," Orellius understands "rather" <note>original Latin: "mãllon"</note> before "than," which is not a bad reading; however, I think a better correction would be "it was some necessity, if virtue led." He does not deny, nor could he, that Cynaegirus's father was a man of

<column-break/>

virtue, yet he denies it in Callimachus, but nevertheless some necessity was present on account of the polemarchy. Let other examples be added of the joining of a feminine noun and the word "absolute" <note>original: "αὐτοκράτωρ" (autokrator) - meaning sovereign, absolute, or having full power.</note>. Thucydides, 4, 126: "absolute battle." Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* 2, 14: "to have absolute command in war." And so Dionysius says elsewhere. Herodian, 1, 9: "youth in orphanage, having taken on absolute and unchecked power."

¹ Thus on page 11, 14: "the prizes of excellence." In my *Greek Anecdotes*, vol. V, p. 367, 7, it is read as "prizes of excellence" <note>The translator notes a slight spelling variation in the Greek root for "excellence" in different editions.</note> due to a slip of the scribe or the typesetter.

</columns>

### ->EXERCISE 11.<-

I begin, then, with the most personal matters. Nature did not give me many sons—so that if not all, at least some might imitate my virtues—but she provided me with only one. He was physically sound and strong, should he choose to exert himself in war. To describe him in an image, he was like the only-born cub of a lion.

However, to the extent that nature provided him the means for what is good and useful to the city, he diverted that advantage toward vice. Every day and every night, he was devoted to revelry, drunkenness, and profligacy. How do you think I felt at that time <note>original: "τῷ τότε" (tō tote) - see page 75, note 2 of the original manuscript. This refers to the specific period of the son's waywardness.</note>, seeing the successor of my lineage standing so far apart from his father’s excellence <term>arete: the Greek concept of excellence or virtue, often associated with fulfillment of purpose and moral character.</term>? He did not care even if someone, out of foresight or a desire to lead him away from evil, reminded him of his father’s diligence and the honor that came from it. 

To him, all that was mine—except for the household property he hoped to inherit—was nothing but nonsense and a useless nuisance. To me, his conduct—besides being forced to look upon the very sun with distaste—brought inconsolable grief and distress. It was a disgrace, a barrier to the honor I received from the many and the joy that should have come with it. 

Thus, I was famously celebrated for my victories on behalf of the city, yet at home I was held fast by terrible misfortunes. I was known as an "Aristeus" <term>Aristeus: a title for a hero who has won the 'aristeia' or prize for the greatest bravery in battle.</term>, yet I was also rumored to be the "father of a bad child." I was considered blessed by everyone for my heroism, but wretched because of my son. The father was occupied with wars by day, and the son spent his days in brothels. The father spent whole nights sleepless, weaving plans for the benefit of the people, while the son passed his nights with prostitutes and the most shameful companions.

I would have preferred not to speak of these things, as they are the ultimate reproaches to my life and my existence. Moreover, since he has paid a sufficient penalty for his actions, to "trample on one who is down" <note>original: "κειμένῳ ἐπεμβαίνειν" (keimenō epembainein) - a Greek idiom meaning to insult or attack someone who is already defeated or, in this context, deceased. See page 105, note 5.</note> and to disparage his character would seem not only unpleasant but malicious to compassionate ears. But this clever and bitter accuser wishes, it seems, to rake up the wound of my misfortune...

## EXERCISE 11.

...I bore the reproaches of his licentiousness; but he seemed as if he were being strewn with roses$^1$ and crowned$^2$. Finally, I threatened him with disinheritance <term>apokeryxis: a formal legal process in ancient Greece where a father publicly disowned his son, stripping him of his inheritance and family status.</term>; and "What is this disinheritance," he said, "that it should be able to cut off my pleasure?" I insulted him; and he mocked me. I wept; and he laughed. I dismissed him from my presence; and he grew shameless, and with a sneer$^3$ he would sneak back in. And since$^4$ I also heard from certain people worthy of belief, how$^5$ he even frequently dared to say with a haughty spirit: "The disciplinarian," speaking of me, "the teacher of one who needs to learn nothing, the tutor of one who is no longer an infant, the admonisher—"

---

...has ceased." It is **kondylos**, a "pen" <note>original Latin: "calamus"</note>. Today they especially use **kondylion** for a writing pen, and even more frequently **kondyli**, with that very common shortening <note>apocope</note> by which they are accustomed to cut down neuter words ending in **-ion**. They no longer use actual **reeds** <note>original Greek: "kalamois"</note> or **stalks** <note>original Greek: "donaxi"</note> for writing—those they have left to the Turks—but feathers [quills]; and yet they say **the kondyli**, not **the feather** <note>original Greek: "to pteron"</note>. Alexander Sutsus <note>A 19th-century Greek satirical poet.</note> says in a Satire: **"Alas! They dare to be pillars of our race, those who never learned how to hold the pen."** Christopulos, another Anacreon <note>A reference to Athanasios Christopoulos, a poet known for his light, lyrical style reminiscent of the ancient poet Anacreon.</note>: **"What hand, what pen could dare to paint you?"** The same man says elsewhere in a very cold sentiment: **"O my most wretched grave, take a pen, write, and I give as ink the tears that I shed."** In transcribing these, I have not followed his 1841 edition. For the editor—a most excellent man and friend of Christopulos who was able to use the poet's own papers—was so excessively accurate and revered his friend's hand with such superstition that he presented **slips of the pen**, for example **kontēli**. There are two faults in a word written thus: the **ē** <note>eta</note> for **y** <note>upsilon</note>, which is common, and **t** for **d** <note>delta</note>, which is very serious. For the sound of the syllable **kond** is changed so that not the Greek **d**, but our *d* is heard. Thus those who are introduced speaking in English comedies or "novellas"—Irishmen or Frenchmen—pronounce "dat," not "that." If Christopulos happened to have

<column-break/>

spoken thus, it should not have been preserved, unless I am mistaken; and I side with those editors who have accepted **kondyli**. He is also worthy of blame who, in the Prologue to the **Political Parallels** of Christopulos (for that eminent man touched upon politics; a disease from which aging poets sometimes suffer), saw to it that this was printed: **"I strive to spend my idle time more busily, playing the game of politics with the pen."** If the decision had been mine, I would have written **with the pen, the game**, sending away the harsher **ch**, since I remember verses edited thus from the poet’s papers: **"And the game begins."**

...[the punishment] being just, specifically the penalty against the son. And just as the shame was raised up in me alone, beyond all others, so too the concern for how to remove this evil belongs to me and to no other. I slaughter him, therefore, not out of ill-will toward the child—may it never be so, O Zeus, Protector of the Lineage! <note>original: "genethlie Zeu"</note>—but rather freeing the city from a shame that cannot be put into words, and freeing both myself and my family from the greatest reproach, one that no person in their right mind would ever accept.

But you, passing over all these things, rush up and down crying "murder!" and "the murder of a son!" as if you had not judged my folly so much as the judges' lack of experience. You hope to snatch them away here to side against me, assuming that I will not defend my rights, and that they will not carefully investigate the motives for the killing, but will instead immediately condemn the one who did the deed simply because it was a "murder."

A murder was committed; but, as I maintain, it was also a just one. For do not look at the deed alone, but also consider my intention <note>original: "dianoia"</note>. For if you were the father of a son—or if not, then wait until you become one—you would know the inviolable laws of nature and that forceful bond. Irrational animals will convince you, even the cruel and wild beasts who face danger for their young. Whether you speak of a bear or a lioness, you would see them protecting their children, throwing themselves in front of the hunters, and if they must suffer the ultimate end, they are willing to suffer everything rather than <note>original Latin note explains the word "rather" is implied here</note> betray their offspring as prey to those who wish to take them. Why then do you not grant even this much to me, which nature gives even to the irrational beasts...

# C. [THE WORKS] OF PACHYMERES

<columns>
2
</columns>

Do I not have a share in this? Am I not also a father and a progenitor, and am I not bound by the inescapable chains of nature? Did I not raise him in freedom? Did I not offer prayers—as I often imagined and hoped many times—that the infant would reach fulfillment and grow into a true man¹ and even surpass his father? But when he traveled the opposite path, overtaken by the envy of some Telchin² <note>The Telchines were mythological figures, often portrayed as spiteful sorcerers or demons who were famously envious of others' success.</note> who cast a spell upon me and my household, did I fail in my own words or deeds to drag him away from that wicked habit? When I saw foreign ranks arrayed for war alongside me, and watched my son wallowing in the most shameful things, how do you think I was disposed then, and with what heart did I endure the war?

But perhaps someone nearby, unable to see my reasoning,³ said to his neighbor: "Wretched man! How miserable!" and added, "It would have been better for him to mind his household affairs and bring his son to his senses." He condemned my lack of feeling, seeing me undertake public duties while suffering at home, desiring to benefit others while I myself was in need of mercy.

So, was I ill-disposed toward the child (for this is what your argument implies) and, envying his life, did I kill him?⁴ Oh—what could anyone say that would rightly describe you?—you who are so utterly heartless toward nature! For he who condemns others for the strange things they have been caught in, first accuses himself of those same things. Just as the simple soul is unsuspicious of vice, so the wicked and complex mind is suspicious of others. Does any man, gentlemen, bear ill-will toward his own offspring? Today, I do not wish for the laws to judge me, but for Nature herself. Will someone readily strike their child with their right hand? No, clearly not. Do you hear, accuser?⁵ This applies to me too...

<column-break/>

...performing the worst deeds and suffering from an incurable disease <note>The author uses medical terminology to describe moral corruption as a sickness that cannot be healed.</note> of character, he was worthy of undergoing punishment. > "But," he says, "one should have pursued the offender in other ways:¹ <gloss>Scholion: metalepsis <note>A rhetorical term referring to a shift in the way an argument is framed or a change in the context of a word.</note></gloss> by depriving him of food and clothing; by dishonoring him, turning away from him, driving him out of the house, or even reporting him to the judges."

You say other ways were needed, and you list the methods. What then? Do you know that I pursued all these ways? If you do not know, ask the neighbors and learn. I turned to him many times, admonishing him first. But he, being admonished, did not gain even a moderate sense of reason, nor did he return to me when I turned away; instead, he acted with utter shamelessness against everything I brought to bear. I deprived him of food; but leaping into the house, he made his spending even greater and beyond necessity, and his pretense of² <gloss>The manuscript reads "by the appearing."</gloss> snatching things away was a demonstration of how much he looked down on me. It was clear he was ready to do the most shameful things to the one who would try to stop him. At times, he even threw out insulting words and mixed these with threats, so that even those in the household were terrified of him, as he nearly drew his sword against them. Did I leave him naked? He dressed himself immediately by snatching my own things. Did I dishonor him? But he wore the insult like a crown,³ <gloss>See p. 215, note 2.</gloss> and took great pride in his disgrace. Did I drive him out of the house? He did not care. Did I threaten to report him? I do not even wish to repeat any of the things he said then about those presiding over the judgment. How many methods of discipline did I attempt? Yet all of them were proven inferior to his impudence. For do not think that I immediately brought the sword against him and, without having first tried every possible effort, carried out the slaughter with my own hands. Rather, a long time measured out his wickedness on one side and my pain on the other, and there was no device by which he could be delivered from his most shameful deeds.

These are the reasons why I, being a father—O Zeus!—and being the kind of man you have known through my deeds, did not think it tolerable in any way for my son to have such a disposition of mind, and to wallow so in his passions.

### BY GEORGE PACHYMERES

<columns>

...not to fall short in zeal, but to bring the young man to his senses¹; but if, despite his doing and saying everything, the boy would not be persuaded, he must look to the sword, and use it to cut out the evils. He argued that it is better for that undisciplined and utterly ruined man to lie dead than to live wickedly, unworthily of himself, and unworthily of his father and his entire lineage.

"But," someone might say², "it is necessary and unavoidable to remove an evil person, yet the father should not become the actual perpetrator of the slaughter³ himself; instead, he should report the matter and seek from the judges either a transformation of the boy's vice or, if he cannot be brought to his senses, his removal. Thus, the act would appear as a punishment for vice, not a satisfaction of his own anger."

I too say that the removal of vice ought to have been managed in this way; for only then, and in that way alone, would I have escaped the accusations of your mouth and others like you. But zeal⁴, I believe, seized me, and the passion of my soul urged me to carry out the slaughter with my own hands. As for his being changed from his vice—even if the entire populace, even if the whole city gave counsel, even if they threatened the most terrifying things, or did anything at all, whether bad or good, toward him—it was entirely hopeless. There was no room for reason to even consider such a thing. As for his being removed from our midst, since it was going to happen by necessity, it would have been well if it had been done by the public. ### III. OF PACHYMERES
### 226

"Again," he said, and another: "But also punish, crush, strike, beat, inflict penalties, and finally kill!" <gloss>1</gloss> If you were saying these things, and I were leaving the judge's bench, what else was left but to kill him again <gloss>1</gloss> and remove one who was altogether incurably diseased? Then, will someone persuade you that this deed—which you would have granted as a just judgment—having now been done, was not done justly, and therefore should not be accepted? And where is the justice in the sentence being just, but the execution of that sentence being held liable for a crime?

Consider <gloss>2</gloss>, I pray you, the legal allowance a father has over a son, and the soul's just passion, and reasonable zeal—consider all these as the father’s justifications. If only he had turned back when being warned! And who would have been more delighted than I? I would not have merely called that day golden, but even beyond those <gloss>3</gloss> celebrated golden ages <gloss>4</gloss>, in which lived certain "golden men." At any rate, if my joy would have been greater than anyone else's had he changed his ways, then certainly my grief is greater because he did not. While someone else might calculate the slaughter, I calculate the daily pain and the inconsolable grief—that a son once so beautiful became, once and for all, unyielding to change from his vices.

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s emotional defense. ### DECLAMATION XI. 227

Therefore, pity this wretched father, no less for these later events than for those that came before. If anyone wishes, let him imitate my zeal; but if not, let each be content with his own lot, and I with mine. If someone has a son who is well-regarded, let him welcome it, and let him consider the child’s life more precious than his own, and let him take greater pride in him—if the boy should prove useful, having often been useful before¹; and if the boy should be undisciplined and unruly, let the father admonish him, let him bring him to his senses <note>original: σωφρονιζέτω</note>², and let him employ every variety of treatment, in case he might somehow train him and win him back. But if he cannot, then let him even kill him. It is better for anyone to be childless <note>original: ἄπαιδα</note> than to be a <term>kakopaida</term> <note>A "bad-child-parent"; one who suffers the misfortune of having a wicked or degenerate child.</note>. For the former state is endurable, and nature understands the suffering; but the latter alienates even nature itself and is among the things that are truly unbearable.

I know that you have often marveled at my <term>aristeia</term> <note>The prize or status awarded for supreme valor and excellence in battle.</note>; I know that I have received from you praises, applause, and gifts; I know you have gathered together with your children to offer sacrifices for my victories. And the hero <note>aristeus</note> was then congratulated for his bravery, but pitied for his misfortune <note>literally: "his bad luck in craft/offspring."</note>. How do you think I bore that day, and what was in my mind as those rites were performed? Was I to reflect on the high praise, or on my own calamity? On the applause for victory, or on the suffering of my soul? Believe me, I often despaired³ of life itself, and I wished I had fallen in the war as a corpse, senseless, rather than to live so miserably, even while being praised as a victor. For the time being, it seemed to me that the only way to release a small portion of my grief was if my son were no longer seen alive in such a state. As for you, however you might wish to receive what has been done—whether it is necessary to punish me or to acquit me—I do not object. It is enough for me that I am not being prosecuted as a "shield-dropper" <note>A coward who flees battle.</note>, nor am I being punished for fleeing from war, nor is my accuser winning your votes by charging me with any other such shameful deeds. I die a hero, caring so much for the affairs of the city that I could not endure it if my entire lineage were not held to the same standard of excellence. There are heroes even in Hades—those who fell gloriously where it is beautiful for young men to fall. When they learn of my deeds, they will marvel; they will, as is likely, accept my decision⁴.

# G. PACHYMERES
### Page 228

<columns>
I used to consider one of my military struggles to be particularly violent—the one where nature resisted on one side, while my judgment <note>original: γνώμη (gnome); referring to his reasoned will or moral purpose</note> fought back on the other. Nature fought because the offender was a child, a seed of my own; but judgment fought because it is not right for a child of a hero <note>original: ἀριστέως (aristeos)</note> to be such a man, nor to live while committing such crimes. Therefore, I have conquered that war as well, with the help of the gods, and nature—the most violent of forces—was defeated by a steady and city-loving judgment.

But now fortune prepares another struggle and war at this tribunal of yours, and the accuser is my opponent. I am confident I shall win this one too. And in what way? I will not be released, I say; for that lies with you and you alone. I will not argue about how I might fall. But even if you choose to kill me, I will gladly accept the slaughter. I will show then that I have conquered nature not only in the case of my legitimate son, but also in my own case and regarding my own life. I accept this other danger on behalf of the city, even if it is not an enemy who kills me, but you—the very people for whom I have accomplished so much.

I ask only this: that everyone be eager on behalf of the city, and in every way lead your sons toward this same goal...

<note>The following section shifts from the rhetorical speech above into a series of scholarly notes and textual corrections on various classical and Byzantine authors.</note>

To Theagenes he promised a herb on the previous day; searching a little way from the lake, he went on his way. The Venice Manuscript <note>Codex Venetus</note> reads *masteuson* <note>search!</note>. By writing *masteuōn* <note>searching</note>, the reading becomes probable. The commentator on Aristides (Vol. III, p. 22) says: "to sail past" <note>paraplein</note> is used of coastal regions; "to sail around" <note>periplein</note> is used of islands. Rather, "upon islands" <note>epi nēsōn</note>. And thus below. Himerius, Oration 3, 8: "O man dear to the gods, and fitting to be likened to the gods." Wernsdorf was able to write "fitting" <note>original: πρέπων (prepon), a masculine participle</note> with confidence, which was found in the manuscripts and left in a note. I myself also found "fitting" <note>prepon</note>. Gregory of Nazianzus, in the Letter to Libanius: "I, a mother, have sent a son to a father; the one by nature, the other by words" <note>referring to a teacher as a spiritual or intellectual father</note>. The manuscript offered me "to the" <note>original: τῷ (tō)</note> which is best, namely "to the father." For Libanius was Gregory's teacher, and teachers are often called "fathers" by their pupils. Michael Choniates, in the *Encomium of Isaac Angelos*, which the learned Tafel recently published for the first time, section 7: "I am present here

<column-break/>

at once a spectator and a daring praiser of royal and divine majesty." Perhaps "daring" <note>original: τολμηρός (tolmeros), the adjective</note> should be read instead of "daringly." Lydus, *On the Magistracies*, p. 38: "that Titus Tatius had that name." It seems it should be read as "in that manner" <note>original: ἐκείνως (ekeinos)</note>. Euripides, Fragment 4 of the *Ino*: "A woman ought to allow such a servant, who will not keep silent about what is just." I once conjectured "of servants" <note>original: προσπόλων (prospolōn)</note>, which Matthias said he did not understand; I certainly thought I understood it thus: "A woman ought to allow such a person from among the servants, who..." The verse follows: "But she hates shameful things and keeps them before her eyes," in which, without changing the sound, I would change the vowels: "may she hate" <note>misoi</note>, "may she have" <note>echoi</note>. Himerius, Oration 23, section 6: "Perhaps there is not enough envy, as long as words are lifted up on golden wings; let us speak again, let us lead the chorus again in envy." The manuscript correctly reads "lifting up" <note>zōn</note> and lacks the preposition "in" <note>en</note>.

## EXERCISE 12 <note>original: ΜΕΛΕΤΗ (Melete); a rhetorical exercise or "mock trial" used in schools to practice legal oratory.</note>

Three hundred of the enemy escaped by night and, arriving at the gates of the city, begged the general <note>original: στρατηγός (strategos)</note> to open the gates so they might enter and be saved. Because there was a law stating that the gates must not be opened at night, the general did not open them. Those in pursuit arrived and slaughtered them. The general is now being tried for public crimes <note>original: δημοσίων ἀδικημάτων (demosion adikematon); a serious charge of harming the state's interests</note>. We are practicing the role of the accuser.

Let no one among you, gentlemen, think that I have brought this indictment against the general out of envy for his reputation. For I consider his glory to be the glory of the entire city. For him to be honored by you for his victories brings him a simple fame; but for you, if one considers it rightly, it brings a manifold fame—both because the city breeds such men, and because it is victorious, and because it rewards its victors in a generous manner from the resources available <note>original: ἐκ τῶν ἐνόντων (ek ton enonton); a common idiom meaning "with what one has on hand" or "to the best of one's ability"</note>. Therefore, to envy a fellow citizen in such a city—

Prisoners of war, having broken their chains, came to the city at night, asking to enter. The general left them outside, not opening the gates. The enemy fell upon them and cut them down. The general is tried for public crimes.</margin>

### GEORGE PACHYMERES

<columns>

...[concerning] these things,¹ it would be as if someone were to look with envy upon his own healthy limbs. But since I too am a citizen, of whatever rank and age, yet still a citizen of your city,² I have suffered terribly in my soul because of what happened. And just as if something good had occurred, I would have joined the many to rejoice with the person responsible and share in your gladness; so too now I have come both to mourn with you the loss of these men, and to remind you of the man responsible, so that he might not secretly escape justice while being a bad man.³ Therefore, I beg and entreat you to set aside your grief for a moment and attend to my words, so that by punishing the offender with the same decrees by which you used to honor him as a victor, you might be seen to act justly in both regards.

I⁴ mix with you only rarely,⁵ and I do not often defile the circle of the council chamber <note>original: bouleuterion; the building where the city council met to deliberate</note>. Nevertheless, I know you have often barely gathered in the council chamber before moving directly from there to the courtroom. You had met initially to deliberate on how to crown someone who seemed to have succeeded, but you then rushed to judge him because someone spoke against him and reported the worst crimes. And this is not a cause for blame, but for praise. For it is right that you must be ready, based on whatever you might hear and discover, either to punish or to crown, so that evil is not neglected, nor good held in contempt. As for the rest of you, just as...

### STUDY 12.
#### 231

...[just like] hunting dogs following a scent,¹ and to see to it that the votes concerning those you might consider become just.

This general present here, who appeared to be "good" at the right moment, seems even today to some to have been the cause of a certain victory, even though many perished. But I, blaming him alone for the evils that followed, am capable, with God’s help, of showing that this great crime belongs to him. And it will be your concern thereafter how you will pursue him. For he did not simply cause a loss; rather, the very flower of the city has fallen because of this "excellent"² man. And if the enemies suffered anything at all, receiving their deserved treatment, they have since caught their breath, while their misfortunes have transferred to our city. Now, a harsh rumor is everywhere, along with wailings, dirges, and tears, as every mother searches for her son.

Rather, as the argument proceeds in its proper course, I will take up the narrative and recount the events.

For³ he should never have been chosen as general from the start for such great struggles—a man whom we had not previously tested in other, more moderate matters. Had he been properly tested, the events of this war would not have failed so miserably, to the point that under the name of "victory" we lost our best men and the courage of such warlike⁴ young men. These youths sometimes rush forward irrationally due to their military habits, and they had no one to manage them with accurate knowledge. For this reason, the victory became, as the saying goes, a "Cadmean victory";⁵ it happened, nonetheless. And as for how large a portion of the...

### BY PACHYMERES
#### 232

...of a general, and the city would have faced the ultimate danger; such was the outcome of the war regarding the remaining strength of the citizens. Therefore, you ought to have sought from the beginning to whom you would entrust the city’s affairs, and not—deceived by the persuasive arguments of the masses and bypassing those truly worthy—elected this man to your own harm, as "the deed itself showed."¹

But since² sudden and highly irrational events enslave one’s thoughts and do not allow for leisure to deliberate on what is beneficial, that enemy invasion was announced to us when we expected nothing. Immediately, everyone was thrown into turmoil; the army was, as usual, capable in battle, but a leader³ was sought for them. What happens to those who suddenly fall from a ship into the sea happened to you then. For they, with the waves overwhelming them and being in danger of "gaping at the water"⁴ <note>A Homeric expression for drowning.</note> and dying, grab onto whatever is at hand as if it were a strong defense, even if it is seaweed or some other cheap and trivial thing. So you, surrounded by terrors, gathered for counsel, and when someone reminded you of him, you immediately accepted the suggestion. Bringing him into your midst, you elected him general—O Zeus and city-protecting gods!—a general! Not as if, by the truth, he would immediately handle affairs with care...

# STUDY 12.
## 233

...expected to fulfill his duty and not be negligent¹ <note>original: "ῥᾳθυμήσοντα"</note>, nor as one who would betray² our allies to the enemies, even if they should often act unexpectedly. Rather, he was expected, through military exercises and all kinds of diligence, to protect his own position and those with him. For what the head is to the body, he was to them; and it was necessary to provide well so that they might both conquer and lack nothing, as it is far better for our people to be preserved with safety than to defeat the enemy precariously.

But this man, having learned military matters from I know not where, chose only to win, even if it should happen that everyone fell.

One must win, my friend, but with good counsel <term>euboulia: the ability to deliberate well or exercise sound judgment</term> and total safety; if safety is missing, victory is vain.

But, as I was saying, when the war was joined and the battle broke out, and the enemies were already rushing in like wild boars³, the general then needed military experience and good counsel to arrange the soldiers in close formation and to unite them in a kind of unbreakable shield-wall <term>synaspismos: a tactical formation where shields are locked together for collective defense</term>, which Homer mentions and compares⁴ to a well-fitted wall. For just as a well-joined⁵ building avoids the violence of the winds, so too does a well-arranged army withstand the charges of the enemy.

But this man, considering the matters of good counsel as nothing, released the young men into war in a frenzy, and their lack of order tripped them up. Not a few fell, many were captured, and finally—if some kind fortune had not held her hand over the city—our affairs would have been utterly destroyed. But along with fortune, the excellence <term>arete: virtue, specifically the martial bravery and merit of the soldiers</term> of the men also overcame the wickedness of the leader; acting on its own, as if they had no general, and managing the war alone, the army suffered much and only with difficulty prevailed over the enemy. And the "second thought," the one without a general, was wiser than the first...

# III. OF PACHYMERES

"I am caught," he says; "For I did not betray the ships; I did not reveal secrets to the enemy; I did not act as a corrupt ambassador; I did not do this and that <note>original: "τὸ καὶ τό" — a Greek idiom equivalent to "such and such."</note>, so as not to list every single thing, have I done."

But is it not a crime to have caused such men to fall so shamefully and miserably before <margin>The Codex reads "your" (ὑμετέρων) instead of "our."</margin> our gates—men with whom Fortune had barely made a truce, while you appeared even more terrible than death itself? You did not betray ships to the enemy, but you betrayed warlike men <note>original: "ἀρεΐκους" — meaning men like Ares, the god of war; martial and brave.</note>. You did not reveal the city's secrets, but you exposed the secrets of nature <note>The orator refers here to the "secrets of nature" as a euphemism for the soldiers' naked bodies being left exposed and dishonored in death.</note> upon our soldiers. You did not act as a corrupt ambassador, but you rejected the embassy of your own kinsmen in their final moments of danger.

Why then, if you did not sin in every possible way of injustice against the city, but only in one—the worst one, as I say—do you try to justify yourself? It is just as if someone, having killed a man with a stone and being judged for murder, were to insistently argue that it was not with a sword, nor with a spear, nor with any other missile. You committed the murder. These details will make no difference, my good man, to the simple fact that a murder occurred. So it is also with—

This note is necessary because I recently came across a passage in Euripides that was misunderstood because of the ambiguity of the word *peiro* (which can be either a verb for "to try" or "to experience"). In Euripides (from Arsenius's *Violetum*), the text reads: "Being born mortal, try to see what pertains to you" <note>original Greek: "θνητὸς πεφυκὼς τἀπί σοι πειρῶ βλέπειν"</note>. The Latin translator rendered this as: "Being born mortal, I suspect seeing the future." But "what pertains to you" (τἀπί σοι) is not "the future," and the word is a middle-voice imperative. I would translate it: "Since you were born a mortal, strive to consider those things that pertain to you and are in your power." A learned man suggests the conjecture "try to see behind you," but the word for "try" is perfectly sound here. Who has ever doubted the integrity of the line from Sophocles's *Philoctetes* (line 149): "Try to attend to the present"? If anything were to be attempted in the Euripides verse, I would write "the things behind" (τἀπίσω) instead of "the things pertaining to you," following the lead of Isidore, whose similar verse is quoted by Arsenius: "Being born mortal, try to look at the things behind." When Stobaeus (Title 22, 27) recites this, he writes "the things behind" (τὰ ὀπίσω) more clearly.

Compare, I pray you $^3$, the preservation of the law with the slaughter of the men, and place these side by side $^4$, and consider whether a law being observed can procure greater benefits for the city, or fewer evils than three hundred men being slaughtered in vain—and whether it was necessary not only to overlook the law for the moment but even to dissolve it for the common good. ### EXERCISE XII.

...since setting it aside is beneficial, why should that rule not be overlooked for the sake of the common interest¹? Provided only that all deceit and malice be absent.

Our ancestors did these things², as did those who succeeded them, and as every man does in his own home. Some burned their own ships so that they might be forced to conquer; others tore down a wall so that they might attack their enemies from a hidden position. The Lacedaemonians³ <note>The Spartans.</note> abolished the law concerning the full moon after they realized that by observing it, they were deprived of their long-held⁴ glory of appearing superior to the Persians. Themistocles⁵ commands the people to remain upon the sea, to abandon the city to its walls, and to transfer themselves to the ships. He urged them not to fixate on the temples of the gods, the tombs of their fathers, the monuments of their kin, nor on any kind of beauty or possessions, nor to care at all if these things should perish. In this way, in all places and at many times, life is renewed through innovation; thus are public affairs managed, and thus are private ones as well.

For there are also laws and ancient customs within every household⁶. For one man, it is the rule to eat but once a day; for another, to inspect and calculate the household accounts on the first day of every month; for another, to carry out a specific task every day—one rule for one man, and another for another. Yet nevertheless, a critical moment arrives⁷, and they overlook these laws, provided only that someone⁸ judges that setting them aside will be beneficial.

Why then⁹ did you appear so devoted to the law, or so cautious—or I know not what to call it—that you would allow so many and such great men to be wiped out? "They died," you say— <note>original: ἀπέθανον. There is a gap in the original manuscript here.</note> "but¹⁰ by the law of war." For it was necessary

# BY GEORGE PACHYMERES
<note>George Pachymeres (1242–1310) was a prominent Byzantine historian and philosopher. This text is a "declamation," a formal rhetorical exercise where the author adopts a persona to argue a specific legal or moral case.</note>

...those men, being true men and justly wishing to pay the debt of their upbringing to their fatherland, kept their souls undefeated even as they endured the fall of their bodies. They showed their enemies that nothing was more precious to them than falling while fighting for freedom. 

But as for you—I want to say "enemy," yet I respect the uniform of the general—nonetheless, as far as those men are concerned, you have done more harm than an enemy could. For they did not fall while drawn up in battle lines, engaging and struggling against the foe; rather, in the manner of swine or domesticated livestock¹, they were slaughtered. 

The King <note>Referring to the Persian King Xerxes I.</note> also killed three hundred at the Gates² <note>The pass of Thermopylae.</note>, but they were blocking his entrance into the land of Pelops <note>The Peloponnese.</note>, and they were eager to fall beforehand if they could not prevail, rather than let him think of victory and do his worst. But you, when our own people sought entrance into the city, you barred the gates of the city, and as if you knew no difference between friends and enemies, you secured the keys. You stood in the path of our people and blocked their salvation. Do you then dare to say that you did not kill them?

-> With your hands³ you did not kill them, I admit, but you did so by your will and your purpose; and any man of sense would consider this both a murder of those men and an act of malice against the city. For they held that place as an anchor of safety and a "sacred anchor," as the saying goes⁴, and... <-

-ime? We will be permitting it if we let this man go for now.

A general must guard the laws and conduct public life according to them. <margin>Objection of the opponent on behalf of the general</margin> However, a general must also provide for and fight for his soldiers, and value their lives above his own soul. If both can be saved—both the laws and the soldiers—one should consider it a success and highly praiseworthy. But if not, <margin>Scholion: Another rebuttal <note>The Greek term 'metalepsis' (μετάληψις) indicates a shift in the legal basis of the argument.</note></margin> and if a law often <note>Regarding the sense of the word "often" (πολλάκις), see page 242, note 6.</note> stands in the way of the soldiers' safety, he must report immediately to the rulers and attempt to persuade them to overlook the law at times for the sake of the soldiers' survival.

If, therefore, <margin>Scholion: Objection by exception <note>An 'enstasis' (ἔνστασις) is a rhetorical tactic used to block a specific claim.</note></margin> he shamelessly claims that as a general it was permissible for him to deliberate about the matters falling under his command, you can say it was not permissible. For I know you did not appoint this man to act on his own whim <note>The phrase "if anything" (εἴ τι) also appears on page 179, note 1.</note> and doing whatever he might feel like, without taking into account the judges, the council, or anything else that holds our state together—lest he be caught and pay the penalty for his audacity when his actions are examined. Even if <margin>Scholion: Counter-pleading</margin> he were such a person, he still should not have reached such a peak of arrogance; <note>original: "ἀπαυθαδίζεσθαι" (to be arrogant). The editor notes a manuscript correction here.</note> he should have been moved by the...

### EXERCISE 12.
<note>A 'Melete' (exercise) is a rhetorical speech written by a student or scholar—in this case, George Pachymeres—practicing the style of ancient Greek orators. These often took the form of imaginary legal cases.</note>

->**THE EPILOGUE**<-

...the fate of the men and the circumstance of the moment, and if nothing else should be considered, then at least the goodwill of the gods. For if the gods, caring for our affairs, put it into the minds of the citizens both to break their bonds and run back to us, yet he himself was negligent and threw away the opportunity that lay within those men. <gloss>1</gloss> <note>The editor notes a small gap in the manuscript here.</note>

Since <gloss>2</gloss> <margin>Scholion: The Epilogue <note>The concluding part of a speech, designed to stir the emotions of the audience.</note></margin> what was in your mind then, when you heard that those who had been taken away into the secure prisons of the enemy were now standing before the gates? They were knocking at the doors, and begging, and again there were those behind them pursuing them from the rear. You perceived that everything rested on you: that if you opened the gates, they would be saved, but if you did not open them, they would be in peril. And while you delayed, the danger itself allowed for no delay. Was it necessary then to calculate laws? Was it necessary to remain silent in any way? <gloss>3</gloss> Was it necessary to wait for the sun, and only then to open up? <note>A reference to military laws that forbade opening city gates after sunset to prevent enemy infiltration.</note>

You did open them then, but you saw only what had already happened—the very thing you seemingly desired. You saw men lying there, stripped corpses. You saw a piteous sight. You saw a strange shambles <gloss>4</gloss> <note>original Greek: "makellon," a loanword from the Latin "macellum," meaning a meat market or slaughterhouse.</note>: heads here, hands there, feet elsewhere, and spilled entrails. These are things truly worthy of your generalship!

Then, even if you died many deaths, how could you pay a worthy penalty? It would be necessary for you to bear upon your own body, one by one, the tortures those men suffered. It would be necessary to endure as many slaughters; to lie there not from one blow, but from the ten thousand blows they received. And even then, perhaps, you might barely have outweighed your crime. But as it is, your single body cannot contain so many wounds.

### 248
# FROM GEORGE PACHYMERES

But why am I speaking to you, and not addressing these men?

I know, gentlemen, that you recognize what has happened, and it needs no words to make its dreadfulness apparent. For what could anyone say to adequately describe the audacity of this man who claims to be a city-lover, a general, and—as he insists—a guardian of the laws? As for how the perpetrator should be punished, you do not need words to urge or stir you. For you possess innate impulses toward **zeal for what is honorable** <note>original: "Ζῆλον". The editor refers back to an earlier discussion of this term on page 224.</note> so that you properly honor the benefactor and worthily punish the criminal. And I know well that if it were possible to kill with one's hands, no one would have refrained from striking, <note>The editor suggests the grammatical particle 'an' is missing here, which would make the sentence 'no one *would have* refrained'.</note> but everyone would have pelted him, and would have considered the injuries inflicted upon him to be like the **showering of leaves** <note>original: "phyllobolia". A traditional Greek custom of throwing leaves or flowers over victors or the dead; here, the speaker uses it ironically to describe a shower of blows.</note> upon the fallen. 

But since you correct this evil through your judgments and votes—which are the means by which you "kill"—do not be negligent. Let a common vote suffice, coming from everyone **as if from one person**, <note>The editor notes this phrasing is a common rhetorical device signifying total unanimity.</note> sentencing this blood-guilty man to death. In the future, there will certainly be a memory and a fair report of you: that once, long ago, there were men in this city who were zealots for the honorable, such that with all their hands they crowned the city’s benefactor and punished the wrongdoer. Thus, while there may be but one stroke of the sword, there are ten thousand "slaughters" from the tongue. In this way, others will be inspired by your zeal, and for the rest of time—not only for the present but also for the future—this vote of yours will benefit the city, if it is delivered justly, as I say and as everyone would surely agree.

---

² It seems the particle *an* <note>A Greek grammatical marker used to indicate a hypothetical or conditional action.</note> is missing. But compare page 225, line 11.
³ The manuscript reads *phylloboulēseis*. He alludes, and quite elegantly, to the ancient custom of *phyllobolia* (showering with leaves) and *anthobolia* (showering with flowers) used as a sign of both mourning and joy. I previously noted this regarding the *Epistles of Diogenes* in the *Notes of Mann*, volume X, page 194; regarding Nicetas Eugenianos, page 396; and regarding Bion 1, 75. Add also Jacobs, 

<column-break/>

*Analecta*, volume VI, page 396; Heraldus on Martial 8, 65, p. 163; Schneidewin on Ibycus p. 120; Tafel, *Clear Explanations*, p. 705, 936.
⁴ I remember reading this antithesis of "as one from all" in Theodoros Rodanthe, book 1, page 21: "Immediately they all cried out with one mingled voice." Likewise on page 37: "The standing crowd, having cried out with one mingled voice in response."

->### FROM GEORGE PACHYMERES<-

...general; but since they were barred by the laws from killing those they had captured and held in their hands<gloss>1</gloss>, unless it were in the heat of battle, they employed other methods of personal violence. They subjected him to bitter tortures and unbearable outrages to eliminate the man who had so often done them the worst injuries<gloss>2</gloss>, concocting—as the saying goes—a **"hollow excuse"**<gloss>3</gloss>: that they wished to learn some of the city's secrets.

But they barely possessed that [secret], I admit; they held it out of that necessity... <note>There is a gap in the original text here.</note>... from the treasures of the heart<gloss>4</gloss> and blurted out what should not have been said. And they, as if ashamed to appear wicked, released him against their will, pretending to regret that they had not demanded the impossible from the start—upon which I would have been stretched to my limit and broken, and they would have been immediately relieved of their future fear.

While those men, then, aimed for that, they were likewise cheated of their hope. But this man here, breathing threats heavily against me, fulfills what they lacked. He wishes to murder the one whom they, despite their desires, could not kill. He attempts to provide a double profit for the enemies: both what they took from me against my will, and what you will do, if you are persuaded by him. I ask you to consider whether this should happen or not. For I do not think it is the same thing for you to kill...

It is dedicated to the memory of **George Pachymeres**, a <term>Dicaeophylax</term> <note>A "Guardian of the Law," a high-ranking judicial official in the Byzantine court</note> in the court of Michael Palaeologus and a <term>Protecdicus</term> <note>A chief legal counsel or advocate for the Church</note> of the Church of Constantinople. He was a man of immense learning—a theologian, historian, philosopher, mathematician, and orator, famous for many literary monuments. I myself

compared this epitaph of Pachymeres to manuscripts 1779 and 1931, which I will designate in the notes with the letters **A** and **B**. I took the title from **A**.

² <note>original: "Editt. χορῷ. W. conjecit σορῷ..."</note> Previous editions read *chorō* <note>meaning "choir" or "dance"</note>. Wernsdorf conjectured *sorō* <note>meaning "coffin" or "sarcophagus"</note>, which the manuscripts actually contain. Regarding the confusion of the letters chi (χ) and rho (ρ), see Bast’s *Commentary on Palaeography*, p. 848; and Jacobs on the *Analecta*, vol. XIII, p. 647. This Jacobs, if I am not mistaken, misused such reasoning regarding an epigram by Antiphilus (7.176) which did not need correcting. There, a dead man speaks whose body was dug up by a plowshare: <note>original: "Ἦ ῥα κακῶν θανάτου τις ἔφη λύσιν..."</note> "Indeed, someone once said death was a release from evils; but for me, stranger, even the grave is not the end of my sufferings." The learned man edited the text based on a guess as "someone *will* say," which ruins the meaning. For that obscure dead man could not imagine that his unholy excavation would be so famous that *no one* would henceforth say death is the end of troubles. Rather, he remembers that this *had* been said by someone, and he is amazed [at its falsity]. The confusion of the letters rho (ρ) and lambda (λ) is much more frequent. # PHILES TO PACHYMERES

...they would immediately have words as their advocates,
<margin>5</margin>as if mixing the strength of breath¹ into the forms;
but since you have died, O teacher,
the graces of your words² seem dead,
and I fear I shall bring a harsh-sounding noise
to a man of wisdom and one free from passions.
<margin>10</margin>Yet if³ while you were still alive, out of a humble heart,
you also applauded the writings of the unlearned,
so that⁴ their nature might take a zealous course,
now that you inhabit a tomb and are covered by the stone of silence,
and have found the bottom of your books deserted,
<margin>15</margin>how could you treat my words as nothing,
and those that are nearly finished⁶ for your sake?
But, O cities⁷, mourn the laws together.
For the pious⁹ Demosthenes among us⁸
no longer stirs the flame of rhetoric.
<margin>20</margin>Lest¹⁰ the throne of the judges appear dry...

# FUNERAL ORATION

<page-num>257</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

For the chest of your books¹
has been overturned into the chest of decay.
O <term>Guardian of the Laws<note>Original: *Dicæophylax*. A high-ranking Byzantine judicial official responsible for overseeing legal matters and the church's canons.</note></term>², if you still have a share
<margin>50</margin>in the guarding of the laws³ and preside over judgments,
decree, establish doctrines, resolve disputes,
bringing forth your impartial judgment;
for your former zeal did not die with you.
Did you not also, while living, contemplate the end,
<margin>55</margin>and perform this life as a tragedy⁴?
O swan, white by the winging of time⁵,
this is that very thing—and alas! for so many labors—
you chose in exchange the three-cubit tomb of the end⁶.

---

¹ Editions read: "our." Manuscripts read: "your." Himerius, Oration 3, 7: "Let no one among you wonder." Wernsdorf cites "our" from a manuscript; I found "your."

² He addresses Pachymeres, who was the *Dicæophylax*. See page 1.

³ Editions: "guarding" (nominative); so too Du Cange, who cites this passage in his *Glossary* under the entry for *Dicæophylax*. Manuscript A: "of the guarding" (genitive). Manuscript B: "guardianships and you preside."

⁴ This phrase, "to perform life as a tragedy" (*tragōdein ton bion*), means to lament human life and to recognize and recount its calamities, which occurs later in verse 61. Wernsdorf says: "It seems to allude to Pachymeres’ poem about his own life." See Fabricius, volume 1, page 786.

⁵ Editions read: "by the wing-like [nature] of time." Manuscripts read: "by the winging," which I have adopted: "O white swan, made so by the swift flight of time." By that noun *pterōsis* [winging], I am led to an epigram in Welcker’s Collection, page 149, which I might attempt to interpret in passing: "Nothing convinced [them], I think, as those of old who said that the race of souls descends from heaven, as much as the winged mind of Iamblichus, running through the upper air and every height of wings." The learned man thought that *pterōn* [of wings] was a participle of the verb "to wing" (to fly), so that "height of wings" is nearly a synonym for the preceding phrase "running through the upper air." Thus the mind of Iamblichus both runs and flies through the upper air and the sublime heaven.

<column-break/>

If we keep the word *pterōn* [of wings], I would prefer to take it as a noun, so that "the height of wings and birds" designates the highest spaces of heaven open to winged creatures. I would also prefer to correct it to *perōn* [passing through], meaning "traversing all the highest spaces." Bastius showed in his *Paleographic Commentary* that the letters *pt* and *p* are often confused. Thus, the inelegant repetition of "winged" (*pterōtos*) and "wings" (*pterōn*) will be avoided.

⁶ Wernsdorf says he sees a flaw here, but not a good correction. I omit what he conjectured. I understand the passage thus: "that very thing—I mean that white hair—and, in exchange for such great labors, alas! you have taken for yourself the three-cubit and final tomb." In the unpublished poem *On Offices* by Philes, verse 113: "We knew the illustrious Chumnus <note>Nicephorus Chumnus, the prefect of the 'Kanikleion' (the imperial inkstand), many of whose short works and letters I have published in the *Greek Anecdotes*</note>, who held a station greater than his previous one; and indeed after him the noble Metochites <note>Theodore Metochites, a great scholar and statesman.</note>, the greatest of the Logothetes, the limit of wisdom, wearing the red golden cap which the illustrious Emperor Andronicus granted to him as he shared in his power. These are the splendors of the scepter below: the forms of presidency, dignity, glory, flowing wealth, and uplifted clay, and the dust of fortune."

## BY HIEROCLES AND PHILAGRIUS
<gloss>┬</gloss> <gloss>_</gloss> <note>These scribal marks serve as decorative fillers or "coronis"-style indicators to separate the author attribution from the main title.</note>

# THE LAUGHTER-LOVER
<note>Original: *Philogelos*. Compiled around the 4th century AD, this is the world's oldest surviving joke book. It contains over 200 jokes, many of which mock "scholasticos" (pedants or absent-minded professors) and residents of certain cities notorious for their perceived stupidity.</note>

<summary>This page is the title page for the "Philogelos" (The Laughter-Lover), a famous collection of ancient Greek jokes attributed to the grammarians Hierocles and Philagrius. It marks the transition in the manuscript from solemn funeral poetry to lighthearted secular humor.</summary>
