...[when asked by] one of his friends why he was doing this, he replied: "It has been a long time since I was sick, and I feel ashamed before him <note>The "him" here likely refers to the doctor or perhaps the personification of Health/Sickness; the pedant feels he is neglecting his 'relationship' with medicine by staying healthy too long.</note>." <insert>1</insert>

7. A pedant <term>Scholasticus: a stereotypical character in Greek humor, often an over-educated fool</term> who had his uvula cut was ordered by the doctor not to speak. He commanded his slave to return the greetings of those who addressed him. Then he himself would say to each person: "Do not take it as an insult if my slave greets you instead of me; for the doctor has ordered me not to speak." <insert>2, 3, 4</insert>

8. A pedant, wanting to catch a mouse that was gnawing on his books, sat in the dark holding a piece of meat in his teeth. <insert>5, 6, 7</insert>

***

<margin>1</margin> **M** <note>Manuscript M</note> reads: "He did this, and replied: 'It has been a long time since I was sick and I am ashamed before it.'"

<margin>2</margin> **This joke is found in M and P. It is absent from the printed Editions and Rh.** <note>Rh refers to the scholar Rhærius.</note>

<margin>3</margin> **A** <note>Manuscript A</note> uses the Ionic form *iētros* for "doctor." **M** uses the standard *iatros*.

<margin>4</margin> **A** writes *epetaxe*. **M** writes *epetaxen*. <note>The difference is a "movable nu," a common grammatical variation.</note> An iambic verse from the *Anthology* (15, 19, 3) correctly begins: "He called a crowd." There, the Palatine reading *ekalesen* was noted. I myself found *ekalese*. I believe not even the smallest details should be omitted.

<margin>5</margin> **This is in M and P as Joke 8; in the Editions and Rh as Joke 7.**

<margin>6</margin> **The Editions** read: "wanting to catch a mouse." **Rh.** reads: "wanting to catch a mouse." Rhærius treats the verb "to catch" <note>original: *piazō*</note> extensively. It also appears in section 28. It was not unknown to the ancient and good writers. See my note in the second edition to Theocritus (4, 35), "having caught the bull by the hooves." Theocritus also used the compound "to seize around" in Epigram 6. It is found everywhere in the books of more recent authors. Theodore Prodromus in the Satire *Against the Abbots* (v. 585) writes: "If a monk falls ill, or if pain seizes him," with a variant "if it catches <note>original: *piasē*</note> him." Corayus, the learned and hardworking interpreter of Theodore, should be consulted on this word in his *Atacta* (vol. 1, p. 140). Andreopulus in *Syntipas* (p. 73): "the one called the night-watchman, having caught me... dragged me away." Symeon Seth in *Ichnelates* (p. 14): "his reproductive organs being squeezed <note>original: *sympiasthentōn*</note> in the cracks of the wood." Nowadays, they say it in the common tongue as

<column-break/>

"to catch" <note>original: *pianō*</note>. Alexander Sutsus in his Satire: "As many as never learned how they catch the pen." Christopulus writes:
->Once Love<-
->[took] his little arrow, bitter,<-
->Rusted in the quiver,<-
->He takes it out slowly,<-
->And catches it, and begins<-
->And rubs it on a stone.<-
I found "takes out" <note>original: *ebganei*</note> published, but I preferred to write in the ancient style <note>original: *aphyganei*</note>, which is better and does not change the sound. For the sake of those readers who are less familiar with these modern formulas, I will advise that a "rusted little arrow" <note>original: *saïttitza skouriasmenē*</note> is a small arrow colored with rust, from the word *skōria* (dross/rust). Often the 'o' sound changes to 'ou'. The author of the *Ciris* (line 245) wrote:
> "I swear... I would rather see all thousands of labors, worthy and unworthy, than suffer you to waste away in such sad filth and such dross (*scoria*)."
Critics cry out that the name is "filthy" and from the dregs of the common people, which cannot be denied. They object, more seriously, that the first syllable in *scoria* is long; but the pronunciation of a rare word could be doubtful, or a "slurring" of sounds <note>original: *synizesis*</note> could occur, as in the word for "walls" (*parjetibus*). Let "dross" (*scoria*) be preserved and understood figuratively regarding the rusty color of a face, or the violet-tinted paleness of lovers.

<margin>7</margin> **Editions and Rh.** read: "biting [meat], he sat opposite." **M** reads "darkness" (*skoteia*). **A** reads "darkness" (*skotia*). Thomas Magister says: "The word *skotia* is not in use." It is found in Micah (3, 6): "it shall be dark (*skotia*) to you from divination." It is indeed in the *Phoenissae*, but in a doubtful passage. An anonymous note in Rhærius says: "Vossius [reads] quietly..."

9. A pedant <term>Scholasticus: a stock character in ancient Greek humor, representing an over-educated but foolish man</term> wanting to teach his donkey not to eat, did not offer it any food. When the donkey died of hunger, he said: “I have suffered a great loss! For just when it had learned not to eat, that is when it died.”

10. A pedant was selling a horse and was asked if it was timid <note>Ancient Greek: "deilos," meaning skittish or easily frightened</note>. He replied: “No, by my father’s salvation! But if "vision" must be changed, and I believe it must, I would prefer to read "habit" or "disposition" <note>original: hexeos</note>. Libanius, volume 4, page 628: "Not these things, my boy, the samples <note>original: deigmata</note> of war, but that sweetest thing for me." ### HIEROCLES

**44.** A <term>pedant</term> <note>original: Σχολαστικός (Scholastikos); the stock character of an over-educated fool.</note>, while sleeping with his father, got up from the bed in the middle of the night and began eating grapes that were hanging above them. His father hid a lamp under a cooking pot, and then, when the son stood up again, he suddenly revealed the light. The son immediately stood upright and began to snore, pretending to be asleep.

**45.** A pedant <note>original: Σχολαστικός</note> visited his grandmother's bed at night. When he was beaten for this by his father, he said: "You have been mounting my mother for all this time without me doing anything to you, and now you are angry at your own mother because you found me with her just once?"

**46.** An agent <note>original: πραγματευτὴς (pragmateutēs); a business manager or factor.</note> reported to a pedant that the river had taken away his land. The pedant cried out in response, saying: "It is using force against us!" <note>The joke relies on the pedant treating a natural disaster as a legal or personal assault (force majeure).</note>

### AND PHILAGRIUS.

**55.** A <term>pedant</term> <note>original: Σχολαστικός (Scholastikos); the stock character of an over-educated fool in Greek comedy.</note>, lacking money for his expenses, was selling off his books. Writing to his father, he said: "Congratulate us, Father! For already our books are providing us with our food." <note>The joke is that he is literally "living off his books" by selling them to buy food, rather than using the knowledge within them to earn a living.</note>

**56.** A pedant, a bald man, and a barber were traveling together. Finding themselves in a wilderness, they agreed that each should stay awake for four hours to guard their belongings. When it fell to the barber to keep the first watch, wanting to play a prank <note>original: μετεωρισθῆναι (meteōristhēnai); to be light-hearted or to make a joke.</note>, he shaved the sleeping pedant's head. When the hours were up, he woke him. The pedant, rubbing his head as he woke from sleep and finding it smooth-shaven, said: "What a great rogue the barber is! He has made a mistake and woken the bald man instead of me!"

**57.** When a pedant had a child by a slave woman, his father advised him to kill the infant <note>Exposing or killing unwanted infants, though discouraged by some, was a historical reality in the ancient world.</note>. But he replied: "First you bury your own children, and then advise me to do away with mine." <note>The pedant implies that his father should have killed him—his own child—if he were so keen on the practice.</note>

### HIEROCLES

...making the secrets of the trial known to the opposing parties, he said: "**Scoundrel!** For should I not mention the essential matters <note>original: τῶν συνεκτικῶν (tōn synektikōn); refers to the binding or central points of a legal case.</note>?"

**69.** A <term>pedant</term> <note>original: Σχολαστικὸς (Scholastikos); an "absent-minded professor" or foolish scholar type.</note> went to visit the parents of a classmate who had died. When the father began to wail and say, "**Child, you have left me in distress** <note>original: ἠπόρησάς με (ēporēsas me); literally "you have left me without resources" or "impoverished me."</note>," and the mother said, "**Child, you have blinded me**," the pedant turned to his companions and said: "If he really did all these things to them, he deserved to be lamented even while he was still alive." <note>The pedant takes the metaphorical expressions of grief literally, assuming the son was a criminal who actually robbed and blinded his parents.</note>

**70.** A pedant went to visit a sick friend. When the man's wife told him that he was already "**outside**" <note>An ancient euphemism meaning the body had been carried out for burial.</note>, he replied: "**Well, if he comes back, tell him that I stopped by.**"

**71.** A pedant, having taken a sample of the length and width of a garment for the purpose of bringing in a <term>hem-border</term> <note>original: ἀκρόπτυχα (akroptycha); a technical term for a folded edge or border, though its exact nature is debated.</note>, began to search and ask which part was the length and which was the width.

**72.** A pedant, after being feasted at a wedding, said as he was departing: "**I pray that you may always do these things, and with good fortune!**" <note>The joke lies in the social blunder; a wedding is intended to be a once-in-a-lifetime event, not something one does "always."</note>

**73.** The same man said that the tomb of Scribonia was beautiful and expensive, but that it had been built in an "**unhealthy**" place. <note>An "unhealthy" location is irrelevant to the dead, making the pedant's observation absurd.</note>

**74.** Someone approached a pedant who owned a very thin horse and said, "**Your horse is looking toward Hades** <note>A common idiom meaning "on the verge of death."</note>." The pedant replied: "**I see it too.**" <note>The pedant either implies he also sees death, or literally sees the horse looking at him, as if he himself were the god of the underworld.</note>

**75.** A pedant who was sick and hungry was told it was not yet the fourth hour <note>roughly 10:00 AM, a standard time for a first meal.</note>. Not believing it, he ordered the **sundial** to be brought to him in bed. <note>The humor comes from treating a fixed, large architectural sundial as a portable device like a modern watch.</note>

### AND PHILAGRIUS <note>Philagrius is named alongside Hierocles as a primary source for this ancient joke book.</note>

**87.** A <term>pedant</term> <note>original: Σχολαστικὸς (Scholastikos); a recurring character in Greek humor representing a foolish intellectual.</note> from the household of a <term>secutor</term> <note>original: σεκούτωρος (sekoutōros); a type of gladiator armed with a shield and sword who "followed" his opponent.</note> was dressed in armor and practicing his moves. When someone suddenly announced that his father was coming, he threw away his weapon and began unfastening his leg-armor. But since his father reached him too quickly, he sat there still wearing his helmet, pretending to read a book.

**88.** A pedant was returning from a journey. While climbing a steep uphill path, he was amazed and said: "When I first traveled this way—when it was manageable <note>original: ἐπαρκεῖν (eparkein); a difficult verb in this context. The editor notes it might mean 'convenient' or refers to the pace of travel.</note>—it was a downhill slope! How has it changed so quickly into an uphill slope?"

**89.** While at sea, a pedant asked the pilot what time it was. When the pilot said he did not know, the pedant asked how long he had been piloting the ship. The man said, "Three years." "How is it," the pedant replied, "that I, who bought a house only six months ago, can tell the hour whenever the sun reaches the courtyard, yet you cannot figure it out from the ship after piloting it for so long?"

...to deliver funeral orations, he wrote a funeral oration for one man who was still alive. When that man complained to him for doing this, the pedant said: "If you people don’t give me advance notice of when you’re going to die, do you want me to embarrass myself by speaking off the cuff?"¹

**91.** A <term>pedant</term> <note>original: Σχολαστικός (Scholastikos); the "egghead" or "pedant" is the protagonist of most jokes in this collection, characterized by a lack of common sense despite his education.</note> invited his classmates to dinner. After they praised the pig's head and asked if they could feast with him again the next day, he went to the cook and said: "Give me another head from that same pig, for the one we had yesterday pleased us very much."⁴ <note>The pedant assumes a single pig has multiple heads to offer.</note>

**92.** A pedant asked his father how much a "five-cup" flask <note>original: πεντακότυλος λήκυθος (pentakotylos lēkythos); a 'kotyle' was a standard liquid measure, roughly a half-pint.</note> actually holds.⁵

**93.** A pedant, hearing of a certain staircase that it had twenty steps for those going up,⁶ asked if there were just as many for those going down.

**94.** While some people were discussing indigestion, a pedant claimed he had never suffered from it. When they asked if he had ever experienced a bitter or unpleasant burp, he said, "I do that every single day!"⁹ <note>The editor notes that he is describing the very symptoms of the indigestion he claims not to have.</note>

**95.** A son was born to a pedant. When people asked what name he would give the child, he said: "He will have my name, and I will keep it for now as well."¹⁰ <note>He speaks as if there is only one "name" to be shared, and he might lose his identity if he gives it away.</note>

**96.** Two pedants were cowards; one hid himself in a well,¹² the other in a reed bed. When some soldiers lowered a helmet into the well to draw up water, the one inside—thinking a soldier was coming down—was caught while pleading for his life.

# AND PHILAGRIOS.

...he suddenly saw his girlfriend¹, turned and called out: "Send me the <term>brooch-cloak</term> too!" <note>original: φιβλατώριον (phiblatōrion); a cloak or garment fastened with a fibula or brooch.</note>

**107.** Another man³, similarly boastful but utterly impoverished⁴, happened to fall ill. When his girlfriend suddenly visited⁵ him and found him lying on a straw mat, he felt ashamed and blamed⁶ the doctors, saying: "The fine and reputable doctors of the city ordered me to be <term>matted</term>⁷." <note>original: ψιαθισθῆναι (psiathisthēnai); the boaster invents a medical-sounding verb from the word for "straw mat" (psiathos) to make his poverty look like a prescription.</note>

**108.** A <term>boaster</term>⁸ <note>original: Ἀλαζὼν (Alazōn); a stock character who pretends to have wealth or status he does not possess.</note> saw his slave in the marketplace newly arrived from the countryside and asked: "How are the sheep doing?" The slave replied: "One is sleeping, and the other⁹ is standing up." <note>The joke is that the "flock" consists of only two sheep.</note>

**109.** A <term>fool</term>¹⁰ <note>original: Μωρὸς (Mōros); a character defined by literal-mindedness or lack of judgment.</note> hearing that the courts in Hades are just, and having a lawsuit pending, hanged himself. <note>He believes he will get a fairer trial in the afterlife than on earth.</note>

## THE ABDERITES¹¹

**110.** In Abdera¹², the city was divided into two parts; those towards...

I propose: *and among the dead*. <note>original Latin: "en de te tethneiōsin"; the editor is correcting a fragmentary Greek phrase.</note>

...living towards the east and those towards the west. **111.** In Abdera⁴, a donkey slipped unnoticed into the <term>gymnasium</term> <note>original: γυμνάσιον; the public place where men trained in the nude and anointed themselves with oil</note> and spilled the oil⁵. <meta>This page continues the series of jokes about the inhabitants of Abdera, a city in Thrace whose people were stereotyped in antiquity as being exceptionally foolish. These entries are attributed to "Hierocles and Philagrios," the traditional compilers of the Philogelos (The Laughter-Lover), the world's oldest surviving jestbook. This page specifically focuses on jokes involving physical ailments and misunderstandings of anatomy.</meta>

->### AND PHILAGRIOS.<-

**116.** An Abderite <term>eunuch</term> <note>original: εὐνοῦχος; a castrated man</note>, having met with misfortune, "produced" a hernia.
<margin>1. This exists in only one manuscript, Manuscript A. With the words slightly changed, it is read again in section 252. 2. Due to great misfortune, this Abderite becomes hernious, which is quite strange if I understand the passage correctly. "To make a hernia" (original: Κήλην ποιεῖν) is used like the common expression "to make a disease" <note>original: faire une maladie</note>. This manner of speaking is not considered among the elegances of our language. Diderot wrote in a certain letter: "while going, I made two diseases... two inflammations of the bowels." Demoustier in *To Women*: "However, I see your face is pale, / and you have at least made a disease." Rousseau of Geneva also spoke this way somewhere. Compare section 200.</margin>

**117.** An Abderite was sleeping with a man who had a hernia. Having gotten up in the night to relieve himself, he accidentally stepped on the hernia while returning in the dark. When the man with the hernia cried out in pain, the Abderite said to him: "Well, why are you sleeping head-first?"
<margin>3. Exists in Manuscript A. 4. Regarding the form of the verb "to sleep" (original: κοιμᾶσαι), see page 268, note 4.</margin>

**118.** An Abderite, while walking, saw a man with a hernia urinating and remarked: "This man will not finish urinating until evening!"
<margin>5. Exists in Manuscript A. 6. The foolish man, looking with indiscreet eyes, believed that the very large tumor of the hernia was actually the bladder, which appeared swollen and prominent because of an abundance of stored liquid.</margin>

**119.** An Abderite saw a man with a hernia coming out of a pool, walking with great difficulty. He said to him: "Why did you load yourself up so greedily, if you weren't able to carry it properly?"
<margin>7. Exists in Manuscript A. 8. It seems that "pool" (original: κολύμβου) is the same as a swimming bath. Compare the words "from the immersion" in the story in section 113. 9. So in Manuscript A. Perhaps it should be "you loaded yourself" (original: ἐγομώσω or γεγόμωσαι). 10. "To carry" (original: Βαστάσαι) is used here in the same sense as "to bear" (original: φέρειν) is often used regarding wine, just as the Latins use *ferre*. Darius Hystaspis had inscribed on his tomb, according to Athenaeus: "I was able to drink much wine and to bear it well." Cyrus the Younger also said he drank more unmixed wine and "bore it better" than his brother Artaxerxes, as seen in Plutarch. Seneca in Letter 36 says: "someone bears that well (meaning good fortune); in the same way as wine." Eunapius says of Sopolis: "not even bearing the pressed drop of Castalia." See my note on page 48.</margin>

<column-break/>

**120.** An Abderite heard that onions and bulbs cause "wind" <note>original: φυσῶσιν; meaning both flatulence and blowing wind</note>. While he was sailing during a great calm, he filled a sack with them and hung it from the stern of the boat.
<margin>11. Exists in Manuscript A. 12. A similar silly joke is found in the book by Abbot Cherrier, *Polissoniana*, page 49. I shall not describe it; it is enough to have pointed it out—perhaps too much. Compare also section 141.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the series of jokes about the inhabitants of Abdera. As established on the previous page, the Abderites were the proverbial "fools" of the ancient world, similar to the "Wise Men of Gotham" in English folklore. These entries (121-127) focus on their literal-mindedness and lack of common sense, particularly regarding language and nature.</meta>

-># HIEROCLES<-

**121.** An Abderite, seeing a runner who had been crucified, said: "By the gods, this man is no longer running; he is flying!"
<margin>1. Found in Manuscript M, entry 92; entry 75 in P. Absent from others. 2. Manuscript M reads "strewn" <note>original: ἐστρωμένον</note> instead of "crucified." Pontanus correctly guessed the meaning, translating it as "suspended" <note>original: suspensum</note>. Manuscript M reads "you fly" <note>original: πέτετε</note>; Pontanus correctly suggests "he flies" <note>original: volat</note>.</margin>

**122.** An Abderite was selling a basin that did not have handles <note>original: ὠτία; literally "ears"</note>. When someone asked why he had removed its "ears," he replied: "In order that it might not hear it is being sold and run away."
<margin>3. In Manuscript M, 93; 80 in P. Absent from others. 4. Manuscript M omits the middle words, reading only "ears he replied." Pontanus perceived the full meaning.</margin>

**123.** An Abderite, having burned his deceased father according to the law, ran into the house and said to his mother, who was ill: "There is still a little wood left over; so, if you want and are able, go ahead and be burned up as well."
<margin>5. This exists only in Manuscript A. 6. Manuscript A uses a grammatically incorrect "if" <note>original: ἐὰν</note>; I have corrected this to the proper form <note>original: εἰ</note>, as these two words for "if" are often swapped, as seen in section 125.</margin>

**124.** An Abderite, in a dream, was selling a piglet and asking one hundred <term>denarii</term> <note>a standard silver coin of the Roman era</note>. When someone offered him fifty, he refused to take them and woke up. Closing his eyes again and stretching out his hand, he said: "Give me at least the fifty!"
<margin>7. In Manuscript M, 94; 81 in P. Absent from others. 8. Manuscript M spells "in a dream" as a single word. 9. In Manuscript M, the verb "woke up" is misspelled. It is an intransitive verb. 10. Regarding the word "closing his eyes," see section 11.</margin>

<column-break/>

**125.** An Abderite's sparrow died. Some time later, seeing an ostrich <note>original: στρουθοκάμηλον; literally "sparrow-camel"</note>, he said: "If my little sparrow had lived, it would be this big by now."
<margin>11. In Manuscript M, 95; 82 in P. Absent from other books. 12. "The ostrich <note>original: struthiocamelus</note> is a type of bird named after the sparrow and the camel, acting as if it were a sparrow equal in size to a camel, about which Pliny wrote in Book 10, Chapter 1. Otherwise called a Struthio." —PONTANUS. Those who say "sparrow-camel" <note>original: στρουθοκάμηλος</note> have a more recent and different compound which pleases me more: "camel-bird" <note>original: καμηλοπούλιον</note>. For it is more similar to a bird in its general kind than to a sparrow.</margin>

**126.** An Abderite, having traveled abroad to Rhodes, began smelling the walls because of the city's name <note>The name Rhodes <original: Ῥόδος</original> sounds identical to the word for Rose <original: ῥόδον</original></note>.
<margin>13. In Manuscript M, 96; 83 in P. Absent from other books. 14. Found in Manuscripts A and M.</margin>

**127.** An Abderite, owing someone a small donkey and not having one, requested that he provide two mules in its place.
<margin>15. Exists only in Manuscript A. Compare sections 12 and 222.</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from jokes about the simpletons of Abdera to a new category of "fools" in the Philogelos: the Sidonians. These entries continue the collection's tradition of attributing absurd logic and linguistic misunderstandings to specific regional groups. The header indicates that these selections are attributed to Philagrius, one of the two purported authors of this ancient joke book.</meta>

->AND PHILAGRIUS.<-

# SIDONIANS<sup>1</sup>.

128. A Sidonian <term>eparch</term> <note>a high-ranking provincial governor</note> was traveling in a carriage. When the mules grew exhausted and were no longer able to walk, the driver unyoked them so that they might recover after grazing for a short while. Once released, they ran off. The governor said to the driver: "Do you see, you scum, that while the mules are running, this carriage—unable to run—just stands here?"

129. A Sidonian rhetorician <note>a professional public speaker or teacher</note> was conversing with two companions. When one of them said it was not right for sheep to be slaughtered because they provide milk and wool, and the other said that a cow should not be killed either since she provides milk and plows the fields, the rhetorician added that it was not right for a pig to be slaughtered either, as she provides liver, udders, and kidneys. <note>The joke relies on the absurdity of the rhetorician's logic: unlike milk or wool, which are produced by living animals, organs like the liver can only be "provided" if the animal is slaughtered.</note>

130. A Sidonian <term>sophist</term> <note>a teacher of philosophy or rhetoric</note>, bathing at the first opening of the bathhouse and finding no one inside, said to his two servants: "As I see it, it doesn't wash." <note>The Greek phrase "οὐ λούει" is a pun. It can mean "nobody is bathing" or, more absurdly, that the bathhouse itself is failing to perform its function because it is empty.</note>

<columns>2</columns>

<sup>1</sup> The manuscripts read "Sidonioi," and so below. I preferred to capitalize <note>original: μεγαλογραφεῖν</note> it, although the author himself might have used a lowercase letter. I will use lowercase <note>original: Μικρογραφία</note> when mentioning the name "Eponichos" in an inscription published by Letronne the Egyptian, vol. II, p. 163. I propose it be corrected to "Eteonikos," which is a very well-known name. The letters TEΩ and the rest, broken and corroded by the "eating" of time, have left behind thin and doubtful strokes, from which one person's guess produces one syllable and another's produces another. My conjecture is not without a certain probability.
<sup>2</sup> Found in Manuscript A. Compare section 100.
<sup>3</sup> Found in Manuscript A. Compare section 103.
<sup>4</sup> Manuscript A reads "dyo" <note>original: δύω</note>, as it does in sections 42 and 103. More appropriately, the form "duo" <note>original: δύο</note> is used elsewhere. Such variations are born of pronunciation and the scribe's carelessness. I happened to come across the variant readings of Memnon by Callistratus, which I once excerpted from manuscript 1038. In inflecting the name Memnon, the scribe everywhere lengthened the second-to-last syllable: "Memnonos," "Mem-

<column-break/>

noni," "Memnona." Most passages in the poets, however, showed the syllable's quantity to be short. But since this Statue of Callistratus has been named, it may be useful to note something: "To that stone of Memnon, nature gave even pleasure, and mixed the rock with pain, and this is the only art we know that has placed thoughts and a voice into stone." Learned men object to the rhetorician—and with no small harshness—claiming he used conflicting ideas by attributing a miracle to nature which he immediately calls a work of art. But to me, the rhetorician seems to have been more clever than absurd. The pronoun "this" <note>original: ταύτην</note> reveals exactly what he intended to say: *That unique art is none other than nature itself.*
<sup>5</sup> Manuscript A reads "providing and plowing" <note>original: παρέχοντα καὶ ἀροτριῶντα</note> (in the masculine). I corrected this using section 103.

<sup>7</sup> Found in Manuscript A. Compare section 23.

->AND PHILAGRIUS.<-

# CYMEANS <note>Residents of Cyme, an Aeolian city in Asia Minor. In the *Philogelos*, they are the "fools" of the ancient world, much like the "Wise Men of Gotham" in English folklore.</note>

<insert>166.</insert> A Cymean, seeing a fig branch hanging down<sup>1</sup> full of ripe<sup>2</sup> figs, grabbed hold of the branch. When his donkey ran out from under him, he was left hanging there. When the gardener<sup>3</sup> asked what he was doing<sup>4</sup> hanging there, he said: "I fell<sup>5</sup> off the donkey."

167.<sup>6</sup> A Cymean saw a sheep tied by its feet and being sheared<sup>7</sup> in that state. He said: "I give thanks to my master that he never tied me up to shave me."

168.<sup>8</sup> A Cymean, whose father was away, fell into a heavy legal charge and was condemned to death. As he was going away to his execution, he begged everyone not to let his father know, lest his father should deal him a fatal beating. <note>The humor lies in his fear of a "deadly" beating from his father when he is already about to be executed.</note>

169.<sup>9</sup> The same man, when someone said, "You robbed me," replied: "May I not return<sup>10</sup> from where I am going if I robbed you."

170.<sup>11</sup> Someone asked a Cymean where<sup>12</sup> Dracontides the rhetorician was staying. "I am alone," he said. "But if you wish, watch<sup>13</sup> the shop, and I will go and show you." <note>The Cymean leaves his business in the hands of a complete stranger just to show the way.</note>

171.<sup>14</sup> A Cymean in Alexandria, after his father had died, gave the body to the embalmers. After some time, he sought to reclaim it. Since the embalmer<sup>15</sup> had other bodies as well and asked what distinguishing mark his father’s coffin had, the Cymean replied: "He had a cough<sup>16</sup>." <note>A cough is a symptom of the living; a corpse in a coffin cannot cough to identify itself.</note>

<meta>This page continues the "Cymean" section of the Philogelos, a joke book from the 4th century CE. The previous page established the Cymeans as the archetypal "fools" of antiquity. These jokes are attributed to Philagrius, one of the two authors named in the collection's title. This page concludes a previous medical joke and provides several anecdotes involving Cymean doctors, legal disputes, and public proclamations.</meta>

->AND PHILAGRIUS.<-

<note>original: "εἰπόντος ὅτι ἀπέθανεν..." — This is the punchline of a joke starting on the previous page regarding a doctor's excuse for a patient's death.</note>
...when someone said that the patient had died, the doctor replied with an oath:
"If he hadn't succumbed to the weakness, he would have burst <note>original: "ἐλάκησεν" — literally 'cracked' or 'shattered,' a crude way to describe an alternative cause of death</note> anyway."

177. A Cymean doctor, while operating on a man who was in terrible pain and screaming, switched to a blunter scalpel. <note>The doctor likely believes that a blunt tool, being less "sharp," will hurt less—a classic piece of fool’s logic.</note>

178. Two Cymeans bought two jars of dried figs. One of them, without the other knowing, began eating not from his own jar, but from his companion's. Eventually, they had both used up the figs in the jars. When each turned back to his own jar, he found it empty. Taking hold of one another, they were led before the magistrate. After considering the case, the magistrate ordered them to exchange the empty jars and to pay back the prices to one another. <note>The judge's "solution" is as nonsensical as the crime, resulting in no change to the situation.</note>

179. In Cyme, a demagogue <note>A political leader who gains support by appealing to popular desires</note> was accused in the assembly. He said: "Citizens, these men are the ones who lied and slandered me; may they be condemned by you. But if I have done any of these things to them, then while all of you are sitting here, let the theater fall on me alone!" <note>The joke lies in the physical impossibility: if the theater falls on him, it falls on everyone sitting in it.</note>

180. A Cymean official made the following public proclamations: "The ephors <note>magistrates</note> immediately after the sacrifice must bring their own hides <note>original: "βύρσας" — referring to the animal skins from the sacrifice, but phrasing it as if it were their own human skin</note> to the priest. And you councilors, enter the council-chamber and do not deliberate. The cooks must throw their own bones <note>Again, the phrasing implies their skeletal bones rather than the meat scraps</note> over the wall. And the cobblers must not possess small lasts." <note>term: lasts <gloss>wooden forms shaped like a human foot used for making or repairing shoes</gloss></note>

181. Some Cymeans met for a vote, and realizing that many people from other cities had failed to show up because of the path, they blamed the road. One said: "Are we not fools, if we also do not stay away in the future?"

<column-break/>

<margin>
<note>Footnote 7: Corayus (At. 1, p. 117) notes that the word for "last" (kalapous) comes from *kalon* (wood) and *pous* (foot), meaning a "wooden little foot" used by shoemakers. This eminent scholar has made this a most worthy digression for the reader.</note>
</margin>

182. A Cymean <note>Cymeans were the subject of many "noodlehead" or "city of fools" jokes in antiquity.</note> was cutting into a wounded head. Having laid the patient on his back, he poured water into his mouth so that he could see through the surgical incision when it would flow out. <note>original: "πότ' ἐκρεύσει" — The doctor assumes the head is a hollow vessel, like a jar, where a leak can be found by filling it with liquid.</note>

### THE GRUMPY ONES <note>original: "ΔΥΣΚΟΛΟΙ" — A character type in Greek comedy and literature referring to a cantankerous, irritable, or anti-social person.</note>

183. A man went to a grumpy doctor and said, "Professor <note>original: "Σοφιστά" — At this time, 'Sophist' was a respectful title for a learned professional, including doctors.</note>, I cannot lie down, nor stand, nor even sit." And the doctor said, "Nothing is left for you then but to hang yourself."

184. Someone says to a grumpy doctor: "What shall I do? I am passing blood <note>original: "αἷμα κάθημαι" — a colloquial way of saying 'I sit for blood,' or 'I have bloody stools.'</note> and bile." And that man said to him: "Even if you pass your very intestines, I won't be moved to bile <note>original: "οὐ χολῶ" — A pun. The doctor means he won't get angry (be 'bilious'), even though the patient is literally losing bile.</note>."

185. A grumpy doctor who was one-eyed asked a patient, "How are you doing?" The patient said, "As you see." The doctor replied, "If you are as I see, then half of you is dead." <note>The doctor only sees half the world with his one eye, and thus jokes that the patient must be half-gone.</note>

186. A man went to a grumpy doctor and, after touching him, said, "You have a bad fever." <note>original: "Κακὰ πυρέττεις" — a common way to describe a high or dangerous fever.</note> The doctor answered and said, "If you can manage to have a better fever, look, there is a bed; lie down and have one."

### AND PHILAGRIUS.

187. A grumpy astrologer was casting the horoscope <note>original: "γένεσιν" — a technical term for a natal chart or the calculation of a life's duration.</note> of a sick child. After promising the mother that the boy would live a long life, he demanded his fee. When she said, "Come tomorrow and I will pay you," he replied: "What then? If he dies during the night, will I lose my fee?"

188. A grumpy man bought a jar of honey. When someone asked him for how much he had bought it, he tipped the jar over and said: "May my blood be poured out just like this if I tell you!"

189. A doctor visited a grumpy patient and ordered him to eat crumbs with soapwort <note>original: "στρουθίου" — *strouthion* refers to the plant soapwort (Saponaria), used medicinally, but it is also a diminutive form of the word for sparrow (*strouthos*).</note>. And the grumpy man said: "How can I get into the cage <note>original: "κλουβίον" — a birdcage or small enclosure.</note> to eat the crumbs with the sparrow?"

### AND PHILAGRIUS.

[...he] said it, you would have believed him; but do I not seem more trustworthy to you than he does?" <note>This is the conclusion of a joke where a man is told his friend has died. The grumpy man replies that the friend himself had told him he was alive just yesterday, and asks why the messenger should be believed over the (now deceased) friend.</note>

194. A grumpy man was going down the stairs <note>original: "σκάλαν" — *skalan*, a term borrowed from Latin</note> when he slipped and fell. When the landlord asked, "Who is there?" he replied: "I have knocked out my rent; <note>original: "ἐλάκησα" — a difficult verb here; it likely puns on "making a noise" from the fall and "paying off" his stay through the injury.</note> what is it to you?"

195. Someone said to a grumpy senator: "I long to see you and to meet with you a little <note>original: "Μικρόν" — *mikron* can mean "for a short time" or "in a small/wretched state."</note>." But the senator replied: "And I want to see you blind and lame." <note>The senator interprets "little" not as a duration of time, but as a wish for the man to be physically diminished or broken.</note>

### THE WITLESS <note>original: "ΑΦΥΕΙΣ" — *aphueis* refers to people who lack natural talent, particularly "dim-witted" or "incompetent" pedants.</note>

196. A witless grammarian was asked: "How should one say it: 'to the two' <note>original: "τοῖς δύο"</note> or 'to the two' <note>original: "τοῖς δυσίν" — the questioner is asking for the correct grammatical case or dialect form.</note>?" He simply held out his hand and pointed to his two fingers.

197. A witless grammarian was asked: "What was the name of Priam's mother?" <note>A typical "trivia" question asked of scholars in antiquity to test their deep knowledge of Homeric lore.</note> Being at a loss, he said: "We call her 'Madam' <note>original: "κυρίαν"</note> out of respect."

205. A witless² soothsayer fell among enemies. ### COWARDS⁴.

206. A coward⁵ was asked: "Which ships are safer, the long warships or the round merchant ships?" He replied: "The ones that have been hauled up on land⁶."

207. A cowardly hunter⁷ was constantly being chased by a bear⁸ in his dreams at night. He eventually hired dogs and kept them in his bed to sleep⁹ with him.

208. Someone said to a cowardly boxer¹⁰: "Who are you going to box with?" That man, pointing out his opponent, replied: "With this gentleman here¹¹." <note>The joke lies in the boxer using an overly polite, submissive title for the man who is about to beat him up.</note>

209. A cowardly boxer¹², who was being constantly "sieved"¹⁴ (pummeled) by his opponent¹³, cried out: "I beg of you! Not all at once!" <note>The boxer is so overwhelmed by the flurry of punches that he feels as though he is being attacked by a whole crowd rather than one man.</note>

### ENVIOUS MEN.

214. An envious man¹ entered a laundry and, because he did not want to urinate², he died. <note>In antiquity, fullers (laundry workers) collected urine in vats to use as a source of ammonia for cleaning and bleaching fabric. The envious man is so spiteful he would rather die of a ruptured bladder than provide the laundryman with a "free" resource.</note>

215. An envious³ homeowner, seeing his tenants prospering, drove them out of his house.

216. An envious man⁴ seeing his neighbor fighting wild beasts in the arena, said to the manager: "A bear!" <note>The original Greek text here is likely missing words. The editor notes that the meaning is unclear, but it may imply the man is calling for a more dangerous animal to kill his neighbor.</note>

217. Another man⁵, out of cowardice, wrote on his forehead: "The place of vital blows⁶." When he was being hit repeatedly, he said to the one striking him: "Does this man not know how to read, and is he trying to kill me?" <note>The humor lies in the coward thinking a warning label would stop a physical assault.</note>

218. A cowardly⁷ boxer being hit repeatedly by his opponent cried out: "I beg of you! Not all at once!" <note>This joke is a repetition of number 209 from the previous section.</note>

### STARVELINGS⁸.

219. A starveling⁹ marrying off his daughter to another starveling was asked what dowry he was giving her. "I am giving a house," he said, "whose windows look out into the bakery." <note>A "starveling" (<term>limoxeros</term> — literally "hunger-parched") is a stock character who is both desperately poor and extremely stingy. The "dowry" is merely the smell of food.</note>

220. A starveling¹⁰ physical trainer, seeing a loaf of bread hanging up, said: "Are you coming down? Are you reporting for duty? Or am I coming up there to finish you off?"

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>HIEROCLES</header>

"...that my uvula has fallen." <note>The patient believes his "staphyle" (uvula, literally "little grape") has become inflamed or descended.</note> And as he gaped open, the doctor turned away and said: "Your uvula hasn't fallen; your anus has risen." <note>original: "Οὐχὶ ἡ σταφυλή σου κατέβη, ἀλλὰ ὁ κῶλός σου ἀνέβη." The doctor is insulting the patient, suggesting his breath smells so much like excrement that his digestive tract must have reversed.</note>

236. A man with bad breath <term>Ozostomos</term> <note>From "ozo" (to smell) and "stoma" (mouth)</note>, flattering his child, chewed up some food to feed it to him. But the child, turning away, said: "I don't want it; Daddy, it's gross!" <note>original: "τατά, κακά" — "Tata" is an ancient nursery word for "Daddy," and "kaka" refers to filth or excrement.</note>

237. A man with bad breath was roasting a sausage <term>loukanikon</term> <note>A "Lucanian" sausage, a popular spiced meat often sold by street vendors</note>, and for a long time...

---

¹ Mynas wrote "your colon," while noting that the manuscript itself says "your anus" <note>Greek: *kolos*</note>. I have written it as *kōlos*, with the proper syllable length. But many use the short vowel, either out of negligence or because they are ignorant of the length and deceived by the pronunciation. From the *Precious Crown* <note>A 16th-century Greek-Latin dictionary</note>: "culo, anus." See Coray, *At.* 4, 270.

² This exists only in manuscript A.

³ Mynas wrote: "said: these things are bad." But he notes the manuscript reads: "I don't want it, daddy, it's bad." In a Greek man of great learning, yet one who often scorns the humble diligence of Western critics, I am not surprised by such negligence in transcription and liberty in changing the text. But I fear many passages have been corrected in this way without the editor warning the reader. I consider *tata* to be a word from infant language, which little children in all regions speak before they can truly talk. "Tata" for father and "mamma" for mother are well known from Latin examples. The books of Greek children preserved the voices *mamme* and *mammia*, though perhaps not *tata*. However, Hierocles had heard this name at home or elsewhere. And "tata" is even native to us. Among us, infants also say "caca" while crying, regarding food they reject, just like that child in the cradle of the scholar spoke to his foul-mouthed father. For who does not remember Aristophanes' character Phidippides shouting "kakka" when he was pressed by the need to defecate? This word...

<column-break/>

...is used by Greek infants, as Coray testifies in his notes on Plutarch vol. III, page 10: "the plural *skata* [dung] has a synonym among us even to this day, *kakka*." Therefore, I have translated: "I don't want it. Daddy, it's poopy!" Who would doubt the Latin *caca*? If a delicate or diligent censor complains that I did not use two 'k's, following the Comic poets and others, the answer is ready: the speech of babbling little Greeks is not yet fixed by the laws of grammar. Add to this the authority of the lexicographer Zalychis: *kaka*, meaning "boar" or "filth."

⁴ This exists only in manuscript A.

⁵ Here too the transcriber behaved rashly; having found *loukanikon*, he "corrected" it to *allantion* <note>a more formal, literary word for sausage</note>. He disliked *loukanikon* because it was a "word from the street." But a learned man acting as an editor should imitate the diligence of a careful scribe. I have therefore restored *loukanikon*, and with that accent. For I believe the word is pronounced that way. Bastius would have preferred *loukanikon*. In a commentary on Lucian's *The Cock*, 14, where "sausage" <note>allantos</note> is noted as "commonly called *lokanika*," he corrected it to *loukanika*. I agree only on the first syllable. In Alciphron 3, 7, I found *loukanikon* as a note on "sausages." Du Cange brings *loukanikon* from the *Precious Crown*. And Zalychis's Lexicon shows *loukanikon*.

...having eaten figs and grapes, he fell asleep <note>original: "katedarthen"</note>. Being prodded by his stomach <note>original: "nygeis," suggesting digestive distress</note>, he seemed to see his friend sitting upon a fig tree in a dream, and this friend was calling him to come eat figs. But after he stood up, it pleased them both to defecate <note>original: "chesai"</note> from the fig tree above. Straining himself, he then defecated upon his bedding <note>original: "stromata"</note>. When he woke up and realized what happened, he washed the bedding and, having greedily eaten again, went back to sleep. And again in his sleep he sees his friend sitting on the fig tree, urging him likewise to come up. <meta>This page continues the "Philogelos" (The Laughter-Lover), specifically a section of jokes traditionally attributed to the grammarian Hierocles. We conclude joke 245 and move into a series of jokes about "misogynists"—a stock character in ancient Greek humor who expresses performative or extreme dislike for marriage and women.</meta>

### HIEROCLES

...he said to his own servants: "Mix a drink for the one, and satisfy the desires <note>original: "aphrodisiasate," literally "perform the rites of Aphrodite"</note> of the other who wishes it." But they replied: "We are not thirsty."

246. A misogynist <term>Misogynaios</term> <note>a "woman-hater," a common target of satire in the ancient world</note> standing in the marketplace was saying: "I am selling my wife tax-free." When some people asked, "Why?" he said: "So that she might be forfeited <note>original: "steresimos." This is a legal pun; the word can mean property that is subject to seizure or loss. He wants to lose her as if she were a confiscated item.</note>."

247. A misogynist, after his wife died, was performing the funeral rites. When someone asked, "Who has found rest <note>original: "anepausato," a common euphemism for death, similar to "passed away"</note>?" he replied: "I have, now that I am rid of her."

***

<note>Scholarly commentary on the text follows below</note>

...[the text is] questioned [reading] *erotomenos*, Rhærius [reads] *eromenas*. However, it was obvious that it should be *erotiomenas* instead of *erotiotas*. A young man <term>Neaniskos</term> about to act as a host (an anonymous source conjectured "having acted as a host," which was corrected in the Voss. manuscript) said to his servants (Voss. [reads] "them"): "Mix a drink for the one who wants it, and satisfy the desires of the one who wants it." And she (reading *kakeine* as in Voss., but it should read *kakeinai*, "they") said: "We are not thirsty."

^1 Manuscript A reads *kerasote*. I have adopted the reading from the Voss. manuscript, *kerasate*. It means "to mix for someone," specifically to offer wine to someone to drink. Pickolos, the most elegant translator of Saint-Pierre, says: "inviting her (a beloved Parisian decorator) to pour <note>original: "nerase"</note> for the fellow drinkers."

^2 This joke exists only in manuscript A.

^3 Thus manuscript A, *steresimos*. If I am not mistaken, there is a play on legal terms here, but I do not fully grasp the riddle.

^4 This is missing from the printed editions. It is joke 57 in the Voss. transcript under the title "On Misogynists"; it is joke 57 in Rh., with the same title. There, it reads: "While a misogynist (so Voss.; an anonymous source conjectured 'of a misogynist'; another 'a misogynist') was burying his wife, someone asked: 'Who has found rest?' and he said: 'Let it be the one who is rid of her' (so Voss.; an anonymous source: 'I, who am rid of her')."

^5 "Found rest" <note>original: "anepausato"</note>, obviously meaning "he died" <note>original: "tethneke" or "ethane"</note>. This is a metaphor that I believe is found in all languages. In the vernacular, it might be aptly said: "Who has found rest? I, who

<column-break/>

am deprived of her." A well-known French epigram says: "Here lies my wife. Oh, how good it is for her rest and for mine!" See Coray, *At.* 4, p. 12. Theocritus, *Idyll* 1, 138: "And he, having said so much, found rest." There is a variation, "rested" <note>original: "anepausato"</note>. The scholarly note <term>Scholium</term> says: "*apepausato* or *anepausato*. He used 'rested' as a euphemism for dying." There are some interpreters who believe the poet signified death here, and I agree with them; however, they should not have translated it as "expired" while keeping the word *apepausato*, since *anepausato* should have been chosen to signify death. Herodian, 3, 15, 3: "Having reigned... he found rest among his young sons as successors." See also Kiesling on Theocritus. Psellus, at the beginning of his funeral oration <term>Monodia</term> for John Patricius—which we are told is an excellent writing—says: "having departed from things here, he rested toward the life above," which is a phrase typical of Christian and Biblical language. However, that word "rest" <note>original: "anapauo"</note> seems to be an error in the letter of Eustathius prefixed to the commentary on Dionysius, p. 71, 32: "I think a seeker of knowledge would desire to hear something about the Mysians, and likewise about the Bebryces; but even the mere name of Libya, or Asia, or Europe will not 'rest' him." I propose it should be rewritten as "will not satisfy" <note>original: "anaplesei"</note>; that is, "it will not satisfy his thirst for knowledge," or as it is well said in Latin, "the naked name of Libya... will not fulfill him."

# HIEROCLES

254. A pedant <term>Scholastikos</term> <note>A stock character in ancient Greek humor, the "Scholastikos" is a man with book-learning but zero common sense.</note> was in a shipwreck during a storm. While the other passengers each grabbed a piece of equipment <note>original: "skeuos," referring to tools or furniture that might float</note> to save themselves, he clung to one of the anchors.

255. A pedant, after burying his son, met the boy's teacher. He asked: "Did the boy come forward?" <note>original: "proēlthen," likely referring to attending class or being present for roll call</note> The teacher replied: "No." "Well then, professor," the pedant said, "he is dead."

256. A pedant gymnastics trainer <term>Paidotribes</term> <note>A teacher of physical education and wrestling for boys.</note>, upon hearing that a student was ill, and on the next day that he had a fever, and later hearing from the father that the boy had died, remarked: "With such excuses, you people don't allow the children to learn anything."

257. A pedant bought some meat and was carrying it home. A kite <term>Loupes</term> <note>original: λούπης, a bird of prey similar to a hawk</note> swooped down and snatched it from his hand. He said: "As I live, let's see if I don't do the same to someone else!" <note>The joke relies on the pedant's absurd logic that he can get revenge on the bird by stealing from another person.</note>

258. A starveling <term>Limoxeros</term> <note>A "hunger-dry" person, often a miserly character in ancient comedy.</note>, because his tribunal was <unclear>corrupt text</unclear>, ordered it to be turned into a bakery.

Page 137, column 2. **Libanius** <note>A famous 4th-century Greek rhetorician.</note> used the phrasing **to blaspheme against** <note>original: βλασφημεῖν εἰς</note> in volume III, page 254, line 13: **insulting a goldsmith** <note>original: βλασφημῶν εἰς χρυσοχόον</note>. **Our author** <note>The writer of the main text being edited in this book.</note>, page 169: **of the insult against that woman** <note>original: τῆς εἰς ἐκείνην βλασφημίας</note>.

Page 140, line 14. The <term>Codex</term> <note>The original manuscript source.</note> reads *storm* <note>original: λαίλαψ</note>.

Page 141, at the end. The <term>Codex</term> reads *hitherto* <note>original: τωτέως</note>.

Page 144, note 5. For page 18, read page 118.

Page 161, note 1. To the illustration I made (which was a little long) regarding the repetition of the phrase **noble born of the noble** <note>original: εὐγενὴς ἐξ εὐγενῶν</note>, I will add the words of **Libanius** concerning the emperors Constans and Constantius from volume III, page 276: **let the words of Plato be said of them—fitting these men more than those for whom they were first spoken—that they became good because they were born from the good.** <note>original: λεγέσθω δὴ τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος ἐπ' αὐτοῖς... ὅτι ἀγαθοὶ δ' ἐγένοντο διὰ τὸ φῦναι ἐξ ἀγαθῶν</note>. He was referring to Plato’s ***Menexenus*** <note>A Socratic dialogue consisting primarily of a funeral oration.</note>, chapter 6. There is also an inscription in **Letronne’s** *Egyptian Collection* <note>original: Sylloge Ægyptiaca</note>, volume II, page 143: **And the great Tourranius born from the great.** <note>original: Καὶ μέγαν ἐκ μεγάλων Τουρράνιον</note>. See that most learned man's comments on page 150.

Page 166, note 1. I have correctly changed the form **he might know** <note>original: εἰδοίη</note>. Some time ago the form **they might know** <note>original: εἰδοῖεν</note> was banished from the *Calliope* <note>The 9th book of Herodotus's Histories.</note> of **Herodotus**, 42, which **Fischer** wrongly derived from the verb *to know* <note>original: εἰδέω</note>, ascribing a non-Ionic contraction to Herodotus. I find **you might know** <note>original: εἰδοίης</note> in **Antonius Byzantius's** *Manual of Good Habits* <note>original: Χρηστοηθείᾳ</note>, section 38: **do not mock anyone while joking; but whomever you know to be taking witty remarks badly, you will never wish to bring words to this person for the sake of wit.** <note>original: μηδένα ἀστειζόμενος σκῶπτε... τούτῳ μηδέποτε λόγους ἐπ' ἀστειότητι προσαγαγεῖν ἐθελήσεις</note>. He ought to have written **you might know** <note>original: εἰδείης</note> from the verb *to know* <note>original: εἴδημι</note>; but the pronunciation of the time deceived him <note>The editor suggests the author wrote what he heard (phonetic spelling) rather than the grammatically correct form.</note>.

Page 174, note 4. I shall bring forward another example of **Rochefort’s** <note>Guillaume de Rochefort (1730–1788), a French translator criticized here for sloppy work.</note> carelessness from an **Aesopic Fable**, which **Coray** <note>Adamantios Korais, a major Greek scholar.</note> published from Rochefort's revision, page 333: **A certain herdsman** <note>original: βουθρέμμων</note> **lost a bull on the mountain. He vowed to sacrifice a bull to the god if he should meet the thief. Suddenly** <note>original: Ἐξ αἴθρης (literally: from a clear sky)</note> **he found him being eaten by a lion...** **Schaefer** wrote **herdsman** <note>original: βουθρέμμων</note>; **Coray** kept the spelling **herdsman** <note>original: βουθρέμων</note> which the manuscript indeed shows, though it should not be kept. For the phrase **from the clear sky** <note>original: ἐξ αἴθρης</note>, which **Rochefort** strangely translated as "from the break of day," both scholars conjectured **suddenly** <note>original: ἐξαίφνης</note>, quite truly; and the manuscript entirely supports this, in which I read it written as **suddenly** <note>original: ἐξαίθνης</note> in very clear letters. Furthermore, the word **he should meet** <note>original: ἐντύχῃ</note> is **Rochefort’s** error; the manuscript has **he might meet** <note>original: ἐντύχοι</note>, and correctly so.

Page 177, line 7. Manuscript: *receive* <note>original: δέχεσθε</note>. — Line 18. For *it was necessary* <note>original: ἔδει</note> perhaps read *he might know* <note>original: εἰδείη</note>.

Page 180, line 8. **He grew up under the care of initiators and tutors** <note>original: Ὑπὸ μυσταγωγοῖς καὶ παιδαγωγοῖς ἀνῆξε</note>] I have already noted similar things on page 172, note 2. See also **Wyttenbach** on the works of Eunapius, page 111: **to have the girl under themselves** <note>original: τὴν παῖδα ἔχειν ὑφ' ἑαυτοῖς</note>. **Aristaenetus** <note>A writer of fictional letters, likely 5th or 6th century.</note>, 2, 5: **a girl... still guarded, and barely peeping out of the house under [the eyes of] guards.** <note>original: κόρην.... ἔτι φρουρουμένην, καὶ μόλις ὑπὸ φύλαξιν ἔσθ' ὅπη προκύπτουσαν τῆς οἰκίας</note>. **Abresch’s** note there in his *Readings* (page 212) is good, but he should not have referred the reader to **Hemsterhuis's** commentary on **Lucian's** *Dialogues of the Dead* 7, 1, since that passage deals with the phrase **to die for someone** <note>original: ἐπί τινι θνήσκειν</note>; and I myself should not have let **Abresch** go blameless in the past. **Lucian**, *Dialogues of the Courtesans* 11: **reared under a thrifty father-**

IX. One born to a prostitute may not speak at the public rostrum; but one born to a male prostitute <note>The Greek "ek pornou" suggests the son of a man who sold himself or lived a profligate life.</note> should not be prohibited. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 159
X. If a courtesan wears gold jewelry, let her (or the jewelry) become public property. . . . . 186
XI. A hero of valor kills his son for committing sexual immorality; he is tried for murder. . . 207
XII. Three hundred soldiers were being pursued at night by the enemy, but the general did not open the gates because the law prohibited it; as they were being slain, he is accused of crimes against the public. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 229
XIII. A general was captured and, being most cruelly tortured, revealed the city's secrets. After returning from captivity, he is accused of crimes against the public. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 249
